afternoon.name: An afternoon
afternoon.line: One sitting, or two. Nothing here needs weeks.
afternoon.after: Done in a day, and it stays done. The room it lives in has more like it.

weeks.name: A few weeks
weeks.line: A little most days, and it is yours before the month is out.
weeks.after: That is the whole ladder. If it caught you, the room it lives in has more.

months.name: A few months
months.line: About three months of a little most days. Every ladder in the school stops around there.
months.after: That is where the ladder stops — about three months in, at something real you can actually do. Nothing in the school runs for years, because a chain you cannot finish stops being a chain. Past here it is yours to carry on, on your own or with your facilitator or with the group.

groups.name: Your body
groups.line: Moving it, making it strong, and what it can do in water.

groups.name: The outdoors
groups.line: Fire, weather, wild things, and everything above your head.

groups.name: Your mind
groups.line: Numbers, words, memory, seeing properly, and saying what you mean.

groups.name: Making things
groups.line: With your hands, with a tune, and with a bit of misdirection.

groups.name: Everyday life
groups.line: Feeding people, earning, fixing, caring, and keeping your head.

categories.name: Body and movement
categories.line: Juggling, skipping, upside down, breath, strength, speed.

tracks.name: Juggling
tracks.line: From one ball thrown hand to hand, to juggling three balls for two whole minutes.
tracks.who: From about eight, and grown-ups
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, and for grown-ups. It starts with one rolled sock thrown from hand to hand, then two balls passing each other in the air, then the first wild throw of three. From there it is counting catches, five, ten, twenty, until three balls stay up for thirty seconds, a minute, and at the end two whole minutes. Most people who practise a few minutes most days get three balls going within a month or two, and it is one of the clearest proofs there is that a thing you could not do before is now yours. Three pairs of rolled socks will do from the first rung to the last.

steps.test: Throw one ball from hand to hand ten times without dropping it.
how: One ball only. A rolled pair of socks works.
Throw it from one hand to the other, up to about eye height.
Aim for the same arc every time rather than for speed.
Ten throws without a drop.
steps.note: The ball should go up and across in front of your face, not straight across between your hands. A rolled pair of socks is better than a real ball at first, because it does not bounce away when you drop it. If you can already do this, count it and go straight on.

steps.test: Throw one ball from hand to hand twenty times, with every throw reaching the same height.
steps.note: Pick a spot on the wall at about eye height, such as a picture corner or a light switch, and make every throw peak level with it. It is slow and it is the whole skill: three balls only work when every throw is the same.

steps.test: Throw one ball from hand to hand twenty times, keeping your eyes on the top of the arc and not on your hands.
steps.note: Look at the spot where the ball turns over at the top. Your hands learn to be in the right place without you watching them. This is the rung that makes three balls possible later, because with three there is no time to look down.

steps.test: Throw one ball twenty times, every throw starting from your weaker hand.
steps.note: The weaker hand is the one you do not write with. Its throws will go wild at first; slow down until they match the other hand. Both hands do exactly the same job in juggling, so the weaker one has to catch up now.

steps.test: Do the two-ball exchange five times, drops allowed.
how: One ball in each hand.
Throw from your right hand. When that ball reaches the top, throw from your left, under it.
Catch the first ball in your left hand, then the second in your right.
That is one exchange. Pick up whatever falls and go again.
steps.note: Throw, throw, catch, catch. The second throw has to go before the first ball lands, and that feels wrong for a while. Clear a space away from anything breakable; a bed behind you saves a lot of bending down.

steps.test: Do the two-ball exchange ten times in a row, catching both balls every time.
steps.note: Throw, throw, catch, catch, then stop, and start the next one. If the second throw keeps going straight across instead of up, you are throwing it too early: wait for the first ball to reach the top.

steps.test: Do the two-ball exchange twenty times in a row, starting each one from your weaker hand.
steps.note: Same as before with the order turned round: the weaker hand throws first. Juggling three balls starts from either hand, so both have to lead.

steps.test: Do the two-ball exchange twenty times in a row without your feet moving.
steps.note: If you keep walking forwards to catch, your throws are drifting forwards. Stand with your toes against the edge of a rug or a line on the floor and throw straight up in front of your face until you stop needing to move.

steps.test: Hold three balls, throw all three once each, and catch at least one.
how: Two balls in your stronger hand, one in the other.
Throw from the hand with two. At the top, throw from the other hand. At the top of that one, throw the last ball.
Throw, throw, throw, and catch whatever you can.
steps.note: It will go everywhere the first few times, and that is the rung. Everybody who juggles went through this. Count it once all three have left your hands in the right order and one has landed in a hand.

steps.test: Throw all three balls once each and catch all three, so you finish with two in one hand and one in the other.
steps.note: Three throws, three catches, then stop. The balls cross over in front of you in a figure eight, and that pattern is called the cascade. A soft thud on the bed is much better than chasing balls round the room, so practise over one.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for five catches before you stop or drop.
steps.note: Carry on past the third throw: every time a ball reaches the top, the next one goes. Count catches out loud. Five is when it stops being a single burst and starts being juggling.

steps.test: Practise three balls for ten minutes on the clock, picking them up every time they drop.
steps.note: Set a timer and keep going until it rings, however many drops. People who can juggle dropped the balls hundreds of times on the way. Ten minutes like this does more than an hour of starting and giving up, and if you already practise this long, set the timer and count it.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for ten catches.
steps.note: Most drops at this stage come from one throw going too far forward or too low. Watch which hand it comes from and give that hand a few one-ball throws before you start again.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for twenty catches.
steps.note: Twenty catches is about ten seconds. Breathe out and let your shoulders drop; tense arms throw unevenly. If it falls apart at fifteen, stop at twelve on purpose a few times, then try for twenty again.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for thirty seconds without a drop.
steps.note: Use a phone timer or have somebody count. By now the balls should be going round at the same height as the spot on the wall from rung two. If they creep higher and higher, bring them back down.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for one full minute without a drop.
steps.note: A minute is well over a hundred catches. It is more about staying calm than about skill now. Pick a steady rhythm in the first ten seconds and do not speed up.

steps.test: Juggle two balls in one hand for twenty throws, the balls going round in a circle.
steps.note: Both balls in the same hand: throw one up, and as it turns over at the top, throw the second up beside it, catching each as it comes down. It is a new move, not a step back, and it makes your weaker hand much steadier. Do the stronger hand first, then the weaker.

steps.test: Juggle three balls while you walk twenty slow steps forward.
steps.note: Walk slowly in a clear room or on grass, and throw a little further forward than usual so the balls move with you. Keep your eyes on the top of the arc and trust your feet. Stop if you get near furniture or a step.

steps.test: Teach somebody the one-ball throw and the two-ball exchange, until they can do five exchanges without you.
steps.note: A friend, a brother or sister, a parent, a child from about eight. Hand them rolled socks, show them rungs one to six in order, and hold back from taking the balls off them. It may take two or three short sessions on different days.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for two whole minutes without a drop.
steps.note: Two minutes is well over two hundred catches. Build to it the way you built to one minute: a steady rhythm, the same height every throw, eyes on the top. Once you can do this, juggling is a thing your hands keep, even after a year without practice.

tracks.name: Skipping
tracks.line: From jumping on the spot to a hundred skips in a row, a criss-cross, and turning a long rope for somebody else.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child from about five and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with small quiet jumps on the spot and a rope set to the right length, then swinging the rope over and stepping across it, then the first few skips in a row. From there the count climbs to fifty and a hundred, with running steps, one-foot skips and a criss-cross on the way. It ends with a long rope turned by two people and somebody else jumping in. A bought rope is cheap, and a length of washing line or thick cord works just as well.

steps.test: Jump on the spot with your feet together twenty times, landing quietly on the balls of your feet.
steps.note: The balls of your feet are the wide part just behind your toes. The jumps only need to leave the floor a little, and quiet landings mean your knees are bending softly. This is exactly how skipping feels without the rope, so if you do this already, count twenty quiet ones.

steps.test: Stand on the middle of your rope and make it the length where the two ends reach your armpits.
steps.note: Stand on the middle with both feet and pull the ends straight up. Too long, tie a knot near each end or wrap it round your hands; too short, find a longer piece. No rope: use a length of washing line or thick cord, about two and a half metres for a grown-up and two metres for a child. A rope is only for skipping: never put it round anybody's neck, and put it away where a small child cannot play with it alone.

steps.test: Hold the rope behind your heels, swing it over your head, and let it land on the floor in front of your feet, ten times.
steps.note: No jumping yet. Turn the rope with your wrists rather than your whole arms, hands a little out from your hips. Outdoors on a flat hard surface is easiest; indoors, check the rope clears the ceiling and the light.

steps.test: Swing the rope over, let it land in front of you, and step across it, ten times.
steps.note: Swing, land, step over, then bring the rope back behind your heels and go again. This teaches the timing of the rope reaching your feet, slowly enough to watch.

steps.test: Swing the rope over and jump it with both feet as it reaches your toes, ten single jumps with a stop between each.
steps.note: One swing, one jump, stop. Jump just as the rope is about to touch the floor in front of your toes. A small jump is enough; the rope only needs a few centimetres.

steps.test: Skip three times in a row without stopping.
steps.note: Now join the single jumps up: as you land, the rope is already coming over again. Keep your elbows close to your sides and let your wrists do the turning. Three is the rung, however long it takes.

steps.test: Skip ten times in a row without stopping.
steps.note: Count out loud. If the rope keeps catching your toes, you are jumping a little late; if it hits your heels as you land, you are turning too slowly. Small, steady jumps win.

steps.test: Skip twenty-five times in a row without stopping.
steps.note: Twenty-five is where breathing starts to matter. Breathe normally through the whole count, and keep landing on the balls of your feet with soft knees.

steps.test: Skip for one whole minute on a timer, starting again straight away each time the rope catches.
steps.note: The rung is the minute, not a count. Every time the rope catches, step back into position and go again without walking away. If you already skip for longer than this, time a minute and count it.

steps.test: Skip fifty times in a row without stopping.
steps.note: Fifty takes under a minute. If you stop near thirty every time, slow the rope down a little and jump lower. Most people get here within a couple of weeks of a few minutes most days.

steps.test: Skip twenty times in a row stepping from one foot to the other, as if running on the spot.
steps.note: One foot takes the first skip, the other foot takes the next. It feels uneven at first and then much easier than two feet, and many boxers skip this way for a long time without stopping. Keep the steps small and quiet.

steps.test: Skip ten times in a row on one foot, then ten on the other foot.
steps.note: Hold the other foot just off the ground. One foot will be much weaker; give it the extra goes. Stop if your ankle or knee hurts and come back to it another day.

steps.test: Skip one hundred times in a row without stopping.
steps.note: A hundred is about a minute and a half. Count in tens so the number stays small in your head. You can use two feet or the running step, whichever you are steadier with.

steps.test: Skip twenty in a row with one criss-cross in the middle: cross your arms as the rope comes over, jump through, and uncross on the next turn.
steps.note: Cross your arms at the wrists in front of your tummy, so your hands end up beside the opposite hips, and the rope makes a loop to jump through. Practise the cross with single jumps and stops first. Then put one into a row of twenty.

steps.test: Run into a long rope turned by two other people, jump it five times, and run out the other side.
how: Use a rope of about four or five metres, turned by one person at each end.
Stand beside one of the turners, close to the rope.
Just after the rope touches the ground and starts going up away from you, run into the middle.
Jump five times facing a turner, then run out on the far side.
steps.note: Long rope is played in playgrounds all over the world. The turners keep it slow and steady and just touching the ground. Nobody needs to be good at it; the first few tries the rope catches you, and everybody laughs.

steps.test: Turn a long rope with another person for a child or a friend, and help them run in, jump five times, and run out.
steps.note: Turn slowly and evenly, and say 'now' as the rope goes up away from them so they know when to run in. Start with the rope swinging from side to side along the ground for a small child, then go all the way round. Keep going until they do it without you calling.

tracks.name: Upside down
tracks.line: From rocking on your back to a forward roll, a cartwheel and a three-second handstand with no wall, one after the other.
tracks.who: Everybody; a grown-up close by for a child
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, with a grown-up close by for a child's first tries at each new rung. It starts with rocking on a rounded back and a forward roll on something soft, builds strong arms with your hands on the floor and your feet up a wall, then learns a cartwheel and a safe way to step down out of a handstand. It ends with a forward roll, a cartwheel and a kick up to a handstand with no wall, held for three seconds, one after the other. Do it on grass, a rug or a mattress on the floor with space all round, warm your wrists first, and stop if anything hurts; if you have a neck, back, wrist or shoulder problem, high blood pressure or eye trouble, ask a doctor before going upside down. There are no headstands here and nothing puts your weight on your neck: a child learns headstands only with a trained coach.

steps.test: Sit on a rug, hug your knees, tuck your chin in, and rock back onto your shoulders and up onto your feet, ten times.
steps.note: This is the shape of every roll: a round back and a tucked chin, so you roll over your shoulders and never onto the top of your head. Rock back far enough that your hips lift, then forward until your feet are on the floor. On a hard floor, fold a blanket under you. If you already roll easily, do ten slowly with the chin tucked on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Do one forward roll on something soft and come up onto your feet.
how: Crouch with your hands flat on the floor in front of you, shoulder-width apart.
Tuck your chin to your chest and look at your tummy.
Push gently with your feet and lift your hips, so you roll over the back of your shoulders.
Hug your knees as you come round and rock up onto your feet.
steps.note: Use a mattress on the floor, a folded duvet or flat grass. The top of your head should never touch the ground; if it does, tuck the chin harder. A grown-up stays beside a child for the first few and stops them if the chin comes untucked.

steps.test: Do three forward rolls in a row, in a straight line, coming up onto your feet each time.
steps.note: Put your hands down straight in front of you each time and push evenly with both feet, or you will roll off to one side. Stand up between rolls if you feel dizzy, and stop for a minute if you still do.

steps.test: Do a forward roll starting from standing, and stand up at the end without a hand touching the floor.
steps.note: Crouch down from standing, roll, and reach your arms forward as you come round so your weight moves over your feet. Standing up without a hand needs the knees hugged tight until your feet are under you.

steps.test: Crouch with your hands flat on the floor and kick both feet up behind you ten times, landing softly.
steps.note: Arms straight, fingers spread, hands shoulder-width apart; your feet only need to leave the floor a little. This teaches your arms to hold your weight while your hips go up, which is the start of a handstand. Warm your wrists first by circling them and pressing them gently back against the floor.

steps.test: Put your hands on the floor and your feet up on a sofa seat or a low step, arms straight and body straight, and hold for twenty seconds.
steps.note: It is like the top of a press-up with your feet raised. Hands under your shoulders, tummy tight, hips in line. No sofa or step: a low sturdy box or the edge of a bed frame.

steps.test: With your feet on the same sofa seat or step, walk your hands back towards it until your hips are over your shoulders, and hold for twenty seconds.
steps.note: Your body makes an upside-down L, with your weight over your hands. Push the floor away so your shoulders are up by your ears. This is most of a handstand's work with your feet safely on something.

steps.test: Start in a press-up position with your feet against a wall, walk your feet up the wall to hip height, hold for ten seconds, and walk back down.
steps.note: Clear space around you and something soft on the floor. Walk your hands in a little as your feet go up, so your body makes an L. To come down, walk your feet down the wall; if your arms tire, bend your knees and bring them to the floor.

steps.test: Walk your feet up the wall and your hands in until your chest is close to the wall, hold for ten seconds, and walk back down.
steps.note: Hands about a hand's width from the wall, arms straight, looking at the floor between your hands. Go only as high as you can walk back down under control. A grown-up stays beside a child for this one.

steps.test: Hold that chest-to-the-wall handstand for thirty seconds.
steps.note: Build from ten seconds, a few more each time, on different days. Squeeze your legs together and push up tall through your shoulders. Come down before your arms shake badly, not after.

steps.test: Do a cartwheel of any shape along a line on grass or a clear floor, and land on your feet.
how: Stand facing along the line, one foot in front, arms up.
Reach down and put the hand on the same side as your front foot on the line, then the other hand beyond it.
Let your legs go over, one after the other, and land one foot then the other.
Bent legs, a small shape, a wobble: all fine for now.
steps.note: A strip of grass is best; indoors, you need a clear space longer than you are tall and soft underneath. Kick lightly at first; the hands on the ground are the part to learn.

steps.test: Do a cartwheel with your legs straight and apart, with both hands and both feet landing on the line.
steps.note: Straight legs go over higher, so you need a stronger kick from the back leg. Imagine your body moving like a wheel along the line, hand, hand, foot, foot.

steps.test: Do a straight-legged cartwheel the other way, leading with your other hand.
steps.note: Almost everybody has a side they always choose. The other side feels like starting again for a few days, and then it comes quicker than the first side did.

steps.test: Kick up to a small handstand shape with no wall, move one hand, turn, and step down to the side, five times.
steps.note: This is the safe way out of any handstand that tips over: move one hand, turn your hips, and your feet come down beside you, like half a cartwheel. Learn it with small kicks, low down, before you go any higher. This ladder never uses a roll to come out of a handstand, because that can put weight on the neck.

steps.test: Kick up to a handstand with your back to a wall and hold for ten seconds.
steps.note: Hands a hand's width from the wall, one foot in front, kick the back leg up and let your heels rest lightly against the wall. Look at the floor between your hands. Come down one foot at a time the way you went up, or step down to the side as you learnt.

steps.test: Hold a handstand with your back to the wall for thirty seconds.
steps.note: Take one heel, then both, a little off the wall for a moment as you get steadier. That small balance with the wall behind you is the next rung starting.

steps.test: Kick up with no wall, balance for one second, and step down.
steps.note: On grass or a mat with space all round. Kick gently: too hard and you go over, too soft and you come straight back. If you go over, move a hand and step down to the side, as in rung fourteen. Count the one second out loud.

steps.test: Teach somebody to rock on their back and do a forward roll on something soft, until they can do three in a row.
steps.note: A child, a friend or a brother or sister. Show them rungs one to three in order, remind them to tuck the chin, and stay beside them. If the person is a child, a grown-up does the teaching.

steps.test: Hold a handstand with no wall for three seconds, and step down to your feet.
steps.note: Fingers pressing into the ground keep you from falling forwards; pushing through the heels of your hands stops you falling back. Many short tries, a few a day, work better than long sessions. Stop when your wrists or arms are tired.

steps.test: Do a forward roll, a cartwheel and a kick up to a handstand held for three seconds, one after the other without stopping.
steps.note: Roll, stand up, turn to face along your line, cartwheel, then lunge and kick up. Give yourself enough room on grass for all three. This is every part of the ladder in one go.

tracks.name: Breath
tracks.line: From ten slow breaths to two minutes held, calmly, and teaching it to somebody.

steps.test: Take ten slow breaths through your nose, with your mouth shut.
how: Sitting up, shoulders down, mouth closed the whole time.
In through the nose to a count of four, out through the nose to a count of six.
Feel your stomach move rather than your chest.
steps.note: Breathing through your nose warms, filters and slows the air. Most of us mouth-breathe all day without noticing, and simply closing your mouth is a real change.

steps.test: Breathe out for twice as long as you breathe in, twenty times.
how: In for four, out for eight. Count it in your head.
Do not force the out-breath — let it be long and loose.
Twenty rounds is about four minutes.
steps.note: The long out-breath is the switch. It is the one thing that reliably slows a racing heart, and it works within about a minute.

steps.test: Breathe in for four, hold four, out for four, hold four — ten rounds.
how: Square, even counts. Sitting up, eyes closed if you like.
If four is a struggle, use three.
Ten rounds is about three minutes.
steps.note: This is the pattern soldiers and divers are taught for staying steady under pressure, and it is simple enough that a child of seven can use it in a dentist's chair.

steps.test: Hold your breath for thirty seconds, sitting still.
how: Sitting down, on dry land, never in or near water.
Two or three slow breaths first, then a normal breath in, then hold.
Stop the moment it is genuinely unpleasant. This is not a competition.
steps.note: On land, a breath hold is completely safe and simply uncomfortable. In water it is dangerous, and people have drowned practising exactly this. Never in water.

steps.test: Use the slow breathing before something you are nervous about.
how: Twenty long out-breaths, in the five minutes before the thing.
A phone call, a talk, a test, a difficult conversation, a needle.
Then go and do the thing.
steps.note: Here is where this stops being an exercise and becomes a tool. Having something to actually do with your hands and your lungs while you wait is half the battle.

steps.test: Hold your breath for forty-five seconds.
how: Sitting still, on dry land, timer running.
Relax your face and shoulders. Tension burns air.
The first urge to breathe is not the end — it comes far earlier than you need to stop.
steps.note: Most of the improvement here is not lung capacity, it is learning that the first strong urge to breathe can be sat through calmly. That transfers to a lot of things.

steps.test: Do the slow breathing every day for a week.
how: Five minutes, same time each day. First thing or last thing.
Any of the patterns you have learned.
Seven days, ticked off.
steps.note: Practising when you are calm is what makes it available when you are not. Nobody can learn a new way of breathing in the middle of a panic.

steps.test: Hold your breath for one minute.
how: Sitting or lying, never in water.
A few slow breaths first, then a full but not stuffed breath in.
Let it out slowly when you finish rather than gasping.
steps.note: A minute sounds impossible before you have done thirty seconds and easy afterwards. Almost everybody gets there within a fortnight of trying every few days.

steps.test: Slow your own pulse down on purpose, and count it before and after.
how: Find your pulse at your wrist or your neck and count the beats for thirty seconds. Double it.
Three minutes of long out-breaths, four in and eight out.
Count it again.
steps.note: Watching a number you thought was out of your control move because you decided it should is the moment this ladder lands. Ten or fifteen beats is a normal change.

steps.test: Hold your breath for ninety seconds.
how: Dry land, sitting still, somebody nearby if you like.
Stay loose. Swallowing once is normal and buys you time.
Never do this standing at the edge of anything, or in a bath.
steps.note: By now the hold is almost entirely a mental job. The lungs are not the limit; the willingness to be uncomfortable calmly is.

steps.test: Hold your breath for two minutes.
how: Lying down, warm, still, on a day you are rested.
Slow breathing for two minutes first, then the hold.
Stop whenever you want to. Nothing here is worth pushing into feeling unwell.
steps.note: Two minutes is the end of this ladder and it is a genuinely surprising thing to own. Longer than this is a thing for trained people with trained supervision, not for an app.

steps.test: Teach somebody the slow breathing until they can do it without you.
how: The long out-breath first. That is the one that works.
Do it with them rather than describing it.
Give them one moment to use it for: before bed, before a test, when they are angry.
steps.note: A child who is given this at six has it for life, and it is the single most useful thing on this ladder. Give them the out-breath and one moment to use it, and nothing else.

tracks.about: Your breathing is the one part of your body that runs itself and that you can also take hold of, which makes it the fastest way there is to calm yourself down on purpose. This ladder is half calm and half capacity: slow breathing that you can use before anything frightening, and breath holds that climb to two minutes. One safety rule runs through all of it, and it is not negotiable: never practise any of this in water, or near water, ever.

tracks.name: Carrying
tracks.line: From two heavy bags to a person on your back.

steps.test: Carry a full bag in each hand the length of your street.
how: Two shopping bags, two full water containers, two bags of books.
Stand tall, shoulders back, walk normally. Do not lean to one side.
If you have to stop, they are too heavy — go a bit lighter and walk the whole way.
steps.note: Two even loads are the easiest way to carry weight and the best place to start. The goal is always to walk normally, not to survive.

steps.test: Carry something heavy in one hand the same distance, then swap.
how: One bag, one side, the whole length, then the same on the other side.
Do not lean away from it — stay upright and let your middle do the holding.
Shorter distance if you find yourself tipping.
steps.note: One-sided carrying is what really trains the sides of your middle, and it is what most of real life is: one heavy bag and a door to open.

steps.test: Carry something awkward up a full flight of stairs.
how: A box, a laundry basket, a bag of sand, a bedside table.
High and close to your chest so you can see the steps.
One step at a time. No rushing the last three.
steps.note: Stairs with something awkward is where carelessness costs most. Slow is not weakness here; it is the skill.

steps.test: Carry two heavy bags for a hundred metres without setting them down.
how: Count the distance out — about a minute and a half of ordinary walking.
Set your grip properly before you start rather than adjusting on the move.
Breathe. People hold their breath when carrying and it is why they stop.
steps.note: A hundred metres is roughly a car park to a front door. This is the rung that makes a big shop a non-event.

steps.test: Carry something heavy on one shoulder for fifty metres.
how: A sack of compost or coal, a heavy holdall, a rolled carpet.
Up to the chest first, then onto the shoulder, one hand steadying it.
Swap sides halfway if it is comfortable.
steps.note: The shoulder carry is how heavy things were moved for most of history, and it is far easier than it looks once the load is properly settled.

steps.test: Carry a full rucksack for a solid hour's walk.
how: Ten to fifteen kilos: water containers, books, tins, whatever is to hand.
Straps tight, load high and close to your back.
An hour, one walk, no sitting down. Rain is fine.
steps.note: A loaded walk is the single best bit of training in this whole ladder and it doubles as a day out. Take it somewhere worth looking at.

steps.test: Carry something heavy in each hand for two hundred metres.
how: Twice the distance of rung four, same load or heavier.
Pick a landmark and walk to it rather than counting steps.
Set down once and finish, if you must — then do it unbroken next time.
steps.note: Grip usually fails before the rest of you does. That is normal, it improves fast, and it is worth having for its own sake.

steps.test: Carry a child on your shoulders for a mile.
how: Hands holding their shins, their hands on your head, both of you agreeing to the plan.
Duck under branches early rather than late.
No child to hand? A rucksack with fifteen kilos in it for the same mile.
steps.note: This is the carrying that everybody actually wants to be able to do. It is also fifteen or twenty kilos for twenty minutes, which is real work.

steps.test: Carry two heavy bags up two flights of stairs without setting them down.
how: Steady pace from the first step. Do not start fast.
Even loads, upright, eyes on the steps.
If your grip is going, that is the rung for another fortnight.
steps.note: Stairs with a load are about three times as hard as flat ground and are exactly what a house move consists of.

steps.test: Carry half your own bodyweight for fifty metres.
how: Split across two hands, or a loaded rucksack plus a bag.
Set up properly, walk tall, breathe.
Do not chase this one if your back complains — go back a rung.
steps.note: Half your bodyweight is a serious carry and it is the point where people start volunteering you for things.

steps.test: Carry somebody your own size ten metres on your back.
how: They climb on from a step or a wall so you are not lifting them from the ground.
Arms under their thighs, lean forward a little, walk tall.
Agree how they get off before you start.
steps.note: A piggyback is a ridiculous amount of fun and a genuinely heavy carry. Ten metres is enough to find out how heavy a person is.

steps.test: Do the carries on three separate days in one week.
how: Two or three carries a session: two bags, one shoulder, one loaded walk.
Ten or fifteen minutes is plenty.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Carrying builds quickly because it is the kind of work your body was built for. Three sessions a week is a month of noticeable change.

steps.test: Carry somebody your own size twenty-five metres.
how: On your back, arms under the thighs, upright rather than bent over.
Short steps, steady breathing, no rushing.
Put them down properly rather than dropping them.
steps.note: Twenty-five metres with a person on your back is the distance that turns this from a game into a thing you could do if you had to.

steps.test: Carry a loaded rucksack up a hill without stopping.
how: Ten to fifteen kilos, any decent hill, all the way to the top.
Short steps and a slow steady pace beat charging and stopping.
No hill nearby? Two flights of stairs, five times over, with the pack on.
steps.note: Hills with weight are the oldest training there is. It also happens to be how you end up at the top of somewhere worth seeing.

steps.test: Carry two full water containers a mile.
how: Ten litres a side is twenty kilos. Five litres a side if that is too much.
Set down as many times as you need the first time, fewer the next.
Water is free and you can pour it out at the end.
steps.note: The cheapest heavy training in the world, and the load gets exactly as heavy as you decide. A mile with it is a proper morning's work.

steps.test: Carry somebody your own size fifty metres.
how: Fifty metres, on your back, no setting them down.
Find your rhythm in the first ten steps and keep it.
Somebody else nearby, just in case.
steps.note: Fifty metres is far enough to get somebody out of a field, off a beach or to the end of a road. That is the reason this rung exists.

steps.test: Carry a heavy load for half an hour over rough ground.
how: A loaded rucksack, a field, a beach, a forest path.
Uneven ground makes everything harder and it is the point.
Watch your feet and slow down on the descents.
steps.note: Rough ground works your ankles, your balance and your attention all at once. Flat pavements never will.

steps.test: Move a household with somebody for a whole day, and still be useful at the end.
how: Offer before you are asked, turn up early, bring gloves.
Take the awkward end and keep your technique when you are tired.
The rung is the last hour, not the first.
steps.note: Everything on this ladder was built for this day. The person who is still careful and cheerful at six o'clock is the one everybody remembers.

steps.test: Carry a loaded pack for a full day's walk.
how: Ten kilos or so, six or seven hours of walking, food and water in the pack.
Start slower than you want to. Eat before you are hungry.
Any long marked path, any decent hill day.
steps.note: A day under a pack is where carrying stops being training and becomes a way of getting somewhere. This is the rung that opens the outdoors.

steps.test: Teach somebody how to lift and carry without hurting themselves.
how: Close to you, back straight, legs doing the work, no twisting under load.
Watch them do it and correct the back before the weight goes up.
Show them the awkward-end rule and the agree-the-plan-first rule.
steps.note: Almost nobody is ever taught this and almost everybody hurts their back at some point. Half an hour of your time can spare somebody that entirely.

tracks.about: Strength that goes somewhere. Lifting is getting a load off the ground; carrying is moving it down a street, up a hill or up two flights of stairs, and it is the sort of strength that actually shows up in a life — shopping, moving house, a child asleep on your shoulder, somebody who has turned an ankle. No equipment: bags, water containers, sacks, and people.

tracks.name: Running
tracks.line: From one minute without stopping to five kilometres.

steps.test: Run for one minute without stopping.
how: Slower than you think — a pace you could hold a conversation at.
One minute on the clock, then walk.
Any shoes that do not hurt. Any pavement, path or field.
steps.note: If one minute is hard, you are going too fast, not too unfit. Halve the speed and try again — it works every time.

steps.test: Run one minute and walk one minute, eight times over.
how: Sixteen minutes in all. Clock or phone timer running.
The running minutes stay slow; the walking minutes are proper walking, not shuffling.
Finish feeling like you could have done another.
steps.note: Run-walk is not a beginner's compromise, it is how nearly every runner is actually built. Do not skip it because it feels too easy.

steps.test: Run for three minutes without stopping.
how: Same slow pace. Breathing through your nose is a good check.
Three minutes, then walk as long as you like.
Two or three of these in one outing is a good session.
steps.note: Three minutes usually arrives within a week of the run-walks. Nothing has got fitter yet — you have just stopped sprinting.

steps.test: Go running three times in one week.
how: Three outings, twenty minutes each, mostly walking at first if you need it.
A day off between where you can.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Three a week is the whole thing. Everything from here is built on it, and one long run on a Sunday builds far less than three short ones.

steps.test: Run for five minutes without stopping.
how: Still slow. If you cannot talk, slow down.
Five minutes, walk five, five more.
Rain is fine. Rain is usually better.
steps.note: Almost everybody can run for five minutes if they go slowly enough, and almost everybody tries to go too fast and learns they cannot.

steps.test: Run for eight minutes without stopping.
how: Pick a route you know so you are not guessing the distance.
Steady. Boring is the correct feeling.
Walk as much as you like afterwards.
steps.note: Eight minutes is where the legs stop being the limit and breathing takes over. Steady breathing in a rhythm is what carries you from here.

steps.test: Run for ten minutes without stopping.
how: Out for five, turn round, back for five.
Same slow pace the whole way, including the last minute.
Get it twice before you move on.
steps.note: Ten minutes without stopping is roughly a mile for most beginners, which means the next rung is already nearly yours.

steps.test: Run a mile without walking any of it.
how: Measure it on a phone map, or use a known lap.
Start slower than you want to. Almost everybody goes out too fast.
Finish it, however slowly.
steps.note: A mile is the first real milestone and the first one worth telling somebody about. It is also a distance you now have for good.

steps.test: Go out and run in the rain on purpose, and finish.
how: Wait for the rain, put your shoes on, go.
You will be wet in the first two minutes and then it stops mattering.
Dry clothes and something warm waiting for you at home.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes you a person who runs, because the weather stops being a decision. It is also more enjoyable than anybody expects.

steps.test: Run for fifteen minutes without stopping.
how: Pace it so the last three minutes are the same speed as the first three.
Steady breathing, easy shoulders, short steps.
Walk home afterwards rather than stopping dead.
steps.note: Fifteen minutes is where a run becomes a thing you can think during. That is when people start looking forward to it.

steps.test: Run three times a week for a fortnight.
how: Six runs in fourteen days. Two short, one longer, each week.
Write the six down first and tick them off.
Miss one? Do it the next day. Do not restart the fortnight.
steps.note: This fortnight is the whole difference between someone who has been for a run and someone who runs. Nothing else on this ladder matters as much.

steps.test: Run for twenty minutes without stopping.
how: Out ten, back ten, at a pace you could talk at.
Take a drink of water beforehand rather than carrying one.
Slow down rather than stopping if it gets hard.
steps.note: Twenty minutes is about two miles for most people and it is the point where fitness starts to show up in the rest of your day.

steps.test: Run two miles without walking.
how: Measure the route, run it, no walking breaks.
Start slow enough that the second mile is the same speed as the first.
It should take twenty to twenty-five minutes.
steps.note: Doubling the mile is mostly patience rather than fitness. Go out slower than feels right and it does itself.

steps.test: Run up a hill without walking any of it.
how: Short steps, lean in slightly, arms working.
Slow right down — the rung is not stopping, not going fast.
No hill nearby? A long steady road bridge, or twenty flights of stairs.
steps.note: Hills are where the actual fitness gets built, and where a slow pace is not embarrassing but correct. One hill a week is plenty.

steps.test: Run for twenty-five minutes without stopping.
how: A new route is easier than a known one at this length.
Take the first five minutes far slower than the rest.
Eat something small an hour or two before.
steps.note: Past twenty minutes the run becomes the easy part of the day rather than the hard part. Most people find this stretch the most enjoyable.

steps.test: Run for thirty minutes without stopping.
how: Fifteen out, fifteen back, steady the whole way.
Walk for five minutes first as a warm-up.
Water afterwards, and something to eat.
steps.note: Half an hour of continuous running is a properly fit adult by any ordinary standard, and it is about three kilometres to four for most people.

steps.test: Run four kilometres without stopping.
how: Measure the route rather than guessing it.
Even pace, no heroics in the first kilometre.
Finish with something left.
steps.note: Four is the last rung before the one everybody has heard of, and by now the distance is a pacing job rather than a fitness one.

steps.test: Run five kilometres without stopping.
how: Measured route, or a parkrun on a Saturday morning, which is free everywhere.
Start at your talking pace and stay there until the last kilometre.
Whatever the time is, the rung is finishing without walking.
steps.note: Five kilometres from a start of one minute, in about three months, with no money spent on anything but shoes. This is the rung the whole ladder was built for.

steps.test: Run five kilometres faster than the first time you did it.
how: Same route, timed, at least a fortnight later.
Hold back for the first two kilometres and spend it in the last one.
Any improvement counts, by a second or by five minutes.
steps.note: Beating your own old number is a cleaner satisfaction than beating anybody else's, and it is available to you for the rest of your life.

steps.test: Run beside somebody doing their first mile, and finish at their pace.
how: Their pace, not yours, the whole way. Talk to them.
Tell them the run-walk method and that going slowly is the trick.
Finish together and make a proper fuss of it.
steps.note: Running somebody else's first mile with them costs you an easy twenty minutes and gives them the thing you have. It is the best use of this ladder there is.

tracks.about: Running from nothing to five kilometres, the way it actually works: slowly. Almost everybody who says they cannot run is simply running too fast, and the whole first half of this ladder is about going slow enough to keep going. It needs shoes that do not hurt and a road. Three times a week for about three months takes most people from a minute to five kilometres without stopping.

tracks.name: Balance
tracks.line: From standing on one foot, to walking a narrow log or beam, turning round in the middle, and coming back without stepping off.
tracks.who: Everybody; a grown-up beside a young child outdoors
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, with a grown-up beside a young child on the outdoor rungs. The first half is done indoors on the floor: one foot, then one foot with your eyes shut, heel to toe along a line, and reaching and bending while you stay up. The second half goes outside to a log, a low wall or a plank lying on the ground, walking it forwards, backwards and slowly, and ends on something narrower, turning round in the middle and coming back. Everything here is at ground level or knee height at most, never higher, and a patch of grass underneath is best. Good balance is useful at every age, from climbing about as a child to staying steady on your feet when you are old.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for thirty seconds without the other foot touching down.
steps.note: Lift the other foot just off the floor, look at something still in front of you, and count or use a timer. Stand near a wall or a chair back in case you tip. If this is already easy, do it on purpose and count it.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for a full minute.
steps.note: Then do the other foot. Brushing your teeth or waiting for the kettle is a good time for this. Small wobbles in the ankle are the balance working; let them happen instead of locking your knee.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Walk heel to toe along a straight line on the floor for twenty steps.
steps.note: The heel of the front foot touches the toes of the back foot every step. Use the edge of a rug, a line of floor tiles or floorboards, or a strip of tape. Arms out to the sides is allowed.

steps.test: Walk heel to toe backwards along the same line for ten steps.
steps.note: Toes of the back foot reach back to touch the heel of the front foot. Glance down at the line when you need to. Clear the floor behind you first.

steps.test: Stand on one foot and pick a sock up off the floor, then stand up tall again without the other foot touching down.
steps.note: Put the sock just in front of your standing foot. Bend at the hips and knee, and let your free leg go out behind you to balance.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for thirty seconds with your eyes shut.
steps.note: Much harder than it sounds, because your eyes do a lot of the balancing. Stand in a corner or next to a chair so you can put a hand out. Start with five seconds and build up.

steps.test: Stand on one foot and touch the floor in front, to the side and behind you with the toes of the other foot, three times round, without putting it down.
steps.note: Reach out, tap lightly, bring the foot back in, then the next direction. Reach only as far as you can and still come back up steady. Do both feet.

steps.test: Stand on one foot holding a full water bottle out in front with both hands, bend your standing knee a little, count five, and straighten, ten times.
steps.note: A small bend is enough; this is about control, not depth. Keep the knee pointing over your toes and not falling inwards. Any tin, bag of rice or book will do instead of a bottle.

steps.test: Walk heel to toe along the line for twenty steps with your eyes shut.
steps.note: Clear the floor ahead of you and have a wall within reach. Open your eyes whenever you feel yourself going, then shut them and carry on. For a child, a grown-up walks beside them.

steps.test: Stand on one foot on a firm cushion or a folded towel for thirty seconds.
steps.note: A soft surface makes your ankle work much harder. Use a sofa cushion or a towel folded several times on the floor, with a wall close by. Do both feet.

steps.test: Walk the length of a log, a low wall or a plank lying on the ground without stepping off.
steps.note: Choose one no higher than your knee, with grass or soft ground on both sides: a fallen tree in a park, the edge of a raised flower bed, a balance beam in a playground, or a plank laid flat on the grass. Never a wall with a drop on either side, and never a kerb beside a road. A grown-up walks beside a young child.

steps.test: Walk the same log, wall or plank slowly, stop halfway, stand still for five seconds, and carry on to the end.
steps.note: Stopping is harder than walking, because moving forwards hides small wobbles. Look at the far end, not your feet. Step off on purpose if you start to fall rather than trying to save it.

steps.test: Walk the length of it backwards without stepping off.
steps.note: Look at it before you start, then feel for it with your toes each step. Go slowly and keep your arms out.

steps.test: Stand on one foot on the log, wall or plank and count to ten.
steps.note: Everything you did on the floor at the start, now on something narrow. Pick the widest, steadiest part to begin. Do both feet.

steps.test: Walk to the middle, turn round to face the way you came, and walk back without stepping off.
steps.note: Turn in small steps on the balls of your feet, keeping them close together. Take as long as you need. Most people wobble most at the moment of turning.

steps.test: Walk to the middle, crouch down until your hands touch it, stand back up, and walk on to the end.
steps.note: Go down slowly, with one foot a little in front of the other. Hands touch lightly, they do not grab. Stand up slowly too.

steps.test: Walk the length of something narrower, such as a round log or a thin balance beam, without stepping off.
steps.note: Narrower means about as wide as your foot or less, still no higher than your knee and with soft ground beside it. In many playgrounds and parks there is a narrow beam or a line of logs. If there is nothing like that near you, a length of wood about as wide as your foot, laid flat on the grass, does the same job.

steps.test: Walk the narrower one with a stop in the middle, standing still for five seconds.
steps.note: The same as rung twelve on something harder. Soft knees and your arms out, and let your hips move under you instead of your shoulders.

steps.test: Walk beside somebody along a log or plank, holding their hand, until they can walk it end to end without you.
steps.note: A child, a friend, a grandparent. Hold their hand below shoulder height and let them lean on you only as much as they need. Let go a little more each time, and stay beside them.

steps.test: Walk the narrower one to the middle, turn round, and walk back to where you started without stepping off.
steps.note: Everything in this ladder is in this one walk: eyes ahead, small steps, soft knees, a still moment, and the turn. Take it slowly. If you have a slackline set up low by somebody who knows how, you can do this rung on that instead.

tracks.name: Riding a bike
tracks.line: From a helmet that fits to a ten-kilometre ride on a route you planned.
tracks.who: Anybody learning; a grown-up with any child near roads
tracks.about: For anybody learning to ride a bike, from a small child to a grown-up who never learnt; a grown-up is with any child, always, on or near roads. It starts off the bike, with a helmet that fits and a bike that is safe. Then the order many children learn in: walking the bike along while sitting on it, braking, gliding with feet up, steering, and only then pedalling. Then starting, stopping on a line, weaving, looking behind and signalling, a hill, and three kilometres on quiet paths. Road rules differ from country to country, so there is a rung for learning yours before the first quiet road, and it ends with a ten-kilometre ride on a route you planned. A bike takes you much further than walking for almost no cost.

steps.test: Put on a bike helmet and adjust it until it sits level and firm, with the straps done up.
how: Level on the head, the front edge about two fingers' width above the eyebrows.
The side straps make a V shape just under each ear.
Buckle it so only one finger fits between the chin strap and the chin.
Shake your head: the helmet should move with it, not slide.
steps.note: No helmet? Borrow one from a friend or a family with older children, or ask whether a school or cycling club near you lends them. A helmet that has been in a crash or is cracked should not be used again. If you already ride, check yours on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Check a bike: both tyres firm, both brakes stop the wheels, and the seat low enough to put both feet flat on the ground.
steps.note: Squeeze each tyre hard with your thumb; it should hardly dent. Push the bike forward and squeeze each brake in turn: that wheel should stop. Lower the seat with its lever or a spanner so the rider sits with both feet flat. No bike? Borrow one, or look for a free bike library or repair group near you. A grown-up uses the tools for a child.

steps.test: On flat ground with no traffic, sit on the bike and walk it along with your feet for twenty metres.
steps.note: A playground, a quiet car park, a park path or a big yard. A balance bike, or a bike with its pedals taken off, stops the pedals knocking your legs; the left pedal unscrews the opposite way to the right one. With the pedals on, keep your feet out to the sides. If you can already ride, do rungs three to ten in one session on purpose and count them.

steps.test: Walk the bike along while sitting on it, and stop with the brakes, not your feet, three times.
steps.note: Squeeze both brakes gently and evenly, never just the front one hard. First practise squeezing them while walking beside the bike, so your hands know where they are. Stop at a mark on the ground each time: a crack, a shoe, a line of chalk.

steps.test: Push off with your feet and glide with both feet lifted for three seconds.
steps.note: Walk it along faster, then lift both feet a little and count 'one, two, three'. Look ahead, not down at the front wheel: the bike tends to go where you look. A very gentle slope of short grass makes gliding easier and falling softer.

steps.test: Glide for ten seconds, steering in a gentle curve round a marker.
steps.note: Put a shoe or a bottle down as the marker. Turn by leaning a little and turning the handlebars a little; big turns of the handlebars at slow speed tip you over. Go round it one way, then the other way.

steps.test: With the pedals on, pedal for ten metres with nobody holding the bike.
steps.note: Start with a glide or a gentle slope, put your feet on the pedals and push. A grown-up helping a child holds the child's shoulders or the back of their top, not the seat or handlebars, lets go early, and says so. Raise the seat a little once pedalling works, so the knee is only slightly bent at the bottom of each push.

steps.test: Start off from standing still on your own, three times.
steps.note: Stand over the bike with one foot on the ground. Lift the other pedal to just past the top, pointing forward. Push down on it hard and bring the other foot onto its pedal as you move. Look ahead. On a slight downhill slope it is easier, so start there if you need to.

steps.test: Ride towards a line on the ground and stop with your front wheel on it, three times in a row.
steps.note: Chalk, a stick or a crack in the path. Slow down early with both brakes, then squeeze a little more to stop on the line, and put one foot down. Stopping exactly where you mean to is what will keep you out of trouble at road junctions later.

steps.test: Ride in a zigzag round five markers without putting a foot down.
steps.note: Shoes, bottles or stones about three big steps apart in a line. Ride slowly and look at the next gap, not the marker. When it is easy, move them a step closer together.

steps.test: Ride in a straight line while you look back over your shoulder for two seconds.
steps.note: This is the skill that matters most on a road later: seeing what is behind you before you move out. Practise where there is no traffic. Turn your head, not the handlebars, and keep your arms loose. Ask somebody to stand behind you and hold up a number of fingers for you to call out.

steps.test: Ride in a straight line with one arm held straight out to the side for three seconds, on each side.
steps.note: This is the hand signal for turning. Take the hand off only once you are riding steadily, and keep the other hand near the brake. Look ahead, not at your arm. Some countries also use other signals, which you will learn on rung fifteen.

steps.test: Ride up a hill without getting off.
steps.note: Choose a short, gentle slope first. If the bike has gears, change to an easier gear before the hill starts, not halfway up. Keep pedalling steadily, and stand up on the pedals for the steepest part if you need to.

steps.test: Ride three kilometres on quiet, traffic-free paths without stopping.
steps.note: Park paths, a traffic-free cycle path, a path along a river or an old railway line; check that bikes are allowed. Slow right down past people walking, and ring a bell or say hello early so nobody is startled. Take water. A grown-up rides with any child.

steps.test: Learn the cycling road rules where you live, and say them out loud to somebody: which side to ride on, the signals, lights, and where children may ride.
steps.note: They differ between countries: which side traffic keeps to, whether children may ride on the pavement, whether a helmet is required by law, and what lights a bike must have after dark. Your national road safety or transport authority publishes them free online. Many schools and councils run free cycling lessons for children and adults; take one if you can.

steps.test: Ride a short loop on a quiet road with an experienced rider, looking back and signalling before every turn.
steps.note: Choose a time with little traffic, such as early on a weekend morning. Ride about a car door's width away from parked cars. With a child, a grown-up rides close behind on the traffic side, or as the local rules allow, and calls out the plan: 'left at the next corner: look back, signal'. Wear something bright in the day and use lights at dusk.

steps.test: Ride to a real place, such as a shop, a park or a friend's home, and back, on quiet roads and paths.
steps.note: Plan the way before you go, choosing quiet streets and paths over main roads even if it is longer. Take a lock and lock the bike to something fixed. A grown-up rides with any child the whole way. If you already ride to places, choose one you have never cycled to and count it.

steps.test: Plan a ride of about ten kilometres on a map, with a stop halfway, and ride it.
steps.note: Use a map app's cycling directions or a paper map to choose quiet roads and paths. Pack water, a snack, a warm layer and a charged phone, and tell somebody at home the route. Stop halfway to rest and eat. A child rides with a grown-up. This is the end of the ladder: the bike is now a way to get somewhere, not only something to practise on.

tracks.name: Hopping and balancing
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One foot, two feet, a straight line and a roll.

steps.test: Stand on one foot while somebody counts to five. Then the other foot.
Stand on one foot while they count to ten.
Hop three times on one foot.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Hop five times on one foot without putting the other one down.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Jump with both feet together, ten times.
Jump over a line with both feet together, ten times.
Jump off a low step and land on two feet without wobbling.
Walk along a line without stepping off it.
Walk along the line heel to toe.
Do a forward roll on something soft.
Hop all the way across the room on one foot.
steps.twist: The foot you would never choose.

steps.test: Hop across the room, swap feet halfway, and land the last one still.
steps.twist: Start on the foot you would never choose.

categories.name: Outdoors and wild
categories.line: Fire, finding your way, shelter, weather, tracks, wild food.

tracks.name: Out the door, part one
tracks.line: From an hour's walk without a phone to a whole day outside.

steps.test: Walk for an hour with the phone in your pocket the whole time.
steps.note: Anywhere: streets count. Notice what you look at when there is nothing to look at.

steps.test: Say which way is north from where you stand, then check.
steps.note: The sun, the time, moss, a landmark. Then a compass or a map to see how you did.

steps.test: Watch the sky at dusk until the first star, and name it if you can.
steps.note: The first "star" is often a planet. A free sky app will tell you which.

steps.test: Go out in the rain on purpose, dressed for it, for twenty minutes.
steps.note: Proper coat, hood up. Nobody else is out; that is what makes it good.

steps.test: Name five trees or plants on one walk.
steps.note: A street, a park, a verge. An app can name them; you have to remember them.

steps.test: Read tomorrow's weather from tonight's sky and wind, write it down, and check.
steps.note: Red sky, wind direction, the kind of cloud. Then see in the morning. Wrong is fine; the looking is the rung.

steps.test: Walk somewhere new with a paper map, or no map at all.
steps.note: Pick a point a mile off and find a way there you have never used.

steps.test: Light a candle with one match.
steps.note: A fire where you have somewhere to make one; a candle where you do not. One match, no second go.

steps.test: Watch the sunrise, out of doors.
steps.note: Look up the time, be outside ten minutes before. Once a year would change most people.

steps.test: Walk ten thousand steps in one day.
steps.note: About five miles. The phone counts them; the legs do the rest.

steps.test: Find the moon, say what phase it is, and where it will be tomorrow.
steps.note: Later each night, by about fifty minutes. Check tomorrow.

steps.test: Sit outside for thirty minutes and write down everything alive you saw.
steps.note: Birds, insects, a cat, a dog, people. A doorstep or a balcony will do.

steps.test: Eat one meal outside.
steps.note: A sandwich on a bench, a flask on a wall. Weather permitting is not a rule; dressing for it is.

steps.test: Walk for two hours in one go.
steps.note: Six or seven miles. Water, a snack, no hurry.

steps.test: Spot three birds and name them.
steps.note: Pigeon, gull and crow count at first. A robin, a blackbird, a wren next.

steps.test: Go for a walk at night with a torch you do not switch on.
steps.note: Twenty minutes. Eyes adjust in about ten. Streets count; somewhere darker is better.

steps.test: Get yourself to somewhere five miles away and back, on foot or by bike.
steps.note: Ten miles in the day. Plan it, pack water, go.

steps.test: Pack a bag for a day out with everything you would need, and go.
steps.note: Water, food, a layer, a waterproof, a map, a plaster. Then a day out with it.

steps.test: Find the highest point you can walk to within an hour of home, and go up it.
steps.note: A hill, a tower, a multi-storey car park roof, a church that lets you climb. Look at your town from above.

steps.test: A whole day outside, dawn to dusk.
steps.note: Sunrise from rung nine, dusk from rung three, and everything between. Part two is the wild proper.

tracks.about: Out the door, wherever you live: an hour without the phone in your hand, north found and checked, the first star, rain on purpose, a sunrise, ten thousand steps, a walk at night with the torch off, and a whole day outside at the end. Every rung works from a town street.

tracks.name: Fire
tracks.line: From finding out where a fire is allowed to teaching somebody else to lay, light and put out a fire safely.
tracks.who: Grown-ups, and teenagers with a grown-up
tracks.about: For grown-ups, and for teenagers with a grown-up beside them at every lit fire; a child never lights a fire alone. The climb starts before any match: finding out where a fire is allowed today, setting up a safe spot with water ready, and gathering and sorting dry wood. Then laying a fire, lighting it, keeping it small and steady, and putting it out until the ashes are cold, leaving the place as you found it. The later rungs are one match, wind, damp wood and a spark striker, and it ends with you teaching somebody else the whole thing. A fire lit well and put out properly is an old, useful skill, and the care it takes is most of the skill.

steps.test: Find out whether you may light a fire in one place you could go, and whether there is a fire ban or high fire danger today.
steps.note: Many parks, woods and beaches do not allow fires at all, and in dry, hot or windy weather there are often bans everywhere. Check the rules for the place (the landowner, the park's website, your local council, a campsite's rules) and your national or regional fire danger rating. A garden fire bowl or a campsite fire pit is often the simplest legal place. If the answer is no, the answer is no; this rung still counts.

steps.test: In a place where a fire is allowed, set up a fire spot with three metres clear all round and a full bucket or bottle of water beside it.
steps.note: Use a fire pit, a fire ring, a fire bowl or a barbecue if there is one. Clear dry leaves and grass, look up for low branches, and keep it well away from tents, fences and hedges. Never set a fire on peat or deep dry leaves, where it can creep underground. The water is ready before the first match, every time from now on.

steps.test: Gather an armful of dead, dry sticks from the ground that snap cleanly when you bend them.
steps.note: If a stick bends instead of snapping, it is too wet or still alive. Take only wood that is already lying on the ground, and never break branches off living trees. Where collecting wood is not allowed, use wood you bring from home.

steps.test: Sort what you gathered into three piles: tinder, kindling, and fuel wood.
steps.note: Tinder catches a flame: dry grass, the thin curls of dead bark, pine needles, or a little scrunched newspaper. Kindling is sticks about as thick as a pencil. Fuel wood is thumb-thick to wrist-thick. Make the kindling pile twice as big as you think you need; running out of it is why most fires fail.

steps.test: Lay a small fire in your fire spot, without lighting it, and have your grown-up or a friend check it would light.
steps.note: A simple way: a fist-sized ball of tinder in the middle, kindling leaned over it in a small cone with a gap on the side the wind comes from, and fuel wood kept to one side for later. Leave spaces for air; a tightly packed fire goes out.

steps.test: Strike five matches, one at a time, away from your body, holding each over a bowl of water until it has nearly burnt down.
steps.note: Hold the box low, strike away from you, and tip the match slightly down so the flame climbs the stick. Drop each one into the water. A teenager does this with a grown-up beside them. If you already strike matches without thinking, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Light the fire you laid with a match, and feed it from small wood to bigger wood until the fuel wood has caught.
steps.note: Light the tinder on the side the wind is coming from, so the wind blows the flame into the fire. Add kindling a few sticks at a time, then fuel wood once the kindling is burning well. Keep it small: a fire the size of a dinner plate is plenty. Somebody stays with a lit fire at all times.
how: Water ready, fire spot clear.
Light the tinder low down, on the side the wind comes from.
Add kindling a few sticks at a time.
Add fuel wood once the kindling is burning well.

steps.test: Put a fire out until the ashes are cold to your hand.
steps.note: Pour water on slowly, stir the ashes with a stick, pour again, and stir again. Hold the back of your hand just above the ashes; if you feel any warmth it is not out. Only then touch them. Warm is not out. If you ever get a burn, cool it under cool running water for at least twenty minutes, as in the First aid ladder.
how: Pour water slowly over everything.
Stir the ashes with a stick.
Pour again and stir again.
Back of the hand above, then touch: cold.

steps.test: After a fire, leave the spot so the next person finds it as you did.
steps.note: Take home every scrap of rubbish, including anything that did not burn. Never burn plastic, foil or painted wood. If there was no fire ring, scatter the cold ashes widely and put back any stones or turf you moved. Leave no trace of the fire at all: that is the rule wherever you go.

steps.test: Keep a small fire going for thirty minutes, adding wood before it needs it, and put it out cold at the end.
steps.note: Add one or two pieces at a time when the flames start to drop, not when the fire is nearly out. Watch how long a piece of fuel wood lasts. The fire should stay the same size the whole time, and never be left alone.

steps.test: Lay and light a fire using a single match.
steps.note: Everything is ready before you strike: tinder dry and fluffed up, plenty of kindling, fuel wood to hand. If it fails, lay it again better and try another day; the one match is the rung.

steps.test: On a breezy day, when there is no fire ban, light a fire in a sheltered fire spot, using your body or a bag as a windbreak.
steps.note: Crouch with your back to the wind and strike the match inside the shelter of your hands. In strong wind, do not light a fire at all: sparks can carry a long way. Saying no on a windy day counts as doing the rung well.

steps.test: After rain, find dry wood and tinder and light a fire with it.
steps.note: Look for dead sticks still hanging in bushes rather than lying on wet ground, and snap them; the inside is often dry. Peel thin curls of bark from fallen dead wood only, never from a living tree. Bringing a little dry tinder from home in a bag is good planning, not cheating.

steps.test: Light a fire with a spark from a fire striker instead of a match.
steps.note: A fire striker (a metal rod and a scraper) throws hot sparks onto very fine tinder: fluffed cotton wool, dry grass rubbed between your hands, or thin bark shavings. Scrape the rod, not the scraper, and hold it close to the tinder. If you do not have one, borrow one from a friend or an outdoor group, or do this rung with matches and a single strike on the finest tinder you can make.

steps.test: Run a fire for a whole evening with other people round it, from checking the rules to putting it out cold.
steps.note: You are the one who checks the fire danger, sets up the spot, puts the water beside it, keeps the fire the right size, and puts it out at the end. Tell everybody the simple rules first: no running near the fire, no throwing things into it.

steps.test: Teach somebody else to lay, light and put out a fire, with you beside them the whole time.
steps.note: Go through the rungs in order with them: the rules, the spot, the water, the three piles, laying, lighting, and putting it out cold. Let them do it with their own hands while you watch and only step in for safety. If they are a child, you are the grown-up beside them. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Finding your way
tracks.line: From pointing to where the sun rises to leading a group on a half-day route you planned and navigated.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; children from ten with a grown-up
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for children from about ten with a grown-up beside them. It starts with no tools at all: where the sun rises and sets, landmarks, and the turns on a route you already walk. Then direction from the sun at midday, from a stick's shadow and from a watch, written for both halves of the world. Then a compass: north, a bearing to something you can see, your own step count, a triangle walked by numbers, and a bearing taken from the map to a place you cannot see. After that come the ways walkers really avoid getting lost: following a wall or stream, aiming to one side on purpose, knowing where you are at any moment, and walking slowly in poor light. It ends with a written route plan left at home and a half-day walk you lead for other people. The Maps ladder teaches reading a map; this one teaches getting across the ground with one, or without one.

steps.test: Stand at your front door and point to where the sun rises and where it sets, then check with a compass app.
steps.note: The sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. It is close to due east and due west only around 21 March and 23 September. Around June it rises north of east and sets north of west; around December it rises south of east and sets south of west; that is true in both halves of the world. Most phones have a free compass app. Not sure where it rose today? Point, and check tomorrow morning.

steps.test: Before walking home from about a kilometre away, name three landmarks you will pass in order, then walk home by them without a map.
steps.note: Landmarks are things that do not move and are easy to see from a distance: a church tower, a tall tree, a bridge, a bright sign, a hill. Say them out loud first: 'the petrol station, then the school, then the big tree'. A child can lead while a grown-up walks behind and says nothing unless it goes wrong. If you walk this way every day, choose a way you use less.

steps.test: Write down every turn from home to a place you go often, with a landmark at each, then walk it and tick them off.
steps.note: Left or right, and what is there: 'right at the post box, left after the bakery'. Most people find they have missed a turn or two in the list, and that is the useful part: you start to notice. If you usually go by car or bus, write the route and walk the last part.

steps.test: Near the middle of the day, turn to face the sun's direction with your eyes on the ground, say which way you are facing, and check.
steps.note: North of the tropics (for example Europe, North America, Japan), the sun is in the south at midday. South of the tropics (for example South Africa, Argentina, most of Australia, New Zealand), it is in the north. Between the tropics it can be nearly overhead at midday, so use the next rung instead. Where clocks go forward for summer, the sun is highest nearer one o'clock. Never look straight at the sun.

steps.test: Push a stick into the ground, mark the tip of its shadow, wait fifteen minutes, mark it again, and say which way is north.
steps.note: The first mark is west and the second is east, because the shadow moves the opposite way to the sun. Stand with the first mark by your left foot and the second by your right: you are facing north. This works in both halves of the world on any sunny day. A pencil in a flowerpot of soil on a balcony works too. Check with a compass app.

steps.test: Find south or north with the sun and a watch that has hands, then check with a compass app.
how: North of the tropics: hold the watch flat and turn it until the hour hand points at the sun; halfway between the hour hand and the 12 is south.
South of the tropics: point the 12 at the sun; halfway between the 12 and the hour hand is north.
Where clocks are forward for summer, use the 1 instead of the 12.
steps.note: No watch with hands? Draw a clock face on paper with the hour hand at the right time. This way is rough: it can be well off depending on the season and the time of day, and it is poor near midday in summer and between the tropics. That is why you check it.

steps.test: Hold a compass flat, away from metal and phones, and point to north, east, south and west from where you stand.
steps.note: A see-through baseplate compass, the kind walkers use, is best for the rest of this ladder; borrow one, or use a phone compass app until you have one. The red end of the needle points to magnetic north. Keys, a railing, a car or a phone in the same hand can pull the needle, so step away from them. The four points go round clockwise: north, east, south, west.

steps.test: Take a bearing to a landmark you can see, walk to it, then turn round and walk back on the opposite bearing.
how: Point the arrow on the compass base at the landmark.
Turn the dial until its north arrow sits under the red end of the needle, and read the number.
At the landmark, add 180 to the number (or take 180 away if it is over 180): that is the way back.
steps.note: A bearing is a direction as a number of degrees, from 0 at north round to 360. Pick something a few hundred metres away across a park or a field with a path: a tree, a gate, a lamp post. Most phone compass apps also show the degrees you are facing.

steps.test: Count your double steps over a hundred metres, three times, and work out your own number.
steps.note: Count one each time your left foot lands. Measure the hundred metres on a sports track, or between two points on a path using a map app's measuring tool. Many adults take somewhere around sixty to seventy double steps; children take more. Your number changes uphill, in mud and in long grass, so try one of those too and write both down.

steps.test: Walk a triangle of three bearings, 0, 120 and 240 degrees, for fifty double steps each, and see how close to your start you finish.
steps.note: Mark the start with a coat or a stick on open ground such as a playing field. Walk 0 degrees for fifty, turn to 120 for fifty, then 240 for fifty. Finishing within a few metres of the coat means your compass work and your counting are good. Take turns: one walks, one watches.

steps.test: Lay the compass on the paper map, turn them together until the needle points to the top of the map, and name three things you can see.
steps.note: This turns the map to match the ground where there is no street to line it up with, such as in fields and woods. The Maps ladder turns the map by the streets; this is the way that works anywhere. The map's north and magnetic north differ by a few degrees in some places and by more than ten in others. The edge of a walking map usually says by how much; for this rung it does not matter.

steps.test: Take a bearing from the map to a place you cannot see from where you stand, walk it counting your steps, and arrive within twenty metres.
how: Lay the edge of the compass on the map from where you are to where you are going.
Turn the dial until its lines run up and down the map, with its north arrow to the top of the map.
If the map gives a magnetic difference for your area, add or take it away as the map says.
Hold the compass flat, turn until the red needle sits over the dial's north arrow, and walk the way the base arrow points.
