steps.note: Choose a target in a park or open woods with paths: a bridge beyond a rise, a gate behind a group of trees. On the way, pick something on your line a short distance ahead, walk to it, and take the bearing again. A grown-up is with any child.

steps.test: Walk a route that follows a wall, a stream or a path to your target, with something beyond it that tells you if you have gone too far.
steps.note: Walkers call the thing you follow a handrail, and the thing beyond a catching feature: a road, a river, the edge of a wood. Plan it first: 'follow the stream to the footbridge; if we reach the road, we have gone past it'. Most good navigation is this, not bearings, because it is the easiest way not to get lost.

steps.test: To reach a gate or a bridge on a long wall or river, aim clearly to one side of it on purpose, so you know which way to turn when you arrive.
steps.note: Aim straight at a gate in a long wall and miss it, and you cannot tell whether it is to the left or the right. Aim to the left of it, and when you reach the wall, turn right. Walkers call this aiming off. Try it where the target is a few hundred metres away across open ground.

steps.test: Partway round a walk, stop, point to where you are on the map, and give three reasons you are sure.
steps.note: The reasons: the last place you were certain of and how long you have walked since; what you can see (a stream on your left, a mast on the hill); and whether the ground under you rises or falls the way the contour lines say. If you cannot give three, walk back to the last place you were sure of. Turning back early is what careful walkers do.

steps.test: Walk a short route you know well at dusk or in mist, using the map and compass slowly, with somebody beside you.
steps.note: Choose paths near home or in a park, never near cliffs, fast rivers or on open hills. Take a torch, warm layers and a turn-back time. Go slower than seems necessary and check the map at every junction. A grown-up is always with any child. No mist this season? Dusk counts.

steps.test: Write a route plan for a half-day walk: each part's bearing, distance and time, a turn-back time, and a shorter way home.
steps.note: One line per part on paper: 'gate to bridge, 110 degrees, 800 metres, 12 minutes'. Add about ten minutes for each hundred metres of climbing. Choose eight to twelve kilometres on paths you have not walked, with a shorter way back from about halfway. Check the forecast before you choose the day; the Weather and tide ladder covers that.

steps.test: Leave the route plan with somebody at home, walk it with a partner while you navigate every part, and tell them when you are back.
steps.note: Tell the person at home the time you expect to be back and what to do if you are two hours late and not answering: ring your emergency number and read them the plan. Keep to your turn-back time. Write the real time for each part next to the plan; the difference shows you your own speed on real ground.

steps.test: Teach somebody to take a bearing and walk it, until they reach a target on their own.
steps.note: A friend, a partner, a teenager. Show them rung eight on something they can see, then let them do it with you saying nothing. Then the triangle from rung ten. Being able to explain it is the best test of whether you really know it.

steps.test: Lead a group on a half-day route you planned, navigating every part, and bring everybody back by the time you set.
steps.note: Family or friends. Use everything: the route plan left at home, the forecast, handrails and catching features, the turn-back time, and stops to check that everybody is warm, fed and not too tired. Tell the group where you are at each stop. This is the end of the ladder: other people can trust you to get them there and back.

tracks.name: Shelter
tracks.line: From a den of chairs and a blanket to a night in a shelter you built, taken down in the morning.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a child always has a grown-up with them in the woods and for the night. It starts indoors with chairs and a blanket, then moves to a sheet or tarp between two trees, two useful knots, choosing a safe spot, and a frame of fallen branches covered in leaves. Then keeping out rain and wind, a warm layer under you, a shelter for two and an hour sitting in it in poor weather. It ends with a night in a shelter you built, taken down in the morning. Every shelter is built only from fallen wood, never from living trees, only where the owner allows it, and taken down afterwards.

steps.test: Build a den indoors from chairs and a sheet or blanket, big enough to sit inside.
steps.note: Two chairs back to back with a gap between them, a blanket over the top, and books on the edges to hold it down. This is the same idea as every shelter after it: a frame, and a cover over it. If you have built plenty of these, build one on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Tie a two-half-hitches knot and a taut-line hitch, each three times, round a chair leg.
steps.note: Two half hitches hold a line to a tree or post. A taut-line hitch makes a loop you can slide to tighten a line without untying it. Any string or cord works. Look up a picture or a short video of each knot and copy it slowly.

steps.test: Tie a line between two trees or posts and hang a sheet over it to make a tent shape, with the edges held down.
steps.note: In a garden, a park where it is allowed, or between two fence posts. Tie one end with two half hitches and the other with a taut-line hitch so you can tighten it. Hold the edges down with stones or sticks pushed through the corners. An old sheet, shower curtain or plastic sheet all work.

steps.test: Find out where you may build a den outdoors, and ask if you need to.
steps.note: Many woods welcome den building; some nature reserves and private land do not. Look for signs, check the rules for the place online, or ask the landowner or the people who look after the wood. A child goes to the woods with a grown-up.

steps.test: In a wood where it is allowed, choose a safe spot for a shelter and say out loud why it is safe.
steps.note: Look up first: no dead branches hanging above you and no dead trees leaning nearby. Look down: not in a dip where rain collects, not beside fast water, not on an ants' nest. Flat, a little higher than the ground around, and near a strong tree is a good spot.
how: Look up for dead branches.
Look down for dips, water and nests.
Say why this spot is safe.

steps.test: Collect fallen branches for a frame, taking only wood already on the ground.
steps.note: Never cut, snap or pull branches off a living tree, and leave rotten logs where they are, as they are home to insects and fungi. You need one long, strong branch for the top and plenty of shorter ones to lean against it.

steps.test: Build a lean-to frame that stands up on its own: a long branch against a tree or wedged in a low fork, with sticks leaned along one side.
steps.note: Push the leaning sticks close together, about a hand's width apart, all at the same slope. Give it a gentle shake: if it wobbles, move the base of the long branch or wedge it better. A child and a grown-up can do this together, the grown-up lifting the heavy branch.

steps.test: Cover the frame with leaves, bracken or ferns until you can barely see daylight through it from inside.
steps.note: Start at the bottom and work upwards, so each layer overlaps the one below, like roof tiles. Use dead leaves from the ground rather than pulling green plants. Sit inside and look for bright gaps, then fill them.

steps.test: Test how dry your shelter is: sit inside for ten minutes of rain, or while somebody pours a watering can over the roof.
steps.note: In a dry place or a dry season, the watering can is the test. Afterwards, feel your clothes and look at where water came in. Add more cover there, and make the roof steeper if water pooled on it.

steps.test: Work out which way the wind is blowing, and build or turn your shelter so the open side faces away from it.
steps.note: Watch leaves and grass move, drop a little dry grass, or wet a finger and hold it up: the cold side is where the wind comes from. Say out loud how you worked it out.

steps.test: Take a shelter down and spread the branches and leaves back out so the place looks as it did.
steps.note: Lay the sticks back on the ground in different places, and scatter the leaves. If you used string, collect every piece. Leave nothing behind: not a knot, not a wrapper. This rung comes with every shelter from now on.

steps.test: Put up a tarp or sheet three ways: a tent shape, a sloping lean-to, and one corner high like a sail.
steps.note: A tarp with holes at the corners is easiest; an old sheet or plastic sheet works with the corners tied round small stones. Pull each shape tight so rain would run off rather than sit in a puddle.

steps.test: Lay a thick bed of dry leaves or a sleeping mat in your shelter, then sit on it for twenty minutes and compare with sitting on bare ground.
steps.note: Cold ground draws warmth out of you faster than cool air does. A pile of dry leaves pressed down to the thickness of your hand, or a foam camping mat, keeps you much warmer. Notice the difference after twenty minutes.

steps.test: Build a shelter two people can lie down in, side by side.
steps.note: The frame needs to be longer than the tallest person and wide enough at the base. Lie in it before you cover it, to check the size. Make the cover as thick as before.

steps.test: Sit in your own shelter for an hour on a cool, wet or windy day, dressed for the weather.
steps.note: Dress as in the Weather and tide ladder, and bring a warm drink. A child does this with a grown-up in or beside the shelter. If you get cold and cannot warm up, stop and go home; that is the right choice.

steps.test: Sleep a whole night in a shelter you built, in a garden or a place where it is allowed, and take it down in the morning.
steps.note: A garden is a good first place: a lean-to of tarp or branches, a mat and sleeping bag, warm clothes, a torch, and a way back indoors if you get too cold. A child always has a grown-up with them for the night. In the morning, take it down and leave no trace. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Weather and tide
tracks.line: From dressing for the weather you can feel to leading a walk in wind and rain that brings everybody home warm.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and the rungs at the shore are always done with a grown-up. It starts at the front door, dressing for what is really outside, then reading a forecast properly: the hour-by-hour, the "feels like" number, the rain map and the warnings. Then daylight, layers, getting dry again, the early signs of somebody getting too cold, and a turn-back time you keep. The middle rungs are the tide: reading a tide table, knowing the dangers, watching the water, and planning a shore walk around it. It ends with you deciding the weather plan for a family day out and leading a walk in wind and rain that everybody enjoys. In many places the weather changes by the hour, so this is the skill that gets people out of the door more often, not less.

steps.test: Step outside the front door for one minute, then choose what to wear for what you felt.
steps.note: Not what the window suggested and not what yesterday was like. Feel the air on your face and hands, check for wind and damp, then dress. A child can do this before school with a grown-up asking "coat or no coat?". If you already do this every morning, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Open today's forecast and say, hour by hour, what to bring if you go out at ten, at two and at six.
steps.note: Use the hour-by-hour view from your national weather service; its website or app is free. For each time, name the actual things: a coat, a hat, sun cream, gloves, nothing extra. The point is that one day can be three different days.

steps.test: Look out at ten, at two and at six today, and write down whether the forecast was right each time.
steps.note: Three ticks or crosses on a scrap of paper, with a word each: "dry, as said", "rain an hour early". Wrong forecasts are useful: they teach you how much to trust them. A child can keep the paper on the fridge.

steps.test: Find the "feels like" temperature in the forecast, go out for ten minutes, and say which number was closer to the truth.
steps.note: Forecasts show two numbers: the air temperature and what it feels like with the wind and damp. On a windy day they can be several degrees apart. After ten minutes out, say which one your hands agreed with. Dress by that one from now on.

steps.test: Open a free rain radar map, find the nearest shower, say when it will reach you, and check.
steps.note: Most national weather services have a free rain map that moves forward through the next few hours. Find where you are, watch the blue patches, and say a time: "about twenty past three". Then look out at that time. Within half an hour is a good result.

steps.test: Look up today's weather warnings for your area, and say what each warning level means.
steps.note: Your national weather service lists them by region, usually in colours or levels. In many countries the lowest means be aware and plan around it, the middle means be prepared for real disruption, and the highest means take action and avoid travel if you can. If there are no warnings today, that counts: say so, and say what each level would mean.

steps.test: Look up today's sunset time, then go for a walk that finishes half an hour before it.
steps.note: In many places the sun sets hours earlier in winter than in summer, so "before dark" means very different things through the year. Pick a walk, work back from the sunset time, and be home or back at the car with half an hour to spare.

steps.test: Go out on a cold day in three thin layers instead of one thick coat, and take one off when you warm up.
steps.note: For example a T-shirt, a jumper and a waterproof, all things you already own. Take the middle layer off before you start to sweat, not after, and put it back on when you stop. Sweat that goes cold is what makes people shiver.

steps.test: After the next wet walk, get everything dry within fifteen minutes of getting home.
steps.note: Newspaper or kitchen roll stuffed into wet shoes, coat hung up, not in a heap, wet things out of the bag, and a dry pair of socks on you. A child can be in charge of the shoes. It is the difference between wanting to go out again tomorrow and not.

steps.test: Learn the early signs that somebody is getting too cold, and say them out loud to somebody else.
steps.note: Health services list them: shivering, pale cold skin, being tired or muddled, clumsy hands, and slurred words. What to do first: out of the wind and wet, dry layers on, a hat, a warm drink if they are fully awake, and ring your emergency number if they stop shivering but are still cold or seem confused. A child can learn it as "shivering, slow and muddled".

steps.test: On your next cold walk with other people, check on each of them every half hour and fix the first one who is cold.
steps.note: Ask plainly: "Warm enough? Hands?" Children and older people often do not say. The fix is usually small: a hat from your bag, a layer swapped, a hot drink from a flask, or just moving faster for a while.

steps.test: Before a walk, pick a turn-back time, and turn back at it even if you feel fine.
steps.note: Say it out loud at the start: "we turn round at half two, wherever we are". Then do it, even when the top is in sight. This is how you learn that turning back is part of a good day, not a failure of it.

steps.test: Look up the tide times for the beach or shore nearest you, and say when high water and low water are today.
steps.note: Free tide times are on tide-times websites and apps, and harbours and shops by the sea often have printed tide tables. There are usually two high tides and two low tides a day, a little over six hours apart, and they come later each day. Write today's four times down.

steps.test: Learn the four rules for the shore, and tell them to whoever you would go with.
steps.note: One: stay off sandbanks, mudflats, rocks and paths to islands when the tide is coming in; it can come round behind you faster than you can walk. Two: know the time of high water before you set off. Three: if somebody is in trouble in the sea, ring your emergency number and ask for the coastguard or sea rescue; do not go in after them. Four: if you fall in, float on your back until you get your breath, which is what sea-rescue services teach.

steps.test: At the shore, watch the edge of the water against one rock for ten minutes and say whether the tide is coming in or going out.
steps.note: Pick a rock, a post or a line of seaweed right at the water's edge. After ten minutes, is the water further up it or further down? Wet, shiny sand above the waterline often means it is going out. Then check against the tide times. A grown-up stays with any child at the water.

steps.test: Plan a shore walk around the tide: set off after high water and be back well before the next one, and do it.
how: Look up today's high water times.
Set off within an hour after the first one.
Turn back at your set time, wherever you have got to.
Be off the sand and rocks at least two hours before the next high water.
steps.note: Starting as the tide goes out gives you the most beach for the longest time. Pick a turn-back time at least two hours before the next high water, and keep it. Tell somebody at home where you are going and when you will be back.

steps.test: Read or listen to the inshore waters forecast for the stretch of coast you would walk, and say what it means for a walk on the coast tomorrow.
steps.note: Many national weather services publish a free forecast for coastal waters, and some read it out on the radio. It usually gives the wind strength on a scale of numbers, the sea state and the visibility. A wind of 6 or more, or a "rough" sea, means a walk well back from the edge of the water, or a walk inland instead.

steps.test: The next time the forecast turns against a plan, change it and say why in one sentence.
steps.note: Change the place, the time or the day: the forest instead of the cliff path, the morning instead of the afternoon, next Saturday instead. The sentence is for the others: "Amber warning for wind, so the woods, not the coast." Changing a plan is harder than going anyway, and it is usually the right choice.

steps.test: Decide the weather plan for a family or friends' day out: where, when, and what everybody brings, and have it go well.
steps.note: Use everything so far: the hour-by-hour forecast, the warnings, the sunset time, and the tide if it is the coast. Tell people the plan the night before, with the list of what to bring. "Go well" means nobody was caught cold, wet or in the dark.

steps.test: Lead a walk of an hour or more in wind and rain, and bring everybody home warm and glad they went.
steps.note: Pick a day with rain and wind but no amber or red warning. Layers, hats, a flask, a turn-back time, a check on everybody every half hour, and something good at the end: a hot drink, a chip shop, a fire. This is the end of the ladder: other people trusting you with the weather.

tracks.who: For everybody; always a grown-up at the shore

tracks.name: Trees and birds
tracks.line: From five fallen leaves to a walk where you show somebody ten trees and birds by name.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a street with trees and a window are enough for most of it. It starts with fallen leaves and one tree near home that becomes your tree, visited through the whole climb. Then ten trees by name and trees with no leaves, then birds: counting them, the commonest where you live, describing one you cannot name, ten on sight, songs by ear, water put out for them, and nests watched from a distance. Free apps such as Seek, Pl@ntNet and Merlin Bird ID, and a guide from the library, help with the naming; you do the remembering. Look and photograph, and never pick or dig up plants: many are protected by law. It ends with a walk where you show somebody else what lives on their own street.

steps.test: Pick up five different leaves from the ground, lay them out side by side, and say one way each is different from the others.
steps.note: Only leaves that have already fallen; never pull them off a plant. A park, a street with trees or a garden. Look at the shape, the edge (smooth, toothed or wavy), and whether it is one leaf or several small leaflets on one stalk. In a season with no fallen leaves, photograph five leaves still on the trees instead. Leave alone any plant with berries, prickles or stinging hairs that you cannot name, and wash your hands afterwards.

steps.test: Photograph one tree's leaf, bark and whole shape, name it with a free app, and check the name in a second source.
steps.note: Free apps such as Seek or Pl@ntNet suggest a name from a photo. They are often right and sometimes badly wrong, so check with a tree guide from your library or a free tree website for your country: do the leaf, the bark and the shape all match? If you have done the 'five trees on your street' extra, choose a tree it did not name.

steps.test: Choose one tree near home as your tree, and make its first page: its name, where it stands, a sketch or photo, and the date.
steps.note: A tree you pass often: on the street, in a park, a school yard or a garden. Write how tall it is compared with a house or a lamp post, how the bark feels, and what is on it now: leaves, flowers, buds, fruit or nothing. You will visit it once a week for the rest of the ladder. A child can add a bark rubbing: paper held against the trunk and the side of a crayon rubbed over it.

steps.test: Name five trees near home from their leaves and bark, with no app, a week after you first looked them up.
steps.note: Look them up first, then leave it a week and walk past them saying the names. Find one thing that marks each one out: a leaf shape, peeling or deeply ridged bark, the smell of a crushed fallen leaf. Choose what is common where you live, since those are the trees you will see most. If you already know five trees, name ten and count it.

steps.test: Measure round your tree's trunk at the height of your chest, and write down a rough guess at its age.
steps.note: Wrap a piece of string round the trunk, then measure the string against a tape measure or a ruler. Some tree groups use a very rough guide of about two and a half centimetres round the trunk for each year, for a tree growing in the open. Trees in a wood, and slow-growing kinds, can be far older than that says, so write it down as a guess, not an answer.

steps.test: Name ten trees near home without any help.
steps.note: The five from rung four and five more. Walk the same route each week and learn one new tree on it each time. Write the ten down with where each one stands, so the walk itself becomes the test.

steps.test: Name three trees that have no leaves on, from the bark, the buds and the shape alone.
steps.note: Where winters are cold, many trees drop their leaves; do this rung then, and if it is the wrong season now, go on and come back to it. Where trees keep their leaves all year, name three from the bark and the outline against the sky, without looking at the leaves. Buds help: their colour, their size, and whether they grow in pairs or one at a time along the twig.

steps.test: Sit still outside or at a window for ten minutes, and count how many birds you see and how many different kinds.
steps.note: Count the most of each kind you see at one moment, not every visit, or one busy bird gets counted ten times. A kind you cannot name still counts: write 'small, brown, pale front'. Many countries run a yearly garden bird count done exactly this way, and you can send your numbers in. A child can keep the tally with marks on paper.

steps.test: Learn the five commonest birds where you live from pictures, then find and name each of them outdoors.
steps.note: The free Merlin Bird ID app shows the birds most likely where you are at this time of year, and a library bird guide has a map for each bird. Learn five from the pictures first, then go and find them. If you have done the 'five birds on your street' extra, learn five more than those.

steps.test: Watch one bird you cannot name, write down four things about it, and then find it in a guide or the app.
steps.note: The four things: its size compared with a bird you know (smaller than a pigeon, bigger than a sparrow), its main colours and any marks, the shape of its beak, and how it moves (hops, walks, climbs a trunk, flies in dips). Those four are usually enough for a guide or for the questions the app asks.

steps.test: Name ten birds on sight, outdoors.
steps.note: The five from rung nine and five more. Water birds, gulls, crows and pigeons all count: most people never learn to tell the different kinds apart. Write the list down with the place you saw each one.

steps.test: Name three birds by their song or call, first with an app and then with your eyes shut.
steps.note: Merlin Bird ID's sound feature listens and shows a name while a bird sings. Pick three you hear every day and play each one's song a few times. Then stand outside, shut your eyes, and name them as they call. Many people remember a song as a few words that match its rhythm; make up your own.

steps.test: Get up at first light once, and name three birds singing, by ear.
steps.note: Where there is a spring, birds sing most at dawn in spring and early summer, starting before sunrise; in many warm countries first light is the busiest time all year. An open window counts, with a blanket round you. Ten minutes is enough. A child does it with a grown-up.

steps.test: Put out a shallow dish of water for birds, keep it clean for two weeks, and write down every kind that comes to it.
steps.note: An old plate or a plant saucer, a few centimetres deep, with a stone in the middle to stand on, placed where a cat cannot hide close by. Empty and refill it every day or two and scrub it once a week, so it does not spread disease between birds. A balcony or a window ledge works. If you want to put out food too, check first which foods are safe for birds where you live.

steps.test: Name five birds by ear on a walk, with no app.
steps.note: The three from rung twelve and two more. As each one calls, say its name, and check with the app afterwards if you were unsure. Wind and traffic make it much harder, so choose a quiet morning.

steps.test: In the nesting season, watch from a distance for a bird carrying twigs or food, and see where it goes, without going near.
steps.note: Stay far enough back that the bird carries on as normal. If it stops, calls in alarm, or waits with food in its beak, you are too close: move away. Never touch or look into a nest and never take eggs; in many countries disturbing a nest is against the law. Where there is a winter, nesting is in spring, roughly March to July north of the equator and August to December south of it; in warm countries it often follows the rains.

steps.test: For one month, keep a list of every tree and bird you name, with the date and place you first saw each one.
steps.note: A page at the back of a notebook or a note on a phone. Add a line only when a name is new to the list. The first days fill quickly; later, a new name is a small event. A family can keep one shared list on the fridge. If you already keep a list like this, count the month.

steps.test: Visit your tree once a week for four weeks, and each time write down one thing that has changed.
steps.note: Buds opening, leaves changing colour, flowers, fruit, seeds falling, a bird using it, a new crack or a fungus at the base. One line and the date, and a photo from the same spot if you have a phone. If you have been visiting it every week since rung three, count four of those weeks.

steps.test: Read back every page about your tree from the first one, and write a few sentences on how it changed while you watched it.
steps.note: By now it may be twelve weeks or more of notes. Lay the photos side by side if you have them. Write what happened first, what came next, and what you expect in the months ahead. Nobody else has a record of that tree.

steps.test: Take somebody on a half-hour walk, name ten trees and birds for them, and let them find and name one of each themselves.
steps.note: A child, a friend, a grandparent. Walk your usual route, stop at your tree first, and tell them one thing about each name, such as how to tell it apart. Then let them spot and name a tree and a bird you showed them. This is the end of the ladder: what lives on the street is now something you can show somebody else.

tracks.name: Wild food
tracks.line: From writing down the safety rules to taking somebody else picking, with every plant checked by a person who is certain.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child only with a grown-up who is certain
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a child never eats anything wild without a grown-up who is certain what it is. The first rule comes before any picking: you never eat a plant unless a person who is certain, not fairly sure, has checked it. The climb stays with a very short list of plants that are easy to know: dandelion leaves, nettles and blackberries. On the way you learn the laws on picking, the dangerous plants where you live, clean places to pick, and the plants that look alike. There are no mushrooms on this ladder except looking at them with an expert in person. It ends with a meal from three things you picked and taking somebody else picking, with the same care. Seasons differ, so do each plant's rungs when it is ready where you live.

steps.test: Write the four rules of wild food on a card and keep it in your coat or bag.
steps.note: One: never eat anything unless a person who is certain has checked it, and certain means certain, not fairly sure. Two: no mushrooms. Three: never pick beside roads, where dogs go, or on ground that may be sprayed. Four: pick only where it is allowed, and only a little. A child can write the card with a grown-up.

steps.test: Find out the rules on picking wild plants where you live, and write down one thing you may do and one you may not.
steps.note: They differ by country. In many places you may pick a little fruit or a few leaves for yourself from public paths, but not in nature reserves, not on private land without permission, and never by pulling a plant up by its roots. Search for the rules from your country's nature or countryside body, or ask your local council.

steps.test: Learn to recognise three plants that are dangerous where you live, from pictures in a trusted guide.
steps.note: Use a guide from your country's botanic garden, a wildlife charity or a poisons information service. In much of Europe, for example, the list includes hemlock, foxglove and giant hogweed, whose sap can burn skin in sunlight; elsewhere the plants are different. Learn what they look like and where they grow, and never touch them.

steps.test: On a walk, find one place that is clean enough to pick from and one that is not, and say why.
steps.note: Not clean: right beside a road, low down where dogs go, at the edge of farm fields, or park and roadside verges that may be sprayed with weedkiller (ask if you do not know). Clean: away from traffic, higher than a dog's height, on land you know is not sprayed.

steps.test: With a person who is certain, find a dandelion plant and say three things that tell it apart.
steps.note: Dandelion leaves grow in a flat circle from the ground and have deep, toothed edges; each flower sits alone on a smooth, hollow stem with no leaves on it; the stem has a milky sap when snapped. Several other yellow flowers look a little similar, so the person with you shows you the differences on real plants. The person who is certain might be a grown-up who has picked for years or a local wild food group.

steps.test: Pick a small handful of young dandelion leaves from a clean spot, have them checked, wash them, and taste a few.
steps.note: Young leaves from the middle of the plant are the least bitter. Wash them well. Eat only a small amount the first time you try any new food, as anybody can react to something new. They can go in a salad or a sandwich.

steps.test: With a person who is certain, find a patch of stinging nettles and learn how to tell them from plants that look like them.
steps.note: Stinging nettles have pointed, heart-shaped leaves with toothed edges, in pairs up the square stem, and fine stinging hairs. Some plants that look similar do not sting; the person with you shows you the difference. Wear long sleeves and gloves.

steps.test: Wearing gloves, pick a bag of the top few leaves of young nettles from a clean spot, and have them checked.
steps.note: Take just the top four to six leaves of each stem, from plants that have not yet flowered. Young nettles are best in spring in many places; if it is not the season where you are, come back to this rung when it is. Gloves on all the way into the kitchen.

steps.test: Cook the nettles into a soup or wilt them like spinach, and eat some.
steps.note: Cooking takes the sting away completely. A simple soup: soften an onion and a potato in a pan, add stock and the washed nettle leaves, simmer for five minutes, and blend or mash. Handle them with gloves or tongs until they are cooked.

steps.test: Learn one pair of plants in your area where a safe plant has a dangerous look-alike, and write down what tells them apart.
steps.note: For example, in much of Europe wild garlic grows near lily of the valley and lords-and-ladies, which are poisonous and have similar leaves; people have been badly poisoned by mixing them up. Find the pair that matters where you live in a trusted guide, and write the differences down. This is why rule one never changes.

steps.test: On a walk, find one plant that looks a little like something you have eaten, and leave it, saying out loud why you are not certain.
steps.note: "The leaves look right but the stem is different, so no." Leaving a plant is the most important skill on this ladder, and the one that keeps experienced people safe. A child says it to the grown-up with them.

steps.test: With a person who is certain, find a blackberry bush and say how you know it is one.
steps.note: Arching, prickly stems; leaves in groups of three or five with toothed edges; white or pink flowers in early summer; berries that go from green to red to shiny black. Blackberries ripen in late summer: around August and September in the northern half of the world, and around February and March in the southern half. Where they do not grow, the person who is certain can show you a common, easy wild fruit that does.

steps.test: Pick a small bowl of ripe blackberries from a clean spot, taking a few from each bush and leaving plenty.
steps.note: Pick only the black, soft ones that come away easily. Take from above a dog's height, leave most of the fruit for birds, animals and other people, and do not trample the plants. Have the first bowl checked.

steps.test: Wash your blackberries and make something with them.
steps.note: Eaten with yoghurt, stirred into porridge, or baked in a crumble with some apple. Soak them in a bowl of cold water for a few minutes first, then drain, to let any tiny insects float out.

steps.test: Go on a walk with an expert in person to look at wild mushrooms, and learn why they stay off this ladder.
steps.note: Many wildlife groups, nature reserves and natural history societies run fungi walks, often free. Look, photograph and listen; do not pick to eat. Some deadly mushrooms look very like ones people eat, and even experts check each one carefully. If there is no walk near you, read about why from a trusted guide and count it.

steps.test: For three months, keep a picking diary: each plant you learn, where it grows, and when it is ready.
steps.note: One line per visit: "Nettles by the old wall, young tops good, early spring." Next year, the diary tells you exactly where and when to go. A child can draw the plants beside each line.

steps.test: Keep some of what you picked for later, using a method from the Keeping food ladder.
steps.note: Blackberries freeze well spread out on a tray and then tipped into a labelled bag. Cooked nettles can be frozen in portions. Blackberry jam from a trusted recipe works too.

steps.test: Make one meal with three things you picked yourself, each one checked.
steps.note: For example: nettle soup, a salad with a few dandelion leaves, and blackberries with yoghurt or in a crumble. Frozen blackberries from earlier count. Tell the people eating what each wild thing is.

steps.test: Give some of what you picked or made to somebody, labelled with what it is, where it came from and the date.
steps.note: A bag of frozen blackberries, a jar of jam, or a pot of nettle soup. Only give plants that a person who is certain has checked, and say what they are so the other person can decide.

steps.test: Take somebody picking for their first time: teach them the four rules and one plant, with a person who is certain checking everything.
steps.note: Start with the card from rung one. Show them one easy plant, a clean place and how much to leave. If you are now the person who is certain about that plant, you can be the one checking; if not, bring somebody who is. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Tracking
tracks.line: From your own footprints in soft ground to showing somebody else an animal track they can read themselves.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with your own footprints, walking and running, then dog, cat and bird prints you can find in any town, and a tray of damp sand that catches prints overnight. Then naming animals from prints, finding their paths and feeding signs, and droppings looked at but never touched. The later rungs are telling fresh from old, reading what an animal was doing, sitting still, moving quietly, and following a trail for a hundred metres. It ends with you showing somebody else a track they can read themselves. Tracking turns an ordinary walk into a story about who else has been there.

steps.test: In soft ground, make a line of your own footprints walking and then running, and say three differences.
steps.note: Mud, damp sand on a beach, snow, or a wet footprint on a dry path all work. Look at the distance between prints, how deep the toe and heel go, and whether the feet land in a straight line. If you already know this, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Find a dog's or a cat's footprint and say which it is, and why.
steps.note: In mud, snow, sand or a dusty path, a park is a good place. Dog prints usually show claw marks and are a little longer than wide. Cat prints are rounder and usually have no claw marks, as cats keep their claws tucked in when walking.

steps.test: Find a bird's footprints, count its toes, and say whether it was walking or hopping.
steps.note: Pigeons, gulls, ducks and crows leave prints on mud, wet sand and snow. Walking birds leave prints one after the other; hopping birds leave them side by side in pairs. Ducks and gulls show webbing between the toes.

steps.test: Put down a tray or patch of smooth, damp sand or mud where animals pass, and check it the next morning for prints.
steps.note: Near a bird feeder, a gap in a hedge, or along a garden wall. Smooth it flat with a board. A little food beside it, like a few seeds, makes a visit more likely. Photograph whatever you find, then smooth it again.

steps.test: Using a free guide for your country, name three kinds of animal from their prints.
steps.note: Wildlife charities and nature groups in many countries publish free print charts. Prints from your sand tray, your dog, a park or a beach all count. Compare the number of toes, the shape of the pads and whether there are claw marks.

steps.test: Have somebody walk across dewy grass or damp sand while you look away, then follow their trail for fifty metres.
steps.note: Early morning dew on grass shows a dark line where somebody has walked. Crouch low and look along the ground towards the light; tracks show up far better that way. Swap over and let them follow yours.

steps.test: Find a path that animals use regularly, and say what makes you think so.
steps.note: A thin line of flattened grass through a field, a gap worn under a fence or hedge, hairs caught on a wire, or a muddy slide down a bank to water. Look where the path goes: to water, food or cover.

steps.test: Find three signs of something eating, and say what you think ate each.
steps.note: A pine cone chewed down to its core, a nut shell split or gnawed, a pecked apple, bitten leaves, or a scatter of feathers. Your country's free guide will show what each animal leaves behind. Look, and photograph; you can touch cones and shells, then wash your hands.

steps.test: Find animal droppings, and name what left them by looking only, using a stick to point.
steps.note: Never touch droppings with your hands, as they can carry germs; point with a stick and photograph them beside a coin for size. Rabbit, deer, dog, fox, goose and owl pellets all look different. Wash your hands with soap and water when you get home, even if you think you did not touch anything.

steps.test: Make a footprint of your own in soft ground and look at it again after one hour and after one day, and describe how it changed.
steps.note: Photograph it each time. Edges crumble, rain softens it, leaves and insects fall in, and the bottom dries paler. Now you have something to compare with an animal's print when you ask "how old is this?".

steps.test: Find an animal's print and say whether you think it is fresh or old, and give two reasons.
steps.note: Compare it with what you learnt from your own print: sharp edges or crumbled, wet or dried, anything fallen into it, rain since. Say "I think this morning, because the edges are sharp and it rained last night." Being unsure is fine; the reasons are the rung.

steps.test: Look at a line of prints and say what the animal was doing: walking, running, stopping or turning.
steps.note: Prints close together in a steady line mean walking. Longer gaps and deeper toes mean running. A cluster of prints means it stopped, perhaps to sniff or eat. Your own walking and running prints from rung one are the key.

steps.test: Sit still outdoors for twenty minutes and write down everything you saw and heard.
steps.note: A garden, a park bench or the edge of a wood. Sit with your back against something, stay quiet and let things settle. Animals often come back after about ten minutes. A child can sit with a grown-up and draw instead of writing.

steps.test: Walk fifty metres through a wood or park as quietly as you can, placing each foot slowly.
steps.note: Put the outside edge of your foot down first, then roll it flat, feeling for twigs before you put weight on it. Stop often and look around. A child and a grown-up can take turns: one walks while the other listens with eyes closed.

steps.test: Follow an animal's trail for a hundred metres, in snow, mud, sand, dew or along a path it uses.
steps.note: When you lose it, stop, mark the last print with a stick, and search in a circle ahead. Stay on land where you are allowed, and stop at fences, water and roads. Where there are dangerous animals, track only with somebody who knows the area, and never follow a fresh trail of one.

steps.test: Take somebody out and help them find and read a track themselves.
steps.note: A child, a friend or a grown-up who has never done it. Take them somewhere you know has prints, ask questions instead of telling ("how many toes?", "walking or running?"), and let them work it out. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Camping
tracks.line: From putting up a tent with help to taking somebody camping for their first time and bringing them home happy.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child with a grown-up
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a child always camps with a grown-up. It starts with putting up and packing a tent, then a night in a garden, then choosing a good pitch, the rules of a campsite and a safety plan. The middle rungs are a night at a legal campsite with a hot meal, staying dry and warm, and leaving no trace. Then carrying everything on your back and two nights in a row. It ends with you taking somebody camping for their first time and bringing them home happy. Where wild camping is allowed is different in every country, so this ladder always says to check, and a borrowed tent is fine for every rung.

steps.test: Put up a tent with somebody helping, in a garden, a park where it is allowed, or a big room.
steps.note: Borrow a tent if you do not have one: friends, family and outdoor groups often lend them. Lay everything out first and read the instructions if there are any. Many tents stand up indoors without pegs, which is a good first go.

steps.test: Take the tent down and pack it back in its bag, with every pole and peg counted.
steps.note: Count the pegs as they come out, fold the tent to the width of its bag, and roll it tightly towards the open end so the air escapes. If it is damp, hang it up to dry at home before it goes away, or it will smell and go mouldy.

steps.test: Put the same tent up on your own.
steps.note: Take your time: lay it out, find the door and point it where you want it, poles in, then pegs pushed in at a slant, leaning away from the tent. A child puts it up while the grown-up only watches.

steps.test: Write a packing list for one night camping, and pack from it with every item ticked.
steps.note: Tent, sleeping bag, sleeping mat, warm layer and hat, waterproof, torch, water, food, a small first-aid kit, a phone, and a bag for rubbish. Tick each item as it goes in. Keep the list for every trip after.

steps.test: Sleep a whole night in a tent in a garden.
steps.note: Your own garden, or a friend's or relative's with their permission. Bring a warm layer and a torch, and remember you can go indoors if you need to. A child's first night out has a grown-up in the tent or nearby. If there is no garden you can use, a night at a campsite later on counts for this rung.

steps.test: Choose the best spot to pitch a tent in a garden or field, lie down on it, and say why you chose it.
steps.note: Flat, not in a dip where rain collects, not under dead branches, and with the door away from the wind. Lie on the ground where you would sleep: any lump or slope you feel now will feel bigger at night.

steps.test: Find one campsite you could get to, and write down its rules on fires, quiet hours, water and toilets.
steps.note: Look on its website or ring and ask. At the same time, find out where wild camping (camping away from a campsite) is allowed where you live: in some countries it is allowed in many places, in others only with the landowner's permission, and in many not at all. Check before you ever try it.

steps.test: Before a night away, write a safety plan and give it to somebody at home.
steps.note: Where you will be, when you will be back, the weather forecast for the night, the nearest place to get help, and your emergency number. Agree a time: if they have not heard from you by then, they call you. Check the forecast again on the day, as in the Weather and tide ladder.
how: Where you are going and when you will be back.
Tonight's forecast.
Nearest help and your emergency number.
A time to check in.

steps.test: Camp a night at a campsite and cook a simple hot meal on a camping stove or the site's barbecue, outside the tent.
steps.note: Something easy: pasta and sauce, soup and bread, or beans and sausages. Never cook, or bring a stove or barbecue, inside a tent or its porch, even to warm up: the fumes can kill. Set the stove on flat ground away from the tent and anything that burns.

steps.test: Stay warm through a cold night in a tent.
steps.note: A mat under your sleeping bag matters more than a thicker bag. Put on dry clothes for sleeping, wear a hat, eat something before bed, and go to the toilet before you get in. Keep tomorrow's clothes in the sleeping bag with you so they are warm in the morning.

steps.test: Keep your sleeping bag and spare clothes completely dry through a wet or dewy night.
steps.note: Pack them in plastic bags inside your rucksack. Nothing touching the tent walls, as water comes through where things press. Wet coats and boots stay in the porch. In a dry place, the heavy dew of a clear night is the test.

steps.test: Leave your pitch so that nobody could tell you were there.
steps.note: Every peg and every scrap of rubbish goes home with you, including tiny things like tea bags and wrappers. Walk over the whole pitch looking at the ground before you go. Leave no trace: that is the rule for every trip after this.

steps.test: Pack everything for one night into one bag you can carry, and walk with it for thirty minutes.
steps.note: Heavy things close to your back and in the middle, light things at the top, waterproof where you can reach it. If it hurts after thirty minutes, take something out or move the weight. Borrowing a big rucksack is fine.

steps.test: Camp a night at a campsite, or a place where it is allowed, that you reach by walking at least two kilometres carrying everything.
steps.note: Use your packing list and safety plan. A campsite with a walk from the bus stop or car park counts. A child does this with a grown-up, and carries only what is comfortable.

steps.test: Camp two nights in a row, keeping yourself and your kit dry and warm the whole time.
steps.note: The second night is the real test: anything wet from the first night must be dried in the day. Hang damp things in the sun or wind, air your sleeping bag, and re-pack neatly each morning.

steps.test: Take somebody camping for their first time, and bring them home happy.
steps.note: A younger child, a friend, or a grown-up who has never camped. Choose an easy place, a good forecast and a short trip. Let them put up the tent with you, cook together, and keep the safety plan yourself. A child never leads this; a grown-up does, with the child helping. That is the far end of this ladder.

categories.name: Water and boats
categories.line: Swimming, cold water, rowing, sailing, fishing, rock pools.

tracks.name: Swimming
tracks.line: From your face in the water to fifty metres without stopping.

steps.test: Put your face in the water and blow bubbles, ten times.
how: Shallow end, hold the side, take a breath, face in, blow out slowly through your nose and mouth.
Ten times, each one a little longer.
Breathing out under the water is the whole foundation. Nobody swims well while holding their breath.
steps.note: This is the rung that adults skip and then wonder why swimming feels like a panic. Blowing out under water is what makes everything above it calm.

steps.test: Hold the side and kick your legs for thirty seconds.
how: Arms straight, holding the rail or the edge, body flat on the surface.
Kick from the hips with straight-ish legs and loose ankles, small and fast.
Small splashes, not big ones — big splashes mean the knees are doing it.
steps.note: The kick does less than people think for moving you and a lot for keeping you flat. Flat is what makes swimming easy.

steps.test: Push off the side and glide with your face in, as far as you can.
how: Feet on the wall, arms stretched out in front, head between your arms, face down.
Push off and go — no kicking, no pulling. Just hold the shape.
See how far the glide takes you before you need to stand up.
steps.note: A good glide is the whole of good swimming. Everything you learn from here is about keeping that shape while you add the arms and legs.

steps.test: Float on your front for five seconds, then stand back up.
how: Face in, arms out, let your legs come up behind you.
Relax — tension sinks and calm floats.
To stand: tuck your knees to your chest, put your feet down, lift your head last.
steps.note: Being able to stop and stand up calmly is what takes the fear out of the deep bit. Practise the standing-up as much as the floating.

steps.test: Float on your back for ten seconds.
how: Head back so your ears are in the water, hips up, arms out to the sides.
Look straight up at the ceiling. Looking at your feet sinks you.
Somebody's hand under your back at first if it helps.
steps.note: Floating on your back is the single most useful thing in the water: it is how anybody in trouble rests. Worth having for its own sake.

steps.test: Push off and glide with a leg kick, three metres.
how: Same glide shape, then add the small fast kick you practised at the side.
Face down, breathing out slowly the whole way.
Three metres, then stand up calmly.
steps.note: Glide plus kick is already swimming — you simply have no arms in it yet. Getting this bit right makes the arms easy.

steps.test: Swim five metres any way you like, without touching the bottom.
how: Doggy paddle, breaststroke, anything. Five metres, feet off the bottom.
Along the shallow end, so you can stand whenever you want.
Calm and slow beats fast and thrashing.
steps.note: Any five metres is a proper milestone: you are now swimming, and everything after this is refinement.

steps.test: Swim ten metres on your front.
how: Face in, breathing out under water, lifting your head only when you must.
Long slow arms rather than fast short ones.
Ten metres is usually about half a short pool.
steps.note: The temptation is to lift your head and rush. Long and slow gets you further with half the effort — that is true for the whole of swimming.

steps.test: Swim ten metres on your back.
how: Ears in the water, hips up, small kick, arms brushing past your ears one at a time.
Look straight up. Glance at the wall behind you as you approach it.
On your back you can always breathe, which is why it is the restful one.
steps.note: Front and back both means you always have a way to keep going when one of them tires. It also means you can rest without touching the bottom.

steps.test: Turn your head to the side, take one breath, and keep swimming.
how: Breathe out under the water first, then turn your head — do not lift it.
One ear stays in the water as you breathe. The head turns, the body stays flat.
Take one breath, put your face back, keep going.
steps.note: This one movement is the difference between swimming ten metres and swimming as far as you like. Practise it at the side of the pool before you swim with it.

steps.test: Swim ten metres taking a breath every three or four strokes.
how: Steady rhythm: stroke, stroke, breathe, stroke, stroke, breathe.
Breathing out continuously between breaths, never holding.
Slow the arms down until the rhythm works.
steps.note: Once the breathing has a rhythm, distance stops being a fitness question. Most people double their distance the week this clicks.

steps.test: Jump in from the side and swim back to it.
how: Water you know the depth of, with somebody watching.
Jump feet first, let yourself come back up, turn and swim to the side.
Do it a second time straight away — the second is far easier.
steps.note: Going under and coming back up without panic is the safety skill hiding inside swimming, and it is worth practising deliberately rather than by accident.

steps.test: Swim fifteen metres without stopping.
how: Long strokes, steady breathing, face in.
Count your strokes — fewer strokes for the same distance means better shape.
Stop calmly at the end rather than lunging for the side.
steps.note: Counting strokes is the swimmer's trick for improving without going faster. Fewer strokes, same distance, is always progress.

steps.test: Pick something up off the bottom in water up to your chest.
how: A diving toy, a coin, anything that sinks.
Breathe out as you go down, eyes open, take it, push off the bottom.
Three or four goes. It gets easy quickly.
steps.note: Going down on purpose and coming back up teaches your body that under the water is a place you can visit, which takes a surprising amount of fear away.

steps.test: Tread water for thirty seconds.
how: Out of your depth, or deep enough that you cannot stand.
Slow circles with your hands, gentle cycling with your legs. Calm and small.
Somebody watching, and the side within reach.
steps.note: Treading water is almost entirely about relaxing. Everybody's first attempt is far too frantic and the second one is easy.

steps.test: Tread water for a full minute.
how: Same slow small movements, breathing normally.
Lie back into a float for a few seconds if you need a rest, then carry on.
Time it rather than guessing.
steps.note: A minute of treading water plus a back float means you could look after yourself in deep water long enough for help to reach you.

steps.test: Swim twenty-five metres on your front without stopping.
how: A full length of most pools. Steady breathing rhythm all the way.
Start slower than you want to — the second half is where people stop.
Finish calmly and hold the side for a moment before standing.
steps.note: A full length is the milestone everybody recognises and the point at which you can call yourself a swimmer without qualifying it.

steps.test: Swim twenty-five metres on your back without stopping.
how: Ears in, hips up, long arms past your ears.
Count strokes so you know when the wall is coming.
Straight line — one arm usually pulls harder and drifts you across.
steps.note: Having a second full length in a different stroke means you can now rest by changing stroke rather than by stopping.

steps.test: Swim there and back with one rest in the middle.
how: Twenty-five metres, a short rest at the wall, twenty-five back.
Same steady rhythm both ways.
Breathe properly before you push off for the second length.
steps.note: This is the rung that turns one length into two, and two into as many as you like. The rest at the wall is a technique, not a weakness.

steps.test: Swim fifty metres without stopping, and climb out unaided.
how: Two lengths, no touching the bottom, no holding the wall at the turn.
Steady from the first stroke. Slow is what finishes it.
Then out at the side on your arms, not up the steps.
steps.note: Fifty metres unbroken from a start of blowing bubbles, in about three months. From here, open water and the cold water ladder are both open to you.

tracks.warn: Never on your own, and never in open water on this ladder. Every step happens at a pool or a lifeguarded beach with somebody beside you who can already swim.
tracks.about: Swimming is the one thing on this list that is a safety skill as well as a fitness one, and the water is patient: it takes almost everybody from blowing bubbles to fifty metres inside a few months. It needs a pool, which is the only cost here — public pools are usually cheap and many have free or low-cost family sessions. Nothing else in the school trains your breathing and your whole body at once like this.

tracks.name: Cold water
tracks.line: From thirty seconds at the end of a shower to a calm four minutes in the sea.

steps.test: Finish a shower with thirty seconds of cold.
how: Normal warm shower, then turn it to full cold for the last thirty seconds.
Head and shoulders under it, not just your feet.
Breathe out slowly and steadily. Do not hold your breath.
steps.note: Thirty seconds, in your own bathroom, costing nothing. The gasp lasts about ten seconds and then it is simply cold, which is a very different thing.

steps.test: Finish a shower with a full minute of cold, three days running.
how: Same routine, longer. A minute is not twice as hard as thirty seconds.
Slow long out-breaths all the way through.
Three days, ticked off.
steps.note: By the third morning you will notice that the dread beforehand is bigger than the cold itself. That gap is the lesson this ladder is really teaching.

steps.test: Stand in the sea or a lough up to your ankles for one minute.
how: Somewhere you know, with somebody with you.
Shoes off, trousers rolled. A minute on the clock.
Any beach, any weather. Free everywhere in this country.
steps.note: Cold feet on a cold day is worse than people expect and is the honest start. The sea is a different thing from a shower and deserves its own first rung.

steps.test: Stand in up to your knees for a minute.
how: Walk in slowly rather than dashing.
Long out-breaths from the moment the water touches you.
Dry socks and shoes waiting on the sand.
steps.note: The cold moves up your body in stages and each stage has its own gasp. Taking them one at a time is exactly how the whole ladder is climbed.

steps.test: Get in up to your waist and stay calm for a minute.
how: This is the one that makes people squeal. Go slowly and keep breathing out.
Hands out of the water at first — hands and wrists feel it worst.
Somebody with you on the shore.
steps.note: Waist deep is the real test of the breathing, because this is where the gasp reflex is strongest. Slow out-breaths beat it every time.

steps.test: Get in up to your shoulders and control your breathing.
how: Lower yourself in rather than jumping. Never dive into cold water.
The first thirty seconds are the worst and then it settles.
Out as soon as the breathing is under control — this rung is not about staying in.
steps.note: Cold water shock is a real thing and it is at its worst in the first thirty seconds. Getting in slowly and breathing out is what makes it safe.

steps.test: Get warm again properly afterwards, and write down how you did it.
how: Dry off completely and dress from the top down, hat on early.
Something warm to drink, and move about — walk, do not sit in the car.
No hot shower straight away; warm up from the inside first.
steps.note: Getting warm again is the part people get wrong, and the cold keeps coming for twenty minutes after you are out. Plan this before you get in, not after.

steps.test: Stay in up to your shoulders for one full minute.
how: Timer on the shore. Somebody watching.
Still, calm, breathing slowly. Not swimming about.
Out on the minute, whatever it feels like.
steps.note: A minute in properly cold water is a real thing to have done. Get out on time rather than proving anything — the people who get into trouble are the ones who stay longer than they planned.

steps.test: Go in on a day you did not feel like it.
how: Decide the night before and go, regardless of the weather or the mood.
Do not renegotiate with yourself at the car park.
Same routine: in slowly, breathe out, warm up properly.
steps.note: This is the rung the whole ladder exists for. Doing the thing you had decided to do, on a day you did not fancy it, is a skill that has nothing to do with water.

steps.test: Stay in for two minutes and get properly warm again afterwards.
how: Two minutes, timed, then straight out and into the warming routine you wrote down.
Watch for shivering that will not stop — that is the point to stop for the day.
Never alone, and never after a drink.
steps.note: Longer is not better in cold water. Two minutes with a good warm-up afterwards is worth far more than five minutes and an afternoon of shivering.

steps.test: Go in once a week for a month, whatever the weather.
how: Four dips, one a week, written in the calendar in advance.
Same place, with the same person, so it needs no arranging.
Whatever the weather does.
steps.note: A month of this changes how you meet cold, rain and discomfort generally. It also tends to become the thing you look forward to most in the week.

steps.test: Take somebody else through their first cold dip, safely.
how: Tell them about the gasp before it happens so it does not frighten them.
In slowly, never diving, long out-breaths, and out on an agreed time.
Their warm clothes, hat and hot drink ready before they get in.
steps.note: Talking somebody through their first thirty seconds is a genuinely useful thing to be able to do, and safety is the whole of it: slow in, breathe out, agreed time, warm afterwards.

tracks.about: Getting into cold water is the shortest route there is to finding out that you can do something you do not want to do, and it takes two minutes. It starts in your own shower, which costs nothing, and moves out to the sea or a lough. The whole skill is the breathing: cold water makes you gasp, and everything else here is learning to take hold of that. Never get into open water alone, never after drinking, and always have dry warm clothes waiting.

tracks.name: Rowing and paddling
tracks.line: From choosing your first kind of boat, to helping a beginner through their first session on the water.
tracks.who: From about eight, always with an instructor or grown-up
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight; a child is always with an instructor or a grown-up, and so is every beginner of any age. The first rungs happen at home and at a pool: choosing a kayak, canoe, paddleboard or rowing boat, finding a club, practising the stroke with a broom, fitting a buoyancy aid and floating in one. Then a proper club or centre takes you onto calm water: getting in and out, going where you mean to, stopping, turning, a practice capsize, and reading the wind and water before you go. It ends with a five-kilometre paddle with a group and helping a beginner through their first session. There is no need to own a boat: clubs and outdoor centres lend them, and many run free or low-cost taster sessions.

steps.test: Look up the four kinds of small boat you can paddle or row, and choose the one you want to try first.
steps.note: A kayak is sat in, with a paddle that has a blade at each end; a canoe is open, and you kneel or sit with a single-blade paddle. A paddleboard is stood or knelt on, and in a rowing boat you pull two oars and face backwards. Any of them is a good start; pick the one a club near you teaches if you are not sure.

steps.test: Find a club, outdoor centre or activity centre near you that teaches your boat, and write down the date of its next beginners' or taster session.
steps.note: Your national paddling or rowing organisation's website usually lists clubs by area, and your local council may list outdoor centres. Many run free or low-cost taster sessions and lend the boat, the paddle and the buoyancy aid. Write down what they ask you to bring, whether you need to be able to swim, and the youngest age they take. In places with a cold season, many clubs move to pool sessions in winter.

steps.test: Sit on the floor with a broom and do twenty forward paddle strokes on each side, turning your body, not just your arms.
steps.note: Hold the broom handle a little wider than your shoulders. Reach forward, put the imagined blade in by your feet, and draw it back to your hip by turning your middle, then lift it out. For a canoe, use one side at a time with one hand on top of the handle. If your boat will be a rowing boat, sit on the floor with your knees bent and practise the rowing movement instead: arms straight out, lean back, pull your hands to your ribs.

steps.test: Put on a buoyancy aid, do up every zip and buckle, and have somebody lift it by the shoulders to check it does not ride up past your chin.
steps.note: This is the lift test, and a buoyancy aid that fails it is the wrong size or too loose. Tighten the straps from the bottom up until it is snug but you can still breathe deeply and move your arms. You wear one on every rung on the water, however calm it looks. If you have no buoyancy aid, do this at the start of your first club session with one they lend you, and count it.

steps.test: At a pool, wearing a buoyancy aid, get into deep water, float on your back for a minute, then swim ten metres to the side.
steps.note: Many clubs run pool sessions for exactly this; public pools often allow it if you ask first. Float first: lie back, let the buoyancy aid hold you, and breathe slowly until you feel calm, then swim. A grown-up or instructor is in the water or at the edge beside any child. If you cannot swim ten metres yet, the swimming ladder is the place to start, and many clubs ask for it.

steps.test: At your first session, before you get in a boat, say back to the instructor what you will do if you fall in.
steps.note: The usual plan is: float first and get your breath, hold on to your boat and your paddle, shout or wave to the instructor, and wait for them to come to you. In moving water, stay on the upstream side of the boat so it cannot pin you. Every club says it a little differently, so use their words. Never go on the water alone, on this rung or any later one.

steps.test: Get into the boat from a bank or low jetty, sit still without tipping it, and get out again, three times.
steps.note: Keep low, keep your weight over the middle of the boat, and hold on to the jetty or bank with one hand while you move. Lay the paddle across the boat and the jetty to steady it. An instructor holds the boat for your first try. Buoyancy aid on, even though you are only getting in.

steps.test: Paddle twenty metres out on calm water and come back to where you started.
steps.note: Short strokes, both sides evenly, and look where you want to go, not at the paddle. Coming back means turning, so go slowly and use extra strokes on one side. The instructor stays close. Buoyancy aid on, and only on calm, sheltered water chosen by the club.

steps.test: Stop the boat within one boat length of a marker, then turn it round on the spot.
steps.note: To stop, put the blade in by your hip and push forward: this is the reverse stroke. To turn on the spot, do wide sweeping strokes forward on one side, then backward on the other. The marker can be a buoy, a post or a spot on the bank. Buoyancy aid on, instructor close by.

steps.test: With an instructor, tip out of your boat on purpose in a capsize practice, float, and get yourself and your boat to the side.
steps.note: Clubs run this in a pool or in warm, shallow, sheltered water, because a capsize you have practised is far calmer than one you have not. Float first and get your breath, then hold the boat and swim it in, or wait for the instructor if they ask you to. In a kayak, the instructor shows you how to get out underwater first. Never try this without an instructor there.

steps.test: Come alongside a jetty or bank, stop next to it, and get out without anybody holding the boat.
steps.note: Come in slowly and at a slight angle, stop with a reverse stroke, and take hold of the jetty before you move. Then the same as getting in, the other way round: low, weight in the middle, one hand on the jetty. If you already do this, do it on purpose today and count it. Buoyancy aid on until you are standing on land.

steps.test: Before a session, look up the wind and the water where you will paddle, decide whether it suits a beginner, and check your answer with the instructor.
steps.note: Look at the wind speed and its direction, and for rain in the last few days, which makes rivers faster. The big warning is wind blowing from the land out over the water: near the shore it looks calm, but it pushes you away and makes coming back hard. On the sea, tides matter too. The instructor has the final word; when they say no, that is a good decision, not a lost day.

steps.test: Paddle five hundred metres in a straight line to a point you chose, without zigzagging.
steps.note: Pick something fixed on the far side, such as a tree or a building, and keep the front of the boat pointed at it. If the boat starts to turn, add a stroke or two on the other side early, before the turn gets big. Buoyancy aid on, with your club or a grown-up who paddles, never alone.

steps.test: Paddle into a light wind for ten minutes and keep your line, then turn and come back.
steps.note: Only on a day the club says suits you. Lean slightly forward, keep strokes short and steady, and aim a little into the wind so it does not turn you. Coming back with the wind behind you is fast, so slow down before any bank or jetty. Buoyancy aid on and a leader on the water with you.

steps.test: Paddle with your club or centre once a week for four weeks.
steps.note: Mark the four dates on a calendar. A week off for bad weather does not end the four; take the next one. Each time, do the checks yourself before you get in: buoyancy aid fitted, the plan if you fall in, the wind and the water. If you already paddle weekly, count the next four on purpose.

steps.test: Paddle five kilometres with a group and a leader, with a rest stop on the way.
steps.note: At a steady pace this takes about an hour and a half, with a rest. Stay in sight of the leader, eat and drink at the stop, and say early if you are cold or tired. A group trip like this is usually on the club calendar; tell somebody at home where you are going and when you will be back. Buoyancy aid on all the way.

steps.test: At a club beginners' session, help one beginner: check their buoyancy aid with the lift test and paddle beside them until they are back on land.
steps.note: Ask the instructor first; they will usually be glad of the help and will still be in charge. Tell the beginner one thing at a time: where to sit, how to hold the paddle, what to do if they fall in. Stay beside them, not ahead. The end of the ladder is somebody else leaving the water wanting to come back.

tracks.name: Sailing
tracks.line: From naming the parts of a dinghy, to taking somebody on their first sail and handing them the tiller.
tracks.who: From about eight, always with a club or instructor
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight; every rung on the water is done with a club or an instructor, whatever your age. The first rungs happen on land and at a pool: the parts of a small boat, finding a club, reading the wind, where a boat can and cannot sail, two knots, fitting a buoyancy aid and floating in one. Then, with an instructor, you crew, rig, steer, change speed, tack, practise a capsize, gybe and come back in. It ends with sailing a course round three marks and taking somebody on their first sail. You do not need a boat of your own: many sailing clubs and centres run free or low-cost try-sailing days and lend boats and buoyancy aids.

steps.test: Find a picture of a small sailing dinghy and name the hull, mast, boom, sail, tiller, rudder, centreboard and mainsheet, saying what each does.
steps.note: The hull is the boat itself; the mast holds the sail up, and the boom holds its bottom edge. The tiller moves the rudder, which steers. The centreboard is the fin under the boat that stops it sliding sideways, and the mainsheet is the rope you pull to bring the sail in. Sailing club websites often have a labelled drawing.

steps.test: Find a sailing club or centre near you, and write down the date of its next try-sailing or beginners' day and what to bring.
steps.note: Your national sailing organisation's website usually lists clubs and centres, including ones on lakes and reservoirs as well as the sea. Many run free or low-cost open days and lend the boat and the buoyancy aid. Write down the youngest age they take and whether they ask you to swim first. In places with a cold season, most sailing stops for the winter, so plan for the start of the warm months.

steps.test: On a walk, say where the wind is coming from five times, using your face, a flag, smoke, trees or the ripples on water.
steps.note: Turn your face until the wind feels the same on both cheeks: that is where it is coming from. Then check against something: a flag streams away from the wind, and ripples move with it. Say it as a direction or a landmark: "from the hill". Sailors check this all the time, so start the habit now.

steps.test: Draw the wind as an arrow at the top of a page, then draw boats pointing in six directions and mark which ones could sail and which could not.
steps.note: A sailing boat cannot sail straight into the wind. Roughly, anything within about 45 degrees either side of where the wind is coming from is the no-go zone; everything else can be sailed. Across the wind is usually the easiest and fastest. Keep the drawing: it explains why a boat has to zigzag to go upwind.

steps.test: Tie a figure-of-eight knot and a bowline, five times each, on a piece of rope or a dressing-gown cord.
steps.note: The figure-of-eight goes in the end of a rope so it cannot run out through a pulley. The bowline makes a loop that does not slip and is easy to undo, for tying a boat up. A sailing club website or a knot guide shows each one in pictures. When you can tie both without looking at the pictures, you are done.

steps.test: Put on a buoyancy aid, do up every zip and buckle, and have somebody lift it by the shoulders to check it does not ride up past your chin.
steps.note: A buoyancy aid that rides up over your chin is too big or too loose; tighten it from the bottom strap up. You wear one on every rung on the water. If you have none, do this at the start of your first club day with one they lend you, and count it.

steps.test: At a pool or in shallow water with an instructor, wearing a buoyancy aid, get in, float on your back for a minute, then swim ten metres.
steps.note: Float first: lie back, let the buoyancy aid hold you, and breathe out slowly until you are calm. That is the first thing to do whenever you land in the water, including from a boat. Many clubs run this at a pool or at the start of a first day. If you cannot swim ten metres yet, start with the swimming ladder.

steps.test: Before you go on the water at your first session, say back to the instructor what you will do if the boat tips over.
steps.note: The usual plan: float first and get your breath, stay with the boat and hold on to it, because a boat is far easier to see than a head, and wait for the instructor or the safety boat. Never swim away from the boat to reach the shore. Every club says it in its own words; use theirs.

steps.test: Go out as crew with an instructor, and say where the wind is coming from three times while you are sailing.
steps.note: Your job is to sit where the instructor says, move across the boat when asked, and keep watching the wind: the flag at the top of the mast, the ripples, your face. Buoyancy aid on. Ask the instructor to check your answers.

steps.test: With the instructor, rig the boat and check it over before it goes in.
steps.note: Look up first: never rig or move a boat under power lines, because a mast can carry electricity without touching them. The checks usually include: the drain bung in, the rudder and centreboard fitted, the sail up, the ropes free and with a figure-of-eight knot at the ends. Say each check out loud as you do it. Buoyancy aid on before the boat goes in.

steps.test: With the instructor on board, hold the tiller and the mainsheet at the same time, and sail in a straight line across the wind for one minute.
steps.note: Tiller in the hand nearest the back of the boat, mainsheet in the other, sitting on the side the wind is coming from. Push the tiller away from you and the boat turns towards the wind; pull it and the boat turns away. Small movements. Pick a landmark and keep pointing at it.

steps.test: Pull the sail in to speed up, let it out to slow down, and let it right out to stop the boat, all on purpose.
