Do it at the same point in the day, so it hangs off something you already do.
Tick the three days off somewhere you can see them.
steps.note: This is the most important rung in the ladder and the least impressive. Three sessions in one week is the thing that turns an afternoon of good intentions into a body that changes. If you already train three days a week, do these rounds inside that and count it.

steps.test: Do twenty squats in one go.
how: Same shape as before: heels down, thighs level, all the way up.
Slow down rather than bounce when it gets hard near the end.
If your form goes at seventeen, stop at seventeen and try again in two days.
Add these to your round from now on.
steps.note: Your round is now twenty squats, five press-ups, twenty seconds. The numbers change, the round does not.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups with your hands on a table.
how: Same table, same shape. Chest to the edge every time.
Do not rush. Two seconds down, one second up.
If you stall at seven, rest ten seconds and finish the last three. Next time, get all ten.
Then lower the height: sofa arm, or a chair against a wall.
steps.note: Doubling the reps is easier than it sounds because your shape is now honest. If ten on a table came easily, move to something lower before you move on — the rung is ten hard ones, not ten easy ones.

steps.test: Hold a plank for forty seconds.
how: Set a timer so you are not counting and guessing.
Squeeze everything from your heels to your shoulders. A plank is a squeeze, not a hang.
If the line breaks at thirty, come down, rest a minute, and hold twice more for twenty.
Two short honest holds beat one long sagging one.
steps.note: Forty seconds is roughly where the plank stops being about your arms and starts being about your middle. If your lower back aches, your hips are too low — lift them a fraction and squeeze harder.

steps.test: Do five press-ups with your hands on the bottom step of the stairs.
how: The lower your hands, the more of you there is to lift. The stairs are the dial.
Same shape: straight line, elbows back, chest to the step.
No stairs? Stack two thick books, or use the edge of a bed frame or a low sturdy box.
When five on the bottom step is comfortable, the floor is next.
steps.note: This is the rung where the programme starts to feel like real training. You are not learning anything new — you are turning the dial down one notch and doing the same five.

steps.test: Do two rounds back to back, with a minute between them.
how: Round one: twenty squats, five press-ups on the step, forty seconds of plank.
One minute of standing about, then round two, the same.
It should take about six minutes in all.
Two rounds is your session from now on.
steps.note: Volume is the quiet ingredient. Two rounds three times a week is six times as much work as one round once, and it still costs you six minutes.

steps.test: Do thirty squats in one go.
how: Thirty is where squats become breathing as much as legs. Let yourself breathe out on the way up.
Keep the last five as clean as the first five.
Legs shaking is normal. Knees caving inwards is not — push them out over your toes.
If thirty is easy, do them with a four-second lowering instead and count that.
steps.note: Thirty good squats a few days a week is enough on its own to change how stairs, hills and getting off the floor feel. Most people notice that before they notice anything in the mirror.

steps.test: Do two press-ups on the floor, chest all the way down.
how: Hands under your shoulders, body one straight line from heels to head.
Down until your chest is a fist's width from the floor, then all the way up. Nothing half-way counts.
Two is the rung. Two proper ones, not five bad ones.
Cannot get one? Go back to the bottom step for another week — it will come.
steps.note: This is the rung people remember. The first real press-up off the floor is a moment, and almost everybody who does the rounds three times a week gets there within a few weeks of starting. If you could already do two on day one, the rung is two slow ones: three seconds down, three seconds up.

steps.test: Hold a plank for one minute.
how: Timer on, hips level, breathing.
Break it into thirty and thirty with a rest if you must, then try the full minute two days later.
Look at the floor, not up — your neck should follow the line of your back.
One honest minute is a real thing to own.
steps.note: A minute is the standard most people will never need to go past for ordinary life. If it is easy, lift one foot off the floor for the last fifteen seconds rather than holding for five minutes.

steps.test: Do ten rows: lie under a sturdy table, grab the edge, and pull your chest up to it.
how: Heels on the floor, body straight, arms straight at the bottom.
Pull until your chest touches the underside of the table edge, then lower all the way down.
Too hard? Bend your knees and put your feet flat — that takes weight off.
No table you trust? A bannister, a low bar in a park, or a broom handle across two chairs.
steps.note: Everything so far has been pushing. This is the first pulling, and it is the half of the body that a floor programme normally forgets. Do it and your shoulders will thank you; skip it and press-ups slowly round your back.

steps.test: Do five press-ups on the floor without stopping.
how: Same shape. Five in a row, no resting at the top.
If you get three, rest twenty seconds and do two more. Next session, go for four in a row.
Add floor press-ups into your round now, even if it is only three.
Chest all the way down, every time.
steps.note: Two to five is usually about two weeks. This is also the point where the easiest mistake appears: chasing the number and letting the depth go. Half press-ups do not build anything. Count only the ones that go all the way down.

steps.test: Do forty squats in one go.
how: Pace yourself from the first one. Steady, not fast.
Breathe in on the way down, out on the way up, every rep.
If your heels lift near the end, that is fatigue — stop there and call it the number.
Split into twenty and twenty if you must, then try the forty again in two days.
steps.note: Forty in one go is a genuine bit of fitness, not a beginner's number. If you are already past forty, do twenty with something heavy held at your chest — a bag of potatoes, a full rucksack, a child — and count that.

steps.test: Do the round three days a week for a fortnight, without missing one.
how: Six sessions in fourteen days. Two rounds each session.
Write the six days down before you start and tick them off.
A session missed gets made up the next day — it does not get skipped.
Anything is better than nothing: one round, half a round, five squats in the kitchen all count as turning up.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes the rest of your life easy. After a fortnight of not missing, the sessions stop needing a decision. If you miss one anyway, do not start the fortnight again — just do the next one.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups on the floor without stopping.
how: Ten in a row, chest to the floor every time, no rest at the top.
Get there by doing more sets of fewer: six, six, six is how you get to ten.
Fresh, at the start of a session, not at the end of it.
When you have it, do it again two days later to be sure it was not a one-off.
steps.note: Ten proper press-ups from a standing start of none is the end of this ladder and it is a real thing. Most people who do the rounds three times a week are here inside three months. Thirty is part two and the press-up ladder; you are now well on the way to both.

steps.test: Write the three numbers again, underneath the first three.
how: Same three: press-ups in one go, squats in one go, seconds of plank.
Same conditions — fresh, with a rest between each.
Write them under the old ones with today's date, so you can see the two sets together.
Then read the first line again.
steps.note: This is the whole point of rung one. Numbers you wrote before you believed anything would happen are the only proof that cannot be argued with. Keep the paper: part two starts by setting the next three.

tracks.name: Getting strong, part two
tracks.line: From ten press-ups to twenty, two minutes of plank, and a body used outside the room.
tracks.about: Part one built the round. Part two makes it heavier and then takes it outdoors: the same three moves going up, pulling added properly, a walk that turns into a run, and something heavy carried down the street. It ends by asking you to pick the one ladder you want to push a long way — press-ups to thirty, squats to a hundred, a first pull-up, five kilometres — because by then you will know which one you actually want.

steps.test: Write down the three you are going for: twenty press-ups, sixty squats, two minutes of plank.
how: Under the two sets of numbers from part one.
Add the date you expect to have them. Be generous: about three months.
These are the ends of this ladder, not a hope.
If you are already past one of them, write the next number up instead and aim there.
steps.note: Named targets beat good intentions because you can tell whether you hit them. Everything in this ladder walks towards these three.

steps.test: Do the round twice through on three days in one week, at part one's finishing numbers.
how: Forty squats, ten floor press-ups, one minute of plank, ten rows. Twice through.
Three days, a rest day between where you can.
About twelve minutes a session now.
Get this week done before you chase any new number.
steps.note: Part one ended at these numbers once. This rung makes them your ordinary Tuesday. If that feels like a step backwards, it is not — comfortable is exactly what it is meant to become.

steps.test: Do twelve press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, at the start of the session.
Chest down to a fist's width from the floor each time.
Get there with sets of eight: eight, eight, eight with a minute between beats one all-out set.
Twelve in a row, no resting at the top.
steps.note: From here on, the press-up number climbs two at a time and every climb is bought with sets you do on the days between.

steps.test: Walk for forty-five minutes without stopping.
how: Out the door, one direction, twenty-two minutes, then turn round.
Proper walking pace — enough that you could talk but would rather not sing.
Phone in your pocket, not in your hand.
Rain is fine. Rain is usually better.
steps.note: A long walk is the base everything else sits on, and it is the one piece of training nobody is too unfit or too tired for. If you already walk this much, do it somewhere you have never walked before and count that.

steps.test: Do fifty squats in one go.
how: Steady from the first rep. This is now a breathing exercise as much as a leg one.
Thighs level every time — the last ten are where depth quietly disappears.
Break as twenty-five and twenty-five with ten seconds between, then close the gap over a fortnight.
Shaking legs afterwards is normal and passes in a minute.
steps.note: Fifty in one go puts you past almost everybody you know. It is also where you stop needing a warm-up for ordinary life.

steps.test: Hold a plank for ninety seconds.
how: Timer on. Hips level the whole way or it does not count.
Squeeze your backside hard — that is the trick that buys the last twenty seconds.
Breathe in a steady rhythm rather than gritting your teeth.
If you break at seventy, hold seventy twice with a minute's rest and go again in two days.
steps.note: Past a minute the plank is mostly a test of whether you will stay calm while something is uncomfortable. That is worth practising on its own.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups slowly — three seconds down, three seconds up.
how: Count it out loud or in your head. Three full seconds each way.
That is sixty seconds of work. It is much harder than ten normal ones.
If you fail at seven, that is the rung for another week.
Do not let the last few speed up. Slow is the whole point.
steps.note: Time under strain, not the number of reps, is what actually builds the muscle. This one rung is why your normal press-up number jumps a fortnight later.

steps.test: Do twenty rows under a table.
how: Body straight, chest all the way to the table edge, arms straight at the bottom.
Twenty in one go. Legs straight out makes it harder, knees bent makes it easier.
Rest your heels on a chair to make it harder still, once twenty is easy.
Keep these in every round — pulling is half of a body.
steps.note: Twenty honest rows is roughly the strength that a first pull-up is built on. If you want the pull-up ladder later, this is the rung that pays for it.

steps.test: Carry something heavy in each hand the length of your street, without putting it down.
how: Two full shopping bags, two water containers, a bag of coal, two full buckets.
Stand tall, shoulders back, walk normally. Do not lean.
If you have to stop, the load is right — pick something slightly lighter and go again.
No heavy things at home? Fill two bags with books, or two containers with water from the tap.
steps.note: This is the strength that actually shows up in a life: shopping, moving house, carrying a child who has fallen asleep. It costs nothing and no gym machine trains it better than two heavy bags.

steps.test: Do fifteen press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, first thing in the session.
Ten, then breathe at the top without dropping your hips, then five more if you must — but aim for fifteen straight.
Depth over number, every single time.
Do it once, then get it again two days later.
steps.note: Fifteen is three quarters of the way to this ladder's target and about half way to the press-up ladder's thirty.

steps.test: Hang from a bar with your feet off the ground for thirty seconds.
how: A park bar, a beam, a strong door frame bar, a low tree branch.
Hands a little wider than your shoulders, arms straight, feet off the ground.
Let your shoulders stretch at first, then pull them down away from your ears and hold that.
Free option: almost every play park and outdoor gym in the country has a bar.
steps.note: A hang decompresses everything that sitting compresses, and it builds the grip that pull-ups, carrying and lifting all need. Thirty seconds is a lot the first time and easy within a fortnight.

steps.test: Hold a plank for two minutes.
how: Timer, level hips, steady breathing.
Pick a spot on the floor and stay with it.
If the line breaks, come down — the two minutes only count if the shape holds.
Once you have it, stop chasing plank time and make it harder instead: lift one foot, then the other.
steps.note: Two minutes is the honest end of the plank for ordinary strength. Anything past it is a party trick, and the side plank and the one-foot version buy you far more.

steps.test: Do sixty squats in one go.
how: Pace it like a run, not a sprint. The first thirty should feel too easy.
Breathe every rep. Holding your breath is what makes fifty feel like a hundred.
Depth to the last one.
Too easy? Hold something heavy at your chest and do thirty instead.
steps.note: That is one of your three targets reached. Write it down next to the date you guessed at the start.

steps.test: Do the round three days a week for a fortnight, without missing one.
how: Six sessions in fourteen days, at your current numbers, two rounds each.
Write the six dates down first, tick them off.
Missed one? Do it the next day. Do not restart the fortnight.
Short and done beats long and skipped.
steps.note: This is the same rung as part one's, and it is here again on purpose: consistency is not a thing you learn once. Two clean fortnights is what makes the rest of this a habit instead of a project.

steps.test: Do ten press-ups with your feet up on a chair.
how: Feet on a chair or the second step, hands on the floor, body in one straight line.
More of your weight goes through your arms, so ten here is worth about fifteen flat.
Chest all the way to the floor, as always.
Higher feet, harder press-up — that is the dial from now on.
steps.note: Now that the floor is comfortable, this is how you keep getting stronger without ever needing weights. Feet up is the same move with the dial turned.

steps.test: Run for five minutes without stopping.
how: Slow. Slower than you think — a pace you could hold a conversation at.
Five minutes, clock running, no walking breaks.
Any shoes that do not hurt. Any road, path or field.
Already a runner? Run five minutes at a pace that makes talking impossible instead.
steps.note: Almost everybody can run for five minutes if they go slowly enough, and almost everybody tries to go too fast and finds out they cannot. Slow it right down and it is yours today.

steps.test: Do twenty press-ups in one go.
how: Fresh, first thing, chest all the way down.
Build it with sets of twelve to fifteen on the days between.
Twenty in a row, no rest at the top.
Get it twice in one week before you call it yours.
steps.note: That is the second of your three targets. Twenty proper press-ups is more than most adults will ever do in one go, and it came from a windowsill.

steps.test: Lower yourself slowly from the top of a pull-up, three times.
how: Jump or step up so your chin is over the bar, then lower yourself as slowly as you can.
Five seconds is good, ten is excellent. Stay in control all the way to straight arms.
Rest a full minute between each one. Three is plenty.
Step off a bench or a low wall to get to the top if you cannot jump there.
steps.note: You can lower far more than you can lift, which is why this is how a first pull-up is built. Three of these twice a week is the whole secret, and it is where the pull-up ladder begins.

steps.test: Do something physical with somebody else, twice in one week.
how: A walk, a swim, a kickabout, a bike ride, a climb up a hill, a game in the garden.
It does not have to be hard. It has to be with somebody.
Ask — most people say yes and nobody ever asks them.
Free option: a walk costs nothing and is the easiest thing in the world to say yes to.
steps.note: Training on your own works until the week it does not. Somebody expecting you is the strongest thing there is for keeping this going, and it turns exercise into time with people, which is a better deal than it sounds.

steps.test: Write your three numbers again, and pick the one ladder you want to push a long way.
how: Press-ups, squats, plank — under the two earlier sets.
Then read the Fitness path and pick one: press-ups to thirty, squats to a hundred, a first pull-up, five kilometres, a hundred metres flat out.
One, not four. The point is to take one thing a long way.
Keep doing the round while you climb it — the round is now your base, not your project.
steps.note: Two programmes, three sets of numbers, and a body that can do things it could not do at the start. From here the single-move ladders go much further than these rounds ever will, and you now know which of them you actually want.

categories.name: Air and sky
categories.line: Kites, rockets, planes, stars, weather in the sky.

tracks.name: Kites
tracks.line: From reading the wind to flying a kite you made yourself, and teaching two children to launch and land it.
tracks.who: Everybody; a grown-up with a child when flying
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a grown-up is with a child whenever a kite is flying. It starts by reading the wind from a window, then making a small kite from paper, straws and thread and getting it into the air. From there you launch and land it on your own, keep it up for ten minutes, make a bigger kite from a bin bag and two sticks, and change its tail to make it fly better. It ends with you teaching two children to launch and land a kite you made. It costs nothing, and the safety rules come first: fly only in a wide open space, never near power lines, roads, railways or airports, and never in rain or thunder.

steps.test: Look out of a window and say whether today is a kite day, from what the trees, leaves and flags are doing.
steps.note: Leaves still and smoke going straight up: too little wind. Leaves and small twigs moving all the time, a flag standing out: good kite wind. Whole branches swaying, hard to walk against: too strong for a first kite. If you have a weather app, the wind speed for a small kite is roughly 10 to 25 kilometres an hour.

steps.test: Make a small sled kite from a sheet of paper, two drinking straws, tape and a long piece of thread.
how: Fold a sheet of printer paper in half and draw a shape like a house turned on its side: a wide middle and narrower ends. Cut it out and open it.
Tape a straw down each side of the middle, from top to bottom.
Put tape over each outer corner, make a small hole through it, and tie one piece of thread to both holes, about three times the width of the kite, as the bridle.
Tie your long flying thread to the middle of the bridle, and tape a paper strip to the bottom as a tail.
steps.note: Paper straws, plastic straws or two thin garden sticks all work. Cotton thread or fishing line on a piece of card to wind it on is enough for a small kite. A child can decorate and tape; a grown-up helps with the holes.

steps.test: Work out which way the wind is blowing in an open space before you launch.
steps.note: Stand still and turn slowly until you feel the wind evenly on your face, or drop a little grass and watch where it goes. For flying, stand with the wind on your back. Choose a field, a beach or a large park with no trees, power lines or roads nearby.

steps.test: Get your kite into the air and keep it up for one minute.
steps.note: With the wind at your back, let out a few metres of thread and let the wind lift the kite from your hand. If it drops, walk backwards a few steps to give it air. A helper holding the kite up a little way away and letting go makes the first flight easier.

steps.test: Launch the kite on your own, with nobody holding it for you.
steps.note: Hold the kite up by the bridle with the wind behind you, and let the wind take it as you let out thread slowly. On a light day, a few quick steps backwards help it climb. Never run towards a road or a slope while looking up.

steps.test: Land your kite on your own without it crashing.
steps.note: Wind the thread in steadily while walking towards the kite, so it comes down gently. If a gust pulls hard, let out a little thread instead of holding tight. Never grab a thread that is pulling fast; it can cut skin.

steps.test: Keep your kite flying for ten minutes without it coming down.
steps.note: When it dips, pull in a little thread; when it pulls strongly and climbs, let some out. Watch the tail: if it spins in circles, it needs a longer tail. Keep well away from other people's kites.

steps.test: Make a bigger sled kite from a bin bag, two sticks about as long as your arm, tape and strong string.
steps.note: The same shape as the paper kite, drawn about four times bigger on a cut-open bin bag. Garden canes, thin dowels or straight sticks work, and so does string from a parcel or a garden shed. A grown-up does any cutting of the sticks.

steps.test: Fly the bigger kite for five minutes, wearing gloves.
steps.note: A bigger kite pulls harder, so wear garden gloves or woolly gloves and wind the string onto a stick or a piece of wood, not round your hand. A child flies it with a grown-up holding the line too. If it lands in a tree or on anything high, leave it; a kite can be made again.

steps.test: Change one thing on the bigger kite, such as the length of the tail or the length of the bridle, and fly it again to see if it flies better.
steps.note: Change only one thing at a time, or you will not know what worked. A longer tail steadies a spinning kite; a longer or shorter bridle changes the angle the kite sits at in the wind. Say out loud what you changed and what happened.

steps.test: Let out about thirty metres of line, fly the kite at that height for ten minutes, and wind it all back in without a tangle.
steps.note: Thirty metres is about forty walking steps; tie a small knot in the line at that length before you go. Keep it much lower than aircraft could ever be, and well away from any airport; some countries set a height limit for kites, so find out yours. If the kite ever touches a power line, let go of the string at once, keep away, and tell the electricity company for your area.

steps.test: Teach two younger children to launch and land a kite you made, until each of them has done both on their own.
steps.note: Children in your family, a friend's children with their grown-up there, or a group at a club. Show them how to read the wind first, then let them hold the line while you stand beside them. Tell them the power line rule before anything else.

tracks.name: Rockets
tracks.line: From a balloon on a string to a rocket afternoon where everybody launches one safely.
tracks.who: From about six; a grown-up for every pressure launch
tracks.about: For everybody from about six, with a grown-up in charge of every water rocket launch and of the pump. The climb starts with a balloon on a string and a paper rocket blown off a straw, then a launcher you stamp on, then a water rocket pushed by air from a bicycle pump: fins, the best amount of water, measuring the height, and a parachute. It ends with a launch afternoon where you keep the safety rules and everybody there launches one. Every rocket here is pushed only by air or water; there are no chemicals, fire or rocket motors anywhere on this ladder, and none should be added. Each rung shows the same idea a real space rocket uses: throw something out of the back, and the rocket goes the other way.

steps.test: Make a balloon rocket that shoots along a string tied across a room.
steps.note: Thread a drinking straw onto a long piece of string and tie the string tight between two chair backs. Blow up a balloon, hold the neck shut, tape it to the straw, then let go. The air rushing out of the back pushes the balloon forwards, and the balloon pushes the air backwards: every rocket works this way.

steps.test: Roll a paper rocket round a pencil, close the top, slide it onto a straw and blow it across the room.
steps.note: Roll a strip of paper around a pencil and tape it, fold and tape the top shut, slide the pencil out and put a straw in its place. Blow a short hard puff. Rule from the start: never aim a rocket at a person or an animal, even a paper one.

steps.test: Make three paper rockets with no fins, small fins and big fins, blow each one five times, and write down which flies furthest on average.
steps.note: Tape the fins at the back end. Blow as evenly as you can each time and add up the five distances for each rocket, then divide by five. Fins at the back keep the rocket pointing forwards, the way the feathers on an arrow do, but big fins also add weight and drag, so the best size is something to find out.

steps.test: Blow the same paper rocket at three different angles, five times each, and find which angle sends it furthest.
steps.note: Try low (almost flat), about halfway up, and steep. With no air to slow it, halfway up (45 degrees) would go furthest; a light paper rocket is slowed a lot by the air, so it often goes furthest a little lower than that. Mark each landing with a coin and pace it out.

steps.test: Explain out loud in three sentences why a rocket moves, and answer one question about it from somebody.
steps.note: A rocket throws something out of its back very fast, and that pushes the rocket the other way, which is what the balloon on the string showed. It does not need to push against the ground or the air, which is why rockets work in space. The faster and the more stuff it throws out, the bigger the push.

steps.test: Build a stamp launcher from an empty plastic drinks bottle and a card tube, and launch a paper rocket by stamping on the bottle.
steps.note: Roll a tube of card that fits snugly into the bottle neck, seal the join all round with tape, and make a paper rocket (closed at the top) that slides over the other end of the tube. Lay the bottle on the ground and stamp on it; blow into the tube to fill the bottle again. Everybody nearby stays behind the launcher, and the rocket points up and away from people, windows and roads.

steps.test: Launch your stamp rocket straight up outside, time how long it stays in the air, and work out roughly how high it went.
steps.note: Use a phone stopwatch from the moment it leaves to the moment it lands. It takes about half that time to go up. Height in metres is about 5 times the going-up time times itself: 1 second up is about 5 metres, 2 seconds up is about 20. Air slows a light rocket, so the real height is a little less than this.

steps.test: Write the safety rules for water rockets and say them out loud to the grown-up who will help, before building anything.
steps.note: The rules: a grown-up runs the pump every time. Use only plastic bottles made for fizzy drinks, which are built to hold pressure; never glass, metal, or a dented or scratched bottle. Only water and air go in, never anything else. Everybody wears glasses or safety glasses and stands well back, at least 5 metres, and nobody stands over the bottle or looks down into it once pumping starts. Launch only in a big open space away from people, roads, buildings and power lines, and never hold, tape or clamp the stopper in to make it hold more pressure.

steps.test: With a grown-up, build a water rocket launcher from a bicycle pump, a ball inflating needle and a cork or rubber stopper that fits a fizzy-drink bottle.
steps.note: The grown-up makes a hole through the stopper and pushes the needle through so it pokes out the other side, then screws it onto the pump. Stand the bottle upside down on a simple stand, such as bricks either side or a board with sticks pushed in, pointing straight up. Many bicycle pumps come with a ball needle; a 1 or 2 litre fizzy-drink bottle is the rocket. The stopper is the safety valve: when the pressure gets high it pushes out on its own, which is why it must never be held in.

steps.test: Launch your first water rocket, a third full of water, with the grown-up pumping and everybody back behind them.
steps.note: Push the stopper in firmly, stand the bottle upside down on the stand, say the rules out loud, and move everybody back. The grown-up pumps from the end of the hose, standing to the side, until the stopper pops and the rocket goes. If nothing happens after a lot of pumping, stop, let the air out through the pump or wait, and check for leaks. Everybody gets wet at the start; wear old clothes.

steps.test: Launch with three different amounts of water, three times each, and find which amount sends it highest.
steps.note: Try a quarter full, a third full and half full. The squashed air pushes the water out, and the water is heavy, so it gives a much bigger push than air alone; too much water and there is not enough air to push it all out. Many people find about a third works best, but your bottle and stopper may differ, so trust your own results.

steps.test: Measure how high one launch went, using a folded paper corner and a known distance.
steps.note: Fold a square of paper in half corner to corner to make a triangle with a 45-degree angle. Somebody stands a measured distance from the launcher, say 15 metres, and looks along the slanted edge with the bottom edge level. If the rocket rises above that line, it went higher than 15 metres plus the height of their eyes; move further away on the next launch until the top just meets the line.
how: Pace or measure a distance from the launcher, such as 15 metres.
Hold the paper triangle at your eye with the long flat edge level.
Watch the top of the flight: above the slanted line means higher than your distance plus your eye height.

steps.test: Add fins and a nose cone with a little weight in its tip, and get the rocket to fly straight up without tumbling.
steps.note: Cut three or four fins from a plastic folder or stiff card and tape them evenly round the bottom end, near the neck. Make a cone from card or the top of a second bottle and put a little modelling clay inside the tip. With the weight near the front and the fins at the back, the air keeps the back behind the front, the way a dart flies point first. Keep the pressure safety rules on every launch.

steps.test: Add a parachute from a plastic bag and string that comes out at the top of the flight and brings the rocket down gently.
steps.note: Cut a circle about 40 centimetres across from a plastic bag, tie four strings to the edge, fold it into a loose-fitting nose cone that sits on the rocket but is not taped. When the rocket slows and tips over at the top, the cone falls off and the parachute pulls out. It takes a lot of tries to fold it so it opens; practise by throwing the folded cone up by hand first.

steps.test: Launch three rockets in a row that all fly straight and come down safely, saying the safety rules out loud before each one.
steps.note: Check the bottle for dents and scratches before every launch, and replace any that are damaged. Keep a written note of water, fins and height for each flight. Three in a row, with nobody breaking a rule, is the finish; one that goes wrong means start the count again.

steps.test: Run a rocket afternoon for family or friends where every person launches a rocket, a grown-up runs the pump, and nobody breaks a safety rule.
steps.note: Start everybody on the balloon and paper rockets, so the youngest have something to launch, then move to the stamp launcher and the water rocket. Say the rules before the first water launch and put a line on the ground that nobody crosses. Let each person choose the water amount and call the countdown for their own launch.

tracks.name: Stars and planets
tracks.line: From finding the Plough to an hour under the stars showing family or friends ten things by name.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a grown-up is always with a child out in the dark. It is written for the northern half of the world; south of the equator the sky is different, so start with the Southern Cross instead. It starts with the one shape you can see on every clear night of the year from most northern countries, the Plough, and uses it to find the North Star and Cassiopeia. Then the sky turning through the night, the big pattern of the season, a planet, the space station, shooting stars and the Moon's craters. It finishes somewhere properly dark with the Milky Way and the Andromeda galaxy, and then an hour of showing other people what you know. Most of it needs nothing but a clear night and a doorstep, and it is one of the best things to share with a child.

steps.test: On a clear night, go outside or to a dark window and find the Plough.
steps.note: The Plough is seven bright stars in the shape of a saucepan: four make the pan and three make the handle. From north of about 40 degrees (most of Europe, North America and northern Asia) it never sets, so it is up on every clear night of the year, somewhere in the northern half of the sky. Turn off the lights behind you. A free sky map such as Stellarium Web can show you where to look, then put the phone away.

steps.test: Follow the two end stars of the Plough's pan to the North Star, and point north.
steps.note: Take the two stars on the side of the pan furthest from the handle. Follow the line they make out of the top of the pan, about five times the gap between them, to a star on its own that is not especially bright. That is the North Star. Face it and you are facing north; check with a compass app if you like. How high it sits matches how far north you live: about halfway up the sky in northern Europe, lower further south. It hardly moves.

steps.test: Find Cassiopeia, the W of five stars on the far side of the North Star from the Plough.
steps.note: Draw an imaginary line from the Plough through the North Star and keep going about the same distance again. Cassiopeia looks like a W or an M depending on the time of year and night. Like the Plough, it never sets from most northern countries.

steps.test: Look for the faint star beside the middle star of the Plough's handle, and say whether you can see it.
steps.note: The middle star of the handle is called Mizar, and right beside it is a fainter one called Alcor. Some people can see the pair at once, some after a minute of looking, and from a bright street some cannot see Alcor at all. Whatever you see, say it; it is a good test of your eyes and of how dark your sky is.

steps.test: Look through a kitchen-roll tube at one patch of sky, count the stars, then count again after twenty minutes in the dark.
steps.note: No torch and no phone screen for the twenty minutes; eyes keep getting better in the dark for twenty minutes or more, and one look at a bright screen sets them back. Write down both numbers. A red light, such as a bike light or a torch with red sweet wrapper over it, lets you see the paper without losing your dark eyes. Dress warmly: standing still gets cold fast.

steps.test: Draw the Plough, the North Star and Cassiopeia from memory, then go out and check your drawing against the sky.
steps.note: Pencil and the back of an envelope. Put the North Star in the middle and the other two either side. Then compare with the real thing and fix what was wrong. A child and a grown-up can each draw one and see whose is closer.

steps.test: Note where the Plough is against a rooftop or tree, look again two hours later, and say which way the sky has turned.
steps.note: The whole sky turns around the North Star once a day, anticlockwise as you face north. In two hours the Plough will have swung round by about a twelfth of a circle. The North Star is the one that stays put, which is why people steered by it.

steps.test: Find the big pattern of the season: Orion in winter, bright Arcturus in spring and early summer, or the Summer Triangle in late summer and autumn.
steps.note: November to March evenings: Orion, low in the south, with three stars in a short straight line for his belt, an orange star above them and a white one below. April to July: follow the curve of the Plough's handle away from the pan to a bright orange star, Arcturus. August to October: three bright stars high overhead, Vega, Deneb and Altair, make the Summer Triangle. Far in the north, the sky in June and early July never gets fully dark, so try late in the evening.

steps.test: Find a bright point that does not twinkle as much as the stars around it, and use a free sky map to name the planet.
steps.note: Planets tend to shine with a steadier light than stars, especially higher up. Venus and Jupiter are the brightest; Venus is only ever seen in the west after sunset or the east before sunrise. Point Stellarium Web or another free sky map at it to check. Some weeks there is no bright planet in the evening; if so, do the next rung and come back to this one.

steps.test: Look up when the space station will next pass over, and watch it cross the sky.
steps.note: NASA's free "Spot the Station" website gives the times and where in the sky to look. It looks like a very bright star moving steadily across the sky for a few minutes, with no flashing lights; a plane has flashing lights. Passes come in runs of a few weeks, so if there are none this week, check again next week.

steps.test: Lie back somewhere safe on a clear night and count shooting stars for thirty minutes.
steps.note: A few can be seen in an hour on most clear nights away from lights. Around 12 August (the Perseids) and 14 December (the Geminids) there can be many more. A garden, a back yard or a car park with a grown-up. Blankets, hats, a flask, and the whole sky in view; do not stare at one spot.

steps.test: Look at the Moon through binoculars when it is half lit, and find three craters along the line between light and dark.
steps.note: Craters show up best near that line, where shadows are long. Rest your elbows on a wall or a car roof to keep the view still. No binoculars? Borrow a pair; many households have one somewhere. Never point binoculars anywhere near the Sun, and a grown-up hands them to a child only once the Sun has set.

steps.test: Stay out two hours later than usual and find the pattern of the next season rising in the east.
steps.note: The stars rise about four minutes earlier each night, which adds up to about two hours a month. So the next season's stars are already up late in the evening: Orion rises in the east late on autumn nights, and the Summer Triangle is up in the east late on spring nights. Name the one you find.

steps.test: With a lamp and a ball, show somebody why Orion is not in the summer evening sky.
steps.note: The lamp is the Sun, the ball is the Earth, and the far walls of the room are the stars. Night is the side of the ball facing away from the lamp. Walk the ball halfway round the lamp and the night side now faces the opposite wall: different stars. In summer Orion is on the same side of the sky as the Sun, so he is up in the daytime, where we cannot see him.

steps.test: Plan a trip to a dark place: pick a night near new moon, check the forecast, and pack for the cold.
steps.note: A dark place means away from town lights: a forest car park, a quiet beach, the hills. Many countries have official Dark Sky Parks; search for the nearest one. The best nights are the week either side of new moon, which most calendars and weather apps show. Pack warm layers, a hat, a flask, a blanket and a red light, and tell somebody where you are going.

steps.test: From your dark place, find the Milky Way.
steps.note: It is a pale band of light, like thin cloud that does not move, running across the sky; it is the light of millions of stars in our own galaxy. From northern countries it is best from August to October in the evening, passing high overhead through Cassiopeia and the Summer Triangle. Give your eyes twenty minutes first. A grown-up with any child, and stay near the car or the path.

steps.test: Find the Andromeda galaxy, another galaxy far beyond our own.
steps.note: It looks like a faint, fuzzy oval smudge, not a point. It is well placed in the evening from about August to February. Find the Great Square of Pegasus, four stars in a big square below Cassiopeia on autumn evenings. From its corner nearest Cassiopeia, count two stars along the curving line that leads away from the Square. At the second, turn towards Cassiopeia, pass one fainter star, and look about the same distance again. Binoculars make it much easier. Its light left it about two and a half million years ago.

steps.test: On one clear night, without a phone or a book, find and name ten things in the sky.
steps.note: Stars, patterns, planets, the Moon, the Milky Way, all count. For example: the Plough, the North Star, Mizar and Alcor, Cassiopeia, Orion, his orange star Betelgeuse, Arcturus, Vega, a planet, the Moon. Write the ten down when you come in.

steps.test: Take one person out and show them three things, then let them find one of those three by themselves.
steps.note: A child, a parent, a friend, a neighbour. Start with the Plough, because they will be able to find it again on their own for the rest of their life. Point with your arm held straight next to their eye line, and wait while they look.

steps.test: Lead an hour under the stars for family or friends, and show them ten things by name.
steps.note: A back garden or a dark car park, blankets and a flask. Start with what never sets, then the season's pattern, a planet if there is one, and finish with something faint that needs dark eyes. Let the children spot the space station or a shooting star. This is the end of the ladder: the sky is something you can give to other people now.

tracks.who: For everybody in the northern half of the world; a grown-up with any child in the dark

tracks.name: Things that fly
tracks.line: From one paper aeroplane across a room to a flying afternoon where you help everybody's plane glide.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, with a grown-up handling any scissors or craft knife for younger children. The climb starts with a folded paper aeroplane, then learns what the bent edges of a wing do, what really holds a plane up, a paper helicopter, a card glider balanced and measured, and a propeller driven by a rubber band. It ends with a flying afternoon where you help everybody there get a plane to glide. Almost all of it needs only paper, card from a cereal box, tape and paper clips, and each rung shows you something real aeroplanes and birds do.

steps.test: Fold a paper aeroplane and throw it gently so it glides across a room.
steps.note: Any sheet of printer paper works. Throw it level and gently, as if sliding it off your hand, not hard. If you already fold paper aeroplanes, fold one on purpose today and count it.
how: Fold the sheet in half the long way, then open it flat.
Fold the two top corners in to the centre line, then fold the new slanted edges in to the centre line again.
Fold it in half along the centre line, then fold each side down to make the wings, level with the bottom edge.

steps.test: Throw the same aeroplane ten times and write down how you held and threw it on the furthest flight.
steps.note: Try a gentle push, a harder throw, the nose a little up, the nose a little down. Mark where it lands each time with a shoe or a coin, and pace out the distance in steps if you have no tape measure. Most paper aeroplanes fly furthest from a smooth, fairly gentle throw with the wings level.

steps.test: Fold two more designs, fly each one five times, and write down which flies furthest on average.
steps.note: Try a wide-winged glider with the nose folded back to make it blunt, or a design from a library book or a free folding website. Add up the five distances for each design and divide by five: that is the average. One lucky flight does not make a design the best.

steps.test: Bend the back edges of both wings up a little and fly it, then bend them down and fly it, and say what each change did.
steps.note: Bent up, the nose usually lifts, so the plane climbs, slows and may swoop or drop. Bent down, it dives. The moving air pushes on the bent edges and tips the whole plane, and on a real aeroplane the flaps that do this are called elevators, on the tail. Flatten the edges again after each try.

steps.test: Bend the back edge of one wing up and the other down, and make the plane turn left and then right on purpose.
steps.note: The air pushes the wing with its edge bent up downwards and the other wing upwards, so the plane leans and turns towards the side bent up. Real aeroplanes do this with flaps near the wing tips called ailerons. Use small bends: a big bend makes it spin to the floor.

steps.test: Sweep a flat piece of card through the air, then sweep it again with the front edge tilted up a little, and feel the difference.
steps.note: Hold the card by its back edge, like a small tray, and move your arm quickly sideways. Flat, it slides through easily. Tilted, you feel the card pushed upwards and backwards, because it is pushing air down and the air pushes back. The upward part of that push is what a wing uses, and the backward part is drag.

steps.test: Explain out loud in four sentences what holds an aeroplane up, and answer one question about it from somebody.
steps.note: A wing meets the air tilted slightly up at the front, and its shape turns the air that flows over and under it downwards behind it. Pushing that air down pushes the wing up, and the same thing can be described as the air pressure being lower above the wing than below it. This push, called lift, only comes while air flows over the wing fast enough, which is why a plane needs speed and why the engines (or, for a glider, gravity) keep it moving forward. A common explanation says the air over the top must go faster to meet the air underneath at the back edge, but the air does not have to meet again, and that part of the story is wrong.

steps.test: Make a paper helicopter, drop it five times from the same height, and time each fall.
steps.note: Cut a strip of paper about 20 centimetres by 5, cut down the middle of the top half to make two blades, fold the blades opposite ways, and put a paper clip on the bottom. Drop it from your raised hand while standing on the floor, and use the stopwatch on a phone. It spins because the falling air pushes on the angled blades, and the spinning blades work like wings and slow the fall, the same way a sycamore or maple seed falls. A child uses scissors with a grown-up close by.

steps.test: Change one thing on your paper helicopter, drop it five times again, and say whether it now falls more slowly.
steps.note: Change only one thing: longer blades, shorter blades, or two paper clips instead of one. Longer blades usually fall more slowly, and more weight usually falls faster but steadier. Changing one thing at a time is the only way to know which change did it.

steps.test: Build a card glider with a body, a wing, a flat tail and an upright fin, using card from a cereal box and tape.
steps.note: A cereal box, tape, scissors and a ruler are all it takes; balsa wood works too if you have it, and a library book or a free website will have plans. Fold a strip for the body so it is stiff, and tape the wing a little way back from the front. Bend the two halves of the wing up very slightly at the tips, which helps it stay level. It will not fly well yet; the next rung sorts that out.
how: Body: a strip of card about 25 by 3 centimetres, folded in half the long way.
Wing: about 20 by 4 centimetres, taped across the body about a third of the way back.
Tail: about 8 by 3 centimetres flat across the back end, with a fin of about 3 by 3 centimetres standing up from it.

steps.test: Add weight to the nose of your glider until a gentle launch gives a smooth glide, not a swoop up or a dive.
steps.note: Use paper clips or a little modelling clay or reusable putty on the nose. If it swoops up, slows and drops, add weight; if it dives straight down, take some off. The balance point should end up under the front part of the wing: rest the glider on two fingertips to find it. A plane balanced like this is stable, because the weight sits ahead of where the lift pushes up.

steps.test: Launch your glider from standing height, measure how far forward it travels, and work out how many times further that is than the height it started from.
steps.note: Use a long hallway, a hall, or outside on a still day. If you launched from 1.5 metres and it travelled 6 metres before landing, it glides four times further than it drops. This number is called the glide ratio: a paper dart may manage three or four, and a well-balanced glider more. Launch it gently and level each time, so you measure the glider and not your throw.

steps.test: Make your glider fly a wide curve to the left and then to the right, by bending the back edge of the fin a little.
steps.note: Bend the back of the fin to the left and the air pushes the tail to the right, so the nose swings left. This moving part on a real aeroplane is the rudder. Make small bends and test after each one, and straighten it again when you are done.

steps.test: Fly your glider outside on a calm day and again in a light breeze, launching into the breeze, and write down what changed.
steps.note: Launched into a breeze, air flows over the wing even at a slow launch, so the glider is often steadier but covers less ground; with the breeze behind, it may drop quickly at first and then travel further over the ground. Choose an open space away from roads, trees and overhead power lines. If a glider lands on a roof, in a tree near cables or on a road, leave it there and make another.

steps.test: Make a propeller from card on a rubber band, wind it up, let it spin in your hand, and feel which way it pushes the air.
steps.note: Cut a propeller about 10 centimetres long from stiff card, twist the two blades opposite ways, and push a straightened paper clip through the middle as the shaft. Hook a rubber band to the shaft, hold the other end, wind the propeller, and let go of the propeller while holding the band. A propeller is a spinning wing: its blades push air backwards, and the air pushes the propeller forwards. That push is called thrust. Keep faces back from anything wound up.

steps.test: Fit a rubber-band propeller to a light glider and get it to fly forward for three metres under its own power.
steps.note: Stretch the rubber band along the underside of a light body, hooked to the propeller shaft at the front and a paper clip at the back. Wind it fifty to a hundred turns, hold the propeller, then let the plane go gently level. Free plans for rubber-band paper and straw aeroplanes are easy to find, and it is fiddly: expect several afternoons. A cheap balsa kit also counts if you have one.

steps.test: Design a glider of your own on paper with measurements, build it, and balance it until it glides further than your first card glider.
steps.note: Change something on purpose: a longer, narrower wing, a lighter body, a bigger tail. Draw it first with every size written on. Use the glide-ratio rung to compare it with your first card glider, and write down what you changed and what it did. Longer, narrower wings usually glide further, which is why gliders and albatrosses have them.

steps.test: Run a flying afternoon where everybody there folds a paper aeroplane and gets it to glide across a room, with your help where a plane dives or swoops.
steps.note: Three or more people is enough: family, friends, children from next door with their grown-ups. Show the fold from the first rung, then help each person bend the back edges or add a paper clip until their plane glides. Finish with a longest-glide contest and a paper helicopter drop. The finish is when every person's plane has glided across the room at least once.

tracks.name: Wind and weather watching
tracks.line: From saying which way the wind is blowing to teaching somebody to call tomorrow's weather from the sky.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. This ladder is about watching the sky yourself, with no forecast in your hand; the Weather and tide ladder is the one for forecasts, warnings and tides. It starts at the door with which way the wind is coming from and how hard it blows, then a streamer to show it, the families of cloud and which way they move, and a weather diary kept for a month. Then the signs: a shower cloud growing, thunder, high cloud thickening, the crossed-winds rule and the air pressure, each one tested against what really happens, and your own calls for tomorrow scored for a week. It ends with you teaching somebody else to make tomorrow's call from the sky. The signs here are the ones used in the middle latitudes of both halves of the world; near the equator the weather follows other patterns, and your own diary is what will show you the pattern where you live.

steps.test: Go outside or open a window, and say which direction the wind is coming from.
steps.note: Turn your face until the wind feels the same on both cheeks: you are now facing where it comes from. Check against a flag, smoke, washing on a line or the tops of trees. A wind is named by where it comes FROM, so a wind blowing towards the south is a north wind. No idea where north is? A free compass app on a phone will tell you, or say it as 'from the park side' for now.

steps.test: Say how strong the wind is in plain words, from calm to gale, by what it is moving.
steps.note: Use what you can see: smoke going straight up is calm; leaves rustling and a flag lifting is a light breeze; small branches moving and paper blowing along is a moderate breeze; whole trees swaying is a strong wind; twigs breaking off and walking being hard is a gale. This is a short version of the Beaufort scale that sailors have used for about two hundred years. A child can learn it as 'still, leaves, branches, trees'.

steps.test: Tie a strip of light material to a railing, a post or a cane outside, where you can see it from a window.
steps.note: A strip cut from a plastic bag, an old ribbon or a length of wool, about as long as your arm, tied where nothing blocks the wind: a balcony rail, a fence post, a garden cane. It streams away from where the wind is coming from. A grown-up does anything that needs a ladder or a window above the ground floor; nobody leans out of a window to do it.

steps.test: Each morning for a week, look at your streamer and write down the wind's direction and strength.
steps.note: One line a day on paper or in the notes on a phone: 'Monday: from the west, branches moving'. The same time each day is best, such as after breakfast. A child can draw an arrow and a small picture instead of words. If you already notice the wind every morning, write it down on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Look at the sky and say whether each cloud you see is a heap, a sheet or a wisp.
steps.note: These are the three families. Heaps are puffy with flat bottoms (cumulus). Sheets are flat grey layers over much of the sky (stratus). Wisps are thin streaks very high up (cirrus). Nearly every cloud is one of these or a mix, and its full name joins them. A clear blue sky? Say so, and do it on the next cloudy day. If you already know the ten cloud types, sort each one into its family and count it.

steps.test: Line one cloud up with a chimney, a roof edge or a tree top, wait a minute, and say which direction it is moving from.
steps.note: Stand still so the fixed point does not move for you. Write down both the wind you feel on the ground and the way the cloud is going: 'ground from the south, clouds from the west'. They are often different, because the wind changes with height. You will use this on rung thirteen.

steps.test: Over one week, name five cloud types on sight, using a free cloud guide from your national weather service.
steps.note: Good ones to start with: cumulus (fair-weather heaps), cumulonimbus (a huge tower, often with a flat top, that brings heavy showers or thunder), stratus (a low grey sheet), nimbostratus (a thick dark sheet with steady rain) and cirrus (high wisps). Tick each off on the day you see it. Clouds change by the hour, so a look out of the window at breakfast, midday and evening finds more than one long look.

steps.test: Start a weather diary: at the same time each day for two weeks, write down the wind, the cloud and whether it rained.
steps.note: One line a day: wind direction, wind strength in your plain words, the cloud family or type, and rain or dry since yesterday. Add warm, mild or cold if you like. A notebook by the window or a note on a phone both work. A child can use drawn symbols: an arrow, a cloud shape, a raindrop. Missed a day? Write 'missed' and carry on.

steps.test: On a clear morning, look out every hour and write down the time the first heap cloud appears.
steps.note: On sunny days the ground warms, warm air rises, and heap clouds often start to form by late morning. Note also whether they stay small and flat or grow taller. In a cold, grey season this may take a few tries; any morning that starts clear will do.

steps.test: Watch a tall heap cloud growing, say whether its shower will reach you and roughly when, and then check.
steps.note: A heap cloud that keeps growing upwards, with a dark base and crisp edges at the top, is often turning into a shower cloud. Use rung six to see which way it is moving and whether it is coming towards you. Say it plainly: 'rain here within the hour'. If you hear thunder, go inside a building or a car and stay there.

steps.test: The next time there is a thunderstorm, count the seconds from a flash to its thunder, and say how far away the storm is.
steps.note: Sound travels about a kilometre in three seconds, so divide the seconds by three for kilometres, or by five for miles. Count again a few minutes later: fewer seconds means the storm is coming closer. Do this from indoors. Many weather services advise that if you can hear thunder you are close enough to be struck, and to stay inside until thirty minutes after the last thunder. No storm this season? Go on and come back to this rung.

steps.test: When high wispy cloud spreads and thickens into a thin milky sheet, write 'rain within a day?' in your diary, and check the next day.
steps.note: In the middle latitudes of both halves of the world, rain often comes with a front, and the first sign is often high cloud spreading across from one side of the sky, turning into a thin sheet, sometimes with a ring of light (a halo) round the sun or moon, then lowering and thickening. It does not always bring rain, which is why you check. Never look straight at the sun: stand where a building hides it and look at the sky beside it.

steps.test: Stand with your back to the wind you feel, watch the high clouds, and say whether the weather is more likely to get worse or better.
steps.note: This is the crossed-winds rule that walkers and sailors have long used. North of the equator: high clouds coming from your left mean the weather is more likely to get worse; from your right, better; from straight behind or in front, little change. South of the equator it is the other way round: from your right, worse. It works best in the middle latitudes and is often wrong near hills. Write your call in the diary and check it.

steps.test: Read the air pressure morning and evening for a week, and write down each time whether it is rising, steady or falling.
steps.note: Many phones have a pressure sensor that a free barometer app can read, and an old barometer on a wall works too. No sensor? Your national weather service publishes free readings from its weather stations; use the nearest. Pressure is given in hectopascals or millibars (the same number), usually between about 970 and 1040. The change matters more than the number: a steady fall often comes before unsettled weather, and a rise before it settles.

steps.test: Keep the weather diary every day for a whole month, adding the pressure whenever you can.
steps.note: Carry straight on from your two weeks. A month with a few gaps still shows a pattern. A child and a grown-up can take it in turns, a day each, and read it back together at the end of each week. If you already keep a diary like this, count the month you have.

steps.test: Read back your month and write down which wind direction came with the most rain, and which with the driest days.
steps.note: Count the rainy days and the wind direction on each, then the dry ones. Where you live, rain may come mostly from the sea side, or over the hills, or with no pattern in the wind at all. Near the equator the pattern may be the time of day instead, such as storms most afternoons. Whatever you find is knowledge about your own place that you worked out yourself.

steps.test: Each evening for a week, write down tomorrow's weather from the sky, the wind and the pressure alone, and count how many you got right.
steps.note: Keep each call short and easy to check: 'dry morning, rain by evening' or 'windier, from the west'. Do not look at a forecast until it is written. Score one for right and a half for close. If you did this once on Out the door, part one, this is the same skill for a week, with a score. Four out of seven is a good start.

steps.test: For ten days, write your own call and the official forecast side by side, and count which was right more often.
steps.note: Forecasts are made with huge computers and trained people, so they will be right more often, and that is fine. The useful days are the ones where you were right and they were not, often a shower or a change they put at a different hour. Those show you what your own eyes on your own sky are good for.

steps.test: Find one local weather sign, such as cloud on a particular hill or mist in a valley, and test it for two weeks.
steps.note: Ask an older neighbour, a gardener, a farmer or somebody who fishes what they watch, or find one in your diary: cloud sitting on the top of a hill, a breeze off the sea on sunny afternoons, fog in low ground on still clear mornings. Each time the sign appears, write down what the weather did next. Some local signs are reliable and some are not, and finding out which is the rung.

steps.test: Take somebody outside, show them the wind, the cloud families and the crossed-winds rule, and let them make tomorrow's call.
steps.note: A child, a friend, a grandparent. Ten minutes outside: face the wind together, name the clouds, then stand with your backs to the wind and look up. Let them say their call, write it down, and check it with them the next day. This is the end of the ladder: reading the sky is now something you can give to somebody else.

tracks.name: Throwing
tracks.line: From a paper ball into a bin, to hitting a target four times out of five from twenty paces, and teaching the throw to somebody else.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts indoors with a scrunched-up paper ball into a bin, then catching, then an overarm throw at a target outdoors from ten and twenty paces, a long throw, and skimming a stone where there is water. It ends with hitting a target four times out of five from twenty paces, and teaching the throw to somebody else. A soft ball, rolled socks or a beanbag are all it needs. Always throw where nobody is in the way, and never at people, animals, windows or cars.

steps.test: Scrunch a sheet of paper into a ball and throw it into a bin from five paces.
steps.note: A pace is one ordinary walking step. Underarm or overarm, whichever you like. Keep going until one goes in, and if you do this every day at a desk already, count it.

steps.test: Throw the paper ball into the bin from five paces, five throws out of five.
steps.note: Five in a row, starting the count again after any miss. Stand the same way each time and look at the bin, not the ball, as you let go.

steps.test: Throw a soft ball against a wall and catch it as it comes back, ten times in a row.
steps.note: A tennis ball, a small rubber ball or a rolled pair of socks. Use a wall with no window in it, such as your own garden wall, the side of a garage or a ball wall in a park, and never a neighbour's wall without asking. Watch the ball all the way into your hands.

steps.test: Catch ten in a row thrown gently to you from five paces.
steps.note: Ask a friend, a parent or a child to throw underarm. Hands out in front, soft, pulling the ball in towards you as it arrives. Step back a pace once ten is easy.

steps.test: Throw overarm and hit a target about the size of a bin lid from ten paces.
how: Stand side-on to the target, throwing arm at the back.
Point your other hand at the target.
Step towards it with the opposite foot as you throw, and let your arm follow through.
Mark the target with chalk on a wall, a bucket on its side, or a hoop on the grass.
steps.note: Overarm is the throw used for distance and aim in almost every sport. Stepping with the opposite foot is the part most people miss, and it is where the power comes from. Check nobody is behind the target before each throw.

steps.test: Hit the same target from ten paces, five throws out of five.
steps.note: Start the count again after any miss. If the misses go left or right, look at where your hand points after you let go: it should point at the target.

steps.test: Hit the target from twenty paces.
steps.note: Further away the ball has to go up a little, not only forwards. Aim slightly above the target and let it drop in. One hit counts for this rung.

steps.test: Hit the target from ten paces with your other hand, three throws out of five.
steps.note: Everything you learnt for the first hand, from the start: side-on, point, step with the opposite foot. It will feel clumsy for a few days. This is how you find out how much of throwing is practice.

steps.test: Throw a ball back and forth with somebody from ten paces, twenty throws without a drop between you.
steps.note: Count every catch out loud together. Throw to the other person's chest, not over their head. A drop by either of you starts the count again.

steps.test: Throw a ball as far as you can in an open space, mark where it lands, and beat that mark by five paces.
steps.note: Use a field or a large park with nobody in front of you, and a soft ball. Mark the first landing with a stick or a jumper. A longer run-up of three steps and a higher throw are the two things that add distance.
steps.twist: Other hand, then beat that too.

steps.test: Skim a flat stone across calm water so it bounces three times.
how: Find a flat, round stone about the size of your palm.
Hold it between thumb and middle finger, first finger along the edge.
Crouch low, throw side-arm, and spin it off your first finger so it lands nearly flat.
steps.note: Only on calm water where nobody is swimming, fishing or boating, and away from birds. Stand on a flat shore, never on a slippery rock or a high edge, and a grown-up is with a child near water. If there is no lake, river or sea near you, this rung and the next wait for a day out.

steps.test: Skim a stone so it bounces six times.
steps.note: Lower and faster. The angle where the stone meets the water matters more than strength: nearly flat to the water, with plenty of spin. Choose the flattest stones you can find and keep them for your best throws.

steps.test: Hit the bin-lid target from twenty paces, four throws out of five.
steps.note: This is the whole ladder in one test: side-on, point, step, follow through, and a little height. Do a few throws from ten paces first. If you already play a throwing sport, count four out of five on your first try.

steps.test: Teach somebody the overarm throw until they hit the target from ten paces, three times out of five.
steps.note: A child, a friend or a parent. Show them one thing at a time: side-on, point at the target, step with the opposite foot. Stand beside them rather than behind the target, and let them take as many throws as they like.

categories.name: Mind and numbers
categories.line: Tables, the cube, chess, memory, codes, puzzles.

tracks.name: Learning to learn, part one
tracks.line: From one thing you wondered about to thinking for half an hour with a pen.

steps.test: Look up one thing you have wondered about and read until you could explain it.
steps.note: Why the sky is blue, how a lock works, where a word comes from. Explain it to the wall if nobody is there.

steps.test: Read for twenty minutes with your phone in another room.
steps.note: Anything on paper. Twenty minutes is longer than it sounds the first time.

steps.test: Write ten lines by hand, slowly and neatly.
steps.note: Copy them from a book. The point is the hand, not the words.

steps.test: Learn five words of a language you do not speak and say them out loud.
steps.note: Hello, thank you, please, yes, no. Pick the language of a place you would like to go.

steps.test: Memorise ten things and say them back an hour later.
steps.note: A shopping list, a poem's first verse, ten capitals. Picture each one somewhere in your house.

steps.test: Do twenty sums in your head, no paper.
steps.note: Adding prices, doubling numbers, splitting a bill. Say the answers out loud.

steps.test: Explain one thing you know well to somebody in three sentences.
steps.note: If it takes more than three, you do not know it as well as you thought. Try again tomorrow.

steps.test: Read one chapter of a book that is a bit too hard for you.
steps.note: Look up nothing. Let the hard words go by and see how much you still got.

steps.test: Find an answer without a screen.
steps.note: A library, a reference book on a shelf, or three people who might know. Slower, and you will remember it.

steps.test: Learn the times table you never quite learned.
steps.note: The sevens, the eights, the twelves. Out loud, forwards and backwards. Have them all? Squares to twenty.

steps.test: Take one bad argument you hear this week and say, kindly, what is wrong with it.
steps.note: "Everybody knows…", "you would say that", two things happening together being called cause. Name the move.

steps.test: Learn twenty words of that language.
steps.note: The five from rung four and fifteen more. Numbers to ten count as ten.

steps.test: Read a whole book, cover to cover.
steps.note: Any book, any length. Finishing is the rung.

steps.test: Write one page about what you learned this month.
steps.note: By hand or typed. What surprised you, what you got wrong, what you want next.

steps.test: Learn one poem by heart and say it to somebody.
steps.note: Short is fine. Four lines said properly beats twenty stumbled.

steps.test: Solve a puzzle that takes more than an hour.
steps.note: A hard crossword, a cube, a logic problem, a jigsaw. Sit with it; do not look up the answer.

steps.test: Teach somebody one thing you learned on this ladder.
steps.note: The sums trick, the poem, the words. Teaching it is how you find out you know it.

steps.test: Hold a short conversation in that language.
steps.note: With a person, or with a recording you answer out loud. Two minutes. Mistakes and all.

steps.test: Read a book written more than a hundred years ago.
steps.note: Old does not mean hard. A short one, all the way through, and notice what has not changed.

steps.test: Sit and think about one question for thirty minutes with nothing but a pen.
steps.note: Write the question at the top. No phone, no book. Whatever you write underneath is yours. Part two goes deeper.

tracks.about: How to learn anything, practised on a few things at once: a language, a poem, sums in your head, a book that is a bit too hard. The rungs are short and the last one is thirty minutes of thinking with only a pen. Nothing to buy; a library card helps.

tracks.name: Times tables
tracks.line: From counting in tens and twos to fifty mixed questions from every table up to twelve in under three minutes, with no mistakes.
tracks.who: From about seven, and grown-ups who never learned them
tracks.about: For anybody from about seven: a child with a grown-up beside them, or a grown-up who never quite learned the tables. It starts with counting in tens and twos, then takes the tables in the order that makes each one easier: ten, two and five, then three, four and eight, then nine, six, eleven and twelve, and seven last, when only one answer in it is new. It ends with fifty mixed questions from every table up to twelve, answered in under three minutes with no mistakes. Knowing them without stopping to think makes every later sum quicker, from sharing out sweets to doubling a recipe. Paper and a pen are all it needs.

steps.test: Count out loud in tens from 10 to 120, then in twos from 2 to 24.
steps.note: Say each number clearly at a steady pace. Twelve steps each, because this ladder goes up to twelve times. If you can already do this without thinking, do it once on purpose, backwards as well, and count the rung.

steps.test: Say the ten times table out loud, from 1 times 10 to 12 times 10, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Say it the full way: one times ten is ten, two times ten is twenty. Any whole number times ten is that number with a nought on the end, so 7 times 10 is 70 and 12 times 10 is 120. If you slip, start again from the top.

steps.test: Say the two times table, from 1 times 2 to 12 times 2, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Two times a number is that number doubled: 2 times 7 is 7 and 7 more, which is 14. Count in twos on your fingers at first if you need to. Say it once more the next day before you go on.

steps.test: Say the five times table, from 1 times 5 to 12 times 5, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Every answer ends in 5 or 0. Five times a number is half of ten times it: 5 times 8 is half of 80, which is 40. The minute marks on a clock face go round in fives, if you have one to look at.

steps.test: Answer twenty mixed questions from the two, five and ten times tables, all correct.
steps.note: Mixed is harder than in order, because you cannot count up from the answer before. In order you are counting; out of order you are remembering, which is the point. A grown-up or an older child can ask the questions instead of the scraps.
how: Write 1 to 12 on twelve scraps of paper and put them in a cup.
Pull one out and multiply it by 2, 5 or 10, choosing a different one each time.
Say the answer out loud, put the scrap back, and pull again.
If you get one wrong, start the twenty again.

steps.test: Draw a grid of 12 rows and 12 columns, fill in every answer you already know, and count the empty squares.
steps.note: Write 1 to 12 along the top and down the side; each square is its row number times its column number. Fill in the rows and columns for 1 (one times a number is the number itself), 2, 5 and 10. You should have 64 empty squares, and because 3 times 4 is the same as 4 times 3, only 36 different answers are left to learn. Keep the grid and fill it in as you go up the ladder.

steps.test: Say the three times table, from 1 times 3 to 12 times 3, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Three times a number is double it and one more of it: 3 times 7 is 14 and 7, which is 21. Count in threes out loud a few times first: 3, 6, 9, 12. Fill the new answers into your grid.

steps.test: Say the four times table, from 1 times 4 to 12 times 4, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Four times a number is double it, then double again: 4 times 7 is 14, then 28. 4 times 12 is 24, then 48. Fill the new answers into your grid.

steps.test: Say the eight times table, from 1 times 8 to 12 times 8, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Eight times a number is double it three times: 8 times 7 is 14, 28, 56. You already know eight times 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 from the other tables, so only 8 times 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are really new. Fill them into your grid.

steps.test: Answer twenty mixed questions from the two, three, four, five, eight and ten times tables, all correct.
steps.note: Use the scraps again, choosing a different table from these six each time. At the end, say any you had to stop and think about three times over. If you got one wrong, do another twenty the next day.

steps.test: Say the nine times table, from 1 times 9 to 12 times 9, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Nine times a number is ten times it, take away one lot: 9 times 7 is 70 take away 7, which is 63. To check an answer from 9 times 2 to 9 times 10, add its two digits: they always come to 9, as in 63 and 36. After that, 9 times 11 is 99 and 9 times 12 is 108.

steps.test: Say the six times table, from 1 times 6 to 12 times 6, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Six times a number is five times it and one more lot: 6 times 7 is 35 and 7, which is 42. When you multiply 6 by an even number, the answer ends in that number: 6 times 4 is 24, 6 times 8 is 48. The only new answers here are 6 times 6, 7, 11 and 12.

steps.test: Say the eleven and the twelve times tables, each from 1 to 12, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Eleven times a number from 1 to 9 is that digit written twice: 11 times 4 is 44. Then 11 times 10 is 110, 11 times 11 is 121 and 11 times 12 is 132. Twelve times a number is ten times it and two times it added: 12 times 7 is 70 and 14, which is 84.

steps.test: Say the seven times table, from 1 times 7 to 12 times 7, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Look at your grid: every answer in the sevens is already there except 7 times 7, which is 49. So this table is answers you know, said in a new order: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56, 63, 70, 77, 84. Your grid should now be full.
