steps.test: Fill in the whole 12 by 12 grid from memory on a clean sheet, with no mistakes and no time limit.
steps.note: Put your old grid in another room first. When you finish, check every square against it. Any square you got wrong goes on a short list that you say out loud each day this week.

steps.test: Answer the ten harder questions in the note, shuffled, twice through with no mistakes.
steps.note: They are 6 times 7 (42), 6 times 8 (48), 6 times 9 (54), 7 times 8 (56), 7 times 9 (63), 8 times 9 (72), 7 times 12 (84), 8 times 12 (96), 9 times 12 (108) and 12 times 12 (144). Write each question on a scrap without its answer, shuffle them, and go. One that helps: 56 is 7 times 8, and the digits run 5, 6, 7, 8.

steps.test: Answer thirty mixed questions in a row from every table up to twelve, all correct.
steps.note: Use the twelve scraps two at a time now: pull out two, multiply them, and put both back. Some will be easy, like 1 times 9, and the next might be 8 times 7. If you get one wrong, start the thirty again.

steps.test: Have somebody ask you thirty mixed questions, and answer each one within three seconds.
steps.note: Anybody who can read two scraps can ask, even a younger child holding your grid to check. They count three in their head; a slow answer counts as a miss, and you get that one again at the end. Done when all thirty have been answered in time.

steps.test: Teach somebody one times table, using the method for it from this ladder, until they can say it with no mistakes.
steps.note: A younger child, a friend, or a grown-up who never learned the eights. Show them the method first, like double three times for the eights, then listen while they say it. It may take a few short goes on different days, and that still counts.

steps.test: Answer fifty mixed questions from every table up to twelve in under three minutes, with no mistakes.
steps.note: Fifty in three minutes is under four seconds each, which leaves time to write. If you go over the time or make a mistake, do a new sheet another day. When you can do this, the tables are there whenever you need them.
how: Ask somebody to write fifty questions on a sheet, or pull two scraps fifty times the day before and write the questions down.
Set a timer for three minutes.
Write each answer next to its question as fast as you can.
Check every answer against your grid.

tracks.name: The cube
tracks.line: From counting the pieces to solving any mix-up somebody hands you, from memory, in under three minutes.
tracks.who: From about eight; anybody who can follow written steps
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight who can follow written steps, and for grown-ups. The cube looks impossible and is not: it is seven short sequences of turns, learned one at a time, and the first one takes an evening. The climb goes layer by layer, from the white cross to the whole cube with the notes in front of you, then from memory, and ends with any mix-up somebody hands you solved in under three minutes. The only thing you need is a standard three-by-three puzzle cube, which costs little and can often be borrowed from a friend, a school or a toy box.

steps.test: Count the centres, edges and corners on the cube, and say which colour centre is opposite which.
steps.note: There are 6 centres with one colour each, 12 edges with two and 8 corners with three. The centres never move against each other, so the colour in the middle of a face is the colour that whole face will be when it is solved. On most cubes white is opposite yellow, but check yours, as some are different.

steps.test: Learn the six letters R, L, U, D, F and B, and turn each face a quarter turn both ways.
steps.note: L, D and B are the hard ones, because clockwise for them feels backwards from where you are holding the cube. Say each letter out loud as you turn it. Every sequence on this ladder is written in these letters.
how: Hold the cube still with one face towards you: that face is F, the front.
R is the right face, L the left, U the top, D the bottom and B the back.
A letter on its own means a quarter turn clockwise, as if you were looking straight at that face.
A letter with a mark after it, like R', means a quarter turn anticlockwise; R2 means a half turn.

steps.test: Do R U R' U' six times in a row, and watch the cube come back to how it started.
steps.note: Start from a solved cube, or take a photo of a mixed one first, so you can see it come back. Keep the same face towards you the whole time and say the letters as you go. This short sequence is the first of the seven you will use to solve the cube.

steps.test: Make the daisy: the yellow centre on top, with a white edge on each of its four sides, white facing up.
steps.note: Turn faces one at a time to bring each white edge up next to the yellow centre. Before bringing in the next one, turn the top so you do not knock out one that is already there. There is no sequence to learn for this: work it out by trying.

steps.test: Turn the daisy into a white cross on the bottom, with each edge's side colour matching the centre next to it.
steps.note: Turn the cube over to check: a white plus sign on the bottom, and a matching colour going up from each arm of it. If one side does not match, that edge went down before it lined up, so bring it back up and try again. Keep white on the bottom from here on.
how: Turn the top until one white edge's side colour matches the centre below it.
Turn that face twice, which takes the white edge down to the bottom.
Do the same for the other three edges.

steps.test: Put one white corner into its place on the bottom, using R U R' U'.
steps.note: It never takes more than five goes of the sequence. If a white corner is in the bottom layer in the wrong place or the wrong way round, hold it at the front right and do R U R' U' once to bring it up, then start again.
how: Find a corner in the top layer that has white on it.
Turn the top until the corner sits above the place it belongs, between the two centres that match its other colours.
Turn the whole cube so that place is at the front right, with white still on the bottom.
Do R U R' U' again and again until the corner is in, with white on the bottom.

steps.test: Finish the white layer: all four white corners in, and the bottom row of every side matching its centre.
steps.note: Do each corner the same way as the last rung, turning the whole cube so the next empty place is at the front right. When it is done, every side has a bottom row of one colour that matches its centre. Look for white corners in the top layer first.

steps.test: Solve the white layer from three different mix-ups, one after another, without looking at the notes.
steps.note: Mix the cube each time with about twenty turns of any faces. Say the stages out loud as you go: daisy, cross, corners. When you can do this three times running, you know the first layer.

steps.test: Put one middle-layer edge in on the right, using U R U' R' U' F' U F.
steps.note: The edge goes down into the gap between the front and right faces. Your white layer comes apart and goes back together during the sequence, so do all eight turns without stopping. If it comes out wrong, check that the top colour of the edge matched the right-hand centre before you started.
how: Hold the cube with white on the bottom.
Find an edge in the top layer with no yellow on it.
Turn the top until the front colour of that edge matches the centre below it.
If its top colour matches the right-hand centre, do U R U' R' U' F' U F.

steps.test: Put one middle-layer edge in on the left, using U' L' U L U F U' F'.
steps.note: Line the edge up the same way as the last rung, but this time its top colour matches the left-hand centre. It is the right-hand sequence done the other way round. If an edge is in the middle layer but in the wrong place or flipped, put any top edge into that gap with either sequence, and the wrong one comes up to the top where you can place it properly.

steps.test: Solve the first two layers: the white layer and all four middle edges.
steps.note: If every edge in the top layer has yellow on it, the edges you still need are in the middle layer the wrong way, so bring one up as on the last rung. When it is done, only the top layer is left to solve. Write down how long it took.

steps.test: Solve the first two layers from three different mix-ups, one after another, without looking at the notes.
steps.note: Mix it with about twenty turns each time. Say the stages out loud: daisy, cross, corners, middle edges. It is common to be slowest at finding the middle edges, so practise spotting the top edge with no yellow on it quickly.

steps.test: Make a yellow cross on top, using F R U R' U' F'.
steps.note: Look only at the yellow edges and the yellow centre; ignore the corners for now. The first two layers are back as they were at the end of each go.
how: Look at the top: the yellow edges make a dot, an L shape, a line, or already a cross.
Dot: do the sequence once, and you get an L.
L: hold it so its arms point to the back and to the left, and do the sequence to get a line.
Line: hold it going from left to right, and do the sequence once more for the cross.

steps.test: Turn the yellow edges so each side colour matches its centre, using R U R' U R U2 R'.
steps.note: The corners will look mixed up after this; that is expected, and the next two rungs put them right. If all four edges already match, go straight on to the next rung.
how: Turn the top until at least two edges match their centres.
If two that match are next to each other, hold them at the back and on the right, do the sequence, then turn the top once more clockwise (U).
If the two that match are opposite each other, do the sequence once from any side, then turn the top until two next to each other match, and do the step above.

steps.test: Put each yellow corner in its right place, whichever way round it is, using U R U' L' U R' U' L.
steps.note: The corner you hold at the front right stays where it is while the other three swap round. Do not turn the top between goes.
how: A corner is in its right place when its three colours match the three centres around it, even if yellow is not facing up.
Find a corner in its right place and hold the cube so that corner is at the front right of the top.
Do the sequence, then check; if the others are not in place yet, do it once more.
If no corner is in its right place, do the sequence once from any side, and then one will be.

steps.test: Twist the last corners using R' D' R D, and solve the whole cube for the first time, with the notes in front of you.
steps.note: Do not turn the whole cube during this stage, or the bottom layers will not come back. If the very last corner will not come right however you twist it, the cube may once have been taken apart and put back wrongly; on most cubes you can twist that one corner round by hand.
how: Hold the cube with yellow on top and an unfinished corner at the front right of the top.
Do R' D' R D, two at a time, until that corner has yellow on top. The rest of the cube will look mixed up: keep going.
Turn only the top (U) to bring the next unfinished corner to the front right, and do the same again.
When every corner has yellow on top, turn the top until the sides match, and the cube is solved.

steps.test: Solve the whole cube three times, from three different mix-ups, with the notes in front of you.
steps.note: Look at the notes only when you need them, and say each stage out loud as you start it. Notice which sequence you still check every time: that is the one to practise. Write down your time for each solve.

steps.test: Solve the whole cube from a mix-up with nothing written in front of you.
steps.note: First say the seven sequences out loud from memory, each with the stage it belongs to, and check them against the notes. If you get stuck during the solve, look up the one you need, then put the notes away and start again from a new mix-up. The rung is one whole solve with no looking.

steps.test: Solve the cube three times in one sitting, each in under five minutes, with nothing in front of you.
steps.note: Use a timer on a phone or a clock with a second hand. Start it when you pick up the mixed cube and stop it when the last face is done. If one goes over five minutes, the three start again.

steps.test: Solve the cube from a mix-up somebody else gives you, from memory, in under three minutes.
steps.note: Ask them to turn it about twenty times while you look away, then start the timer as you pick it up. Speed comes from not stopping to hunt for pieces, so practise finding the next piece while your hands finish the last sequence. When you can do this, you can solve any cube anybody hands you.

tracks.name: Chess
tracks.line: From setting up the board to teaching a complete beginner to play a whole game.
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with setting up the board and learning how each piece moves, then a first whole game, the special moves, and how to finish a game with checkmate. After that come the ideas that win games: a good start, checking what the other player is threatening, puzzles, forks and pins, and going back over a game you lost. It ends with you teaching a complete beginner until they can play a whole game by the rules. A board and pieces are ideal, but a free chess app, or a board drawn on paper with pieces written on scraps, does every rung.
tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side

steps.test: Set up the board and pieces correctly, and name every piece as you put it down.
steps.note: Turn the board so each player has a light square in the bottom right-hand corner. Rooks go in the corners, then knights, then bishops; the queen goes on the square of her own colour, and the king on the one left. The eight pawns go in the row in front. No set? Draw eight rows of eight squares on paper and write the pieces on small scraps, or use a free chess app.

steps.test: Show somebody, or say out loud, how each of the six kinds of piece moves and takes.
steps.note: Rook: straight along rows and columns. Bishop: diagonally. Queen: both. King: one square any way. Knight: an L shape, two squares one way and one to the side, and it can jump over pieces. Pawn: one square forward (two on its first move), but it takes one square diagonally forward, which is the move beginners most often get wrong.

steps.test: On the board, put a king in check, then in checkmate, then in stalemate, and say the difference.
steps.note: Check: the king is attacked and must get out of it. Checkmate: the king is attacked and there is no way out, so the game is won. Stalemate: the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, and the game is a draw. Set each one up with just a few pieces.

steps.test: Play one whole game to the end, checkmate or draw, with every move legal.
steps.note: White moves first. Play slowly and check each other's moves; there is no hurry. No other player? A free chess app on its easiest setting counts. A child and a grown-up playing each other is ideal.

steps.test: Castle in a game, and say the four rules that allow it.
steps.note: The king moves two squares towards a rook, and that rook jumps to the square on the king's other side. You may only castle if neither piece has moved, nothing stands between them, your king is not in check, and it does not pass through or land on an attacked square. It tucks the king away and brings the rook out in one move.

steps.test: Set up and show the two special pawn moves: reaching the far row, and taking "en passant".
steps.note: A pawn that reaches the far row becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight, almost always a queen. En passant: if a pawn moves two squares from its start and lands right beside an enemy pawn, that enemy pawn may take it as if it had moved only one, but only on the very next move.

steps.test: Say the usual value of each piece, then play a game counting what you give and what you get before every capture.
steps.note: Pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king cannot be swapped, so it has no number. Giving a knight to take a pawn loses 2. A free app counts as the other player.

steps.test: Checkmate a lone king using your king and queen, on a board or an app with only those three pieces.
steps.note: Use the queen to push the lone king to the edge of the board, then bring your own king up to help. Watch for stalemate: leave the lone king at least one square to move to until the final move. Many free apps let you set up this position; so does a board.

steps.test: Checkmate a lone king using only your king and one rook.
steps.note: It takes longer than with a queen. The rook cuts the king off one row at a time while your king walks alongside to guard the rook. If you already know how, do it on purpose from a new starting position and count it.

steps.test: In three games, in your first ten moves: move a pawn to the centre, bring out both knights and both bishops, and castle.
steps.note: The centre is the four squares in the middle. Try not to move the same piece twice early, and keep the queen on its starting square for the first few moves. Write a tick for each game where you did all three.

steps.test: For one whole game, before every move of yours, ask "What does the other player's last move attack?"
steps.note: Look at the piece that just moved and every square it now reaches. Most lost pieces are lost because nobody asked. It makes the game slower; that is fine.

steps.test: Solve ten "mate in one" puzzles, where one move gives checkmate.
steps.note: Free chess apps and websites have thousands, and a library chess book will have pages of them. Look at every check you can give before choosing. If a puzzle beats you, set it up on a board and try each move.

steps.test: Find the fork in five puzzles: one piece attacking two of the other player's pieces at once.
steps.note: Knights are the best at forks, because their L-shaped move is hard to see coming. A knight that attacks the king and the queen at once wins the queen. Search "fork" in a free puzzle app, or ask somebody who plays to set some up.

steps.test: Find the pin in five puzzles: a piece that cannot move without leaving a more valuable piece behind it open to capture.
steps.note: A bishop attacking a knight that has the queen standing behind it on the same diagonal is a pin: if the knight moves, the queen is taken. Only rooks, bishops and queens can pin.

steps.test: Solve ten "mate in two" puzzles, finding both of your moves before you play the first.
steps.note: Look for checks and captures first, then for quiet moves that leave the king no way out. Write down both moves before you check the answer.

steps.test: Write down every move of one game in chess notation, both players' moves.
steps.note: The columns are a to h from White's left, the rows 1 to 8 from White's side. Pieces are K, Q, R, B and N (knight); a pawn has no letter. "Nf3" means knight to f3, "x" means takes, "+" means check, "O-O" means castling. Many free apps show the notation as you play, so you can check yourself.

steps.test: Play five whole games in one week, and write down the moves of each.
steps.note: Against people, or a free app on a setting that wins about half the time. Online, a child plays with a grown-up nearby and with chat turned off. Keep the written games; the next rung uses one.

steps.test: Go back through one game you lost, move by move, and mark the first move where it went wrong.
steps.note: Replay it on a board from your notation. Stop at each of your moves and ask what else you could have played. Many free apps will also check a game for you, but find your answer first and check it after.

steps.test: Win a game against somebody who is playing their best, not letting you win.
steps.note: A friend, a relative, somebody at a chess club, or a free app one setting above the one you usually beat. Ask them before you start to play properly. Losing on the way is part of the rung; keep playing until the win comes.

steps.test: Teach a complete beginner until they can set up the board and play one whole game by the rules.
steps.note: Use the same order you climbed: the board, the moves, check and checkmate, then a game. Let them make mistakes and ask them what they see before you tell them. A child can teach a grown-up, and a grown-up a child.

tracks.name: Memory
tracks.line: From six digits held for a minute to thirty things, read to you once, said back in order.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. A trained memory is a method anybody can learn: you turn things into pictures, put the pictures in places you know, and walk past them again. The climb starts with a six-digit number held for a minute, builds a route of ten places in your head, then twenty, then thirty, and adds names and numbers along the way. It ends with somebody reading you thirty things once and you saying them all back in order. It looks like a gift, and it is a method.

steps.test: Memorise a six-digit number as three pairs, cover it, and say it back one minute later.
steps.note: Take six digits from a barcode or a receipt, or have somebody write them for you. Say them as three pairs: 4, 7, 1, 8, 9, 2 becomes forty-seven, eighteen, ninety-two. Wait a minute, say it, then uncover it and check.

steps.test: Learn the phone number of one person you would call if you lost your phone, and say it the next day without looking.
steps.note: Many people now know no phone numbers from memory, and this is the one worth having. Split it into groups of three or four digits, say it out loud five times, and again at bedtime. A child learns the number of a parent or carer.

steps.test: Turn five words into five pictures in your head, and say the words back five minutes later.
steps.note: Use these: bell, carrot, ladder, umbrella, fish. Make each picture big, moving or noisy: not just a bell, but a huge bell ringing on your kitchen table. The clearer and stranger the picture, the easier it is to find again.

steps.test: Link ten words into one short story in your head, and say the ten back in order.
steps.note: Use these: kite, bread, shoe, lion, clock, bucket, star, piano, spoon, tree. Each thing does something to the next: the kite lands on a loaf of bread, the bread is squashed by a shoe, a lion is wearing the shoe. Go through the story once more in your head, then say the list.

steps.test: Learn the names of three people you have just met, say each name back to them, and write all three down that evening.
steps.note: A new classmate, a neighbour, somebody at a club, or a shop worker with a name badge. Say the name back as you meet ("Nice to meet you, Amira") and link it to a picture, like a Rose holding a rose. A child does this with a grown-up nearby; if you meet nobody new this week, learn the names of three people you see often but have never asked.

steps.test: Choose ten places in your home in the order you walk past them, and say them with your eyes closed, forwards and backwards.
steps.note: For example: front door, doormat, coat hook, mirror, stairs, kitchen door, sink, fridge, table, window. Pick places that look different from each other and will not move. Write the list down, because you will use these ten places in this order for the rest of the ladder.

steps.test: Put ten things on your ten places, and say them back in order and then backwards.
steps.note: Use these, or ask somebody to write ten: hammer, apple, feather, rabbit, cup, glove, egg, whistle, basket, crown. Make each thing do something at its place: the hammer knocking on the front door, an apple squashed on the doormat. To say them back, walk the route again in your head and look at each place.

steps.test: Say the same ten things back the next morning, in order, without looking.
steps.note: Walk the route once in your head before you start. If a place seems empty, look at it for a moment longer, as the picture often comes back. Make the pictures for any you missed stranger for next time.

steps.test: Give each digit from 0 to 9 a picture by its shape, and say all ten pictures in order without looking.
steps.note: For example: 0 a ball, 1 a candle, 2 a swan, 3 a pair of lips turned on its side, 4 a sailing boat, 5 a hook, 6 a cherry on its stalk, 7 a boomerang, 8 a snowman, 9 a balloon on a string. Use these or your own, but once chosen, never change them. Numbers are hard to picture and these pictures are easy, which is why this works.

steps.test: Memorise the first twenty digits of pi, two digit pictures at each of your ten places, and say them back.
steps.note: Pi is the distance round any circle divided by the distance across it, and it starts 3.1415926535897932384. Split the digits into pairs: 31 41 59 26 53 58 97 93 23 84. At each place, put the two pictures doing something together: at the front door, a pair of lips (3) blowing out a candle (1).

steps.test: Memorise a shopping list of ten things and do the shop without looking at the list.
steps.note: Put the ten things on your ten places before you leave, and keep the written list in a pocket to check only at the end. A child can do this for part of a family shop with a grown-up. For an online shop, fill the basket from memory, then compare it with the list.

steps.test: Add ten more places to your route, and walk all twenty in your head, forwards and backwards.
steps.note: Carry on through the house, or go outside: the gate, the path, a tree, a lamp post, the corner. Keep to places you know well and that will still be there next year. Write the new ten under the first ten.

steps.test: Put twenty things on your twenty places and say them back in order, with no more than two missed.
steps.note: Have somebody write twenty words you have not seen, or take twenty names of things from one page of a book. Look at each for a few seconds and make it do something at its place before you move on. If you miss more than two, try a new list another day.

steps.test: Go over a new list of twenty on the day, the next day and three days later, then say it back a week after you learned it, with none missed.
steps.note: Each time, walk the route once and say the list out loud; it takes about a minute. Going back over it at growing gaps is what keeps it: without that, many people find much of a list has gone within days. Write the list down and fold it away so you can check honestly at the end.

steps.test: Memorise the first forty digits of pi, two digit pictures at each of your twenty places, and say them back.
steps.note: The twenty digits after the ones you know are 62 64 33 83 27 95 02 88 41 97. So the first forty are 3.141592653589793238462643383279502884197. Keep the first twenty where they are and put the new pairs on places eleven to twenty.

steps.test: Learn the names of everybody in a group of eight or more people, and say every name out loud to the group.
steps.note: A class, a sports team, a club, or the guests at a family meal. Link each name to a picture, as on rung five, and go round the group in your head more than once while you are with them. Asking somebody their name again early on is fine; saying all of them at the end is the rung.

steps.test: Add ten more places, and walk all thirty in your head, forwards and backwards.
steps.note: Carry on the same route, or add a second route you know well, like the way to school, work or a friend's home. Keep the places in a fixed order and write all thirty down. This route will hold the list on the last rung.

steps.test: Have somebody read you twenty things once, at a steady pace, and say them back in order, with no more than two missed.
steps.note: They read one thing about every five seconds and do not repeat any. You put each one on its place as it is read, with no time to go back. If you miss more than two, try again another day with a new list.

steps.test: Have somebody read you a twenty-digit number once, in pairs, and say it back with no mistakes.
steps.note: They read it as pairs, like "fifty-eight, zero seven, ninety-one", with a short pause between each. You turn each pair into two digit pictures at the next place on your route. They check you against what they wrote.

steps.test: Have somebody read you thirty things once, and say all thirty back in order.
steps.note: Done the same way as rung eighteen, with a list of their choosing and all thirty places. A mistake or two on the first go is normal, so try a new list on another day. When you can do this, you can hold a list of jobs or a day's plan the same way.

tracks.name: Mental arithmetic
tracks.line: From adding two small numbers to twenty mixed sums, set by somebody else, done in your head in under ten minutes.
tracks.who: From about eight; grown-ups too
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight who can add small numbers, and for grown-ups who would like to stop reaching for a calculator. It starts with adding two small numbers and moves through taking away, doubling and halving, multiplying, dividing and percentages, with one method for each that works every time. Then the sums go into real shopping: a running total, the change, a shared bill, and which size is better value. It ends with twenty mixed sums set by somebody else, done in your head in under ten minutes. The Times tables ladder helps with the multiplying rungs, and nothing needs buying.

steps.test: Add twenty pairs of numbers from 1 to 9 in your head, all correct.
steps.note: Write 1 to 9 on nine scraps of paper, put them in a cup and pull out two at a time, or have somebody call out pairs. Pairs that make ten help most: 8 and 7 is 8 and 2, which makes 10, then 5 more, so 15. If this is already easy, do the twenty on purpose as fast as you can and count the rung.

steps.test: Answer twenty take-away sums inside twenty, like 15 take away 8, all correct.
steps.note: Count up from the smaller number instead of back from the bigger: from 8 to 10 is 2, from 10 to 15 is 5, so the answer is 7. Use the same scraps: pull two, add 10 to the bigger, and take the smaller away. Say each answer out loud.

steps.test: Answer ten sums like 47 plus 8 in your head, where the answer goes past the next ten, all correct.
steps.note: Fill up to the next ten first: 47 and 3 is 50, and the 5 left over makes 55. For questions, pull a scrap and add it to a two-digit number you can see: a page number, a date, a number on a packet. Check each one on paper afterwards.

steps.test: Add ten pairs of two-digit numbers in your head, like 46 plus 37, all correct.
steps.note: Tens first, then ones: 40 and 30 is 70, 6 and 7 is 13, and 70 and 13 is 83. For questions, open a book at two pages and use the last two digits of each page number, or have somebody read pairs out. Check each one on paper after you say it.

steps.test: Answer ten sums by rounding one number to a ten and putting it right afterwards, like 47 plus 38.
steps.note: 38 is 2 less than 40, so work out 47 plus 40, which is 87, then take away the 2: 85. It works for taking away too: 63 take away 29 is 63 take away 30, which is 33, then add the 1 back: 34. This one method does much of the work in the rest of the ladder.

steps.test: Take one two-digit number from another ten times in your head, like 72 take away 45, all correct.
steps.note: Count up in jumps: 45 to 50 is 5, 50 to 72 is 22, and 5 and 22 is 27. Or round: 72 take away 50 is 22, then add back the 5 you took away too many: 27. Use whichever is quicker for you, and check on paper.

steps.test: Add four two-digit numbers in your head, five times, all correct.
steps.note: Look for pairs that make a round number first: 27, 45, 33 and 15 become 27 and 33, which is 60, and 45 and 15, which is 60, so 120. Use the ages of four people you know, or the last two digits of four prices on a receipt. Say the running total out loud as you go.

steps.test: Double ten two-digit numbers and halve ten others in your head, all correct.
steps.note: Double the tens, double the ones, then add: double 68 is 120 and 16, which is 136. Halve the same way: half of 74 is half of 70, which is 35, and half of 4, which is 2, so 37. Half of an odd number ends in a half: half of 57 is 28 and a half, written 28.5.

steps.test: Multiply ten two-digit numbers by a one-digit number in your head, like 34 times 7, all correct.
steps.note: Split the bigger number into tens and ones: 30 times 7 is 210, 4 times 7 is 28, so 238. Say the first part out loud so you keep hold of it while you work out the second. The Times tables ladder makes this rung much quicker.

steps.test: Multiply ten numbers by 5 and ten numbers by 9 using ten lots, all correct.
steps.note: Times 5 is times 10, then halve: 46 times 5 is 460 halved, which is 230. Times 9 is times 10, then take away one lot: 36 times 9 is 360 take away 36, which is 324. Check two or three on paper to be sure of the method.

steps.test: Divide ten numbers by a one-digit number in your head, like 156 divided by 6, all correct.
steps.note: Split the number into parts that divide easily: 156 is 120 and 36, 120 divided by 6 is 20, 36 divided by 6 is 6, so 26. To divide by 4, halve twice: 96, 48, 24. Make questions that come out exactly by multiplying first, and check each answer by multiplying back: 26 times 6 should be 156.

steps.test: Work out 50, 25, 20 and 75 per cent of five different numbers in your head.
steps.note: Fifty per cent is half, and 25 per cent is half again: 25 per cent of 64 is 32, then 16. Twenty per cent is ten per cent doubled: 20 per cent of 45 is 4.5 doubled, which is 9. Seventy-five per cent is the whole take away a quarter: 75 per cent of 48 is 48 take away 12, which is 36.

steps.test: Before working out ten sums, say roughly what each answer will be, then work it out and see how close you were.
steps.note: Round each number to one that is easy to use: 48 times 21 is about 50 times 20, which is 1000, and the real answer is 1008. A rough answer first catches the big mistakes, like a missing nought. Use sums from the rungs before, or prices on a receipt.

steps.test: Multiply ten pairs of two-digit numbers in your head, like 23 times 14, and get at least eight right when you check on paper.
steps.note: Split the smaller number into tens and ones: 23 times 10 is 230, 23 times 4 is 92, and 230 and 92 is 322. Say 230 out loud to keep hold of it while you work out the rest. Make a rough answer first, as on the last rung, so you know about where you should land.

steps.test: Keep a running total in your head for a shop of ten or more things, and be within 1 of the total at the till.
steps.note: Round each price to one place after the point as you go: 2.49 becomes 2.50 and 1.85 becomes 1.90. A child can do this for a grown-up's shop, and an online basket works too if you add it up before looking at the total. If prices where you live are in large whole numbers, like 1250, aim to be within 100 instead.

steps.test: Work out your change before the till shows it, on three separate things you pay for.
steps.note: Count up from the price to what you handed over: from 7.35 to 7.40 is 0.05, to 8 is 0.60 more, to 20 is 12 more, so 12.65. If you pay by card, work out the change you would get from the next round number, like 10, 20 or 50, and check it on a calculator later. A child can do this while a grown-up pays.

steps.test: Take a real receipt or bill and split it evenly between three or four people in your head, then check it on a calculator.
steps.note: Split the whole number and the part after the point separately: 87.60 between 4 is 80 divided by 4, which is 20, and 7.60 divided by 4, which is 1.90, so 21.90 each. If it does not divide exactly, round each share up and say how much is left over. A shopping receipt, a household bill or a take-away order all work.

steps.test: In a shop or on a shop's website, work out which of two sizes of the same thing is better value, three times.
steps.note: Work out the price of the same amount of each: 500 g for 2.40 is 0.48 for each 100 g, and 750 g for 3.30 is 0.44 for each 100 g, so the bigger one costs less for each 100 g. Some shelf labels print this in small type, so you can check yourself. The bigger size is only better value if you will use it all before it spoils.

steps.test: Teach somebody one method from this ladder until they use it correctly on three sums of their own.
steps.note: Rounding and putting it right (rung five) and counting up for change (rung sixteen) are good ones to start with. Show one worked example, then give them three to try and say nothing unless they ask. If they get stuck, work the next one together and let them do the one after alone.

steps.test: Answer twenty mixed sums that somebody else sets from this ladder, in your head, in under ten minutes, with at least eighteen right.
steps.note: Give them this ladder to choose from: some adding, taking away, multiplying, dividing, percentages and change. They read each sum out, you say the answer, and they check it on a calculator. If you get fewer than eighteen, practise the kind you missed for a few days and try again with new sums.

tracks.name: Codes and ciphers
tracks.line: From one message in a shift cipher to a treasure hunt of five coded clues that other people follow to the end.
tracks.who: From about eight; best with a friend or a grown-up
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, and best done with a friend, a brother or sister, or a grown-up. It starts with one of the oldest ciphers, moving each letter along the alphabet, then goes on to keyword alphabets, counting letters to read a message without its key, book ciphers, Morse code, and messages hidden inside ordinary writing. It ends with a treasure hunt of five clues, each in a different code, that other people follow to the end. Codes are puzzles, spelling and careful counting all at once, and they need only paper and a pen.

steps.test: Write a short message in a shift-of-three cipher, then turn it back into plain words to check it.
steps.note: MEET AT FOUR becomes PHHW DW IRXU. Leave the spaces between words in for now, as it makes the next rungs easier. Julius Caesar is said to have used this shift in his letters.
how: Write the alphabet in a line.
Under it, write the alphabet again starting from D, with A, B and C at the end.
For each letter of your message, find it on the top line and write the letter under it.
To read it back, find each letter on the bottom line and write the one above it.

steps.test: Send a message in a shift cipher to somebody, tell them the shift, and have them read it correctly.
steps.note: Choose any shift from 1 to 25 and tell them the number, not the message. A note on the table, a message on the fridge or a text all work. Then ask them to send one back for you to read.

steps.test: Read the shift cipher in the note without being told the shift.
steps.note: Here it is: AOL JHRL PZ PU AOL ISBL APU. There are only 25 possible shifts, so you could try them one by one, but short words are quicker: a three-letter word that appears twice is often THE. Count how far it is from T to A to find the shift, then read the rest.

steps.test: Make a keyword alphabet, write a message with it, and read it back.
steps.note: Write a keyword with no letter used twice, like GARDEN, then the rest of the alphabet in order without those letters: GARDENBCFHIJKLMOPQSTUVWXYZ. Write the normal alphabet above it, so A becomes G, B becomes A and C becomes R. HELLO becomes CEJJM.

steps.test: Count how often each letter appears in the first 200 letters of a page of a book, and write down the five most common.
steps.note: Tally marks against A to Z down the side of a page make it quick. In ordinary English writing E is usually the most common letter, with T, A, O and I close behind; other languages have a different order, so count a page in the language you write your messages in. These counts are what let you read a cipher without its key on the next rung.

steps.test: Read a message somebody else wrote in a mixed-up alphabet of their own, without the key, and read the whole message.
steps.note: Ask somebody to write at least three sentences with every letter swapped for another, keeping the spaces. Count its letters: the most common is probably E. Then look for one-letter words (often A or I), three-letter words that repeat (often THE or AND) and double letters, and pencil in your guesses as you go.

steps.test: Send a message to somebody using a book cipher, giving each word as page, line and word numbers from a book you both have.
steps.note: 12-3-4 means page 12, line 3, the fourth word. You both need the same edition, because page numbers change between editions: two copies of the same school reading book or two library copies of the same printing work. Find each word you need anywhere in the book and write its numbers down in order.

steps.test: Learn the Morse code for the letters of your name, and tap your name for somebody who writes it down from the taps.
steps.note: Copy the Morse alphabet from a library book or a free page: each letter is a pattern of short and long signals, like A, which is short then long. Tap short taps and long presses on a table, with a clear gap between letters. SOS is short-short-short, long-long-long, short-short-short; practise it indoors, and never signal it outside for fun, where somebody could take it as a real call for help.

steps.test: Hide a word in an ordinary note using the first letter of each line, have somebody read the note without noticing, then show them.
steps.note: To hide HELLO, write five lines starting with H, E, L, L and O: Home soon. Eggs for dinner? Lots of rain here. Lunch was good. Out at six tomorrow. Keep each line an ordinary sentence so nothing looks odd. With this kind of hiding, nobody knows there is a message at all; with a cipher, people can see a message but cannot read it.

steps.test: Write a message where a keyword sets a different shift for each letter, then read it back.
steps.note: With the keyword CAT the shifts are 2, 0 and 19, so SEE YOU AT NOON becomes UEX AON CT GQOG. The same letter no longer always turns into the same letter, so counting letters does not read it. This way of writing was used for hundreds of years and was once called the cipher nobody could read.
how: Turn each letter of the keyword into a shift: A is 0, B is 1, C is 2, and so on.
Write the keyword again and again under your message, one keyword letter under each message letter.
Move each message letter along by the shift of the keyword letter under it.
To read it back, move each letter back the same number of places.

steps.test: Invent a cipher of your own and give a message in it to a friend, who tries for ten minutes to read it without the key.
steps.note: Mix ideas from this ladder: a shift and then the message written backwards, numbers for letters, or a drawn symbol for each letter. Write the key down and keep it somewhere safe. Whether they read it or not, show them the key at the end and ask what helped them or what stopped them.

steps.test: Run a treasure hunt of five clues, each written in a different code from this ladder, that other people follow to the end.
steps.note: Each clue says where the next one is hidden, and the last one leads to a small treasure: a snack, a drawing or a note. Put a hint with each clue so it can be solved, like "shift of 3" or "the blue book on the shelf". Indoors or in a garden is best; if any clue goes outside, a grown-up checks that every hiding place is safe.

tracks.name: Puzzles
tracks.line: From one easy puzzle finished to a puzzle of your own that three people try and at least one solves.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up together
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can work on most rungs together. It starts with one easy puzzle finished, then goes through a river-crossing riddle, sudoku, logic grids, crosswords and puzzles you solve by asking questions. Along the way it practises two habits: staying with a puzzle while you are stuck, and coming back to it the next day. It ends with a puzzle of your own that three people try and at least one solves. Everything is free: paper and a pen, the puzzle pages of the newspapers at a library, library puzzle books, or free printable puzzle pages online.

steps.test: Finish one easy puzzle on your own, from start to end: a word search, a maze or a small jigsaw.
steps.note: A jigsaw of about 50 pieces if your household has one; otherwise a word search or maze from a newspaper, a library puzzle book or a free printable page. For a jigsaw, do the edge pieces first, then sort the rest by colour. If easy puzzles are nothing new to you, do one on purpose against a timer and count the rung.

steps.test: Solve the farmer's river crossing in the note, moving scraps of paper, without being told the answer.
steps.note: A farmer must take a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river in a boat that holds the farmer and only one of them. If they are left alone together, the wolf eats the goat, and the goat eats the cabbage. Draw the river on paper, write the four names on scraps, and move them across: there is a way with nothing eaten.

steps.test: Finish an easy sudoku with no help.
steps.note: Every row, every column and every 3 by 3 box needs the numbers 1 to 9 once each. Start with a row, column or box that has only one or two empty squares. Use a pencil, and younger children can start with a small 4 by 4 grid that uses 1 to 4.

steps.test: Spend twenty minutes on the nine-dot puzzle in the note, writing down each thing you try, without looking up the answer.
steps.note: Draw nine dots in three rows of three, then join all nine with four straight lines, without lifting your pen or going back along a line. Being stuck is the part where the thinking happens, so the rung is the twenty minutes, solved or not. If you do solve it, keep the answer to yourself so you can give the puzzle to somebody else.

steps.test: Finish a medium sudoku with no help.
steps.note: Now look at one empty square at a time and check its row, column and box together to see which numbers are left. Write the possible numbers small in the corner of a square, and cross them out as you find they cannot go there. If you make a mistake you cannot find, start a fresh one rather than looking at the answer.

steps.test: Finish a logic grid puzzle, where clues tell you who has what, by crossing things off in a grid.
steps.note: A small one might have three friends, three pets and clues such as "the girl with the cat is not called Mia". Put a cross in the grid where a clue says no and a tick where you are sure; each tick lets you cross off the rest of its row and column. Choose the smallest size for your first one, from a library puzzle book or a free printable page.

steps.test: Solve a lateral thinking puzzle that somebody else reads to you, asking only questions they can answer with yes or no.
steps.note: These are short stories that seem not to make sense, and the other person picks one from a puzzle book or a free page and keeps the answer to themselves. Ask things like "Is it night-time?" or "Does the weather matter?" until you can say what happened. There is no limit on questions, and the rung is done when you give the whole answer.

steps.test: Solve the two working-backwards puzzles in the note by starting from the end.
steps.note: Here is how it works: I think of a number, double it, add 6 and get 20, so work back: 20 take away 6 is 14, and half of 14 is 7. Now try: I think of a number, add 5, double it and get 36; what was it? Then: a water lily doubles in size every day and covers a whole pond on day 30; on which day did it cover half the pond?

steps.test: Finish a whole crossword, using a dictionary if you need one.
steps.note: Start with a quick or easy crossword, where each clue is simply a meaning, not a riddle. Fill in the answers you are sure of first, because each one gives you letters for the answers that cross it. Library newspapers, puzzle books and free printable pages all have them, and children's puzzle books have smaller ones.

steps.test: Put away a puzzle you are stuck on, come back to it the next day or the day after, and solve it.
steps.note: A sudoku, a crossword clue or a riddle from a book. Stop when you have tried everything you can think of, write down where you got to, and look again the next day before you do anything else with it. It is common to see what to do straight away after a break; if not, give it one more day before looking at the answer.

steps.test: Finish a hard sudoku or a large logic grid puzzle with no help.
steps.note: You will need the small pencil numbers from rung five. One useful rule: when two squares in the same row can only hold the same two numbers, those two numbers cannot go anywhere else in that row, and the same is true for a column or a box. Expect it to take more than one sitting, and come back to it as on the last rung.

steps.test: Make a puzzle of your own, give it to three people, and have at least one of them solve it.
steps.note: A river crossing with new characters, a number to work back to, a small logic grid, or a riddle about something in your home. Solve it yourself first and write the answer down, so you know it can be done. If nobody gets it after a fair try, give a clue, and if that is not enough, make it a little easier and try new people.

tracks.name: Finding things out
tracks.line: From three questions written down to a week spent answering one, with the sources shown to somebody else.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about twelve. The climb starts with writing down what you wonder about and asking the people around you, then moves to searching well, checking one source against another, finding where a saying really came from, and ringing the person who would actually know. It ends with one bigger question answered properly over a week, written on a page with the three places the answer came from, and shown to somebody so they can check it for themselves. Everything answers confidently now, from websites to AI tools, and being able to tell a checked answer from a guess is a skill you use every day.

steps.test: Write down three questions you have wondered about this week, each one ending with a question mark.
steps.note: Real ones, not quiz questions: why does the kettle switch itself off, when was my street built, what does the name of my town mean. A note on your phone or the back of an envelope is fine. If you already keep a list like this, add three today and count it. You will use these questions for the next few rungs.

steps.test: Ask somebody one of your three questions, and keep asking until you understand the answer or you are both sure they do not know.
steps.note: Somebody in the house, a friend, a grandparent, a colleague at the tea break. Useful follow-ups are "How do you know?" and "What do you mean by that?". Finding out that they do not know is a proper finish too: it tells you where to look next.

steps.test: Search for one of your questions online using three or four key words, and find the answer on the first page of results.
steps.note: Type the words that matter, not the whole sentence: "kettle switch off how" works better than "why does my kettle turn itself off". If the first page has nothing useful, change one word and try again. Any free search engine will do.
how: Pick the three or four words that carry the question.
Read the page titles and the short text under each before you open one.
Open the most likely one and find the sentence that answers it.

steps.test: Read the answer to that question on two different websites, and write down whether they agree.
steps.note: Choose two that are not copying each other: a museum or a university page and a newspaper, or a council page and an encyclopaedia. If they agree, good. If they do not, write down what each one says; that is the start of the next rung.

steps.test: For one of those pages, find who wrote it and when, and write both down.
steps.note: Look at the top and the bottom of the page, or an "About us" link. A named person or organisation and a date make a page easier to trust. If you cannot find either, write that down too, and trust the page a little less.

steps.test: Find out how to do one practical thing you have never done, and do it the same day.
steps.note: Fold a fitted sheet, tie a tie, restart the internet router, set the timer on the oven, or plant a potato. Written steps, a video or a person all count. It is done when the thing is done, not when you have read about it. A younger teenager chooses the job with a grown-up.

steps.test: Ask an AI chat tool one question with who you are, what you need and why written into it, and get a useful first answer.
steps.note: Compare "radiator cold" with "I rent a flat and one radiator is cold at the top and warm at the bottom. What can I safely check myself before I ring the landlord?" The second one gets a better answer first time. If you do not use them, put the same full question to a search engine or a person and count it.

steps.test: Check one answer from an AI tool or a website against a second, better source, and write down whether it was right.
steps.note: A better source is one closer to the facts: the official page of the council, the maker of the product, the museum that holds the thing. Answers can sound certain and still be wrong, so this is worth doing even when the first answer looks fine. Right or wrong, you have done the rung once you have checked.

steps.test: Take one saying that is shared under a famous name, and find where it first appeared or that there is no record of it.
steps.note: Sayings passed around as Einstein, Churchill or Abraham Lincoln are good ones to try. Search the exact words in quotation marks along with the word "quote" or "source", and look for a page that names the book, speech or letter it came from. Sometimes the honest answer is that nobody can find it, and that counts.

steps.test: Read the original of one thing people are talking about, rather than somebody talking about it.
steps.note: A council planning application instead of the local Facebook post about it, the report itself instead of the news story, or the actual letter from school instead of what another parent said. Then write one sentence on what the original says that the talk left out. Most originals are free to read online or at a library.

steps.test: Ring or email the place that would actually know, and ask one clear question.
steps.note: The council about bin days, the library about an old photograph of your street, a museum about an object, a shop about a product. Write the question down before you ring, and write the answer down while they are talking. A younger teenager can do this with a grown-up sitting beside them.

steps.test: Write down what you believe about one thing, look it up properly in two good sources, and write down what you believe now.
steps.note: Pick something you are fairly sure of, not something you care a lot about, for the first go: how long a goldfish remembers, whether cracking your knuckles does any harm, how old your town is. Sometimes your view stays the same and sometimes it changes. The rung is being willing to write the second line honestly.

steps.test: Spend a week answering one bigger question, and write the answer on one page with the three places you got it from.
steps.note: Bigger means it needs more than one search: when was my house built and who lived there first, where does our tap water come from, why is my town where it is. Ten minutes a day is enough. Use at least one source that is not a website, like a person, a library book or an old map.

steps.test: Show somebody how you found the answer to your bigger question, step by step, so they could check it themselves.
steps.note: Go through your page with them: the question, where you looked first, what did not work, and the three sources. Let them ask questions. If they could follow the same steps and reach the same answer, you have finished this ladder.

tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about twelve

tracks.name: Maps
tracks.line: From finding yourself on a phone map to planning a day out on a paper map and leading it.
tracks.who: From about eight, with a grown-up out of doors; grown-ups
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, with a grown-up for the rungs out of doors, and for grown-ups who have always let the phone decide. It starts on a phone map: the dot that is you, then the view from above. Then a paper map: finding home, the key, the scale, how long a walk takes, turning the map to match the street, and a first walk with the paper map alone. The middle rungs are the numbers and lines on a map: grid references, latitude and longitude (which can bring help to exactly where you are), and contour lines that show hills. It ends with drawing a map yourself, planning a walk somewhere new, and planning a day out for other people and leading it. A person who can read a map knows where they are and what is around them, even when the phone battery is empty.

steps.test: Open a map app on a phone, find the dot that shows where you are, and name your street and the nearest street that crosses it.
steps.note: Any free map app works. Zoom out with two fingers until the next street shows. Tap the button that makes the map turn as you turn, and watch it line up with the way you are facing. No phone? A computer shows the same map; find your home by typing the address.

steps.test: Switch the map to the satellite view and find your home, the nearest park and a place you go every week.
steps.note: Satellite view is photos taken from above, so roofs, trees and car parks look as they really are. Find the three places, then switch back to the plain map and find them again. A child can say what each looks like from above: 'our roof is the grey one with the big tree behind'.

steps.test: Get a paper map that shows your home, and mark your home on it with a pencil cross.
steps.note: Free ways to get one: borrow a local or walking map from the library, pick one up at a tourist office, or print one from a free online map such as OpenStreetMap. A walking map with contour lines (the thin brown or orange lines) is the most useful for later rungs. If you already have one at home, this takes a minute: count it.

steps.test: Find the key on the paper map, then find eight of its symbols on the map itself.
steps.note: The key (sometimes called the legend) is the box explaining what each symbol means: a church, a car park, a railway, a footpath, woodland, water, a viewpoint, a bus station. Point to one of each on the map. A child can read out a symbol from the key while the grown-up finds it, then swap.

steps.test: Measure the straight-line distance from home to a place you know with the map's scale bar, then check it on the phone map.
steps.note: Lay the edge of a strip of paper on the map between the two places and mark both ends. Hold the strip against the scale bar and read off the distance. Most map apps can measure a straight line, often by pressing and holding a point and choosing to measure. Say how far off you were.

steps.test: Measure a walking route of about one kilometre on the map, say how long it will take, then walk it and time yourself.
steps.note: Lay a piece of thread along the roads and paths, then hold it against the scale bar. On flat ground many adults walk about five kilometres an hour, which is twelve minutes for one kilometre; children, hills and busy crossings are slower. Write your guess before you set off. A grown-up walks with any child.

steps.test: Stand at a street corner, find it on the paper map, and turn the map until the streets on it point the same way as the real streets.
steps.note: Turn the whole map, not yourself. When it is right, what is on your left in real life is on the left of the map too. The writing may end up sideways or upside down; that is fine. Walk to the next corner and turn it again.

steps.test: Walk to a place about a kilometre away that you have never walked to, using only the paper map and turning it at every corner.
steps.note: Pick the place on the map first: a park, a church, a bridge. Keep the phone in your pocket for safety, not for directions. At each corner, stop, turn the map, and choose. If you go wrong, walk back to the last place you were sure of. A grown-up is with any child and lets the child hold the map.

steps.test: Say which grid square your home is in, and find three places on the map from the grid references in its index.
steps.note: Many walking maps have numbered lines across and up. Read the number along the bottom first, then the number up the side; a square takes the numbers of the line on its left and the line below it. If your map has letters along one edge and numbers along the other, give the letter and number of the square. Street maps often have an index of streets with their squares at the back.

steps.test: Give a six-figure grid reference for one landmark, and have somebody find the landmark from your numbers alone.
steps.note: Split each side of the square into ten by eye. Across: the line number, then how many tenths across. Up: the line number, then how many tenths up. That points to a spot about a hundred metres across on most walking maps. If your map has no numbered lines, do this with the next rung instead, which works on every map in the world.

steps.test: Find your latitude and longitude on the phone map, send them to somebody, and have them find your exact spot.
steps.note: In most map apps, press and hold on your dot to see two numbers, such as 48.858, 2.294, which is the Eiffel Tower. They work on every map in the world, paper or phone. In an emergency, reading them out to your emergency number can bring help to exactly where you are, so practise finding them now, calmly, and try it without looking at these steps.

steps.test: Find a hill on a map with contour lines, and point to where its sides are steep and where they are gentle.
steps.note: Contour lines join places of the same height; the numbers on them are metres (or on some maps, feet) above the sea. Lines close together mean steep; lines far apart mean gentle; a circle in the middle is the top. A walking map has them, and the free website OpenTopoMap shows them for the whole world. A child can make a hill of play dough, slice it into layers with a thread, and draw round each layer on paper.

steps.test: Choose the gentler of two ways up a hill from the contour lines, walk up that way, and say whether you chose right.
steps.note: A hill in a park or at the edge of town with paths. The gentler way crosses fewer contour lines for its length. Walk up it, and if you can, come down the steeper way to feel the difference. Stay on paths. A grown-up is with any child.

steps.test: Draw a map of your street and the streets around it from memory, with a north arrow and a scale bar.
steps.note: Pencil and paper. Put in what a visitor would look for: the corners, a school, a bus stop, a big tree, your gate. Then use the phone map to check which way is north and roughly how far each street is, and fix your drawing. Give it to somebody at home and ask them to point to where you live on it.

steps.test: On the paper map, plan a walk of about five kilometres to somewhere you have never walked, writing every turn and how long each part should take.
steps.note: Choose a place with a reason to go: a viewpoint, a lake, a café, a friend's home. Write it as a list: 'left at the church, 10 minutes; footpath across the field, 15 minutes'. Add about ten minutes for every hundred metres of climbing, using the contour lines. Pick a shorter way back too, such as a bus or a different road.

steps.test: Walk the route you planned with only the paper map, and write the real time next to each part.
steps.note: Phone in the pocket, switched on, for safety. Tell somebody at home where you are going and when you expect to be back. At each turn, find it on the map before you take it. The difference between your planned times and the real ones is your own walking speed, which you now know. A grown-up is with any child.

steps.test: Plan a day out for other people on a paper map, with the route, the times and a stop for food, and then lead it.
steps.note: Family, friends, or a child's friends with their grown-ups. Use everything: the scale for distances, the contour lines for hills, your own walking speed for times, and a shorter way back if people get tired. Tell everybody the plan the night before. This is the end of the ladder: other people can follow you because you can read the map.

categories.name: Words and languages
categories.line: A new language, reading, books, handwriting, poems, stories, signing.

tracks.name: A new language
tracks.line: From saying hello and your name to a ten-minute conversation about your life with somebody who grew up speaking it.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can learn the same language together, and it works for any language you choose. It starts with the sounds, a few greetings and numbers, and saying who you are, then builds the words for your home, your food and your day. The middle adds questions, what you did yesterday and what you will do tomorrow, and the first short talks with other people. It ends with a ten-minute conversation about your life with somebody who grew up speaking it. Everything here can be done with free tools: free lessons and a free dictionary online, library courses, and people nearby or online who speak the language.

steps.test: Choose one language and one free way to learn it, and say 'Hello, my name is' and your name in it, out loud.
steps.note: Choose a language you will hear or use: a family language, the language of a place you want to visit, or one spoken by people near you. Free ways in: a language app with free lessons, free video lessons on a video website, a course borrowed from the library. Copy a recording of a real speaker so the sounds are right from the first day.

steps.test: Listen to the main sounds of the language, and copy each one out loud after the recording.
steps.note: Search for the name of the language and the word 'pronunciation', and choose a video by a speaker. Pay most attention to the sounds your own language does not have. If the language uses its own letters, such as Greek, Arabic or Japanese, learn the first five letters and their sounds now and add a few each week.

steps.test: Say hello, goodbye, please, thank you, sorry, yes and no without looking.
steps.note: Write the seven on a small card and read them aloud morning and evening for a few days. Test yourself by covering the card. If you already know these, say them on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Count from one to ten and back down to one, out loud.
steps.note: Say them on the stairs, one step each, or while laying the table. Counting backwards shows whether you really know them or are only saying a string of sounds. Numbers come up in every price, time and address, so they are worth having early.

steps.test: Say four sentences about yourself: your name, your age, where you live, and one thing you like.
steps.note: Use a free online dictionary or your lessons for the words, and keep the sentences short: 'I am ten. I live in a flat. I like football.' Write them down, then say them without the paper. These four sentences are the start of nearly every first conversation.

steps.test: Learn the words for ten things in your home, and put a paper label on each one.
steps.note: Door, table, chair, window, bed, cup, fridge, book, lamp, shoes. Small strips of paper and a bit of tape work fine. Say the word each time you touch the thing, and take the labels off after a week to test yourself.

steps.test: Learn five questions and how to answer each one: what is your name, how are you, where do you live, what is this, and how much is it.
steps.note: Write each question with a short answer underneath. Ask yourself the questions out loud and answer them. Notice how questions are made in this language: some change the order of the words, some only change the voice.

steps.test: Say your four sentences about yourself to another person.
steps.note: A family member counts, even if they do not speak the language; tell them what you said afterwards. A child and a grown-up learning together can take turns. Saying it to a real face is harder than saying it to the wall, which is why it is a rung.

steps.test: Count to a hundred in tens, then say five numbers somebody picks between one and a hundred.
steps.note: Ten, twenty, thirty and so on first, then the numbers in between. Some languages build numbers in an unusual way, such as French saying 'four twenties' for eighty; notice the pattern in yours. Ages, prices and bus numbers are good practice.

steps.test: Learn fifty everyday words over a week: food, family, weather and time.
steps.note: Seven or eight new words a day. Make small paper cards with the word on one side and a quick drawing on the other, and go through the pile each morning. Take out the cards you know every time, so you spend your time on the hard ones.

steps.test: Watch ten minutes of a children's programme or song in the language, and write down every word you recognise.
steps.note: Free video websites have children's programmes and songs in most languages. Children's programmes speak slowly and show what they mean. Do not stop to look words up; just catch what you can, and count the words at the end.

steps.test: Say five sentences about what you are doing today.
steps.note: 'I get up. I eat bread. I go to school. I see my friend. I read a book.' Use the words from rung ten. Say them to yourself while you do the thing, and write them down afterwards to check.

steps.test: Learn how to talk about the past with five common verbs, go, eat, see, do and say, and make one sentence with each.
steps.note: Your free lessons or a grammar page online will show the past forms. Make sentences about yesterday: 'I went to the shop. I ate soup.' If the language has several past forms, learn the one used most in everyday talk first.

steps.test: Write five sentences about your weekend, and have somebody who speaks the language correct them.
steps.note: A speaker you know, a teacher, or a free language-learning forum where speakers correct learners' writing; a grown-up helps a child post there. Write the corrections underneath in a different colour and read the correct version aloud. Every mistake corrected is a sentence you will not get wrong next time.

steps.test: Have a two-minute conversation in the language with another learner or a speaker.
steps.note: Ask each other the five questions from rung seven and answer with your sentences about yourself. Look for a conversation group at a library or community centre, or a free language-exchange website where you help each other. Anybody under sixteen does online exchanges with a grown-up in the room, and nobody gives out their address or school.

steps.test: Read a short children's story in the language and understand most of it.
steps.note: Free children's stories in many languages are online, and some libraries lend picture books in other languages. Read the whole story once without a dictionary, then look up only the words you needed to follow it. Tell yourself the story in your own language to check.

steps.test: Say three things you will do tomorrow.
steps.note: 'Tomorrow I will go to the park. I will cook dinner. I will phone my grandmother.' Your lessons will show how the future is made; some languages simply add a word for 'tomorrow' to the present. Say them tonight, then check the next evening what you really did.

steps.test: Watch a short video made for learners at normal speed, twice, and say in the language three things it was about.
steps.note: Search for the language and 'for learners' or 'easy', and choose a video of about five minutes with real people talking. The first time, just listen; the second time, catch the details. Watching with subtitles in the same language is allowed on the second go.

steps.test: Have a five-minute conversation with somebody who speaks the language well, about your day and what you did yesterday.
steps.note: The person from rung fourteen or fifteen, a speaker in your area, or a language-exchange partner. Ask them to speak a bit slowly and not switch into your own language. When you do not know a word, describe it with the words you have.

steps.test: Have a ten-minute conversation about your life with somebody who grew up speaking the language, and understand most of what they say.
steps.note: Your family, your work or school, what you like doing, where you would like to go. Mistakes are fine; ten minutes of staying in the language is the rung. That is the far end of this ladder; talking with speakers often is what keeps the language growing from here.

tracks.name: The old language of your place
tracks.line: From the language's own name to half an hour at a gathering of speakers, speaking only that language when you speak.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It is about the old or heritage language of where you live or where your family comes from: Irish, Welsh, Scottish Gaelic, Māori, Hawaiian, Basque, Yiddish, and many more. It starts with the language's own name, a few greetings and your own name, then the place names around you and what they mean, the words for family, and an old saying. The middle adds songs, stories and listening to speakers, and it ends with half an hour at a class, gathering or online group of speakers, speaking only that language when you speak. These languages carry the names of the land and the people, and every new speaker helps keep one alive.

steps.test: Find out the old language of where you live or where your family comes from, and learn to say its name in that language.
steps.note: Irish is Gaeilge, Welsh is Cymraeg, Scottish Gaelic is Gàidhlig, Māori is te reo Māori, Hawaiian is ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi and Basque is euskara. If there are several, choose the one that means most to you. Listen to a speaker saying the name on a free video and copy it until it sounds the same.

steps.test: Say hello, goodbye and thank you in the language, copying a recording of a speaker.
steps.note: Search for the name of the language and 'greetings'. Choose a recording by somebody who speaks it, and copy each word five times. Many of these languages have sounds your everyday language does not; take your time with those.

steps.test: Say in a full sentence your name and where you live.
steps.note: Your free lessons or a free online dictionary will show the pattern, such as 'I am Sam and I live in ...'. Some of these languages have their own form of common first names; find out whether yours has one. Write the sentence down and say it until you do not need the paper.

steps.test: Find out what the name of your town, area or street means in the old language.
steps.note: In many places, the names on road signs came from an older language underneath, and they often describe the land: a hill, a ford, a church, an oak wood. Search for the place name and the word 'meaning', or ask at your local library. If your family's language comes from somewhere else, find the meaning of a place name from there.

steps.test: Learn what five place names near you mean, and tell somebody while you pass them.
steps.note: Hills, rivers, villages, a road you use every day. Tell a child in the car or a friend on a walk: 'This place means the black pool.' If the place names near you did not come from this language, choose five from where your family came from and show them on a map.

steps.test: Count from one to ten in the language, and back down.
steps.note: Count stairs, spoons, or steps on a walk. Counting backwards shows you really know them. Some of these languages count in an unusual way, such as in twenties; notice whether yours does.

steps.test: Ask somebody at home how they are in the language, and answer when they ask you.
steps.note: Learn the question and two or three answers: well, not bad, tired. If nobody at home speaks it, teach them the question and the answers first; learning together is how many families bring these languages back. Do it every morning for a few days.

steps.test: Learn the words for ten things in your home, and put a paper label on each one.
steps.note: Door, table, window, bed, cup, bread, water, fire, book, shoes. Strips of paper and tape are all you need. Say the word each time you touch the thing.

steps.test: Learn the words for mother, father, grandmother, grandfather, sister, brother and friend, and say who is in your family.
steps.note: 'My mother is Ana. My grandfather is Tom.' If your family comes from the place the language belongs to, ask an older relative whether they remember words or family names in it. Write down anything they tell you, with who said it.

steps.test: Learn one old saying in the language, what each word means, and when people say it.
steps.note: Most of these languages have proverbs about weather, work, family or friendship. Search for the language and 'proverbs', and choose one short enough to remember. Say it at the right moment this week, and explain it to somebody.

steps.test: Every morning for a week, say in the language what day it is and what the weather is like.
steps.note: Learn the days of the week and five weather words: sun, rain, wind, cold, warm. Say them at the window before breakfast. Seasons and weather differ from place to place, so learn the words for the weather you actually get.

steps.test: Find out the story of the language in about ten lines: where it was spoken, what happened to it, and who speaks it now.
steps.note: Use a library book or two good websites and write it down in your own words. Some of these languages were once spoken by nearly everybody in a place, lost speakers, and are now growing again through schools and families. Knowing its story makes it easier to carry on learning it.

steps.test: Listen to ten minutes of radio, a video or a podcast in the language, and write down every word you recognise.
steps.note: Many of these languages have their own radio, television or online channels, often free to watch. Choose something for children or learners to begin with. Do not stop to look words up; count the words you caught at the end.

steps.test: Learn a short song or poem in the language, and say or sing it from memory.
steps.note: A lullaby, a children's song, or a short poem that people there know. Learn the meaning line by line first, then two lines a day. Songs are how many of these languages were passed down, and they help with the sounds too.

steps.test: Say five sentences about what you are doing today.
steps.note: 'I get up. I drink tea. I walk to school. I see my friend. I read.' Use the words from your labels and your family words. Say each one while you do the thing, and write them down afterwards to check.

steps.test: Read a short children's story in the language and understand most of it.
steps.note: Free children's stories are online for many of these languages, and some libraries lend books in them. Read it once without a dictionary, then look up only what you needed. Tell the story to somebody in your everyday language to check.

steps.test: Tell somebody in the language, in three sentences, what you did yesterday.
