steps.note: Your lessons will show how to talk about the past; learn went, ate, saw and did first. A learner at home, a speaker, or a voice message to somebody learning with you all count. Getting the meaning across is the rung; small mistakes are fine.

steps.test: Find a class, conversation group or online group of speakers and learners, and join in once, even if you mostly listen.
steps.note: Libraries, cultural centres, community halls and churches often host them; for a language spoken far from where you live, an online group is the way. Say your name and where you live in the language when you arrive. Anybody under sixteen goes with a grown-up, or joins online with a grown-up in the room.

steps.test: Have a five-minute conversation with somebody who speaks the language well.
steps.note: Somebody from the group on rung eighteen, an older relative, or a teacher. Ask them to speak slowly and not to switch into your everyday language. Talk about your family, your day and what you did yesterday.

steps.test: Spend half an hour at a gathering of speakers, and speak only that language whenever you speak.
steps.note: The group from rung eighteen, a language evening, a sports club or a church service held in the language, or an online gathering. Listening for most of it is fine; the rung is that every word you say is in the language. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Reading
tracks.line: From hearing the first sound in a word to reading a book you have never seen, aloud, with no help.
tracks.who: A child from about four with a grown-up; grown-ups learning
tracks.about: For a child from about four with a grown-up beside them, and for any grown-up who is still learning to read. It starts with sounds, not letter names: first hearing the sounds inside spoken words, then learning which letters make them, then pushing the sounds together to read a word. Letters and sound patterns come in small groups, each followed by real words and sentences to read, and it ends with a book you have never seen, read aloud from start to finish with no help. The rungs are for reading English, and ten minutes most days is plenty. A grown-up learner needs a helper too: a friend, a relative, or a volunteer, and many libraries and adult learning centres run reading help at no cost.

steps.test: Listen to your helper say five short words, and say the first sound of each one.
steps.note: Your helper says words like sun, map, dog, fish and tap, and you say 'sss', 'mmm', 'd', 'fff', 't'. No letters yet: this rung is only listening. Say each sound short, with no 'uh' on the end, so 'd' and not 'duh'. Your helper is a grown-up for a child, or a friend or tutor for a grown-up.

steps.test: Listen to your helper say the sounds of five words slowly, one sound at a time, and say each whole word.
steps.note: Your helper says 'c... a... t' and you say 'cat'. Good ones to start with: s-u-n, m-a-p, d-o-g, p-i-g, h-a-t. Still no letters: reading is this same pushing-together, done with your eyes later. If it is hard, your helper leaves shorter gaps between the sounds.

steps.test: Learn the sounds of the letters s, a, t, p, i and n, and say each sound when your helper points to the letter.
steps.note: Say the sound, not the name: s is 'sss', a is the sound at the start of 'ant', t is a short 't', p is a short 'p', i is the sound at the start of 'ink', n is 'nnn'. Your helper writes the six letters large on paper and points in a mixed-up order. Say the sounds the way people around you say them. You know this rung when you get all six right twice in a row.
how: Your helper writes s a t p i n on a sheet of paper.
They say each sound and you copy it.
They point in a mixed-up order and you say each sound.

steps.test: Read six words made from those letters by saying each sound and pushing the sounds together: sat, pin, tap, nap, tip, pan.
steps.note: Point under each letter as you say its sound, then say the sounds again faster until they make the word, just like on rung two. Your helper writes the words on paper, big and clear. If a word comes out wrong, go back to the first sound and try once more. Plenty more words work with these six letters: pat, tin, nip, sit.

steps.test: Learn the sounds of m, d, g, o, c and k, and say each one when your helper points to it.
steps.note: m is 'mmm', d is a short 'd', g is the hard sound at the start of 'got', o is the sound at the start of 'on'. The letters c and k make the same sound, the one at the start of 'cat' and 'kit'. Mix these six with the first six when your helper points, so the old ones stay fresh.

steps.test: Read ten words made from the twelve letters you know, sounding each one out.
steps.note: For example: dog, cat, mop, kid, map, pot, dig, cot, mat, got. Your helper writes them in a list and you read down it. Words you read quickly without sounding out still count; that is where reading is going.

steps.test: Listen to your helper say five words, and for each one say its sounds and point to the letters on a sheet.
steps.note: This is reading turned round, and it makes reading stronger. Your helper says 'map', you say 'm... a... p' and point to m, a and p on the sheet from rung three. A child who can hold a pencil can write the letters instead of pointing.

steps.test: Learn the sounds of e, u, r, h, b, f and l.
steps.note: e is the sound at the start of 'egg', u is the sound at the start of 'up', r is 'rrr', h is a soft breath, b is a short 'b', f is 'fff', l is 'lll'. Read a few words with them straight away: red, bus, hut, bed, fun, leg. Take two or three days over this rung if you need to.

steps.test: Learn the sounds of j, v, w, x, y, z and qu.
steps.note: j is the sound at the start of 'jam', v is 'vvv', w is the sound at the start of 'wet', y is the sound at the start of 'yes', z is 'zzz'. x makes two sounds together, 'ks', as at the end of 'box'. The letters q and u nearly always go together and say 'kw', as in 'quiz'. After this rung you know a sound for every letter.

steps.test: Learn to read five everyday words that do not follow the sounds: the, to, I, no and go.
steps.note: Some very common words cannot be sounded out, so you learn them by sight. Your helper writes each one on a small piece of paper; you read them in a mixed-up order until you get all five right without stopping. Keep the papers and mix them in with the later word lists.

steps.test: Read three short sentences made of sound-out words and those five sight words.
steps.note: For example: 'The cat is on the bed.' 'I got a red hat.' 'The dog can go on the mat.' Your helper writes them out. Point under each word as you read, and read the whole sentence again once you have worked out every word.

steps.test: Learn the sounds that two letters make together, sh, ch, th, ng and ck, and read ten words with them in.
steps.note: Two letters, one sound: sh as in 'ship', ch as in 'chip', th as in 'thin', ng as at the end of 'ring', ck as at the end of 'duck' (the same sound as c and k). Words to read: shop, fish, chin, much, this, moth, song, king, back, sock. Point under the two letters together, because they make one sound.

steps.test: Read ten words where two sounds sit side by side, like stop and milk, saying every sound.
steps.note: stop, frog, milk, jump, hand, best, crab, swim, lost, plan. Each letter still makes its own sound, so 'stop' is s... t... o... p. These words are longer, so take them slowly and push all the sounds together at the end.

steps.test: Learn ten more everyday sight words: he, she, we, me, be, was, you, they, said and my.
steps.note: Use small pieces of paper again and mix them with the first five from rung ten. Some of these nearly follow the sounds, and noticing which part is odd helps you remember them. You know this rung when you read all fifteen in a mixed-up pile without stopping.

steps.test: Learn the sounds ai, ee, igh, oa and oo, and read ten words with them in.
steps.note: ai as in 'rain', ee as in 'feet', igh as in 'night', oa as in 'boat', oo as in 'moon'. Words to read: rain, tail, see, green, high, light, coat, road, food, soon. oo sometimes makes the shorter sound in 'book' and 'look'; if one way does not make a word you know, try the other.

steps.test: Read one page of a first reading book aloud, sounding out any word you do not know.
steps.note: A first reading book uses only the sounds taught so far, and many libraries lend them at no cost. You can also find free printable ones online, or your helper can write five short sentences on a sheet about something in your day. If you already read pages like this, read one on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Learn the sounds ar, or, ur, ow, oi and er, and read ten words with them in.
steps.note: ar as in 'car', or as in 'fork', ur as in 'burn', ow as in 'cow', oi as in 'coin', er as in 'her'. Words to read: park, star, horse, short, turn, down, town, soil, boil, sister. ow can also say the sound in 'snow'; try both and choose the one that makes a word.

steps.test: Read ten words where an e on the end changes the sound in the middle, like cake and bike.
steps.note: Read 'cap', then 'cape': the e at the end makes no sound, but it makes the a say its own name. The same happens with the other vowels. Words to read: cake, game, bike, time, home, rope, cube, tube, late, five.

steps.test: Read a whole first reading book on your own over a few days, then tell your helper what happened in it.
steps.note: Read a few pages a day, aloud or quietly, choosing a book at the level of rung sixteen or a little harder. When you finish, tell your helper who was in it and what happened, in your own words. Understanding the story is the point: sounding out is how you get there.

steps.test: Read a short book you have never seen before aloud to somebody, from start to finish, with no help.
steps.note: Choose a short first reading book or picture book from a library or a friend's shelf that you have not read before. Your listener only listens; if you cannot read a word, sound it out, just as you have done since rung four. That is the far end of this ladder, and the Reading books ladder starts from here.

tracks.name: Reading books
tracks.line: From one page tonight to a whole book of about two hundred pages in one day.
tracks.about: For grown-ups, and for any child who can already read a chapter book on their own (the Reading ladder comes before this one). The climb starts with one page at bedtime and a book you actually want, then builds the habit a few days a week, then the length of a sitting, from ten pages to an hour, then a hundred and fifty pages in a day. It ends with a whole book of about two hundred pages read between getting up and going to bed. Nothing to buy: joining a public library is free in most places, and you can ask a library to get in a book it does not have on the shelf.

steps.test: Read one page of a book tonight before you sleep.
steps.note: Any book in the house counts: a novel, a cookbook, a book a child left lying about. One page is the whole rung, and reading on is allowed. If you already read in bed most nights, do it on purpose tonight and count it.

steps.test: Get one book you want to read and put it beside your bed.
steps.note: Want is the important word: not one you think you ought to read. Take it from your own shelf, borrow it from a friend, or get it free from the library. Putting it where you will see it at bedtime is half of this rung.

steps.test: Read ten pages of that book in one sitting.
steps.note: Ten pages is usually fifteen to twenty minutes. Sit somewhere you will not be interrupted and put the phone face down or in another room. If you stop at eight, read the last two before bed and count it.

steps.test: Read on three separate days in one week.
steps.note: Any amount on each day, even a page. Tie it to something you already do, like the first cup of tea or getting into bed. Tick the days off somewhere you can see them.

steps.test: Read for thirty minutes, count the pages, and write the number down.
steps.note: That number is your reading speed for this kind of book, and the rungs further up are measured against it. Do not hurry to make it bigger; read the way you normally read. Write the date beside it so you can compare in a couple of months.

steps.test: Read something every day for a week, even if it is one page.
steps.note: Seven days, no gaps. On a busy day one page before sleep keeps the week going. If you miss a day, start the seven again from the next day; nothing is lost.

steps.test: Read twenty-five pages in one sitting.
steps.note: At the speed from rung five, work out roughly how long this will take and put that time aside. A weekend morning or a quiet evening is ideal. Get up and stretch at the halfway point if you need to, but stay with the book.

steps.test: Finish the book you chose on rung two.
steps.note: If you no longer like it, you are allowed to stop and choose another one you want more. Then finish that one. Finishing a book is the rung, whatever the book and however long it took.

steps.test: Ask somebody who reads a lot what you should read next, and start it within a week.
steps.note: A friend who always has a book, a librarian, a bookseller, a relative. Tell them one book you liked and ask for something like it. Having the next book ready means there is never a gap after finishing one.

steps.test: Read fifty pages in one day.
steps.note: Split it however you like: twenty in the morning, thirty in the evening. A day off is easiest for the first go. If you are already past fifty pages a day, read fifty on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Read for a whole hour without stopping.
steps.note: Set a timer and put it out of sight so you are not checking it. Phone in another room, a drink beside you before you start. An hour is a good length to get properly into a book.

steps.test: Take your book out and read twenty pages somewhere other than your home.
steps.note: On the bus or train, on a park bench, in a café, in the library, in the car while waiting at a school gate. If it is cold, a library or a café is fine. Noticing that you can read in any spare twenty minutes is the point.

steps.test: Read a hundred pages in one day.
steps.note: At most speeds this is between two and four hours of reading, spread through the day. Choose a book you are enjoying and a day with nothing much in it. Plan three or four sittings with breaks for food and a walk.

steps.test: Read every day for a month without missing a day.
steps.note: Any amount each day, as on rung six, but for about thirty days. Keep the book with you, so a queue or a wait becomes a few pages. If you miss one, carry on the next day and add a day at the end.

steps.test: Read two books inside one month.
steps.note: Pick two you want to read before the month starts, so you are never stuck choosing. Shorter books are allowed; this rung is about keeping going. The library can have both ready for you to collect.

steps.test: Finish a book of a kind you never read.
steps.note: If you read stories, choose a history or a biography. If you read facts, choose a novel. Poetry, a play or a book of letters all count too. Ask a librarian for a good first one of that kind.

steps.test: Tell somebody about a book you finished, well enough that they ask to borrow it.
steps.note: Say what it is about in two sentences, then the one part you remember most, without giving the ending away. Then offer to lend it. If they ask for it, you have done the rung.

steps.test: Read a hundred and fifty pages in one day.
steps.note: The same plan as the hundred-page day, with one more sitting. Choose a book you are enjoying and want to keep reading, not the hardest one on the shelf. Short walks and proper meals between sittings help more than coffee.

steps.test: Read one book a week for four weeks in a row.
steps.note: Four books in about a month. Have the next one ready before you finish the one you are on. Choose books of a length you can honestly finish in a week at your speed from rung five.

steps.test: Read a whole book of about two hundred pages in one day.
steps.note: From getting up to going to bed, with meals, walks and rests in between. Choose a book you are looking forward to and a day with nothing else planned. Plenty of people do not believe they can do this until they have. Write the title and the date on the first page of your notebook.

tracks.who: Grown-ups, and children who read chapter books alone

tracks.name: Writing by hand
tracks.line: From how you sit and hold the pen to a one-page letter by hand that somebody reads without asking what a word says.
tracks.who: From about six; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a grown-up whose writing has gone untidy since keyboards will find it useful too. It starts with how you sit and hold the pen, then where each letter starts, then letters sitting properly on a line with even gaps between words. The middle adds joined letters, copying, and a quick timed test of how much you can write clearly. It ends with a one-page letter by hand that the person you give it to reads without having to ask what a word says. A pen or pencil and any paper is all it needs; lined paper helps, and you can draw lines with a ruler.

steps.test: Sit with both feet flat, the paper tilted, and the pen held lightly, and write your name three times.
steps.note: Hold the pen between your thumb and first finger, resting on your middle finger, a finger's width up from the tip, and do not squeeze. Tilt the paper a little so it lines up with your writing arm; if you are left-handed, tilt it the other way and keep your hand below the line you are writing. If you already write comfortably, sit and hold the pen this way on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Write the whole small alphabet, a to z, starting every letter in the right place.
steps.note: Where a letter starts decides whether it can be written quickly later. Most letters start at the top. The round letters c, a, d, g, o and q start just below the top on the right and go round to the left; e starts in the middle. Write slowly and check each one against a printed alphabet.
how: Write c, a, d, g, o, q: start near the top right, go round to the left.
Write l, i, t, u, y, j: start at the top, go down.
Write r, n, m, h, b, p, k: go down, then back up and over.
Write e, s, f, v, w, x, z last.

steps.test: Write the capital letters A to Z, then your full name with a capital at the start of each part.
steps.note: Capitals all stand the same height, as tall as the tallest small letters. Most start at the top. Check each one against a printed alphabet and write any you got wrong three more times.

steps.test: On lined paper, write 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' with every letter sitting on the line.
steps.note: This sentence has every letter of the alphabet in it. Small letters like a, e and o sit on the line; tall letters like b, d, h, k, l and t reach up; letters with tails like g, j, p, q and y hang below. No lined paper? Draw lines two finger-widths apart on plain paper with a ruler or the edge of a book.

steps.test: Write three sentences about your day with an even gap between every word.
steps.note: The gap between words is about the width of one small letter o; a child can put a finger down as a spacer. Words squashed together are the most common reason handwriting is hard to read. Look at the three lines when you finish and fix any gap that is too big or too small by writing that line again.

steps.test: Write the numbers 0 to 9 clearly, then a list of ten things with a number next to each.
steps.note: A shopping list works well: 6 eggs, 2 onions, 1 loaf. Numbers get misread more than letters, so make 1 and 7 look different, close the top of 4 or leave it open but always the same way, and give 9 a straight or curved tail every time. Ask somebody to read the list back to you.

steps.test: Write the fox sentence five times, circle the worst letter, and write that letter ten times on its own.
steps.note: Look for the one that leans the wrong way, sits off the line, or looks like a different letter. Write it ten times slowly, then write the whole sentence once more. Doing this once a day for a few days fixes letters faster than filling pages.

steps.test: Join the letters in five short words, in, an, it, up and us, writing each word three times without lifting the pen.
steps.note: Joining lets the pen travel from the bottom of one letter up to the start of the next, so you write faster with less effort. The line leaves the first letter at the bottom and slides up to where the next letter begins. Some countries teach joined writing and some keep letters printed; try it here, and if clear printed letters suit you better, keep them and use the later rungs to get quicker.

steps.test: Write the fox sentence joined, or in quick clear print, three times.
steps.note: Letters that do not join easily, like x, z and capitals, can stand apart; most joined writers leave some gaps. Keep the letters on the line and the gaps between words even, as on rungs four and five. Compare your third try with your first.

steps.test: Copy a paragraph of about fifty words from a book, clearly, and write down how many minutes it took.
steps.note: Any book in the house works: a story, a recipe, instructions. Read a few words, write them without looking back at the book halfway, then read the next few. Write the time at the bottom; you will use it on rung twelve.

steps.test: Write a short note by hand to somebody in your home and leave it where they will find it.
steps.note: Three or four lines: thank you for something, a plan for the weekend, or something you like about them. Put it on their pillow, a plate or a shoe. The test is that they read it without asking you what any word says.

steps.test: Copy another paragraph of about fifty words, clearly, and do it faster than on rung ten.
steps.note: Use a different paragraph of about the same length. Read a longer chunk each time before you write it, and keep the pen moving rather than going back over letters. If it is faster but hard to read, it does not count yet: clear first, then quick.

steps.test: Write half a page by hand every day for seven days.
steps.note: A diary of the day, a list of plans, a copied poem, a recipe: anything, as long as it is by hand. The back of an old envelope counts. If you miss a day, carry on the next day and add a day at the end.

steps.test: Write a one-page letter by hand to somebody outside your home, and post it or give it to them.
steps.note: A grandparent, a friend, an old teacher, a neighbour. Tell them a few things that have happened and ask them something. Handing it over costs nothing; posting it needs a stamp. The far end of this ladder is a whole page they read without having to ask what a word says.

tracks.name: Beautiful writing
tracks.line: From two pencils taped together to a quotation with a decorated capital, written well enough to hang on a wall.
tracks.who: From about nine; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about nine: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with two pencils taped together, which show how a broad pen makes thick and thin strokes, then guide lines, a pen held at one angle, and the italic small letters in families. Then come spacing, capitals, a first quotation and a better second one, a planned page and a decorated letter, and it ends with a quotation beautiful enough to hang on a wall. Cheap pens and pencils are fine: two taped pencils, a chisel-tip marker or an inexpensive italic pen does everything here. Beautiful writing is slow writing, and many people find ten minutes of it one of the calmest parts of the day.

steps.test: Tape two pencils together with their points level, and draw a row of zigzags and a row of circles without turning the pencils.
steps.note: Hold the pencils so the two points sit at a slant, and keep that slant the whole time. Where you move along the slant, the two lines come close together; where you move across it, they spread apart. That is exactly what a broad calligraphy pen does, and two pens taped together work too.

steps.test: Rule pairs of guide lines five pen-widths apart, and fill one line with downstrokes all the same length.
steps.note: Make five short sideways marks with your pen, one stacked on top of the next, and measure the height: that is how tall a small letter such as a, n or o will be. For taped pencils, a pen-width is the distance across both points. Rule the lines lightly in pencil with a ruler, and leave the same gap again above and below for tall letters and tails.

steps.test: Write a whole line of the letter o and a whole line of n with the pen held at the same angle all the way.
steps.note: Hold the flat edge of the pen at about halfway between flat and upright to the guide line. The pen makes the thick and thin parts for you; your only job is to stop it twisting. Check along the line: the thin parts of every letter should fall in the same places.

steps.test: Write a line each of i, l, t and j in italic, every letter leaning forward by the same small amount.
steps.note: Italic leans forward only a little, about as much as a clock's minute hand at one minute past the hour. Rule a few faint slanting lines across the page to keep every letter at the same lean. Italic is used on this ladder because it is quick to learn, easy to read and works with a cheap pen.

steps.test: Write a line each of n, m, h, r, b and p in italic, with the arch starting high up the downstroke.
steps.note: In italic the arch comes out of the downstroke about two-thirds of the way up, not from the bottom, which gives the letters their narrow shape. Look at a printed italic alphabet, from a library book or found online, to check each shape. Get n right first and the rest follow from it.

steps.test: Write a line each of a, d, g, q, u and y in italic, all built on the same narrow slanting oval.
steps.note: Each one starts at the top right of the oval and goes round to the left and down, then up again into a downstroke. Make u like an n turned upside down. If one letter looks wider than the others, its oval has usually become too round.

steps.test: Write the rest of the small letters, c, e, o, s, v, w, x, z, k and f, then the whole alphabet in one row.
steps.note: The whole row is the test: every letter the same height, the same lean and the same pen angle. Circle the three letters that look least like the others, write each one for a line, then write the alphabet once more.

steps.test: Practise italic letters for ten minutes a day for seven days, and date and keep every page.
steps.note: Each day, write one line of a letter family and one line of words that use it, such as minimum, button, quiet or daylight. If you miss a day, carry on the next day and add a day at the end. On the seventh day lay the first page beside the last and write down what has changed.

steps.test: Write the word minimum five times, changing only the spacing, and pick the one where the gaps look most even.
steps.note: Minimum is hard to space because it is nearly all upright strokes. Two straight strokes side by side need the most room, two round letters side by side the least, and a straight beside a round somewhere between. Even spacing is about how the gaps look, not measuring them with a ruler.

steps.test: Write the italic capitals A to Z, about one and a half times the height of the small letters, then your full name.
steps.note: Keep the capitals plain: the same pen angle, the same lean, no swirls yet. The round ones, C, D, G, O and Q, are wider than the others, and that is correct. Rule an extra guide line for the capital height.

steps.test: Write out a quotation of about fifteen words in italic with no mistakes in letters or spelling.
steps.note: Choose words you like: a line of a poem, a proverb, a sentence from a favourite book. Write it in pencil first to see where the lines break, rule your guide lines, then write it in pen. One mistake means starting that copy again, and that is part of the rung.

steps.test: Circle three faults in your quotation, then write it again with those three better.
steps.note: Faults to look for: a letter taller than its neighbours, a lean that changes, a word crowded against the next one. Put both copies side by side when you finish. The second being better, however small the difference, is the rung.

steps.test: Draw three small rough plans of a page for your quotation, and choose the one with the best space around the words.
steps.note: Draw three rectangles the shape of your paper, each about the size of a playing card, and draw lines where the words would go: centred, all on the left, or broken at different words. Leave a little more space at the bottom than at the top, which usually looks more settled. Mark the sizes of the plan you choose onto your real sheet.

steps.test: Draw the first letter of your quotation as a large decorated capital, and colour it in.
steps.note: Draw it about five small letters high in pencil, give it a double outline, fill it with colour and add a simple pattern round it such as leaves, dots or a border. Old handwritten books, many of them shown free online by museums and libraries, are full of these for ideas. Coloured pencils or felt-tips are enough.

steps.test: Write somebody's name beautifully on a card, with a decorated first letter, and give it to them.
steps.note: A name for a bedroom door, a place card for a meal, or a label for a book they own. Rule guide lines, write it in pencil, then in pen, and rub out the pencil once the ink is fully dry. Hand it over in person if you can.

steps.test: Write your quotation on its own page with your decorated capital and your chosen plan, well enough to hang on a wall.
steps.note: Use everything on this ladder: ruled lines, one steady pen angle, even spacing, the page plan from rung thirteen and the capital from rung fourteen. Write it twice if you need to and keep the better one. When it is hanging on a wall, yours or the wall of somebody you gave it to, this ladder is done.

tracks.name: Poems: learning them and writing them
tracks.line: From choosing one short poem to a poem evening at home where you say one by heart and read one of your own.
tracks.who: From about six; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, each with a poem that suits them. It starts with reading a few short poems aloud and choosing one you like, then learning it by heart, finding its beat, and saying it to one person slowly enough that every word is heard. Writing your own comes in small pieces alongside: a three-line poem, then four lines that rhyme, then eight lines you change until they sound right. It ends with a poem evening at home where everybody says or reads one, and you say one by heart and read one you wrote. Poems are free in any library and on many websites, and a poem learned by heart stays with you for years.

steps.test: Read three short poems aloud and choose the one you like best.
steps.note: Short means four to twelve lines. Some to look for: 'Who Has Seen the Wind?' by Christina Rossetti, 'Rain' by Robert Louis Stevenson, 'Hope is the thing with feathers' by Emily Dickinson, or a book of poems for children from the library. Choose the one whose sound you like, not the one you think is best. If you already have a favourite, read it aloud on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Learn the first four lines of your poem, and say them with the page turned face down.
steps.note: Read one line aloud three times, then say it without looking; add the next line the same way. Say all four together at the end. A small mistake is fine on this rung; say them again tomorrow morning and you will usually find they are still there.

steps.test: Clap the beat of those four lines as you say them.
steps.note: Most poems have a beat, like a song. Clap on the words or parts of words that sound strongest: 'WHO has SEEN the WIND?' Some poems do not have a steady beat; if yours does not, clap each line's strong words anyway and notice where the pauses fall.

steps.test: Learn the rest of your poem, and say the whole of it the next morning without the page.
steps.note: Add two lines a day, always saying the whole poem from the top. Saying it next morning is the test, because that is when you find out whether you really remember it. If a line goes missing, look once, then say the whole poem again.

steps.test: Say your poem to one person, slowly, with a short pause at the end of every line.
steps.note: Nearly everybody says a poem too fast the first time. Stand or sit facing them, take a breath, and leave a half-second at the end of each line. Ask them afterwards which line they remember; that tells you it was heard.

steps.test: Write a three-line poem about something you can see from a window: five syllables, then seven, then five.
steps.note: This shape is called a haiku, and it comes from Japan. A syllable is each separate sound you can clap in a word: 'window' has two, and 'the cat on the wall' has five. Write about one real thing you can see right now, such as rain on a car, a bird or a washing line. The count matters less than a clear picture.

steps.test: Choose a longer poem of sixteen to twenty-four lines, and learn it by heart over a week.
steps.note: 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' by Robert Frost has sixteen lines; 'The Tyger' by William Blake has twenty-four. A child might choose a funny poem of the same length. Four lines a day is enough, always saying the whole poem from the top.

steps.test: Say the longer poem standing up to two or more people.
steps.note: At a meal, after dinner, or on a video call to relatives. Tell them the name of the poem and who wrote it, then begin. Keep the pauses from rung five; if you lose a line, stop, breathe, and carry on from the next line you remember.

steps.test: Write four lines about something that happened this week, with the second and fourth lines ending in words that rhyme.
steps.note: Pick a small real thing: a dog that barked at you, a burnt piece of toast, a bus that came early. Write what happened in plain words first, then move the words around until lines two and four end in a rhyme, such as rain and again, or toast and most. Clap it to hear whether it runs smoothly.

steps.test: Copy five poems you like into a notebook by hand, one a day for five days.
steps.note: Any notebook or a few sheets stapled together. Write the title and who wrote it above each one. Copying a poem slowly shows you how it was built: where the lines break and which words were chosen. This becomes a book of your own to choose from later.

steps.test: Write eight lines of your own, read them aloud, and change at least one word that sounds wrong.
steps.note: About a person, a place or a day you remember well. Read it out loud: a word that makes you stumble, or sounds flat, is the one to change. Rhyme or no rhyme, both are allowed; keep a beat you can clap.

steps.test: Read your eight lines aloud to one person.
steps.note: Tell them first what it is about in one sentence, then read it slowly with the pauses you have practised. You do not need to ask what they thought; reading it aloud to somebody is the rung. If they say one line they liked, write that down.

steps.test: Learn a poem of about thirty lines by heart.
steps.note: 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat' by Edward Lear and 'If' by Rudyard Kipling are both a little over thirty lines. Use the notebook from rung ten to choose. Four or five lines a day for a week is plenty, saying the whole poem from the top each time.

steps.test: Hold a poem evening at home where everybody says or reads one poem, and you say one by heart and read one of your own.
steps.note: Tell people a few days ahead so each can choose a poem; a child can say a four-line rhyme. Sit in a circle, take turns, and clap after each one. You say your thirty-line poem and read your eight lines. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Sign language
tracks.line: From spelling your own name with your hands to a five-minute conversation in sign with a Deaf person, without using your voice.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. Learn the sign language used where you live, because sign languages differ from country to country: British Sign Language, American Sign Language and Auslan are three different languages. It starts with the finger-spelling alphabet and your own name, then everyday signs, family, numbers, and the way the face asks a question. The middle adds sentences about yourself and your day, watching signers at their own speed, and how to get a Deaf person's attention politely. It ends with a five-minute conversation in sign with a Deaf person, without using your voice. Free video dictionaries and lessons, many made by Deaf signers, are all it needs.

steps.test: Find the sign language used where you live, watch its finger-spelling alphabet on a free video, and spell your own name with your hands.
steps.note: Search for the name of your country and 'sign language alphabet'. Some sign languages spell with two hands, such as British Sign Language and Auslan, and some with one, such as American Sign Language. If you are left-handed, use your left hand where the video uses the right.

steps.test: Finger-spell the whole alphabet slowly, checking each letter against the video.
steps.note: Go through it in groups of five letters. Watch your hands in a mirror or on a phone camera, so you see what the other person sees. Letters that look alike are the ones to practise most.

steps.test: Sign hello, please, thank you, sorry, yes and no, copied from a video by a Deaf signer.
steps.note: Many free video dictionaries show each sign with a Deaf person signing it. Copy the hand shape, where the hand is, and how it moves. If you already know these, sign them on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Finger-spell three names to somebody learning with you, and read three names they spell to you.
steps.note: Spell slowly and hold each letter still for a moment. Reading finger-spelling is harder than doing it, which is why this rung needs two people. If nobody at home is learning, teach one person the alphabet first; a child and a grown-up can learn it together.

steps.test: Sign 'My name is' followed by your finger-spelled name, and 'Nice to meet you'.
steps.note: These are the first things you sign when you meet somebody. Some sign languages leave out small words like 'is'; copy the order the video uses. Look at the person's face, not your own hands, while you sign.

steps.test: Learn the signs for mother, father, sister, brother, baby, grandmother, grandfather, friend and family, and sign who is in your family.
steps.note: Use a free video dictionary for your sign language. Sign 'my mother' and point or finger-spell her name. Nine signs is a lot for one day, so take two or three days if you need them.

steps.test: Sign the numbers from one to ten, and back down.
steps.note: Number signs differ between sign languages, so use the video for yours. Sign your age, and the number of people in your home. Counting backwards shows you really know them.

steps.test: In front of a mirror, ask three questions in sign with the right face for each.
steps.note: In many sign languages the face is part of the grammar. A question with a yes or no answer usually has raised eyebrows; a question starting with what, where or who usually has the eyebrows drawn down. Find a video that shows this for your sign language, and copy the face as well as the hands.

steps.test: Learn the signs for what, where, who, when, how and why, and ask somebody their name and where they live.
steps.note: Use the face from rung eight with each one. The question sign often comes at the end of the sentence in sign; check the order on a video. A family member learning with you can answer.

steps.test: Learn ten everyday signs: eat, drink, sleep, work, school, home, go, want, like and help.
steps.note: Two or three a day from the video dictionary. Use them at home while you do the thing: sign 'eat' at dinner, 'sleep' at bedtime. Signs you use in real moments stay with you.

steps.test: Sign five short sentences about yourself, such as where you live, what you like and what you do in the day.
steps.note: The order of signs is often different from the order of words in speech, so find a learners' video with example sentences and copy its order. Keep each sentence short. Write the five in your own language first so you know what you want to sign.

steps.test: Film yourself signing those five sentences on a phone, watch it back, and fix one thing.
steps.note: Compare it with the video you learned from. Look at hand shapes, where your hands are, and your face. Film the sentences again with the one thing fixed and delete the first go if you like.

steps.test: Learn the signs for today, tomorrow, yesterday, morning, evening and the days of the week.
steps.note: Many sign languages show time by where the hand is: forwards for the future, back over the shoulder for the past. Check whether yours does. Sign the day each morning for a week to keep them.

steps.test: Sign three sentences about what you did yesterday to somebody learning with you, or film them and send them.
steps.note: 'Yesterday I went to school. I ate pasta. I saw my grandmother.' Use the time signs from rung thirteen and the everyday signs from rung ten. If nobody is learning with you, send the video to a friend or a learners' group.

steps.test: Watch a short video of a Deaf person signing at their own speed, twice, and say three things it was about.
steps.note: Look for videos in your sign language made for learners, or short news or stories signed by Deaf people. The first time, just watch the face and hands without stopping; the second time, catch details. Catching three things is the rung, even if much of it went past.

steps.test: Learn how to get a Deaf person's attention politely, and how to keep a conversation going when you do not understand.
steps.note: A small wave where they can see it, or a light tap on the shoulder, is usual; a quick flick of the room light is used too, to reach a whole room. Keep looking at the person's face while they sign, and learn the signs for 'again, please', 'slower, please' and 'I am learning'.

steps.test: Sign sixty signs you know without looking, while somebody says or points to each thing.
steps.note: Make a list of sixty from the rungs so far and a few more you need, like colours and food. The other person calls them out in a mixed-up order, and you sign each one. Put any you miss on a card and practise them that week.

steps.test: Have a two-minute conversation in sign with another learner, without using your voice.
steps.note: Ask each other names, where you live, who is in your family and what you did yesterday. When you do not know a sign, finger-spell the word or point. Keeping your voice off the whole time is part of the rung.

steps.test: Go to a sign-language class, Deaf club event or signing social, and introduce yourself in sign.
steps.note: Search for your sign language and 'social' or 'club' near you; many welcome learners. If there is nothing near you, an online signing group for learners counts. Anybody under sixteen goes with a grown-up. Sign your name, that you are learning, and 'nice to meet you'.

steps.test: Have a five-minute conversation in sign with a Deaf person, without using your voice.
steps.note: At the group from rung nineteen, or with a Deaf person you know who is happy to chat with a learner. Talk about yourself, your family and your week, and use 'again, please' when you need it. That is the far end of this ladder.

categories.name: Speaking and people
categories.line: Strangers, the stage, listening, hard things, humour, teaching.

tracks.name: Meeting people, part one
tracks.line: From a smile to a second conversation, in twenty small steps.

steps.test: Smile at three people you pass today, with your eyes on theirs for a second.
steps.note: That is the whole rung. Count them on your fingers. Most people look at the ground; you are already doing the rare thing.

steps.test: Say good morning, or hello, to three people you pass, and mean it.
steps.note: Out loud, not a nod. A dog walker, somebody at the bus stop, the person on the till. If one does not answer, that is theirs, not yours; the count is what you said.

steps.test: Thank somebody by their name today: read the badge, or ask it.
steps.note: "Thanks, Claire." The name changes the whole thing. If nobody wears a badge, "Sorry, what is your name?" is the rung.

steps.test: Ask a stranger the time, or whether this is the right road for somewhere.
steps.note: You already know the answer; the point is the asking. Pick somebody standing still. One sentence, a thank you, done.

steps.test: Ask somebody for directions to a place you can name, and listen to the whole answer.
steps.note: "Excuse me, do you know the way to the library?" Let them finish, say the first turn back to them, thank them.

steps.test: In a shop, ask where something is, then ask one more question about it.
steps.note: "Where is the honey?" then "Is that one any good?" You do not have to buy anything. A library, a market stall or a garden centre counts just as well as a shop.

steps.test: Give one honest compliment to a stranger.
steps.note: Their dog, their garden, their coat, how they handled a child. Say it and move on; do not wait for anything back. It has to be true.

steps.test: Keep a conversation with somebody you do not know going for one minute.
steps.note: Three questions will do it: where are you from, what brings you here, what is good round here. Bus stops, queues and dog walks are where these happen.

steps.test: Ask somebody for a recommendation: a book, a walk, a podcast, a place.
steps.note: "What is the best walk round here?" People love being asked. Write the answer down; you will use it on rung eighteen.

steps.test: Phone a shop or business and ask one simple question.
steps.note: Opening hours, or do they stock a thing. Under a minute. Write the question down before you dial. If you never phone anywhere, this is a bigger rung than it looks, and it counts double in your own book.

steps.test: Phone somewhere with a slightly bigger ask.
steps.note: Can they order something in, hold something for you, or could a small group visit one afternoon. You are enquiring, not demanding; a no is a fine answer and the rung is still done.

steps.test: Send a message to somebody whose work you enjoy, saying the one thing it did for you.
steps.note: An author, a maker, a podcaster, a musician. An email, or a message wherever they are. Three sentences, no ask, no link. Most of them are never told; you will be remembered.

steps.test: Send the same kind of message to somebody local.
steps.note: A shop, a club, a coach, a band, the people who run the market. "Just to say Saturday was brilliant, thank you for running it." Local people answer.

steps.test: Talk to a neighbour you have never properly spoken to.
steps.note: Their name, how long they have been here, that is enough. Over the fence, at the bins, at the car. Say your own name first.

steps.test: Ask somebody about themselves and listen for two minutes without talking about you.
steps.note: "How did you get into that?" Then only questions. Two minutes is longer than you think; most people have never been listened to that long.

steps.test: Ask a cheerful, slightly odd question somewhere, and see what happens.
steps.note: "Do you ever get people asking to bring a picnic in here?" or "Has anybody ever proposed in this shop?" Respectful, smiling, one minute. The discovery is that nobody minds and most people enjoy it.

steps.test: Do one useful thing for a stranger today.
steps.note: Hold a door, carry a bag to a car, tell somebody the queue is shorter next door, pass on a recommendation of your own. Small and real.

steps.test: Get one person's name and a way to reach them, with a reason.
steps.note: "I will send you that walk." "Let me know when the market is on again." A number, an email, a handle. The reason is what makes it natural. Somebody from rungs eight, nine or fourteen is ideal.

steps.test: Send what you said you would send, within a day.
steps.note: The walk, the book title, the photo. Short, friendly, no questions. This is the rung almost nobody does, and it is the one that makes you somebody people remember.

steps.test: Have a second conversation with somebody you met on this ladder.
steps.note: Same person, another day. "Did you try that walk?" If it goes well, suggest something: a coffee, the market, the children at the park, a talk you both want to hear. That is a friend beginning. Part two starts here.

tracks.about: Twenty small steps from a smile to a second conversation with somebody you did not know a month ago. Nothing here needs money or a café; the shop rungs need no buying and the calls take a minute. It is written for the person who finds this genuinely hard, so the first rungs are tiny and the later ones are where the friends come from.

tracks.name: Meeting people, part two
tracks.line: From one small thing together to a room full of people you brought together.
tracks.about: Part one got you talking to people; part two turns talk into friends. Reconnecting, inviting, hosting a pot of tea, organising the walk, running a small regular thing, and finally putting on an event of your own. Nothing needs money: tea at yours, a bench, a park. It ends by counting the people you could call on a bad day.

steps.test: Send a one-line message to three people you have not spoken to in a year.
steps.note: "Saw this and thought of you." "Hope the new job is going well." No ask, no catch-up demand. Some will answer this week; that is enough.

steps.test: Ask somebody you met in part one to do one small thing together.
steps.note: A walk, the market, a look at that view you were told about. Twenty minutes is plenty. Costs nothing.

steps.test: Learn and use the name of everybody you meet this week.
steps.note: Say it back straight away, use it once in the conversation, and once at the end. Write them down that night.

steps.test: Introduce two people to each other who did not know each other.
steps.note: "You two should meet, you both…" That sentence is the whole rung, and people remember who did it.

steps.test: Ask somebody for help with something small, and accept it.
steps.note: A hand with a box, a lift, an opinion, a recipe. Asking for help is the fastest road to a friend there is.

steps.test: Say yes to the next invitation you would normally turn down.
steps.note: The thing you would have made an excuse for. Go, stay an hour, then leave if you want to. Count it.

steps.test: Turn up at the same regular thing twice in one week.
steps.note: A run, a class, a market, a service, a group. The second time in a week is when you stop being a visitor.

steps.test: Have a proper conversation with somebody twenty years older than you, and one with somebody twenty years younger.
steps.note: Ask them about their week. Most people only ever talk to their own age.

steps.test: Ask three people what they are working on, and follow up with one of them within a week.
steps.note: "How did the thing go?" A week later, unprompted. Almost nobody does this; you will be remembered for it.

steps.test: Invite one person for a walk, a picnic, or a cup of tea at yours.
steps.note: Tea at home costs nothing. A sandwich on a bench is a picnic. The invitation is the rung, whether or not they can make it.

steps.test: Tell somebody something true about yourself that you usually keep back.
steps.note: Not a confession; a real thing. What you are afraid of, what you want, what you were like at fifteen. It is how acquaintances become friends.

steps.test: Be the one who organises: pick the day, the place, and the time, and tell people.
steps.note: Three people or more. Most gatherings never happen because nobody names a day. Name it.

steps.test: Host two or three people for a simple meal or a pot of tea.
steps.note: Soup and bread is a meal. A pot of tea and a packet of biscuits is enough. The place from the Home ladder is ready in ten minutes.

steps.test: Reconnect with an old friend and meet in person.
steps.note: Somebody you were close to and drifted from. A message, then a walk. The first ten minutes are awkward and then they are not.

steps.test: Do a favour that costs you an hour.
steps.note: Help somebody move something, mind a child, fix a bike, sit with somebody's parent. An hour of yours, given properly.

steps.test: Start a small regular thing and run it three times.
steps.note: A weekly walk, a game night, a Sunday call, a Saturday parkrun with two others. Three weeks running. After three it exists.

steps.test: Ask for an introduction to somebody you would like to meet, and follow it through.
steps.note: "Do you know anyone who…?" Then a message the same day it is offered, and the meeting inside a fortnight.

steps.test: Go somewhere alone where you know nobody, and leave with one name and a way to reach them.
steps.note: A talk, a club night, a fair, a class. The rung is the name, not the hour.

steps.test: Put on a small event of your own: six people or more.
steps.note: A picnic, a games afternoon, a talk in your front room, a walk with a flask at the end. You choose the day and you tell people. Then it happens.

steps.test: Write down the names of the people you could call on a bad day.
steps.note: If the list is longer than it was when you started part one, both ladders worked. That list is the point of all of it. From here a facilitator, and the network you build on purpose.

tracks.name: Talking to people you do not know
tracks.line: From ordering at a counter yourself, to a half-hour interview with somebody you had never met.
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, and for grown-ups; a child does every rung with a grown-up beside them. Where Meeting people is about making friends, this ladder is about asking people you do not know for what you need, and then for what they know: ordering, asking for things that are not on show, asking for advice, and finally interviewing people about their work. It ends with a half-hour interview with somebody you had never met, written up and given back to them. Everybody you meet knows something you do not; this is how you find out what.

steps.test: Order something for yourself at a counter, out loud, and say thank you at the end.
steps.note: A chip shop, a bakery, a café, a post office. A child does the talking while the grown-up stands beside them and says nothing. No money to spend: ask at the library to renew a book, or at a station for a timetable. If you do this every day already, do it today with your eyes on theirs and count it.

steps.test: Ask somebody at a desk or counter for something that is not on show.
steps.note: A free map at the tourist office, a glass of tap water, a library card form, a bus timetable, a spare bag. You are asking for something they have and you cannot see. A yes or a no both finish the rung.

steps.test: Ask the person serving you one question that is not about what you are buying.
steps.note: "Is it always this busy on a Saturday?" "Do you bake these here?" "How long have you worked here?" Pick a quiet moment, not when there is a queue behind you.

steps.test: Ask somebody working in a public place what they are doing today.
steps.note: A park keeper, a market trader setting up, a lifeguard, somebody painting railings, a librarian shelving. Only ask somebody who can stop safely: never somebody working near traffic or with machines running.

steps.test: Ask somebody at work two questions in a row, where the second comes from their first answer.
steps.note: They say they start at six; you ask what the first job of the morning is. The second question shows you were listening, and that is when people start to tell you more.

steps.test: Ask somebody who knows their trade for advice on a real problem you have, then follow it.
steps.note: A butcher on how to cook a cheap cut, a hardware shop on which screw holds a shelf, a garden centre on why a plant is dying, a librarian for a book like the last one you loved. You do not have to buy anything to ask.

steps.test: Go back to the person who gave you the advice and tell them how it went.
steps.note: "You told me to cook it slowly; it was brilliant." People who give advice almost never hear what happened. This is often the start of being known in a place.

steps.test: Ask somebody who has run a local shop or business for years how they started, and listen to the whole story.
steps.note: The shoe mender, the family butcher, the hairdresser, the person at the market stall. Pick a quiet time of day. Five minutes of their story is plenty.

steps.test: Write down ten questions you could ask anybody about their work or their life.
steps.note: "How did you get into this?" "What does a normal day look like?" "What is the hardest part?" "What do people get wrong about your job?" "What would you tell somebody starting?" Questions that cannot be answered with yes or no.

steps.test: Try three of your questions on somebody you already know, and mark which gave the longest answers.
steps.note: A grandparent, a neighbour, a friend's parent, a colleague. Cross out any question that got a one-word answer and write a better one.

steps.test: Ask somebody at work if they could answer three of your questions now, and ask them.
steps.note: "I am practising asking people about their jobs; could I ask you three quick questions?" A shop worker in a quiet moment, a librarian, a postal worker. If they say not now, thank them; asking was the rung, and try somebody else.

steps.test: Ask somebody if you could come back another day for ten minutes of questions about their work, and fix a time.
steps.note: Somebody from the last few rungs is ideal. Agree a day, a time and a place they choose, and write it down. A child asks with their grown-up there, and the grown-up is at the interview too.

steps.test: Do that ten-minute interview with your questions, and write notes as they talk.
steps.note: Arrive on time, say thank you first, ask your questions, and let them wander off the list if they want to; that is often the best part. Stop at ten minutes unless they want to keep going.

steps.test: Write up what they told you on one page, and give or send them a copy.
steps.note: Their name, their work, the best things they said, in your words. Let them correct anything. Very few people have ever had their story written down.

steps.test: Ask somebody whose work you know nothing about for twenty minutes of questions, and fix a time.
steps.note: A farmer, a bus driver, a nurse, a vet, a baker who starts at four in the morning, a boat builder. Ask through somebody you know, or at their place of work. A no is fine; ask the next one.

steps.test: Do the twenty-minute interview, and ask their permission before you record or write it down.
steps.note: "Is it all right if I take notes?" A phone can record the sound if they agree. Use your questions, then ask one you had not planned, about the part that surprised you.

steps.test: At the end of an interview, ask "Who else should I talk to?", and ask them to introduce you.
steps.note: People almost always know somebody. Ask for one name and whether they would send a message or tell that person you will be in touch.

steps.test: Interview the person you were introduced to, somebody you had never met, for half an hour, and give them a written copy.
steps.note: Fix the time, bring your questions, write it up afterwards and send it to them, and a note of thanks to whoever introduced you. That is the far end of this ladder: you can walk up to a stranger and come away knowing their story.

tracks.who: From about eight, with a grown-up beside a child

tracks.name: Standing up in front of people
tracks.line: From reading one page aloud in an empty room, to a fifteen-minute talk to thirty people, with questions at the end.
tracks.who: From about eight; a grown-up arranges a child's audiences
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, and for grown-ups; for a child the audiences are family, class and club, and a grown-up arranges the later rungs. This is prepared speaking: a talk you have written and practised, given to people sitting and listening. It starts with reading one page aloud to an empty room, then to one or two people, then a one-minute talk from a card. In the middle it builds a five-minute talk with a real opening, pauses, a voice that reaches the back, and a way to carry on when something goes wrong. It ends with a fifteen-minute talk to thirty people, with questions at the end.

steps.test: Read one page of a book aloud, standing up, in an empty room, slowly enough that every word is clear.
steps.note: Any page of any book: a story, a recipe, a newspaper article. Nerves make everybody speed up, so read slower than feels right. If you read aloud often, read standing today and count it.

steps.test: Record yourself reading the same page on a phone, listen back once, and write down one thing to change.
steps.note: Too fast, too quiet, dropping the ends of sentences, a voice that stays on one note. Most people dislike their recorded voice at first; listen for the one thing, not the sound of it. With no phone, read it to somebody and ask them for the one thing instead.

steps.test: Read a page aloud, standing, to one or two people at home, fixing the thing you wrote down.
steps.note: A partner, a parent, a child, a grandparent on a video call. Ask them afterwards whether they heard every word.

steps.test: Read aloud to somebody standing still, feet apart, hands resting, and ask them to tell you each time you move.
steps.note: Swaying, shifting from foot to foot and fiddling with hands all make people watch you move instead of listening. Hold the page in one hand if you need to. Standing still feels strange at first and looks calm from the outside.

steps.test: Choose a subject you know well, and write three points about it on a small card.
steps.note: How to look after a dog, the best walk near you, how your job works, a game you love, a trip you took. Three short points, a few words each, big enough to read at arm's length. The back of an envelope works as well as a card.

steps.test: Talk for one minute from your card, standing, to an empty room, with a timer.
steps.note: Say each point and give one example for it. If you finish early, add another example; if you run over, cut. Do it three times.

steps.test: Give that one-minute talk to one or two people, looking at each of them in turn.
steps.note: Look at one person for a sentence, then the next. Glance at the card only between points. Ask them what they remember; it tells you which point they took in.

steps.test: Write a first sentence for your talk that is not "Hello, my name is", and a last sentence that ends it clearly.
steps.note: Start with a question ("Who here has ever been lost?"), a surprising fact, or a very short story. End with the one thing you want people to remember, then "Thank you." Write both out in full; they are the two sentences worth learning by heart.

steps.test: Give a two-minute talk to three or more people, with your new first and last sentences.
steps.note: Family after a meal, friends, a few people at a club. Stand where everybody can see you. Say your first sentence, then look up before you go on.

steps.test: In a talk, leave a pause of three full seconds after your most important sentence.
steps.note: Count three in your head. It will feel far too long to you and sound right to them. The pause is what tells listeners that sentence mattered. Give the two-minute talk again with the pause in it.

steps.test: In a hall or a big room, speak until a person standing against the far wall hears every word without you shouting.
steps.note: A school hall, a church hall, a community centre, a large room at home with the doors open, or outdoors across a garden. Breathe in low, stand tall, and aim your voice at the back wall, not the floor. Ask them to put a hand up if a word goes missing.

steps.test: Read something aloud to a group outside your home.
steps.note: A reading at a club or a place of worship, a story to younger children at a library session, a poem at a class, a notice at a meeting. Use everything so far: slow, still, heard at the back, a pause. Ask the person running it beforehand whether you may.

steps.test: Plan a five-minute talk on paper, then practise it aloud three times, timing each one.
steps.note: Pick a subject you know or want to find out about. Aim for about five minutes; people nearly always run long on the day. Put your three points on one card.
how: An opening sentence.
Three points, each with one example.
A closing sentence, then thank you.

steps.test: Practise the five-minute talk with somebody who interrupts you on purpose twice, and carry on each time from where you stopped.
steps.note: They drop a book, their phone rings, or they ask "sorry, what?" in the middle of a sentence. Pause, glance at your card, and pick up the sentence you were in. Something going a bit wrong happens at almost every real talk, and practising it takes most of the fear away.

steps.test: Give the five-minute talk to five or more people, then take questions for two minutes.
steps.note: Before the talk, write the three questions you are most likely to be asked and a short answer to each. Repeat each question out loud before you answer, so everybody hears it. Keep answers short.

steps.test: Ask two people from that audience for one thing that worked and one thing to change, and make the change in your notes.
steps.note: "What is one thing that worked, and one thing I should change?" Write down both answers exactly, without arguing. Change your talk before you give it again.

steps.test: Offer a ten-minute talk to a group that has meetings, and fix a date.
steps.note: A club, a class, a youth group, a care home's afternoon, a local history society, a team meeting at work, a school assembly for a child with their teacher's say-so. Say what the talk is about in one sentence. If the first says no, ask the next.

steps.test: Give a ten-minute talk to fifteen or more people, with one card of notes, and take questions.
steps.note: Extend your five-minute talk or write a new one, and practise it aloud three times first. Arrive early and stand where you will speak before anybody comes in. Use the interruption practice if anything goes wrong.

steps.test: Plan a fifteen-minute talk, practise it aloud three times, and give it once to two or three people at home.
steps.note: Use the changes from rung sixteen and what you learned at rung eighteen. Time every practice. Ask your home audience where it felt slow, and cut there.

steps.test: Give a fifteen-minute talk to thirty or more people, with one card of notes, and take questions at the end.
steps.note: The group from rung seventeen may invite you back, or offer the talk to a bigger one: an assembly, a society meeting, a larger club night. That is the far end of this ladder: a room of thirty listening to you, and you able to answer what they ask.

tracks.name: Listening
tracks.line: From putting your phone down when somebody talks, to helping somebody reach their own answer with only questions.
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with the plain things (phone down, face the person, let them finish) and moves to saying back what you heard, asking instead of telling, and staying quiet when somebody is upset. The last rungs are listening to people you disagree with, and helping somebody think a real decision through using nothing but questions. Being properly listened to is rare, and the people who can do it are the people others come back to.

steps.test: Put down whatever is in your hands and turn to face the next person who talks to you.
steps.note: Your phone, the remote, a book, a pen. Turn your shoulders, not just your head, and look at them until they have finished. That is the whole rung, and it changes the conversation more than you would expect.

steps.test: Let somebody tell you about their day, and say nothing until they have stopped.
steps.note: At tea, in the car, on the walk home from school. Nods are allowed; words are not. If you live alone, ring somebody and ask about their day. If you find you already do this, do it on purpose tonight and count it.

steps.test: Let somebody finish every sentence for a whole conversation, even when you know how it ends.
steps.note: Catch yourself when you want to jump in and finish it for them. Wait for the full stop. A conversation of five minutes is enough.

steps.test: Listen to a short piece on the radio or a podcast, then say its three main points out loud.
steps.note: Pick something three to five minutes long: a news item, a talk, a story. Listen once, no rewinding, then say the three points to the room or to somebody nearby. This is the practice for the next rung, without a person waiting on you.

steps.test: Say back what somebody told you, in your own words, and ask "Have I got that right?"
steps.note: "So the bus was late and you missed the start, have I got that right?" If they correct you, say the corrected version back. Getting it right on the second go still counts.

steps.test: When somebody tells you something, ask one question about it instead of telling a story of your own.
steps.note: They say they went to the beach; you ask which beach, not tell them about your beach. Wanting to tell your own story is normal. Noticing the moment you want to is half of this rung.

steps.test: Keep somebody you know talking for five minutes, using only questions about what they have just said.
steps.note: A parent, a friend, a brother or sister. "What happened then?" "Why do you think that was?" "What was the best bit?" Use a timer if it helps. If you did the two minutes in Meeting people, this is the same thing, longer, with somebody you know.

steps.test: Notice when somebody has stopped listening to you, and finish what you are saying in one sentence.
steps.note: The signs: they look away, check a phone, say "mm" a lot, start moving. When you see one, finish your point in a sentence and ask them something. Then it is their turn.

steps.test: Listen to a talk of about thirty minutes, then write down its main points from memory.
steps.note: A lecture online, a sermon, a talk at the library, a long radio programme. No notes while you listen. Three to five points afterwards is a good result.

steps.test: Ask somebody close to you how they are, and if they say "fine", ask once more and wait.
steps.note: "Fine, and how are you really?" Then say nothing for a few seconds. Most of the time it is fine, and that is good to know. Sometimes the second answer is the real one.

steps.test: Listen to somebody who is upset until they have finished, without giving any advice.
steps.note: A friend after a bad day, a child whose game went wrong, a parent who is tired. No "you should", no "at least". "That sounds hard" and "What happened?" are enough. The urge to fix it is kind, and it is also what stops people talking.

steps.test: Ask somebody "Do you want help with this, or do you want me to listen?", and do what they choose.
steps.note: Use it the next time somebody brings you a problem. If they want help, help. If they want you to listen, the last rung was the practice.

steps.test: Listen to somebody who disagrees with you about something that matters to them, all the way through, without interrupting.
steps.note: Pick something real but not bitter: whether children should have phones, which school is best, whether the town needs a new road, which team is better. Your turn to talk comes after. Do not argue it back in your head while they speak; that is not listening.

steps.test: Say their side back so well that they say "Yes, that is what I mean."
steps.note: Same person, or another disagreement. You do not have to agree with it; you have to say it fairly. If they say "not quite", try again. When they say yes, the rung is done.

steps.test: When two people are disagreeing about something small, say each side back to them fairly, without taking a side.
steps.note: Where to go on Saturday, what to watch, whose turn it is. "So you want the park because it is dry, and you want the cinema because you have been waiting all week." Small things only; a serious row is for grown-ups to handle, not for this rung.

steps.test: Let somebody talk through a small problem for ten minutes while you ask only questions, until they say what they will do.
steps.note: What to make for tea, how to fit in a job, what to say to a friend. Questions like "What have you tried?" and "What would make it easier?" No suggestions. It feels slow; that is fine.

steps.test: Help somebody think through a real decision for twenty minutes, using only questions, until they tell you their next step.
steps.note: A job, a move, a course, a hard conversation they need to have; for a child, which club to join or how to make up with a friend. "What matters most to you here?" "What would you do if you were not afraid of getting it wrong?" "What is the first thing you could do?" The answer is theirs, and that is why they will act on it. That is the far end of this ladder.
how: Ask what the decision is, and what they have thought of so far.
Ask what matters most, and what worries them.
Ask what they could do first.
Say their next step back to them, and stop.

tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side

tracks.name: Saying the hard thing
tracks.line: From a two-sentence apology, to calmly saying the thing a whole group has been avoiding.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child can practise the early rungs with their own family. It starts with the plain ones: a real apology with no "but", saying no kindly without an invented excuse, and saying "I was wrong". Then it moves to hearing criticism without defending yourself, disagreeing with one calm reason, giving honest feedback, and writing down and then having a conversation you have been putting off. It ends with calmly saying the thing a whole group has been avoiding, and suggesting a way forward. Every rung is done kindly; the aim is fewer silent grudges and more honest, warm relationships.

steps.test: Think of one thing you did this week that upset somebody, and write an apology of two sentences: what you did, and what you will do instead.
steps.note: "I snapped at you when you asked about dinner. Next time I am tired I will say so instead." Name the thing plainly, with no excuse and no "if you were upset". If nothing comes to mind, write one for the last small thing, like being late or forgetting to reply.

steps.test: Say that apology to the person, with no "but" in it.
steps.note: "But" cancels whatever came before it: "Sorry, but you were annoying me" is not an apology. Say your two sentences, then stop and let them answer. A message is fine if you cannot see them; in person is better.

steps.test: Over the next week, do what you said you would do instead, without mentioning it.
steps.note: The apology is the promise; this is keeping it. If you slip once, say so quickly and carry on. Tick the rung at the end of the week.

steps.test: Say no to the next small request you do not want to do, kindly and in one sentence.
steps.note: "No, thank you, not this time." A lift you cannot give, a club you do not want to join, a second helping. Smile, and do not say it three different ways. For a child, practise with a grown-up at home first.

steps.test: Say no without making up an excuse.
steps.note: "I would rather not" is enough. An invented reason ("I am busy that day") invites the other person to solve it for you. The truth, said kindly, is easier to keep up. If you say this one already, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Tell somebody "I was wrong about that", naming the thing, on the same day you realise it.
steps.note: "I said the shop shut at five. I was wrong, it is six." Start with small facts; they are practice for bigger things. No excuse after it.

steps.test: Ask somebody close to you, "What is one thing I could do better?", and answer only "Thank you".
steps.note: A partner, a parent, a brother or sister, a friend, a colleague. Do not explain, defend or give your side, even if it feels unfair. Thinking about it later is allowed; arguing now is not.

steps.test: Do that one thing better for a week, then tell the person you tried.
steps.note: "You said I interrupt. I have been trying not to this week." You do not need to ask whether it worked. The telling shows them their honesty was safe with you.

steps.test: Give somebody honest feedback on something they made or did: one thing that works and one clear thing to change.
steps.note: A drawing, a meal, a piece of work, a speech. "The opening made me laugh. The middle part was hard to follow; could you cut it shorter?" Be specific in both halves, and ask first: "Would you like my honest thoughts?"

steps.test: Disagree with somebody about something small, out loud and calmly, with one reason.
steps.note: "I see it differently: I think the park is better, because it is dry." Which film, which route, whether it will rain. Keep your voice the same as for any other sentence. You do not need to win; saying it is the rung.

steps.test: Disagree politely with somebody older than you or in charge, giving one reason and asking one question.
steps.note: A parent, a teacher, a manager, a coach. "I do not think that will work, because the room is too small. Could we try the hall?" Pick a calm moment, not in the middle of an argument.

steps.test: Write down, in three sentences, a hard thing you need to say to somebody: what you have noticed, how it affects things, and what you would like.
steps.note: "The last three times we met, you arrived half an hour late. I end up waiting on my own and feeling a bit silly. Could you text me if you are running late?" Facts, not labels: "late three times", not "you are rude".

steps.test: Say it to them kindly, then listen to their side all the way through.
steps.note: Choose a private moment. Say your three sentences, then stop. They may have a reason you did not know about. The rung is done when both of you have been heard, whether or not anything changes yet.

steps.test: Write down the conversation you have been putting off longest, and have it within a week.
steps.note: Money you lent, a job that keeps falling to you, something said that hurt. Use the three-sentence shape. If it is with somebody who could harm you, do not do it alone: talk it over with somebody you trust first, and choose a safe place.

steps.test: Go back to somebody you have fallen out with, even a little, and be the first to try to put it right.
steps.note: "I am sorry for my part in the other day. Can we start again?" Say sorry for your part only; you cannot apologise for theirs. If there is nobody, do this after the next small disagreement, within a day.

steps.test: Speak up with one calm sentence when somebody is being left out, talked over or unfairly blamed.
