steps.note: "Wait, Sam was about to say something." "That was not Mia, she was with me." Only where it is safe; if anybody is in danger, get help from somebody in charge or ring your emergency number instead.

steps.test: At a meeting or a family table, calmly say the thing everybody has been avoiding, and suggest one way forward.
steps.note: "We keep planning the holiday and never booking it. Shall we each say one date that works, now?" Or the chores nobody does, the club that is running out of money. Say it as a fact, suggest one next step, then let others speak. This is the far end of the ladder.

tracks.name: Storytelling
tracks.line: From telling somebody what happened today, to keeping ten or more people listening to a story told from memory.
tracks.who: From about six; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with telling what happened today in order, then true stories with a beginning, a middle and an end, then made-up stories where somebody wants something and something is in the way. Along the way come pauses, voices, a story learned from memory and a true story from your own family. It ends with a story told from memory to ten or more people, with everybody listening to the end. Stories are how people have passed on what matters for as long as there have been people, and anybody can learn to tell one well.

steps.test: Tell somebody what happened to you today, in the order it happened, in under two minutes.
steps.note: Start with where you were, then what happened, then how it ended. At dinner, in the car, on a phone call. If you tend to jump about, say "first", "then" and "in the end" out loud to keep the order.

steps.test: Tell a short true story with a clear beginning, middle and end, and stop as soon as it has ended.
steps.note: The time the dog got out, the day you got lost, a surprise that went wrong. Beginning: where and who. Middle: what happened. End: how it turned out. Then stop; do not add "anyway, so yes".

steps.test: Retell a story everybody knows, without the book, in under three minutes.
steps.note: The Tortoise and the Hare, Cinderella, a folk tale from your own family's tradition, the story of a film you love. Getting the order right from memory is the whole rung. A child can tell it to a grown-up, and a grown-up to a child.

steps.test: Make up a story out loud about three objects in the room, and record it on a phone.
steps.note: Pick three things you can see, such as a spoon, a shoe and a clock, and let them all matter in the story. Record it so nobody needs to be there. No phone? Tell it out loud to yourself and count it.

steps.test: Listen back to your recording and write down one thing to change.
steps.note: A part that went on too long, an ending that was not clear, lots of "um". Only one thing. Tell the story again with that change, and notice the difference.

steps.test: Tell a made-up story in which somebody wants something, and something is in the way.
steps.note: A mouse wants the cheese and the cat is asleep beside it. A girl wants to win the race and her shoe breaks. Nearly every story ever told works this way: somebody wants something, something is in the way, and the story is how it turns out.

steps.test: In the next story you tell, stop for a slow count of two just before the most important moment.
steps.note: "She opened the box, and inside was..." one, two "...a tiny grey kitten." Watch your listener lean in during the pause. That is the pause working.

steps.test: Tell a story with at least two characters, and give each of them a different voice.
steps.note: A deep slow voice for the giant, a quick high one for the mouse. Voices do not need to be good impressions, just different enough that the listener knows who is speaking without being told.

steps.test: Tell a younger child a bedtime story without a book, and keep them listening to the end.
steps.note: Keep it short and gentle, with one character they can picture and a happy ending. If they ask questions, answer inside the story. A child climbing this ladder can tell one to a younger brother, sister or cousin, or to a grown-up at bedtime.

steps.test: Ask somebody older in your family for a true story from their past, and ask two questions to get the details.
steps.note: "What was the naughtiest thing you did at school?" "How did you and Grandad meet?" Then ask "What did it look like?" and "What happened next?" If you have no older relative nearby, ring one, or ask an older friend or neighbour.

steps.test: Tell that family story to somebody else, with the details you learned.
steps.note: Say whose story it is at the start: "This happened to my gran." Keep the details that make it real, such as the name of the street or the colour of the bike. Tell the person it came from that you told it; most people are glad to hear it.

steps.test: Tell a round-the-table story with two or more people, each adding one sentence in turn until it ends.
steps.note: You start: "Once there was a baker who could not stop sneezing." The next person adds a sentence, and so on. Your job as the storyteller is to steer it towards an ending when it has gone round a few times. Good for a meal or a long journey.

steps.test: Learn a folk tale by reading it three times, then tell it from memory to somebody.
steps.note: Any tradition in the world: Anansi and the pot of wisdom, the Pied Piper, Momotaro the peach boy, Stone Soup. Your library will have a book of them. Do not learn the words; learn the order of what happens, and tell it in your own words.

steps.test: Tell the same story to two different people, and make the second telling better by one change you chose.
steps.note: Cut a slow part, add a pause, open with the most exciting moment instead of the weather. Decide the change before the second telling. It still counts if the second telling does not feel better; you tried something on purpose.

steps.test: Tell a story that makes your listeners laugh at a point you planned in advance.
steps.note: Choose the funny moment before you start, build up to it, pause, then say it plainly. Kind stories only: laugh at what happened, not at a person. A true story from your own life is the easiest place to start.

steps.test: Tell a story that makes your listeners go completely quiet at a point you planned in advance.
steps.note: A moment of danger, a surprise, a sad or tender ending. Slow down, speak more softly, and leave a silence after the moment. Choose a story that suits the listeners' ages.

steps.test: Tell a story for five minutes to three or more people, from memory, without being interrupted.
steps.note: The folk tale or the family story, made a little longer. Ask first: "Can I tell you a story?" Sit or stand where everybody can see your face. If somebody interrupts, smile, answer briefly, and carry on.

steps.test: Teach a younger person the three parts of a story, and listen while they tell one of their own.
steps.note: Somebody wants something, something is in the way, and how it turns out. Help them with one question if they get stuck, and otherwise say nothing until they have finished. Then tell them the best part of it.

steps.test: Tell a story from memory to ten or more people, and keep everybody listening to the end.
steps.note: A family gathering, a class, a club, a campfire, a birthday. Five to ten minutes, a story you have told at least twice before. Watch the faces as you go; if people start to look away or fidget, move to the next exciting part. This is the far end of the ladder.

tracks.name: Being funny
tracks.line: From one clean joke learned word for word, to five minutes of your own kind, funny stories told to a group of ten or more.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with one joke learned word for word and told with a pause in the right place, moves to noticing what really makes people laugh, telling funny things that happened to you, and writing jokes of your own. It ends with five minutes of your own funny stories told to a group of ten or more. One rule runs through every rung: no joke ever makes fun of a real person, and every joke is one you could tell in front of a grandparent and a small child at the same time.

steps.test: Choose one short clean joke and say it out loud until you can tell it word for word.
steps.note: For example: "Why did the scarecrow win a prize? Because he was outstanding in his field." Find one in a joke book from the library, or ask somebody for their favourite. Say it five times. Check it passes the rule for this whole ladder: fine to tell to a grandparent and a small child at once.

steps.test: Tell that joke to somebody, with a short pause just before the last line.
steps.note: Set it up, stop for one beat, then say the last line clearly and do not laugh first. The pause is most of the skill. If they do not laugh, the rung still counts; you told it properly.

steps.test: This evening, write down three things that made somebody laugh today.
steps.note: A face somebody pulled, a word said wrong, the dog stealing a sock, something on the radio. Write what it was, not whether it was clever. Most laughs come from surprise and from things everybody recognises.

steps.test: Learn five clean jokes and tell one a day to five different people.
steps.note: Keep them on a card in your pocket until you know them. Notice which one gets the biggest laugh, and which one you tell best. Both are useful to know.

steps.test: Tell a joke that gets no laugh at all, then smile and carry on talking.
steps.note: It will happen on its own if you keep telling jokes; count the first time it does. "Well, I liked it" and a smile is all you need. Everybody who is funny has told jokes that got silence.

steps.test: Tell somebody a funny thing that really happened to you, and keep the funniest part for the very last sentence.
steps.note: For example, the day you searched the house for your glasses while wearing them. Tell it in order, leave out anything that does not help, and stop straight after the funny part. Do not explain it.

steps.test: Make a small joke about a mistake you made today, not about anybody else.
steps.note: "I put the milk in the cupboard and the cereal in the fridge. The cereal was very cold." Laughing at your own small mistakes helps other people relax. Keep it light; this is not about saying bad things about yourself.

steps.test: Say one funny thing you notice in the moment, out loud, after checking it is kind.
steps.note: The check is quick: would the person it is about laugh too? If the answer is no, or not sure, keep it in. If yes, say it instead of saving it for later.

steps.test: Write down ten things you find funny, and one sentence on what most of them have in common.
steps.note: A scene from a film, a comic strip, a family story, a comedian, a funny book. What they share might be surprise, somebody being very serious about something silly, or a thing going wrong slowly. That is the kind of funny that suits you.

steps.test: Write one joke of your own: a set-up, then a last line that surprises.
steps.note: Start from something ordinary you know well: your cat, your school bus, your kitchen. Write the set-up as a plain statement or question, then look for a last line that turns it round. A play on words is a fine first one. Write several and keep the best.

steps.test: Tell your own joke to two people, and change one thing after the first if it got no laugh.
steps.note: Change one thing only: a shorter set-up, a longer pause, a different last word. Then tell the second person. Notice whether the change helped.

steps.test: Play "Yes, and" with somebody for five minutes, building a silly story where each of you adds to what the other just said.
steps.note: One says "We opened the fridge and found a penguin." The other says "Yes, and it was eating all the cheese." Never say "No". This is how comedy actors practise, and it works at a kitchen table or on a car journey.

steps.test: Get a laugh from somebody without saying a word.
steps.note: Act out trying to open a jar that will not open, a very slow sneeze, or walking into a strong wind. Big, clear movements, and a straight face. Children are often much better at this than grown-ups.

steps.test: Cheer up somebody who is having a hard day with something light, and stop if they would rather you did not.
steps.note: A funny story from your week, a silly photo, your jar mime. Watch their face; if a smile does not come, stop and just be with them. Sometimes listening helps more than a laugh, and knowing that is part of being funny.

steps.test: Write three minutes of funny true stories from your own life, with at least three places where you hope people laugh.
steps.note: Three minutes spoken is about 400 words. Two or three short stories is plenty. Mark the three laughs. Read it aloud with a timer and cut anything that slows it down. The kindness rule still applies to every line.

steps.test: Tell your three minutes to one person you trust, then cut or change the part that got no laugh.
steps.note: Ask them afterwards which bit they liked most. Keep that, and cut or rewrite the flattest part. Then say the whole new version aloud once on your own.

steps.test: Tell your three minutes to a group of five or more people you know.
steps.note: At a family meal, a birthday, a class, a club. Ask first: "Can I tell you something that happened?" Stand where everybody can see you. Tell it the way you practised, and let the laughs finish before you carry on.

steps.test: Tell five minutes of your own kind, funny stories to a group of ten or more.
steps.note: A family party, a club night, a school or community talent evening, a gathering of friends. Add two minutes of new stories to your three and try the whole thing on one person first. A laugh every half a minute or so is a very good result. This is the far end of the ladder.

tracks.name: Teaching
tracks.line: From writing down the steps of one thing you can do, to teaching a group over three sessions until everybody can do it without you.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child can teach a grown-up too
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight: a child can teach a grown-up and a grown-up can teach a child. You start with one small thing you can already do and write its steps down. The rungs go from teaching one person with your hands off, to checking a week later, to changing how you teach when somebody finds it hard, to three short lessons, and end with teaching a group over three sessions until everybody can do it without you. Teaching shows you quickly whether you really know something, and it is useful to somebody every time.

steps.test: Choose one small thing you can do that somebody near you cannot, and write down its steps in order.
steps.note: Folding a paper aeroplane, tying a bowline, boiling an egg, shuffling cards, a trick for the nine times table, a phone shortcut. Number the steps. Five to eight steps is plenty.

steps.test: Do the thing yourself following only your written steps, and add any step you had left out.
steps.note: Read one step, do exactly that, and nothing more. You will almost always find a step you do without thinking, like "fold it in half first" or "wait for the water to boil". Write it in.

steps.test: Teach that thing to one person using your steps, showing each step slowly once.
steps.note: Somebody at home, a friend, a brother or sister, a grandparent. Show one step, then let them do that step, then the next. If they already know it, choose another thing from your list.

steps.test: Let them do it all the way through while you keep your hands behind your back and speak only when they ask.
steps.note: Taking it off them to show them again is the most common mistake in teaching. If they go wrong, let them notice. Wait until they ask, then answer only that question.

steps.test: Ask them to teach it back to you, and write down the step where they went wrong.
steps.note: Pretend you do not know it and do exactly what they say. The step they miss or muddle is the step your teaching did not make clear.

steps.test: Change that step in your written steps, and teach the thing to a different person.
steps.note: Make the step smaller, add a picture, or say it a different way. Then see whether the second person gets past it without trouble.

steps.test: A week later, ask the first person to do the thing again without help, and go over it once if they need to.
steps.note: Whatever they have forgotten after a week is what needed practising. Go over only that part, then let them do it all again.

steps.test: When somebody asks you a question you cannot answer, say "I do not know, so let us find out", and find out together.
steps.note: Look it up, try it, or ask somebody who knows. Pretending to know is the one thing that loses a learner's trust. If nobody asks you such a question this week, ask your learner for the hardest question they can think of.

steps.test: Teach one thing to two people at once, so both can do it by the end.
steps.note: Stand where both can see your hands. Let them take turns, and let the one who gets it first help the other. Two friends, two people at home, two children with their grown-up there.

steps.test: Teach somebody who is finding it hard by showing it a different way from the first.
steps.note: Draw it instead of saying it, do it in slow motion, break one step into three smaller ones, or use their own hands with yours beside them doing the same. Keep going until one way works.

steps.test: Choose a bigger skill that needs more than one session, and split it into three short lessons on paper.
steps.note: Juggling three balls (one ball, two balls, three), the rules of chess (how pieces move, check, a first game), a simple recipe (chopping, cooking, the whole dish). Write what the learner should be able to do at the end of each lesson.

steps.test: Teach those three lessons to one person on three different days.
steps.note: Start each lesson by asking them to show you what they remember from the last one. Only move on when they can do the part before.

steps.test: Teach one small thing to a group of four or more at once.
steps.note: A family gathering, a class, a club, friends. Show it once where everybody can see, then walk round and watch each person try. A grown-up teaching children does it with the children's own grown-ups there.

steps.test: Teach a group your three lessons over three sessions, until everybody can do the skill without you.
steps.note: Use the lessons from rung eleven, changed by what you learned on rung twelve. At the end, ask each person to do it with you standing back. If one person cannot yet, give them a fourth short session.

tracks.name: Saying it yourself
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Your name, a hello, a please, a thank you, a question, a story.

steps.test: Say your name and how old you are to somebody you have not met, looking at them.
Say hello first to somebody you know, before they say it to you.
Say goodbye and their name when you leave.
Ask for something in a whole sentence with a please in it, instead of pointing.
Say thank you to the person at the shop, loud enough that they hear it.
Answer a grown-up who asks you a question, without hiding behind anybody.
Ask a grown-up a question you really want the answer to, and listen to all of it.
Tell somebody you do not want to, in words, instead of crying.
Say sorry to somebody yourself, in your own words.
Order your own food or drink while somebody stands beside you.
Tell somebody something that happened today, with a beginning, a middle and an end.
Tell it to somebody who was not there, so that they understand it.

tracks.name: Keeping in touch
tracks.line: From writing down ten people you like, to twelve weeks in which every one of them has heard from you at least twice.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child can keep in touch with grandparents, cousins and old friends with a grown-up's help. This is not about meeting new people (that is Meeting people, parts one and two); it is about not losing the people you already have. It starts with a list of ten names and one thing going on in each life, then messages that ask about real news, calls, birthdays, and a regular time with a few people. It ends with twelve weeks in which every person on your list has heard from you at least twice. Friendships rarely end in a row; far more often they fade because nobody got in touch.

steps.test: Write down the names of ten people you like but have not been in touch with this month.
steps.note: Old friends, cousins, a former neighbour, a grandparent, somebody from a club you left. Paper or a note on your phone. Ten is the list for this whole ladder, so choose people you would be glad to hear from.

steps.test: Next to each name, write roughly when you last spoke and one thing going on in their life.
steps.note: A new baby, a house move, an exam, a new job, a parent who is ill. If you do not know anything, write "do not know"; that is useful to see too.

steps.test: Send one person on the list a short message asking about the thing going on in their life.
steps.note: "How did the move go? Is the new place feeling like home yet?" One or two lines. A question about their news shows you remembered, which is worth more than "Hi, how are you?"

steps.test: Ring one person on the list, just to ask how they are, and talk for at least five minutes.
steps.note: No reason needed: "I was thinking about you, so I thought I would ring." If they do not answer, leave a short cheerful voice message and count it. A video call counts too.

steps.test: Tell one person on the list a piece of your own news, so it is not only questions.
steps.note: Something small and real: a thing you made, a walk you took, what you are reading, a funny moment from your week. Keeping in touch works when both people share.

steps.test: When you see something that makes you think of somebody on the list, send it with one line.
steps.note: A photo of a place you went together, a song, a recipe, an article about their hobby. "This made me think of you." If nothing turns up today, look back through your photos for one to send.

steps.test: Write the birthdays you know from your list into a calendar, and ask for any you do not know.
steps.note: A paper calendar on the wall or the one on your phone, with a reminder on the day. "When is your birthday? I want to put it in my calendar" is a message people like to get.

steps.test: On the next birthday from your list, send a message that says one real thing, not only "Happy birthday".
steps.note: "Happy birthday! I still laugh about the day we got the tent up in the rain." If no birthday comes up soon, send one to anybody you know whose birthday it is.

steps.test: When somebody tells you about something coming up, put a reminder in your calendar and ask how it went on the day.
steps.note: An interview, a hospital appointment, a first day, a driving test, a match. "Thinking of you today, how did it go?" Being remembered on the day is one of the kindest things one person can do for another.

steps.test: Send a handwritten note or card to somebody on your list.
steps.note: Four or five lines is plenty. Post it, or put it through their door if they live nearby. If a stamp is not in reach, write it by hand and send a photo of it instead; it still counts.

steps.test: Agree a regular time with one person on your list: a call, a walk or a meal, on a set day each month or each fortnight.
steps.note: "Shall we ring each other on the first Sunday of every month?" A fixed day means neither of you has to wonder who should get in touch next. Put it in both calendars.

steps.test: Keep that regular time twice in a row.
steps.note: If one of you has to miss it, set the new date there and then. Two in a row is when it starts to feel normal.

steps.test: Send one kind message to somebody on your list who has not replied to you for a while, with no question about why.
steps.note: "No need to reply, just wanted to say I hope you are well." People go quiet for all sorts of reasons: work, illness, a new baby, a hard time. A message with no pressure in it is easy to answer when they are ready.

steps.test: For four weeks, get in touch with two people from your list each week, and tick them off.
steps.note: A message, a call, a note: any of the ways from the earlier rungs. Choose the two at the start of each week. Update the "one thing going on" column as you learn their news.

steps.test: Remember a hard date for somebody on your list, and send them a message on the day.
steps.note: The anniversary of somebody dying, a first birthday without a parent, the date of a big operation. "Thinking of you today." Nothing more is needed. Put the date in your calendar so next year you remember too.

steps.test: Agree a regular time with two more people on your list, and keep each one at least once.
steps.note: That makes three people with a set day. Different shapes suit different people: a monthly call with one, a walk every fortnight with another, a meal every season with a third.

steps.test: Send a short round-up to a group of family or old friends: three lines of your news and one question for them, and do it twice, a month apart.
steps.note: A group message or an email. "The garden is full of weeds, I have started a pottery class, and Mum is well. What is everybody reading?" It keeps a whole group in contact, not just you with each person.

steps.test: Reach twelve weeks from the start of your list, with every one of the ten having heard from you at least twice.
steps.note: Look down your list and count. Three of them now have a regular time with you. If somebody has not heard from you twice yet, send them something today, then tick this rung. This is the far end of the ladder.

categories.name: Making and building
categories.line: Wood, cloth, clay, drawing, knots, electronics, machines, code.

tracks.name: Make something, part one
tracks.line: From a ten-minute drawing to a thing somebody asks where you bought.

steps.test: Draw one thing in front of you for ten minutes, mostly without looking at the paper.
steps.note: A mug, a hand, a plant. It will look wrong; that is the point. Keep it.

steps.test: Tie three knots you can name, and undo them.
steps.note: A reef knot, a bowline, a clove hitch. Rope, a shoelace, a phone cable will all do.

steps.test: Fold a paper aeroplane that flies across a room.
steps.note: Any paper. Fold, throw, adjust, throw again. The adjusting is the making.

steps.test: Draw the same thing every day for five days and keep all five.
steps.note: Same mug, same chair. Lay the five out in a row and see what happened.

steps.test: Make something from a cardboard box.
steps.note: A house, a mask, a shelf, a castle. Scissors and tape. It has to stand up.

steps.test: Sew two pieces of cloth together by hand, ten even stitches.
steps.note: Any two scraps. Even matters more than small.

steps.test: Take ten photographs of one ordinary thing until one is good.
steps.note: A cup, a doorway, a puddle. Move, wait for the light, try again. Keep the one.

steps.test: Build something that stands on its own from what is in the recycling.
steps.note: A tower, a bridge, a creature. It stands without your hand for one minute.

steps.test: Draw a face that looks like the person.
steps.note: Somebody sitting still for ten minutes, or a photo. Eyes halfway down the head, not at the top.

steps.test: Shape one thing from wood, clay, or a bar of soap.
steps.note: A spoon, a bird, a bowl. A knife and a bar of soap is enough for a first carving.

steps.test: Make a simple circuit: a battery, a wire, and a bulb or buzzer.
steps.note: A cheap kit, or a lemon, two different coins and a small LED. Light comes on: done.

steps.test: Take a broken thing apart and see how it worked.
steps.note: A clock, a toaster, a toy. Unplugged. Lay the parts out in order.

steps.test: Draw a room in perspective, the lines meeting at one point.
steps.note: Dot in the middle, floor and ceiling lines running to it. Then the furniture.

steps.test: Make a gift by hand and give it.
steps.note: A card, a small carving, a drawing framed, a jar of something. Given, not kept.

steps.test: Mend one thing with glue, thread, or a screw so it works again.
steps.note: A chair, a book, a bag strap, a toy. Working is the test.

steps.test: Write your name beautifully twenty times, until the last one is good.
steps.note: A proper pen, slow. Compare the first and the twentieth.

steps.test: Make a kite, a boat, or a rocket, and fly, float, or launch it.
steps.note: Paper and string, a bottle and a cork, a balloon on a straw. It has to actually go.

steps.test: Follow written instructions to build something with more than twenty steps.
steps.note: A model, flat-pack furniture, a recipe with stages. Every step, in order, no skipping.

steps.test: Design something on paper first, then make it.
steps.note: A drawing with sizes, then the thing. Notice where the drawing was wrong.

steps.test: Make one thing good enough that somebody asks where you bought it.
steps.note: That is the bar. Part two is a craft you keep.

tracks.about: Making, tried from every side: drawing, knots, paper, card, cloth, a photograph, soap carving, a circuit, a thing taken apart, a gift made and given. By the end one thing you made is good enough that somebody asks where you bought it. Scraps, tape and what is in the recycling.

tracks.name: Wood
tracks.line: From sanding a scrap of wood to a low step stool you planned, built with halving joints, and stood on.
tracks.who: From about eight with a grown-up; hand tools only
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight with a grown-up beside them for every saw and chisel rung, and for grown-ups and teenagers learning woodwork for the first time. Everything is done with hand tools: sandpaper, a hand saw, a try square, a hand drill, a screwdriver, clamps and a chisel, and no power tools for children. The climb goes from sanding and reading the grain, to marking and sawing square, to screws and glue, a plan and a small box, then a chisel, a sharp edge and a proper joint. It ends with a low step stool you planned and built yourself, standing on it. Offcuts from a timber yard or a builder are often free, and borrowed tools are enough to start.

steps.test: Sand a scrap of wood smooth along the grain with sandpaper wrapped round a small block.
steps.note: Any clean offcut works, such as a piece of old shelf or a length of plain timber; avoid old painted wood and pallet wood, which can carry lead paint or chemicals. Wrap the paper round a block so the surface stays flat. Keep going until your fingers find no rough patches.

steps.test: Sand one patch across the grain and one along it, first with coarse paper and then with fine, and feel the difference.
steps.note: The grain is the lines that run along the wood. Sanding across it leaves scratches that show when the wood is oiled; sanding along it hides them. Coarse paper has a low number on the back, such as 80, and fine paper a higher one, such as 180: always go from coarse to fine.

steps.test: Measure a length twice, then mark a line square all the way round the wood with a try square and a sharp pencil.
steps.note: Hold the thick edge of the try square tight against the wood and draw along the metal blade, then carry the line round all four sides. If the line meets itself where it started, you held the square tight. Measuring twice catches most mistakes before they are cut into the wood.

steps.test: With the wood clamped down and a grown-up beside you, saw off a piece just on the waste side of your line.
steps.note: Clamp the wood to a table or bench so both hands are clear of the saw's path; never hold it with your knee or your other hand near the blade. Start with two or three gentle backward strokes to make a groove, then long easy strokes using most of the blade. Saw beside the line on the side you will throw away, so the piece you keep is the right length.

steps.test: Saw a cut straight and square, and check the end with the try square.
steps.note: Stand so your arm, the saw and the line are in one straight row, and look down on the line from above. Let the saw's own weight do most of the cutting. If light shows under the try square's blade, the end is not square, so cut another and compare.

steps.test: Saw three pieces to exactly the same length, and stand them side by side to check.
steps.note: Mark all three from the same end of the tape or ruler, not each one from the last, so small errors do not add up. Stand them on end on a flat table and look along the tops. Within a millimetre of each other is good.

steps.test: Drill a straight hole right through a clamped piece of wood with a hand drill, with a scrap underneath so the back does not split.
steps.note: A hand drill with a turning handle, or a gimlet for small holes, is all you need; no power drill on this ladder. Make a small dent where the hole goes with a bradawl or a nail so the bit does not wander, then turn steadily while keeping the drill upright. The scrap underneath stops the wood breaking out as the bit comes through.

steps.test: Screw two pieces of wood together in an L shape, drilling a pilot hole first so neither piece splits.
steps.note: The pilot hole is a little narrower than the screw's thread and goes through the top piece into the bottom one. Use a screwdriver that fits the screw head exactly, press hard and turn slowly so the head does not get chewed. Stop when the head sits level with the wood.

steps.test: Glue two pieces of wood together, clamp them, leave them a full day, and check the joint holds.
steps.note: Spread a thin, even coat of wood glue on both faces, press them together and clamp until a little glue squeezes out, then wipe that off with a damp cloth. After a day, try to pull them apart by hand. A good glued joint along the grain is often stronger than the wood beside it.

steps.test: Draw a plan of a small open box with every size written on it, and a list of the pieces to cut.
steps.note: A box for pencils, seeds or small tools: a base and four sides. Draw it from the front, the side and above, and write the length, width and thickness of every piece, remembering that where sides overlap the ends, the lengths change. Check the plan against the wood you actually have before you cut anything.

steps.test: Build the box from your plan, glued and screwed, and write down everything the plan got wrong.
steps.note: Cut all the pieces first and check each one against the list. Fix two sides to the base, then the two ends, drilling pilot holes as on rung eight. A plan is rarely right the first time, and that list of mistakes makes the stool plan at the end of this ladder better.

steps.test: With a grown-up beside you, cut thin shavings off the corner of a clamped piece of wood with a chisel, both hands behind the blade.
steps.note: Clamp the wood so it cannot move. Hold the handle with one hand and the blade near its tip with the other, both behind the cutting edge, and push away from your body in small cuts. Never hold the wood in one hand while you chisel with the other, and wear safety glasses if you have them.

steps.test: Sharpen a chisel on fine sandpaper laid on a flat tile, and cut the end of a piece of wood before and after to feel the difference.
steps.note: Hold the slanted face of the blade flat on the paper and rub back and forth until you can feel a tiny rough edge along the flat back, then rub the flat back on the paper once or twice to remove it. A blunt chisel needs pushing hard and slips; a sharp one cuts with less force, which is safer. Younger children watch a grown-up sharpen it, then feel the difference themselves.

steps.test: Cut a halving joint so two pieces of wood cross each other with their faces level and no gap.
steps.note: Tight is better than loose, because a tight joint can be pared down to fit and a loose one cannot be made bigger. A grown-up stays beside younger children for the saw and the chisel.
how: Lay one piece across the other and mark both its edges.
Mark half the thickness down each side with the try square.
Saw down to that line at both edges, plus a few cuts in between.
Chisel out the waste, working in from both sides towards the middle.

steps.test: Mend a gap or a mistake in one of your joints instead of starting again.
steps.note: Glue a thin sliver of wood into a gap, glue and clamp a small split, or fill a hole with glue mixed with fine sawdust from the same wood and sand it flat when dry. Most old furniture has a mended mistake somewhere in it. If all your joints fit, cut one loose on a scrap on purpose and mend that.

steps.test: Finish one thing you have made with two thin coats of oil or wax, a day apart, so the grain shows.
steps.note: Sand to fine paper first, rub on a thin coat, wait a quarter of an hour and wipe off whatever has not soaked in. Cloths used with linseed oil and similar oil finishes can catch fire on their own as they dry, so lay them out flat outdoors to dry, or soak them in water, before you throw them away. Wax needs no such care and is fine for a first finish.

steps.test: Draw a plan for a low step stool with halving joints, check it with a grown-up, and cut every piece on the list.
steps.note: A simple design: two end frames, each two legs joined by a rail near the floor with halving joints, and a top board screwed and glued across them, about 20 to 25 centimetres high. Use wood at least as thick as your thumb, mark every piece with its name in pencil, and use the list of mistakes from your box. Spread it over several days.

steps.test: Build the step stool, finish it, and stand on it on a flat floor after a grown-up has checked it.
steps.note: Put the frames together without glue first to check the fit, then glue and screw them and leave the glue a full day before the finish. A grown-up checks every joint and pushes it for any wobble, then you step on in the middle with both feet. When it holds you without moving, this ladder is done.

tracks.name: Cloth and thread
tracks.line: From threading a needle to a pair of pull-on shorts or a skirt, sewn by hand and worn out of the house.
tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, with a grown-up handling the iron for younger children. It starts with a needle, a knot and three stitches, then a button, a seam and a small filled pouch, then a hem, a stitched edge, a drawstring bag and a cushion cover. It ends with a pattern traced from clothes that already fit, and a pair of shorts or a skirt you sew and wear out of the house. Everything is sewn by hand, so there is no machine to buy: a needle, thread, pins, scissors and old sheets, pillowcases or shirts are enough.

steps.test: Thread a needle and tie a knot in the long end of the thread that does not pull through the cloth.
steps.note: Cut the thread about as long as your arm, because longer thread tangles. Snip the end cleanly, wet it, and push it through the eye while holding the needle against something white. For the knot, wrap the end twice round your fingertip, roll it off with your thumb and pull it tight.

steps.test: Sew a running stitch along a pencil line on a scrap of cloth, with every stitch the same length.
steps.note: In and out along the line, each stitch about half a centimetre long. Pull the thread snug but not so tight that the cloth bunches up. Old sheets, pillowcases and shirts all make good practice scraps.

steps.test: Sew a line of back stitch that looks like one unbroken line on the front.
steps.note: Come up one stitch-length ahead, go back down at the end of the last stitch, and come up one stitch-length ahead again. It is the strongest hand stitch and the one that sews the seams on this ladder. On the back the stitches are longer and overlap, and that is correct.

steps.test: Finish a line of stitching with three tiny knotted stitches on the back, and trim the thread.
steps.note: Take a tiny stitch, pull it nearly tight, and pass the needle through the little loop before it closes; do that three times in the same place. Tug the cloth gently and nothing should move. Every rung from here ends this way.

steps.test: Sew a four-hole button onto a scrap of cloth so it holds when you pull it hard.
steps.note: Double the thread. Lay a pin across the top of the button and sew over it four or five times through each pair of holes, then pull out the pin, wind the thread three times round the stitches under the button and finish on the back. The pin leaves room for the cloth of the buttonhole. If you already sew buttons on, sew one onto clothing that needs it and count it.

steps.test: Sew two pieces of cloth together with back stitch one centimetre from the edge, then open them out.
steps.note: Put the pieces with their better sides facing each other, pin them, and draw a pencil line one centimetre in from the edge. Sew along the line, then open the pieces out: the stitches are hidden and the seam sits on the back. Nearly all clothes are joined this way.

steps.test: Sew a small pouch from two squares, turn it right side out through a gap, fill it, and sew the gap shut.
steps.note: Two squares about the size of your palm, sewn round three sides and part of the fourth. Turn it through the gap, push the corners out with a pencil, fill it with dried rice or lentils, and close the gap with small stitches over the edge. It makes a beanbag for throwing and catching; keep filled bags away from babies.

steps.test: Press a seam open with an iron, and compare it with a seam you did not press.
steps.note: Open the two edges of the seam apart on the back and press down with the iron rather than sliding it. The pressed seam lies flat and looks finished; the other one bulges. A grown-up does the iron for younger children, and with no iron, running a thumbnail firmly along the opened seam does a smaller version of the same job.

steps.test: Hem the edge of a square of cloth: fold it over twice, pin it, and sew it down with small slanting stitches.
steps.note: Fold the edge over about half a centimetre, then again about one centimetre, and press the folds. Each stitch catches a thread or two of the main cloth and then the fold; on the front only tiny dots should show. A square of old shirt hemmed on all four sides makes a handkerchief.

steps.test: Sew blanket stitch along the edge of a piece of felt or fleece, with every stitch the same height and the same distance apart.
steps.note: Push the needle in from the front a little way in from the edge, and before you pull it tight, pass the needle through the loop of thread at the edge. An old fleece jumper cut up works as well as felt. Fleece does not fray, so it is good for a first pencil case.

steps.test: Measure and cut a rectangle of cloth 30 centimetres by 40 centimetres with straight edges and square corners.
steps.note: Lay the cloth flat on a table, draw the lines with a ruler and a pencil or chalk, and check the corners against the corner of a book. Cut with long strokes of sharp scissors along the line, not little snips. Lining the edges up with the threads that run through the cloth makes it hang straight.

steps.test: Sew a drawstring bag from your rectangle, with a channel at the top and a cord that pulls it closed.
steps.note: Fold the rectangle in half, back stitch the side and the bottom but stop five centimetres from the top, then fold the top edge over twice to make a channel wide enough for the cord and sew it down. Pin a safety pin to one end of a cord, a shoelace or a ribbon and push it through the channel. Use it for shoes, marbles or a packed lunch.

steps.test: Trace a paper pattern from a pillowcase, with an extra centimetre added all the way round for the seams.
steps.note: Lay the pillowcase flat on newspaper or wrapping paper and draw round it, then draw a second line one centimetre outside the first. That extra centimetre is what the seams use. Write on the pattern what it is and which edge sits on a fold of the cloth.

steps.test: Make a cushion cover with an overlapping back and no zip, using your own paper pattern.
steps.note: Cut one front piece the size of the cushion plus the seam allowance, and two back pieces that overlap by about ten centimetres, each hemmed along the edge that overlaps. Lay the backs on the front with the better sides facing, sew all round, turn it out through the overlap and push the cushion in. No cushion? The same cover makes a pillowcase for a small pillow.

steps.test: Sew a split seam or a loose button back together on a piece of clothing belonging to somebody in your home, and give it back.
steps.note: Ask around: a coat with a loose button, a pocket coming away, a seam open under an arm. Turn the clothing inside out and back stitch along the old seam line, starting a little before the split and ending a little after it. If you live alone, do it for a friend or neighbour who asks.

steps.test: Shorten or take in one piece of your own clothing that does not fit, and wear it.
steps.note: The easiest are trousers or sleeves a little too long, or a waist a little too loose. Put it on inside out, pin where it should be, take it off, and sew along the pins, then try it on before you cut away any extra cloth. Children often have trousers that are too long, which makes a good first one.

steps.test: Trace a pattern from a pair of pull-on shorts or a skirt that fits you, and cut the pieces out of cloth.
steps.note: For shorts, fold them in half so one leg lies flat, trace the front and then the back (the back is deeper at the seat), and add one centimetre for seams, two at the hems and three at the waist for the elastic. For a simple skirt, a rectangle half as wide again as your hips is enough, as long as you want it plus the hem and the waist. An old sheet or a large cotton shirt gives enough cloth.

steps.test: Sew the shorts or skirt, thread elastic through the waist, and wear them out of the house.
steps.note: Back stitch the seams, press them, hem the legs or the bottom edge, then make the waist channel the way you did on the drawstring bag and feed the elastic through with a safety pin, sewing its ends together. Try it on before you sew the last gap in the channel shut. Spread it over a week of evenings; when you wear it out of the house, this ladder is done.

tracks.name: Knots and rope
tracks.line: From a stopper knot in a dressing-gown cord to five sticks lashed into a firm square frame.
tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with the knot that stops a rope pulling through a hole, then the handful of knots that do most everyday jobs: tying up a bundle, tying to a post, a loop that does not close up, joining two ropes and pulling a line tight. Then you tie them all with your eyes closed, stop a rope end fraying, and lash sticks together into a frame that holds its shape. Any rope or cord about two metres long will do, such as a dressing-gown cord, a skipping rope or an old washing line. These knots are for everyday jobs, never for climbing or for holding a person's weight.

steps.test: Tie a figure-of-eight knot in the end of a rope, pull it tight, and undo it.
steps.note: Make a loop, take the end round behind the rope and back down through the loop: before you pull it tight it looks like the number eight. It is a stopper knot, the one that stops a rope pulling through a hole or a ring. If you know it already, tie it three times quickly and count it.

steps.test: Tie a reef knot round a rolled-up towel, then tie a granny knot and see which one slips.
steps.note: Right over left and under, then left over right and under: the two ends come out lying flat beside the rope. Do the second half the same way as the first and you get a granny knot, which twists and slides when you pull the ends. A reef knot is for tying up a bundle or a bandage, not for joining two ropes that will be pulled hard.

steps.test: Tie a clove hitch round a chair leg, pull the long end, and check that it grips.
steps.note: Wrap the rope round the leg, cross over the first turn, wrap round again and tuck the end under that second turn. It grips when pulled and slides off easily when loose, which is why it starts the lashings at the end of this ladder. A table leg, a banister or a fence post all work.

steps.test: Tie a rope to the back of a heavy chair with a round turn and two half hitches, and hang a bag with a few books in it from the rope.
steps.note: Wrap the rope twice round the bar of the chair (the round turn), then take the end round the long part of the rope and back through itself, twice. The two wraps take the pull and the two hitches hold them there. Lift the bag just off the floor and check the knot does not slide.

steps.test: Tie a bowline, a loop that stays the same size however hard you pull it, five times.
steps.note: Many people learn it with a little story: the rabbit comes up out of the hole, runs round the back of the tree and goes back down the hole. The loop holds its size under a hard pull and still unties easily afterwards. Five in a row with no mistakes is the rung.
how: Make a small loop in the rope, with the long part underneath it.
Bring the end up through the small loop.
Take it round behind the long part of the rope.
Send it back down through the small loop, and pull tight.

steps.test: Tie a bowline round your own waist, pull on the long end hard, and check the loop does not get tighter.
steps.note: This is harder than rung five because you are tying it from the other side, against your own body. Use a rope long enough to go round you with an arm's length to spare. It trains you to tie a loop round something you cannot see well, like a post or a tree trunk; a knot learned from an app is never for climbing or lifting a person.

steps.test: Join two ropes of different thicknesses with a sheet bend, and pull hard on both ends.
steps.note: Make a U shape in the thicker rope. Push the thin rope up through the U, round behind both sides of it, and tuck it under itself. A shoelace joined to a dressing-gown cord is a good test: a reef knot slips here, and the sheet bend holds.

steps.test: Tie a line between two chairs with a taut-line hitch, and slide the knot to make the line tight.
steps.note: Tie one end to the first chair with a bowline. Take the other end round the second chair leg and back towards the line, wrap it twice round the line inside the loop, then once more round the line outside the loop, and pull it snug. Slide the knot and the line tightens; let go and it stays. It is the knot for a tent rope or a washing line.

steps.test: Tie all seven knots from this ladder from memory, then tie them again with your eyes closed.
steps.note: Figure of eight, reef knot, clove hitch, round turn and two half hitches, bowline, sheet bend, taut-line hitch. Say each name before you tie it, and if one fails with your eyes closed, tie it three times with your eyes open and try again. Tying by feel is what you need in the dark, in the rain or behind your back.

steps.test: Stop the end of a rope fraying by winding strong thread tightly round it and tucking the thread in.
steps.note: Lay a loop of thread along the rope end, wind the thread tightly round the rope and over the loop for about as far as the rope is wide, then push the thread end through the loop and pull the loop back under the windings. Trim both ends. Tape wound tightly round the end also works as a quick fix, but do the thread version at least once.

steps.test: Lash two sticks into a cross with a square lashing so they do not twist when you turn them.
steps.note: Garden canes, old broom handles or straight sticks found on the ground all work; about as thick as a thumb is easiest. Wind the rope round the two sticks three or four times, then wind it two or three times between the sticks, round the wraps, to pull everything tight.
how: Tie a clove hitch on the upright stick, just below where the cross stick sits.
Wrap over the cross stick, behind the upright, over the cross stick and behind the upright, three or four times.
Wind two or three turns between the sticks, round all the wraps, pulling hard.
Finish with a clove hitch on the cross stick.

steps.test: Lash five sticks into a square frame with the fifth stick across the diagonal, so it does not lean when you push a corner.
steps.note: Four square lashings make the corners, then lash the diagonal stick to two opposite corners; without it, a square frame leans over into a diamond. Use it to hold up a climbing plant, as the side of a play den or as a frame on a wall. If you push a corner and it keeps its shape, this ladder is done.

tracks.name: Clay and carving
tracks.line: From a pinch pot the size of an egg cup to a butter spreader you carved, oiled and used at a meal.
tracks.who: From about five; the knife rungs for teenagers up
tracks.about: For everybody from about five for the clay rungs; the knife rungs are for grown-ups, and for teenagers with a grown-up beside them, and each of those rungs gives younger children another way to do it. The climb starts with a pinch pot, a coil, a proper join and slow drying, then a patterned slab, a model animal, a painted and sealed piece, a box and a pot with a lid that fits. Then it turns to carving: a block of clay, a whittled stick, and a wooden butter spreader you sand, oil and use at the table. Clay is forgiving, because if it goes wrong you squash it and start again. Air-drying clay needs no kiln, only a table and a little water, and what you make from it is for keeping and looking at, not for food or for holding water.

steps.test: Roll a lump of clay into a smooth ball and press it into a pinch pot about the size of an egg cup.
steps.note: Use a lump the size of a small egg. Push your thumb into the middle, then pinch gently between thumb and fingers while you turn the ball round in your other hand. Air-drying clay costs little; for the first few rungs, a dough of two cups of flour, one cup of salt and about one cup of water works too.

steps.test: Make a second pinch pot, cut it in half with a piece of thread, and check the walls are the same thickness all the way round.
steps.note: Hold the thread tight between two hands and pull it down through the pot. Where the wall is thick, pinch more next time; where it is thin, pinch less. Aim for walls about as thick as a pencil, then squash both halves back into a ball to use again.

steps.test: Roll a coil as even as a pencil and as long as your forearm, without it cracking.
steps.note: Roll with flat hands from the middle outwards, moving your hands apart as you go. If it goes flat, turn it a quarter and roll again; if it cracks, the clay is too dry, so wet your hands a little. Make three and keep the best.

steps.test: Add a handle to a pinch pot by scratching both joining faces, wetting them, and pressing them together.
steps.note: Score both faces and wet them: scratch criss-cross lines with a fork or a cocktail stick, dab on a little water, press together with a small wiggle and smooth the join with a damp finger. Clay that is only pressed together usually comes apart as it dries. This join is used on nearly every rung after this one.

steps.test: Build a small pot from a flat base and four or five coils, each one scratched, wetted and smoothed onto the one below.
steps.note: Make the base a flat round about the size of the palm of your hand. Lay each coil round the edge, then smooth clay down from each coil onto the one below, inside and outside, until no gaps show. Keep the walls upright by turning the pot as you go rather than reaching round it.

steps.test: Dry a pot slowly over three days so it does not crack.
steps.note: Put it somewhere cool, away from sun and heaters, with a loose plastic bag or a damp cloth over it for the first day, and turn it upside down on the second day so the base dries too. In a hot, dry place, keep it covered for longer. Most cracks come from drying too fast or from joins that were not scratched and wetted.

steps.test: Roll a flat slab between two guide sticks so it is the same thickness everywhere, press a pattern into it, and cut it into a neat square tile.
steps.note: Lay two pencils or two strips of thick card either side of the clay and roll a rolling pin or a bottle across them: the sticks set the thickness. Press in a leaf, a fork, a piece of lace or a shell. Cut the square with a blunt table knife against a ruler.

steps.test: Model an animal from one lump of clay, pulling the legs, head and tail out of the lump rather than sticking them on.
steps.note: A cat, a hedgehog, a bird or a tortoise is a good first animal. Pulled-out parts stay on when the clay dries; anything you have to add, join by scratching and wetting. Keep it small and chunky, because thin legs snap.

steps.test: Write down one thing to fix on your animal, then make it again with that thing fixed.
steps.note: One sentence is enough: the head too big, the legs too thin, a crack at the neck. Make the second animal with that one thing put right. Keep both side by side so you can see the difference.

steps.test: Smooth a dry piece with a barely damp sponge, paint it, and seal it with clear varnish or watered-down white glue.
steps.note: Wipe rough edges with the sponge rather than sanding them, which makes dust. Any water-based paint works; when it is dry, brush on varnish or white PVA glue mixed with a little water. Sealed air-drying clay is still not safe for food or for holding water, so it is for keeping things like rings, pens or seeds.

steps.test: Carve a repeating pattern into a half-dry pot with a cocktail stick, with clean lines that do not tear the clay.
steps.note: Clay that has dried for about half a day is firm but not hard, and that is when it carves cleanly. Draw the pattern very lightly first, then cut over it. One simple shape repeated all round, such as waves, dots or leaves, looks planned rather than accidental.

steps.test: Build a small open box from five slabs, four sides and a base, with every corner scratched, wetted and smoothed.
steps.note: Let the slabs firm up for an hour first so they stand up on their own. Cut them against a ruler, join every edge that touches, and press a thin coil into each inside corner to make it strong. A box big enough for paper clips or a few coins is plenty.

steps.test: Make a pot with a lid that sits on it without sliding off, and let the two dry together.
steps.note: Make the pot, then roll a round slab a little wider than its top, and join a ring of thin coil under the lid so it fits just inside the rim. Dry the lid sitting on the pot with a scrap of kitchen paper between them, so both shrink together. A small knob on top makes it easy to lift.

steps.test: Press clay into a thick block, let it firm up for a day, and carve a fish out of it by cutting away everything that is not the fish.
steps.note: Draw the outline on the top with a cocktail stick, then take off thin slices with a lolly stick, a teaspoon or a blunt table knife, working from the outside in. Take a little at a time, because clay you cut away cannot go back. Carving in wood works the same way, only slower.

steps.test: Whittle a green stick into a point, then cut a notch and a flat face into it, always cutting away from your body.
steps.note: For grown-ups, and for teenagers with a grown-up beside them; younger children carve a second clay block into a different animal and count it. Use a small knife with a blade that locks open, and a freshly cut stick as thick as a thumb, which is softer than dry wood. Sit down with your elbows on your knees, keep the blade moving away from you and your other hand behind it, and close the knife whenever you stop.

steps.test: Carve a flat butter spreader from a piece of soft wood, down to a pencil outline drawn on both sides.
steps.note: A flat piece of soft wood about as long as your hand and as thick as a finger: lime (also called basswood), birch, or a soft offcut, which timber yards often give away. A grown-up saws off the big waste, then whittle thin shavings down to the line; if you are pushing hard, the cuts are too big. Younger children: a grown-up does the knife cuts while you draw the shape, and you do the next two rungs yourself.

steps.test: Sand the spreader with coarse and then fine sandpaper until you cannot feel any knife marks.
steps.note: Wrap sandpaper round a scrap of wood for the flat parts and hold it loose over a finger for the curves. Sand along the grain, the lines in the wood, not across them. Wet the spreader lightly, let it dry and sand once more, so the tiny fibres that water lifts are gone before its first wash.

steps.test: Rub oil into the spreader, leave it overnight, and use it to spread butter at a meal.
steps.note: Use an oil sold as safe for wooden chopping boards, or a little cooking oil if that is what you have. Rub on a thin coat, wait twenty minutes, wipe off what has not soaked in, and leave it overnight; wash it by hand afterwards and dry it straight away. When it spreads butter on bread at a meal, this ladder is done.

tracks.name: Drawing
tracks.line: From three kitchen things in two minutes each to a drawing of somebody's favourite thing, given to them to keep.
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a grown-up who finds a rung easy can do it with the other hand. The climb starts with quick drawings of real things in front of you, then teaches looking: one continuous line, the simple shapes underneath, light and shade, the space around a chair, your own hand, measuring with a pencil. It ends with people, a view from a window, and a careful drawing of something a person loves, given to them. Drawing is mostly looking, and it improves with practice the way handwriting does; a pencil and any paper is all you need.

steps.test: Draw three things from the kitchen, two minutes each, looking at them while you draw.
steps.note: A mug, a spoon, a key, a tin: whatever is on the table. Look at the thing more than at the paper. Wobbly lines are fine; the rung is three honest two-minute drawings. The back of an envelope and a biro will do.

steps.test: Draw the same thing three times and pick the best one.
steps.note: Choose one of the three from rung one. Each time, look for one thing you got wrong last time and fix it: the handle too small, the lid too flat. Write "best" on the one you choose.

steps.test: Draw something in front of you without lifting the pencil off the paper.
steps.note: A shoe, a plant, a bunch of keys. One line from start to finish, going slowly round every edge you can see. It will look strange; it is training your eye to follow an edge, not making a picture.

steps.test: Draw an object by starting with the simple shapes underneath it.
steps.note: A kettle is a box with a cylinder spout; a cat is a circle on an oval. Draw the shapes lightly first, then draw the real edges over them, then rub out the shapes or leave them faint. A teapot, a lamp or a cuddly toy is a good one.

steps.test: Draw a cereal box, a tin and an orange so each one looks solid, not flat.
steps.note: For the box, draw the top as a slanted shape so you can see two sides at once. For the tin, the top is an oval, not a circle, and the bottom curves the same way. The orange comes next rung. If you do not have these, any box, anything round and any ball will do.

steps.test: Shade a round thing so it looks round, with the light coming from one side.
steps.note: Put the orange or a ball beside a window or a lamp. Leave the part nearest the light white, press gradually harder as you go round to the far side, and add a darker shadow on the table on the side away from the light. Squinting at it helps you see the light and dark.

steps.test: Draw something small every day for a week in the same notebook.
steps.note: Five or ten minutes a day: your breakfast, your shoes, a houseplant, the view from a chair. A cheap notebook or a few sheets of paper folded and stapled is enough. Keep them all, including the ones you do not like.

steps.test: Draw only the empty spaces around and between the legs of a chair.
steps.note: Look at the gaps between the legs and the bars as if they were shapes, and draw those shapes, not the chair. When you have drawn the gaps, the chair appears. Your eye stops drawing what it expects and starts drawing what is there.

steps.test: Draw a whole chair, with the legs going the right way.
steps.note: Use what the last rung showed you: the gaps between the legs tell you where each leg goes. The back legs look shorter and higher on the page than the front ones. Check each leg against the gap beside it before you move on.

steps.test: Draw your own hand from life.
steps.note: Rest the hand you do not draw with on the table in a relaxed position. Start with the shape of the whole hand, then the fingers, then the creases. Hands are hard for everybody, so ten minutes and an honest attempt is the rung.
steps.twist: Draw the hand you draw with, using the other one.

steps.test: Fill one page with small drawings of the same thing from different sides.
steps.note: A shoe works well: from the front, the side, the back, from above, lying down. Aim for eight to ten small drawings. Turning an object round teaches you more about its shape than one big drawing.
steps.twist: Half of them with the other hand.

steps.test: Measure with your pencil held at arm's length, and draw a door or a window with its height and width the right size against each other.
steps.note: Close one eye, hold the pencil straight out with your arm locked, and line the tip up with the top of the door. Put your thumb where the bottom is. Then turn the pencil sideways and see how many of those widths fit into the height. Draw it to match.

steps.test: Copy a drawing by an artist you admire, line for line.
steps.note: Libraries have books of drawings, and many museums put old drawings online free: search a name like Rembrandt, Dürer or Beatrix Potter with the word "drawings". Copy slowly and look at where each line starts and stops. Artists have always learned this way.

steps.test: Draw for ten minutes a day for two weeks without missing a day.
steps.note: The same as the notebook week, twice as long. Mix it up: an object, a shaded ball, your hand, a copy. If you miss a day, carry on the next and add a day at the end.

steps.test: Draw a view from a window, with near things bigger and lower on the page than far things.
steps.note: The window frame is your edge. A fence post near you is tall on the page; the same kind of post far away is small and higher up. Things in front hide part of what is behind them, so draw the front things first.

steps.test: Draw five quick one-minute drawings of somebody while they move about.
steps.note: Somebody washing up, playing a game, reading on the sofa. One minute each: just the shape of the body and which way it leans, no faces or details. Set a timer. Most people are happy to be drawn if you ask first.

steps.test: Draw somebody sitting still in front of you, head to feet, in fifteen minutes.
steps.note: Somebody watching television or reading is ideal. Use the pencil-measuring from rung twelve: see how many heads fit into their whole height and draw it that way. Leave the face simple; the rung is the whole body in the right proportions.

steps.test: Draw one place from life for an hour, with shading and near and far things.
steps.note: A corner of your kitchen, the view down the garden or the street from a window, a café table if you are out. Start with light lines for the big shapes, then the edges, then the shading last. Take breaks, but stay with the same drawing.

steps.test: Draw the favourite thing of somebody you know, as carefully as you can, and give it to them.
steps.note: Their dog, their bike, their house, their teapot: from life if you can, or from a photograph they send you. Take several sittings if you need them, and use everything from this ladder: shapes first, measuring, light and shade. Write their name and the date on the back. When they keep it, you have finished this ladder.

tracks.who: For everybody from about six, side by side

tracks.name: Electricity
tracks.line: From tracing the loop inside a torch to a battery-powered gadget of your own that does a job somebody asked for, still working a month later.
tracks.who: From about eight with a grown-up; teens and grown-ups
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for children from about eight with a grown-up beside them. Everything on this ladder runs on ordinary batteries of 9 volts or less. Mains electricity, from the sockets in the wall, kills: nothing on this ladder is ever connected to it, opened, or plugged in. The climb starts inside a battery torch, then a bulb lit with kitchen foil, a home-made switch, series and parallel, an electromagnet, a meter, an LED with the right resistor, a breadboard, a light that comes on in the dark, and a small computer chip you program. It ends with a battery gadget of your own that does a job somebody asked for and keeps working for a month.

steps.test: Open a battery torch, take the batteries out, and trace with your finger the path electricity takes from the battery, through the switch, to the bulb and back.
steps.note: Use a torch that takes ordinary AA or AAA batteries, not one you charge with a lead. Unscrew the end or the front, take the batteries out, and look for the metal strips and springs that touch each end of the batteries, the switch and the bulb. Electricity only flows when there is an unbroken loop from one end of the battery back to the other: that loop is called a circuit. The switch simply opens a gap in the loop and closes it again. Put it back together and check it still lights.

steps.test: Write the four safety rules for this ladder and read them out to somebody.
steps.note: One: batteries of 9 volts or less only, and never anything that plugs into the wall, because mains electricity kills. Two: never join the two ends of a battery with just a wire or foil and nothing else in the loop, because the wire gets hot fast (this is a short circuit). Three: never cut, pierce, crush or short-circuit a lithium or rechargeable battery, such as the ones in phones, laptops, electric toothbrushes and power packs, because they can catch fire; and keep button batteries away from small children. Four: if anything gets hot, smells or smokes, disconnect it and step back. Outside, keep well away from power lines and electricity substations.

steps.test: Light the torch bulb with one or two batteries and two strips of kitchen foil, then take it apart again.
steps.note: Fold two strips of foil a finger wide and long enough to reach. One strip goes from the raised end of the battery (plus) to the tip at the bottom of the bulb; the other from the flat end (minus) to the metal side of the bulb. Use a torch bulb for this rung, not an LED: an LED needs a resistor in the loop, and that comes on rung thirteen. If the foil gets warm, the strips are touching each other: separate them.
how: Tape one strip to each end of the battery.
Hold the other end of one strip against the tip of the bulb.
Touch the other strip to the metal side of the bulb.

steps.test: Draw the circuit you made as a diagram using the standard symbols for a battery, a bulb, a switch and a wire.
steps.note: A single battery cell is a long thin line (plus) beside a short thick line (minus). A bulb is a circle with a cross in it. A wire is a straight line, drawn with square corners. A switch is a short line tilted up away from a gap. Look these up on any free science site if you want to check; diagrams let anybody in any country read your circuit.

steps.test: Put ten different things into a gap in your circuit, one at a time, and sort them into ones that light the bulb and ones that do not.
steps.note: Try a coin, a key, a metal spoon, a pencil sharpened at both ends (touch the lead), a rubber band, paper, plastic, a wooden spoon, a piece of foil, a glass of tap water with the two foil ends dipped in. Metals let electricity through easily (conductors); plastic, rubber, wood and paper do not (insulators). Pencil lead and water let a little through, often too little to light the bulb, which is a real result and worth writing down.

steps.test: Make a switch from a paper clip and two drawing pins pushed into card, put it in your circuit, and turn the bulb on and off.
steps.note: Push two drawing pins into a piece of thick card a paper clip's length apart, with a foil strip under each pin. Hook the paper clip under one pin so it can swing across to touch the other. Swinging it across closes the gap and completes the loop; swinging it away opens the gap. A light switch on the wall does the same job, but that one is mains: never open it.

steps.test: Put two batteries end to end in your circuit, see what happens to the brightness, and say why.
steps.note: Check the voltage printed on the bulb or on the torch first, and do not use more batteries than that, or the bulb will burn out. Batteries end to end, raised end to flat end, add their voltages: two 1.5-volt batteries give 3 volts. Voltage is the push; more push makes more electricity flow through the same bulb, so it glows brighter. Turned the wrong way round, one battery cancels the other.

steps.test: Wire two bulbs one after the other (series), then side by side (parallel), and say in which one they shine brighter and why.
steps.note: You need a second bulb of the same kind: from a second torch, or a cheap pack. In series, all the electricity goes through both bulbs in turn, the push of the battery is shared between them, and both glow dimmer; take one out and both go off. In parallel, each bulb has its own path straight to the battery, so each glows about as bright as one bulb alone, and the battery runs down faster. Most homes are wired in parallel, which is why one lamp can be off while another is on.

steps.test: Make an electromagnet: wind plastic-coated wire thirty times round a steel nail, connect it to one battery for a few seconds, and pick up paper clips.
steps.note: Use thin plastic-coated wire and a single ordinary (not rechargeable, not lithium) 1.5-volt battery. Electricity flowing through a coil of wire makes it a magnet, and the steel nail inside makes it much stronger. The coil is almost a short circuit, so connect it only for a few seconds at a time and let go if the wire or battery gets warm. Try twenty turns and forty turns and count the paper clips each time.

steps.test: Explain voltage, current and resistance out loud using water in a pipe, and answer one question about it from somebody.
steps.note: Voltage is like the pressure pushing water along a pipe; it is measured in volts. Current is how much flows past a point each second; it is measured in amps. Resistance is like a narrow part of the pipe that makes it harder to flow; it is measured in ohms. More push or less resistance gives more current. The comparison helps but is not perfect: electricity does not leak out of an open wire the way water leaks out of an open pipe.

steps.test: Use a multimeter to measure the voltage of a new battery and a used one, and write both numbers down.
steps.note: Borrow a meter if you can: from a relative, a school, a library or a makers' club; basic ones are cheap. Turn the dial to DC volts (a V with a straight line) on the 20 range, touch the red probe to the raised end and the black to the flat end. A new AA battery usually reads a little over 1.5 volts; a used one reads less. Never put the probes anywhere near a wall socket.

steps.test: Use the multimeter's beep setting to find which of three wires somebody has secretly broken.
steps.note: Ask somebody to cut through the metal inside one of three plastic-coated wires without cutting the plastic, or to break one foil strip under tape. Turn the meter to the setting with a sound symbol, touch the probes together to hear the beep, then touch one probe to each end of each wire. A beep means a complete path; silence means a break. Testing like this, instead of guessing, is how faults are found in every kind of machine.

steps.test: Work out on paper the resistor an LED needs on a 9-volt battery, then build it and light the LED.
steps.note: Without a resistor, too much current flows and the LED burns out, often in a second. A typical red LED uses about 2 volts and is happy with 0.02 amps, so the resistor takes the other 7 volts: 7 divided by 0.02 is 350 ohms; use the next size up, such as 390 or 470. Resistor values are shown by coloured bands, and a free online chart or your meter will read them. The LED's longer leg goes towards plus.
how: Take the LED voltage away from the battery voltage.
Divide what is left by 0.02.
Choose the nearest resistor with a bigger number, and put it in the loop with the LED.

steps.test: Build a circuit with an LED, a resistor and a push button on a solderless breadboard, from a diagram.
steps.note: A breadboard has hidden metal strips under its holes: the holes in each short row are joined, and the long rows down the sides carry the battery. Push the parts in, follow the diagram one wire at a time, and check each connection against it before connecting the battery. With no breadboard, build the same circuit in a free online circuit simulator first, which also counts for this rung.

steps.test: Build a light that comes on by itself when it gets dark, from a diagram, using a light sensor and a transistor.
steps.note: The light sensor is a light-dependent resistor or a phototransistor. As the room gets darker, the sensor's resistance changes, and the transistor, which works like a switch controlled by a small current, turns the LED on. Library books on electronics and free electronics sites have this exact circuit. Test it by covering the sensor with your hand.

steps.test: Make a small programmable computer chip blink an LED, either on a real board or in a free online simulator.
steps.note: Microcontroller boards such as Arduino-type boards or the micro:bit run from batteries or from a USB lead to a computer, and are used in many schools and clubs, which often lend them. Free online simulators, such as Wokwi, let you write and run the same code with no board at all. The code turns a pin on, waits half a second, turns it off, waits, and repeats. Only ever power it from batteries or a USB lead, never from anything wired to the wall.

steps.test: Program the chip to do one thing when a button is pressed and something different when a light sensor reads dark.
steps.note: The chip reads the button as on or off, and reads the light sensor as a number. Use an if: if the button is pressed, flash quickly; if the light number is below a value you choose, turn the LED on steadily. Print the sensor number to the screen first so you can see what dark and light read in your room.

steps.test: Build a battery gadget in a box that does a job somebody at home asked for, and keep it working for a month.
steps.note: Ask first: a light that comes on when a cupboard opens, a buzzer when the fridge door is left open, a reaction-time game, a night light for a hallway, a light that shows when a plant's soil is dry.
