Put it in a small box with the wires tidy and the battery easy to change. Write down every time it stops working and what you fixed. The finish is a month of it being used, still running on batteries only.

tracks.name: Making things with code
tracks.line: From exact instructions on paper to a web page you made that somebody asked for a change to, and then used on three different days.
tracks.who: From about eight, a grown-up nearby online; grown-ups too
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight, with a grown-up close by for anything online and in charge of any account; grown-ups start at the same first rung. The climb starts on paper with no computer, then moves blocks on a free site to make a small game, then typed code: a web page, colours, a button, error messages, a list that remembers what you typed. It ends with putting your page online at a free address, watching somebody use it, fixing what confused them, adding the thing they asked for, and seeing them use it on three different days. All of it can be done with free sites and a computer or tablet already in the house, and it teaches you to see how the apps you use every day are made.

steps.test: Write exact step-by-step instructions for drawing a simple picture, and have somebody follow them word for word without seeing the picture.
steps.note: Draw a house from a square, a triangle and a door first, and hide it. Write steps like "Draw a square with sides as long as your thumb" and "Draw a triangle sitting on top of the square". The other person does exactly what the words say, even when it is clearly wrong. Where their drawing goes wrong, your instructions were not exact enough, and a computer is even more literal than a person.

steps.test: Agree five online safety rules with a grown-up, or write them for your household, before using any coding site.
steps.note: Good rules: a grown-up sets up and owns any account for a child, and reads its age rules first. Never put your full name, school, address, photo or where you are into a project or a profile. Do not chat with or reply to people you do not know, and never move a conversation to another app. Tell a grown-up straight away about anything that feels wrong, and nobody is in trouble for telling. Never type a password or personal details into code somebody else gave you. Grown-ups keep the same rules for themselves, and use a strong password.

steps.test: Make a character move across the screen with code blocks on a free coding site that needs no account.
steps.note: The Scratch editor (scratch.mit.edu, choose Create) and the Hour of Code activities at code.org both work in a browser without an account. In Scratch, drag a "when green flag clicked" block, then "move 10 steps" under it, and click the green flag. A computer or tablet is best; the blocks are hard to drag on a phone.

steps.test: Make a character that keeps moving and bounces off the edges of the screen, using a loop.
steps.note: In Scratch, put "move 10 steps" and "if on edge, bounce" inside a "forever" block. A loop repeats the blocks inside it, which saves writing the same thing a hundred times. To keep your work without an account, use File, then Save to your computer.

steps.test: Make something happen only when a key is pressed or when two characters touch, using an if.
steps.note: In Scratch, try "if key space pressed then" with "change y by 10" inside, placed inside the forever loop, or "if touching" another sprite, then "say Got you!". An if checks a question and only runs its blocks when the answer is yes. Nearly every program you use is full of these.

steps.test: Add a score that goes up by one each time something is caught, using a variable.
steps.note: In Scratch, make a variable called score, set it to 0 when the green flag is clicked, and "change score by 1" when the catch happens. A variable is a named box that holds a value the program can change. Check that the score starts at 0 every time the game restarts.

steps.test: Finish a small game with a start, a way to win or lose, and an end screen, save it, and have somebody play it.
steps.note: Keep it small: catch ten falling apples before a timer runs out, or dodge five balls. Watch the other person play and do not explain anything; notice where they are confused. Save the game file to the computer so it is kept.

steps.test: Make a web page with your first name as a heading, in a plain text editor, and open it in a web browser.
steps.note:
Open a plain text editor (Notepad on Windows; TextEdit on a Mac, set to plain text in its menu) and type

Sam

with your own first name, or any word. Save it as index.html and double-click the file; it opens in the browser. On a tablet, a free in-browser code editor does the same job. Everything on this page is only on your computer until the rung where it goes online.
how: Open a plain text editor.

Type

Your name

and a line of

Some words

under it.
Save it as index.html, then open that file in a browser.

steps.test: Change the colours, the font and the spacing of your page with CSS until it looks how you want.
steps.note: Add a <style> section at the top with lines such as body { background: lightyellow; font-family: sans-serif; } and h1 { color: teal; }. Save, then reload the browser to see each change. Change one thing at a time so you can see what each line does.

steps.test: Add a button that changes the words on the page when you press it, using JavaScript.
steps.note: Give a paragraph an id, add a <button>, and in a <script> section at the bottom write a line that sets that paragraph's text when the button is clicked. Free beginner lessons on sites such as MDN Web Docs or freeCodeCamp show exactly this. Copy the example, then change the words to your own, so you understand each part.

steps.test: Break your button on purpose, read the error message in the browser's console, and fix it.
steps.note: Misspell a word in your script, save, and reload. On a computer, open the console with F12, or right-click the page, choose Inspect, then the Console tab. The red message usually names the line number and what went wrong, such as a name that does not exist. Reading error messages carefully fixes most problems faster than guessing.

steps.test: Draw on paper how a to-do list page will look, and write one sentence for what each button does, before writing any code.
steps.note: Draw the box you type into, the Add button, the list, and a Delete button beside each item. Write, for example: "Add puts what I typed at the bottom of the list and empties the box." Deciding this on paper first is quicker than changing code later.

steps.test: Build the list page from your drawing: type something, add it to the list, and delete any item.
steps.note: You need a text box, an Add button, and a list that your script adds a new item to. Each item gets its own Delete button that removes it. Build the Add part first and check it works before starting the Delete part.

steps.test: Make the list still be there after you close the page and open it again.
steps.note: Browsers have a small store called localStorage: save the list into it every time it changes, and read it back when the page opens. It only keeps the list in that browser on that device, and clearing the browser's data empties it. Test by adding three items, closing the tab, and opening the page again.

steps.test: Ask an AI chat tool to explain one line of your code you do not fully understand, then change that line to do something new and check it works.
steps.note: Many AI tools have a minimum age in their rules, often 13 or 18: a child does this with a grown-up using the grown-up's tool. Paste the one line, not your whole project, and never paste passwords or personal details. The explanation can be wrong, so the test is whether your change works when you reload the page.

steps.test: Make your list page work on a narrow phone-sized screen, checked in the browser's device view.
steps.note: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> inside the <head>. Open the browser's Inspect tools and choose the phone or device icon to see the page at a phone's width. Make buttons big enough for a finger and make sure nothing runs off the side of the screen.

steps.test: Put your page online at a free web address, and open it on a phone.
steps.note: Free hosting sites such as GitHub Pages or Netlify let you upload a folder and give you an address. Their rules usually need you to be 13 or older, so a grown-up creates and owns the account for a younger child. Check the page first: no full name, school, address or photo on it.

steps.test: Send the address to one person, watch them use the page for the first time without helping, and write down where they got stuck.
steps.note: Choose somebody you know: a family member or a friend. Sit beside them or watch on a video call, and do not point or explain, even when they struggle. Every place they hesitate goes on your list; that list is more useful than anything you could guess.

steps.test: Fix the first thing they got stuck on, and put the new version online without losing the working one.
steps.note: Before changing anything, copy the whole working folder and name the copy with the date, so you can always go back. Make the fix, test it on your computer, then upload. Open the address on a phone afterwards to check the live page works.

steps.test: Ask your user for one thing they would like the page to do, add it, and see them use the page on three different days.
steps.note: Keep the request small enough to build in a few sessions: a tick box for done items, a count of items, a second list. Tell them when it is ready and do not remind them to use it. The finish is three separate days on which they chose to open it.

tracks.name: Photography
tracks.line: From one sharp photo of a cup to a small show of your ten best photographs for family or friends.
tracks.who: From about six; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, sharing one phone. It starts with holding the camera still and getting the thing you meant in focus, then light, background, where things sit in the picture, height, low light, time of day and movement. Then come people, choosing your best, light editing, a week of one photo a day and a family occasion, and it ends with a small show of your ten best photographs for family or friends. A phone camera is all you need. Two rules run through every rung: ask before you photograph any person, and never photograph children you do not know.

steps.test: Wipe the camera lens, hold the phone in both hands, and take a sharp photo of a cup on a table.
steps.note: Phone lenses collect fingerprints, and a soft cloth or a clean T-shirt corner fixes a lot of blurry photos straight away. Tuck your elbows against your body and press the button gently. Zoom into the photo afterwards: if the rim of the cup is crisp, it counts.

steps.test: Photograph a small thing close up, tapping it on the screen first so it is the sharpest part of the picture.
steps.note: A button, a leaf, the pattern on a spoon handle. Tap the thing on the screen and wait a moment for it to sharpen before you press. If the background comes out sharp and the thing is soft, tap and take it again.

steps.test: Photograph one object from where you stand, then walk closer until it fills the picture, and take it again.
steps.note: A plant, a shoe or a bowl of fruit. Walk closer rather than zooming, because zooming on many phones makes the picture softer. Compare the two: a great many disappointing photographs were simply taken from too far away.

steps.test: Photograph the same object by a window twice: once with the light falling on its side, once with the window behind it.
steps.note: Turn the object or move yourself, not the window. Light from the side shows shape and texture; light from behind makes the object dark with a bright edge. Say which you like better and why; with no window, a lamp does the same job.

steps.test: Photograph a thing with a messy background, then move yourself until the background is plain, and take it again.
steps.note: Crouch, step sideways or turn the thing round until behind it there is only a wall, the sky, a tablecloth or grass. Look at the edges of the screen as well as the middle before you press. The same care stops a lamp post or a plant appearing to stick out of somebody's head.

steps.test: Turn on the grid lines in your camera settings and take three photos with the main thing on a grid line, not in the middle.
steps.note: The grid splits the screen into nine boxes. Put a horizon along the top or bottom line, or a tree or a toy on one of the upright lines, with space on the side it faces. Then take the same photo with the thing exactly in the centre and compare them.

steps.test: Photograph one thing from three heights: lying on the ground, standing, and from straight above.
steps.note: A toy, a flower, a pair of shoes or a sleeping cat. From low down small things look big and important; from above you see patterns and shapes. Keep the one that shows the thing best.

steps.test: Take a sharp photo in a room lit by one lamp, with the phone resting on something steady and the flash off.
steps.note: Rest the phone on a table, a pile of books or the back of a chair, tap to focus, and keep still for a second after pressing, because many phones take longer in low light. The flash makes everything look flat. Evening is the easiest time to try this.

steps.test: Photograph the same outdoor view in the hour after sunrise or before sunset, and again around the middle of the day.
steps.note: From a doorstep or through an open window is fine. Low sun makes long shadows and warm colours; high sun makes short shadows and flatter light. Near the equator the low-sun time is short, so be ready a little early; put the two photos side by side.

steps.test: Take a sharp photo of something moving, such as a ball in the air, a running dog or water pouring.
steps.note: Hold the button down, or use burst mode, to take many photos in a row, then keep the sharpest one. Bright light helps, because the phone takes each picture faster. Or follow the moving thing with the phone as you press, so it stays sharp while the background blurs.

steps.test: Ask somebody in your home if you may photograph them, take their photo facing a window, and show it to them.
steps.note: Ask first, every time, and if they say no, that is the answer. Stand them facing the window so the light falls on their face, come close enough that their face fills much of the picture, and tap on their eyes to focus. Show them straight away and delete it if they ask you to.

steps.test: Take twenty photos of things and places on one walk, pick the best three, and say one reason for each.
steps.note: Gates, puddles, clouds, a bird on a wall, a shadow on a path. This walk is for things, not people: ask before photographing any person, and never photograph children you do not know. Mark the three as favourites so you can find them again.

steps.test: Edit one photo on the phone: straighten it, crop it, and adjust the brightness, keeping the original.
steps.note: Most phones have all three under the edit button, with nothing extra to buy. Straighten the horizon first, crop away what does not help, then brighten or darken a little. Put the edit next to the original, and if it looks edited, go back and do less.

steps.test: Take one photo a day for seven days of the same view or the same kind of thing, and keep all seven.
steps.note: The view from one window, your breakfast, or the sky at the same time each day. Keeping the place and the time the same makes the changes easy to see. At the end, lay them out in order and choose your favourite.

steps.test: Photograph a family meal or celebration so that everybody who was there appears in at least one good photo.
steps.note: Tell everybody you are taking photos, and for anybody else's children, ask their parents first. Take a few of everybody together and some of people talking, not only posed ones. Send the best to the family afterwards, including one of the person who is usually the one holding the camera.

steps.test: Print one photo, or have it printed, and give it to the person who is in it.
steps.note: Many libraries, chemists and photo counters print from a phone for a small price. If printing is not possible, send the photo to them on its own with a sentence about why you like it. A printed photograph is often kept for years.

steps.test: Choose your ten best photographs from this ladder and show them to family or friends, each with a short title.
steps.note: Print them and pin them to a wall or peg them to a string, or show them one at a time on a laptop or a television. Put them in an order where each leads to the next, and write a title for each. When people have looked at all ten and you have answered their questions, this ladder is done.

tracks.name: Scissors
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Cutting, and cutting where you meant to.

steps.test: Open and shut the scissors ten times with nothing in them.
Hold them the right way round, thumb on top, and show somebody.
Cut a piece of paper in two, any way you like.
Snip all along the edge of a piece of paper to make a fringe.
Cut along a straight line somebody drew for you.
Cut a square out.
Cut along a curvy line, all the way, without leaving it.
Cut out a circle and hold it up.
Cut out a shape and turn the paper instead of the scissors.
Fold paper, cut, and open it out to see what happened.
Cut out three shapes and stick them down to make a picture.
Tell somebody what your picture is, while they look at it.

tracks.name: Crayons
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Colouring in, then drawing what you see.

steps.test: Colour one shape in and stay inside the line.
Colour it all the way in, with no white bits left.
Colour a whole picture, every part of it, with more than one colour.
Press hard for a dark colour and softly for a pale one.
Draw a circle that joins up where it started.
Draw a square and a triangle.
Draw a person with a head, a body, two arms and two legs.
Give the person a face, and say who it is.
Draw your house.
Draw somebody standing outside your house.
Draw something that happened today.
Tell the story of your picture to somebody while they look at it.

categories.name: Music and voice
categories.line: Singing, an instrument, rhythm, songs, whistling, reading music.

tracks.name: Play, part one
tracks.line: From a song sung alone to a five-minute show for two people.

steps.test: Sing one whole song out loud, alone, start to finish.
steps.note: In the car, the shower, the kitchen. All the verses you know.

steps.test: Clap a rhythm back to somebody, and have them clap yours.
steps.note: Four beats, then eight. A table and two spoons if hands are boring.

steps.test: Learn one coin or card trick well enough to fool yourself in a mirror.
steps.note: A coin vanish, or the trick where the chosen card comes to the top. Ten minutes a day for three days.

steps.test: Throw and catch one ball a hundred times without dropping it.
steps.note: A rolled sock counts. Same height every throw; that is the whole secret of juggling.

steps.test: Whistle a tune somebody can name.
steps.note: Cannot whistle? Hum it, and whistling is a rung in the Music room when you want it.

steps.test: Stand on one leg for a minute, then the other.
steps.note: Eyes on one spot. Then, when it is easy, eyes shut.

steps.test: Learn a three-line joke and tell it to somebody.
steps.note: Short, clean, told slowly. The pause before the last line is the joke.

steps.test: Do one trick for one person.
steps.note: The trick from rung three. If they see how it works, that is how you learn where to look.

steps.test: Juggle two balls in one hand, or three balls for three throws.
steps.note: Socks again. Three throws and a drop still counts.

steps.test: Dance for a whole song with nobody watching.
steps.note: Curtains closed if you like. All the way to the end of the song.

steps.test: Play five notes on any instrument that make a tune somebody recognises.
steps.note: A keyboard app on a phone counts. Ode to Joy is five notes. An instrument you own is better.

steps.test: Skip ten times in a row.
steps.note: A rope, a washing line, a length of anything. Ten without a stumble.

steps.test: Learn a second trick and do both, one after the other, for somebody.
steps.note: Two tricks is an act. Say something between them.

steps.test: Sing with another person, both of you singing.
steps.note: Any song you both know. Out loud, together, to the end.

steps.test: Do a cartwheel, a handstand against a wall, or a forward roll.
steps.note: On grass or a carpet. Whichever you have never done, or not for twenty years.

steps.test: Make up a game with rules and play it with somebody.
steps.note: A cup, a coin, a hallway. Write the rules down in three lines.

steps.test: Play a whole tune for one person.
steps.note: Start to finish, mistakes and all. The instrument from rung eleven.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for ten throws.
steps.note: This is the one people remember learning. A month of a few minutes a day.

steps.test: Be somebody else for ten minutes: a voice, a hat, a face painted on.
steps.note: A character with a name. Children are the best audience for this one.

steps.test: Put on a five-minute show for two or more people.
steps.note: A song, a trick, a joke, a tune. Introduce it. Bow at the end. Part two is a real act.

tracks.about: Songs, tricks, juggling, dancing, a joke, a tune on anything, a cartwheel, a character with a hat. Twenty rungs of play that end in a five-minute show for two people. Socks for juggling, a phone keyboard for the tune, and no audience until you are ready.

tracks.name: Singing
tracks.line: From one steady hummed note to starting a song that everybody in the room joins in with.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. The climb starts on your own with one long hummed note and a two-minute warm-up, then learns to breathe low, to match a note, and to sing a song through with the recording turned off. Only then does anybody else hear you: one person, then a round with somebody, then a group. It ends with you starting a song that the whole room joins in with. Nothing to buy; a free piano app or website gives you the notes, and no rung asks anybody to listen until you have practised alone.

steps.test: Hum one long, steady note for as long as one breath lasts, and time it.
steps.note: Pick a comfortable note in the middle of your voice, not high or low. Keep it the same, without wobbling up or down, until the breath runs out. Write down the seconds; you will beat it on rung three.

steps.test: Do a two-minute voice warm-up: humming, a lip buzz, and slides from low to high.
steps.note: It loosens the voice before singing, the way a stretch does before running. Do it quietly; it does not need to be loud.
how: Hum gently on a comfortable note for thirty seconds.
Blow air through loose closed lips so they buzz, and slide the note up and down, for thirty seconds.
Sing "oo" sliding slowly from your lowest comfortable note to your highest and back, four times.
Finish with a long, easy hum.

steps.test: Breathe in so your stomach moves out and your shoulders stay still, then hum one note for longer than on rung one.
steps.note: Put one hand on your stomach and one on your chest. Breathe in through your nose so the lower hand moves and the upper hand hardly moves. Let the breath out slowly on the hum. If your shoulders rise, start again, slower.

steps.test: Do the warm-up three mornings running.
steps.note: In the shower, making breakfast, or in the car. The same two minutes as rung two. Tick off the three mornings.

steps.test: Match one note: play it on a free piano app or website, and hum it until your note and that note sound the same.
steps.note: Search "online piano" for a free keyboard. Pick a note in the middle, play it, and hum. When you are slightly off you hear a wobble or a buzz between the two sounds; when you match, the two sounds blend into one. Slide your hum slowly up or down until the wobble stops, or ask somebody to sing you the note instead.

steps.test: Match five different notes in a row on the piano app.
steps.note: Choose five notes close together, one at a time. Play, listen, then hum. If one goes wrong, play it again and slide to it before moving on.

steps.test: Sing the first five notes of a scale up and back down, in tune with the piano app.
steps.note: On the piano app, start on any white key and play the next four white keys to the right; that is five notes going up. Sing them on "la", one per note, then back down. Play each note first if you need to, then try singing all five without it.

steps.test: Write out the words of one song you like from memory, check them, and sing it through without looking.
steps.note: A song you already half know is easiest: a hymn, a football song, a song from a film, a folk song. Fix the lines you got wrong, then sing it all through at a normal speaking volume. Nobody else needs to hear this one.

steps.test: Record yourself singing that song on your phone, and listen back to all of it once.
steps.note: Many people do not like hearing their own recorded voice at first, and that is normal. Listen once to the end and write down one part that was in tune and one that was not. The recording is only for you; delete it afterwards if you like.

steps.test: Do the warm-up every morning for one week.
steps.note: The same two minutes, seven days. Add rung seven's five notes at the end. If you miss a day, carry on the next.

steps.test: Sing along with the recording of your song, turn the sound off halfway, and still be in time and in tune when you turn it back on.
steps.note: Use a music app or a video. Sing with it for the first verse, mute it, keep singing, and unmute at the chorus. If you have drifted away, try again; it usually takes a few goes. This is what singing without backing feels like.

steps.test: Sing the same song louder, without it going shouty.
steps.note: Loud singing comes from breathing low, as on rung three, not from squeezing your throat. Stand up, open your mouth wider, and let the sound out on each breath. If your throat hurts, stop and try again quieter tomorrow. Pick a time when nobody in the house is sleeping.

steps.test: Learn a second song properly, words and all.
steps.note: A different kind from the first: if the first was slow, make this one quicker. Use the same method: write the words out, check them, sing it with and then without the recording.

steps.test: Sing one of your two songs all the way through to one person.
steps.note: Somebody in your family, a friend, a grandparent on a phone call. Tell them you are practising singing and ask them to just listen. Stand up, breathe low, and do not stop to apologise; carry on to the end.

steps.test: Sing a round with somebody else, each of you holding your own part.
steps.note: "Row, Row, Row Your Boat", "London's Burning" and "Frère Jacques" are rounds. One person starts, and the second starts from the beginning when the first reaches the end of the first line. Keep going until you can each sing through twice without joining the other person's part.

steps.test: Do the warm-up every morning for thirty days.
steps.note: Two or three minutes each morning for a month. By now it is warm-up, five notes up and down, and one song. If you miss a day, carry on the next and add a day at the end.

steps.test: Sing three songs from memory, back to back, with no words in front of you.
steps.note: Your two songs and one more. Sing them standing up, one straight after the other, as if somebody were listening. If you forget a line, keep the tune going on "la" until the words come back.

steps.test: Join in with a group singing, and sing every word out loud from beginning to end.
steps.note: A church service, a choir's open rehearsal, a carol service, a match, a singing session in a pub or community hall, a birthday. Many choirs welcome a newcomer who wants to listen or try; ask before you go. Sing at full voice, not mouthing along.

steps.test: Sing one song on your own to a group of three or more people.
steps.note: A family gathering, a friend's birthday, a car full of people. Say what you are going to sing, stand up if you can, and sing the whole thing. A child can sing to the family at teatime.

steps.test: Start a song yourself and get everybody in the room singing along with you.
steps.note: Happy Birthday at a party, a round at a family gathering, a song everybody knows on a long car journey. Start clearly on a note that suits most voices, not too high, and keep singing loudly so others can follow. When the whole room is singing, you have finished this ladder.

tracks.who: For everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side

tracks.name: An instrument
tracks.line: From one clear note to playing a song all the way through for a few people who sing along.
tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child and a grown-up can each learn one, side by side. It does not matter which instrument: one borrowed from family or a friend, a school or library loan, a low-cost recorder, whistle or ukulele, or a free piano app on a phone for the first rungs. The climb goes one clear note, a tune on five notes, playing in time, ten minutes a day, then working a tune out by ear and from the page, and a song you like played from memory. It ends with that song played all the way through for two or three people who know it and sing along. Free tuner and metronome apps are all the extra kit you need.

steps.test: Get hold of an instrument you can use today and make one clear note on it.
steps.note: Borrow one from family or a friend, ask whether a school or library lends them, or use a low-cost recorder, tin whistle or ukulele. With nothing to hand, a free piano app on a phone is enough for the first nine rungs. A clear note means no squeak, buzz or rattle; if you already play, count it and choose a piece you cannot play yet for the rungs ahead.

steps.test: Tune your instrument with a free tuner app, or play one note into the app and read which note it is.
steps.note: Search your app store for a free tuner. String instruments such as a guitar, ukulele or violin need tuning every time you play; a beginner video for your instrument shows which notes the strings should be. A keyboard, piano app, recorder or whistle stays in tune, so just play one note and see its name.

steps.test: Play three different notes cleanly, one after another, and say the name of each.
steps.note: Find a free beginner video for your instrument that shows how to hold it and where the first notes are. The tuner app tells you the name if the video does not. Slowly and clean beats quick and blurred.

steps.test: Play five notes going up in order and back down, without a squeak or a buzz.
steps.note: On a keyboard these are C, D, E, F and G, the white keys starting from the C just to the left of two black keys. On other instruments the beginner video usually starts with the same five. Play it three times.

steps.test: Play "Ode to Joy" or "Mary Had a Little Lamb" on those five notes, well enough that somebody could name it.
steps.note: Starting from C, "Ode to Joy" begins E E F G G F E D C C D E E D D, and "Mary Had a Little Lamb" begins E D C D E E E, D D D, E G G. Play it slowly, note by note, until it flows. If you know a different five-note tune from where you grew up, that counts too.

steps.test: Play that tune three times in a row without a mistake.
steps.note: If you slip, start again from the beginning and count again from one. Slow down until three in a row is possible; speed comes later.

steps.test: Play the tune in time with a free metronome app set slowly, or with your own foot tapping.
steps.note: Set the metronome to about 60 clicks a minute, one note to each click, and hold longer notes for two clicks. In time matters more than fast: slow and steady always sounds better than quick and uneven.

steps.test: Practise ten minutes a day for seven days in a row, and tick each day off.
steps.note: The same time each day helps, such as after breakfast or before the evening meal. Start each session with the five notes, then the tune, then something new. Ten minutes most days does more than an hour once a week.

steps.test: Learn a second, longer tune on your own from a free beginner video or book.
steps.note: Choose one a little harder than the first, such as a folk tune, a hymn, or a simple theme from a film. Learn it a line at a time, and join each line to the one before.

steps.test: Take the bar you keep getting wrong, play it slowly ten times with no mistakes, then play the whole tune.
steps.note: A bar is one small section of the tune, a few notes long. Play it slowly enough that it is never wrong, ten times, then a little faster. This is the most useful practice skill there is, and fixing one bar teaches more than playing the whole tune again.

steps.test: Play three tunes from memory, one after another, with nothing in front of you.
steps.note: Your two tunes and one more. Choose the order first so there is no gap. If one breaks down, carry on to the next and come back to it tomorrow.

steps.test: Play a whole tune for one person in the room, from start to end without stopping.
steps.note: A family member, a friend, or somebody on a video call. Most listeners notice a stop far more than a wrong note, so keep going through any mistake.

steps.test: Work out a short tune by ear, with nobody showing you the notes.
steps.note: Choose something you can hum, such as "Happy Birthday" or a song everybody in your house knows. Find the first note, then try notes until the next one sounds right. It takes longer than you expect and it changes how you listen to music.

steps.test: Learn a tune you do not know from written music or from tab, on your own.
steps.note: Tab is a simple written form for guitar and ukulele that shows which string and fret to press. Free beginner sheet music and tab are easy to find online, and the Reading music ladder teaches the notes. Choose something short.

steps.test: Practise ten minutes a day for thirty days, ticking each one off.
steps.note: The same shape as rung eight, for a month. A missed day is not a reason to stop; tick the next one. By the end you will hear the difference in a recording from day one.

steps.test: Learn the beginner version of a song you really like.
steps.note: Search the song name with "easy" and your instrument. On a guitar, ukulele or keyboard, a great many songs use just three or four chords; on a whistle or recorder, learn the tune. The simple version is a real way to play it.

steps.test: Play that song all the way through, three times, without stopping.
steps.note: Use the bar-fixing from rung ten on any part that breaks down, then go back to playing it through. Three complete times in one sitting.

steps.test: Play the song from memory, with nothing in front of you.
steps.note: Look at the music or chords once, then put them face down and play. If a part is missing, look at only that part, then put it away again.

steps.test: Play the song in time with somebody else singing or playing along, from start to end.
steps.note: A family member singing, a friend with another instrument, or a recording of the song played quietly if nobody is free. Count "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud before you both start.

steps.test: Play the song all the way through for two or three people who know it, and have them sing along.
steps.note: After a meal, on a birthday, or at a family visit. Tell them the song first and count them in. Play steadily and keep going through any mistake; people singing along carry a song past a wrong note.

tracks.name: Rhythm
tracks.line: From clapping along to one song to leading a group in a clapped or tapped rhythm that stops together on your signal.
tracks.who: From about six; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts by clapping along to a song, then counting, then keeping time with a free metronome app, and checking yourself with a recording. After that you clap the rhythm of words, tap your foot and clap at the same time, clap between the beats, hear music in three and in four, and play a simple drum pattern on a table with both hands. It ends with you leading three or more people in a clapped or tapped rhythm that stops together when you signal. You need nothing but your hands, a table, and a phone.

steps.test: Put on a song you like and clap on every beat, all the way to the end.
steps.note: The beat is the steady pulse you would tap your foot to. Choose a song with a clear, strong beat, such as a pop song, a march or a folk dance tune. If you drift, stop clapping, listen for four beats, then join in again. If you already do this without thinking, do it with a song you have never heard.

steps.test: Count "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud over and over, clapping on every number, for one minute by a timer.
steps.note: Keep the numbers evenly spaced, like the ticking of a clock. Clap a little louder on each "1". This is the counting that every later rung uses.

steps.test: Clap along with a free metronome app or website set to 80 beats a minute for two minutes.
steps.note: Search "online metronome". A metronome clicks at an exact, steady speed. When you are exactly together, your clap covers the click and you stop hearing it; when you hear two sounds, you are early or late.

steps.test: With the metronome going, turn the sound down to nothing for eight claps, then turn it back up and check you are still together.
steps.note: Count the eight silent claps in your head. If you have drifted, notice whether you went faster or slower, and try again. When eight is easy, try sixteen.

steps.test: Record yourself clapping a steady beat for two minutes with no music, and listen back for any place it speeds up.
steps.note: Most people speed up without noticing, and a recording shows it. Start the metronome while you listen back, at the speed you started on, and hear where the two separate. Write down whether you sped up, slowed down, or held it.

steps.test: Say a nursery rhyme or short poem and clap once on every syllable, then clap it again with the words only in your head.
steps.note: For example, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star" is seven claps: twin-kle twin-kle lit-tle star. That pattern of long and short sounds is the rhythm, which is different from the steady beat underneath it.

steps.test: Tap your foot on the steady beat while you clap the rhythm of the same rhyme.
steps.note: Say the rhyme out loud to start. Your foot keeps going evenly; your hands follow the words. If one of them falls apart, stop, start the foot alone, and add the claps again.

steps.test: Have somebody clap you a rhythm four beats long, and clap it back correctly five times in a row.
steps.note: Take turns: they clap, you copy, then swap. Keep the rhythms short and simple at first. With nobody to hand, search for a free "clap back rhythm" video, which claps a rhythm and leaves a gap for you.

steps.test: With the metronome at 80, clap exactly halfway between the clicks for one minute.
steps.note: Count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" out loud, with the numbers on the clicks, and clap only on each "and". This is called the offbeat, and it is harder than it sounds. Slow the metronome to 60 if you keep landing on the click.

steps.test: Clap a bar of three and a bar of four with a louder clap on each "1", then say whether "Happy Birthday" is in three or four.
steps.note: Count "1, 2, 3" several times, then "1, 2, 3, 4" several times. Then sing "Happy Birthday" and clap along, trying each count. It fits in three, like a waltz; "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" fits in four. Try one more song you know and decide which it is.

steps.test: On a table, tap every beat with your right hand and every other beat with your left for one minute, then swap hands.
steps.note: Count "1, 2, 3, 4": the right hand taps on all four, the left hand only on 1 and 3. Start slowly with the metronome. When it is steady, swap so the left hand taps every beat.

steps.test: Tap a simple drum pattern on a table for one minute: right hand on every beat, left hand on 2 and 4, a foot on 1 and 3.
steps.note: This is the pattern under a great many songs. The foot is the low drum, the left hand the sharp drum, the right hand keeps time. Build it one part at a time: right hand alone, then add the left hand, then the foot.
how: Tap the right hand on every beat, counting 1, 2, 3, 4.
Add the left hand on 2 and 4.
Add your foot on the floor on 1 and 3.
Hold all three for one minute with the metronome, slowly.

steps.test: Play that drum pattern along with a whole song, without stopping.
steps.note: Choose a song with a steady beat, not too fast. If you lose it, keep only the right hand going until you find the beat again, then add the rest.

steps.test: Along with a song, stop tapping for four bars while counting silently, and come back in exactly on a "1".
steps.note: A bar is one count of "1, 2, 3, 4", so four bars is sixteen beats. Count them in your head and start again on the next "1". This is how drummers and players know when to come back in.

steps.test: Keep a steady beat on a table, a box or an upturned pot while somebody sings or plays a whole song over it.
steps.note: Agree the speed first by counting "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud before they start. Your job is to stay steady even when they speed up or make a mistake. With nobody to hand, do it under a family member singing along to the radio.

steps.test: Lead three or more people in a clapped or tapped rhythm: set the beat, give each a pattern, and end all together on your signal.
steps.note: Family at a table works well. Start everybody on the steady beat, then give one person the rung-six rhythm and another the offbeat. Agree the signal beforehand, such as a raised hand and "4, 3, 2, 1, stop". Try it twice and let somebody else lead the second time.

tracks.name: Whistling
tracks.line: From a first faint whistle to teaching somebody who could not whistle to make a clear note.
tracks.who: From about six; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about six: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with any whistled sound at all, then one clear note, then moving the note up and down with your tongue. After that come real tunes, checked against a piano app and a recording, whistling while breathing in, and a loud whistle with two fingers. It ends with you teaching somebody who cannot whistle to make their first clear note. Nothing to buy, and a tune whistled well is a small, cheerful thing you carry everywhere.

steps.test: Round your lips and blow gently until you hear any whistled sound at all, even a faint one.
steps.note: Shape your lips as if saying "oo", leaving a small round hole, and rest the tip of your tongue just behind your bottom teeth. Wet your lips and blow softly, not hard. Moving your lips a little tighter or looser finds the sound; a mirror helps. Some people get it in a minute and some take a few days of trying for a few minutes; if you already whistle, whistle one note on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Whistle one clear note and hold it for three seconds without the sound of rushing air drowning it.
steps.note: Blow more gently than feels natural; too much air turns the note into a hiss. Count three slowly in your head. If the note keeps cutting out, make the hole in your lips a little smaller.

steps.test: Whistle one note, then a higher one, by moving your tongue while your lips stay still.
steps.note: Keep your lips the same and slide your tongue slowly forward and up inside your mouth, as if moving from "oo" towards "ee", and listen for the note to rise. Moving it back brings the note down. Go slowly; the change is small.

steps.test: Slide slowly from your lowest whistled note to your highest and back down, without the sound cutting out.
steps.note: Like a siren, but slow. If the sound stops at the top or the bottom, that is the edge of your range for now; slide up to just below it. Do it three times.

steps.test: Whistle the first five notes of a scale going up and down, checked against a free piano app.
steps.note: Search "online piano" for a free keyboard. Start on any white key and play it and the next four white keys to the right, one at a time. Play a note, whistle it until the two sound the same, then move to the next. When a note is slightly off you hear a wobble between the two sounds; slide until it stops.

steps.test: Whistle a short tune everybody knows, such as "Happy Birthday" or "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", all the way through.
steps.note: Hum it once first so the tune is in your head. Whistle slowly; getting every note matters more than speed. If one jump is hard, whistle just those two notes a few times, then go back to the start.

steps.test: Whistle that tune to somebody without saying what it is, and see whether they can name it.
steps.note: A family member, a friend, or somebody on a video call. If they cannot name it, ask which part sounded wrong and try once more. If they name it, the tune is clear enough for other people to hear.

steps.test: Whistle along with a recording of a song and stay in tune with it from start to end.
steps.note: Choose a slow song with a clear tune: a folk song, a hymn, a song from a film. Keep the recording quiet enough to hear yourself. Where you drift off the note, stop, listen for a line, and join in again.

steps.test: Whistle three different tunes from memory, one after another, without stopping.
steps.note: The tune from rung six, the song from rung eight, and one more you know well. Choose them before you start so there is no gap to think. If you already whistle many tunes, choose three you have never whistled before.

steps.test: Whistle a note while breathing in, then whistle out and in again without a break in the sound.
steps.note: Keep the same lip shape and draw air in gently through the small hole. The breathed-in note is usually quieter and a little different; that is normal. Being able to whistle both ways lets a tune carry on while you breathe.

steps.test: Whistle one loud note with two fingers in your mouth.
steps.note: Wash your hands first. Put the tips of your thumb and first finger, or two first fingers, together under your tongue, fold the tongue back, close your lips tightly round the fingers and blow hard through the gap. Practise outside or where a loud noise does not matter, never close to somebody's ear. It often takes a week or more of short tries; there are many free videos showing it slowly.

steps.test: Teach somebody who cannot whistle yet until they make one clear note.
steps.note: A child, a friend, or a grown-up who never learned. Show them rung one: the "oo" lips, the tongue behind the bottom teeth, blowing gently. Most people blow too hard, so tell them to blow as if cooling a spoonful of soup. It may take a few short sessions over several days; stay cheerful, and the note is theirs when it comes.

tracks.name: Writing a song
tracks.line: From new words to a tune everybody knows to a song of your own that a group joins in with on the last chorus.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and writing one together counts. It starts with new words to a tune everybody knows, then choosing what your own song is about and finding the one line that says it. From there the chorus gets a tune, recorded on a phone, then two verses, cutting, singing it to somebody and changing it, and a simple beat or chords underneath. It ends with a second song written for a person you know, and one of your songs sung for a group who join in on the last chorus. No instrument is needed; your voice and a phone to record on are enough.

steps.test: Write four new lines to the tune of a song everybody knows, and sing them through.
steps.note: For example "Happy Birthday" or "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", with new words about your day, your pet, or the weather this morning. Each new line needs the same number of beats as the old line, so sing it as you write. If you already write songs, count this and start the next rungs on a new song.

steps.test: Choose what your own song is about, and write it at the top of a page in one plain sentence.
steps.note: One real thing: a day you remember, a person, a place you love, a feeling you had this week. For example "The morning we saw the sea for the first time." Everything else in the song will serve this sentence.

steps.test: Under your sentence, write eight lines of plain words about it: what you saw, heard, did and felt, with no rhymes yet.
steps.note: Real details, such as "the cold sand under my feet" or "Dad counting the waves", work better than big words. Write fast and do not fix anything yet.

steps.test: Choose the one line that says the whole thing best, and build a four-line chorus that starts and ends with it.
steps.note: The chorus is the part that comes back and that people remember. Rewrite your best line into something short enough to sing easily, then write two lines to go between its two appearances.

steps.test: Say the chorus out loud while clapping a steady beat, and change words until every line fits the beat.
steps.note: Clap "1, 2, 3, 4" as you speak. Where a line feels crowded, cut a word; where it feels thin, add one. Two lines ending with a rhyme helps people remember it, but a clear line matters more than a rhyme.

steps.test: Sing the chorus on a tune you make up, and record it on your phone so it is not lost.
steps.note: Sing the first tune that comes, even a very simple one that moves only a few notes. Record three different tries and choose the one you like best. Nobody else needs to hear these.

steps.test: The next day, sing the chorus from memory, then check it against the recording.
steps.note: If the tune came out differently, decide which version is better and record that one. A tune you can remember a day later is one other people will be able to remember too.

steps.test: Write a first verse of four lines that says where, when and who, leading into the chorus.
steps.note: The verse tells the story; the chorus says what it means. Use details from your eight lines on rung three. Try to have the second and fourth lines end in a rhyme or a near-rhyme.

steps.test: Give the verse its own tune, different from the chorus, and record verse and chorus together.
steps.note: Many songs sing the verse lower or more quietly and lift for the chorus, so you hear when the chorus arrives. Try two or three tunes and keep the one that leads most naturally into the chorus.

steps.test: Write a second verse that moves the story on: what happened next, or what changed.
steps.note: Same number of lines and the same tune as the first verse, with new words. If verse one was the morning, verse two could be the drive home, or years later.

steps.test: Sing the whole song through and cut every word you stumble over or do not need.
steps.note: Read it aloud first, then sing it. Mark every place you trip, and try the line with a word gone. Shorter lines are nearly always easier to sing.

steps.test: Sing verse, chorus, verse, chorus without stopping, time it, and get it under three minutes.
steps.note: If it runs long, cut a repeated line or shorten a long held note. Record this full version; it is your first finished draft.

steps.test: Sing the song to one person, and afterwards ask them which line they remember.
steps.note: A family member, a friend, or somebody on a video call. Tell them it is a first draft. The line they remember is working; a line nobody remembers is the one to look at.

steps.test: Change one line because of what they said, or because of what they did not remember.
steps.note: Only one line, so the song stays yours. Sing the new version through and keep whichever of the two you prefer.

steps.test: Sing the song while clapping or tapping a steady beat, or playing two or three chords, all the way through.
steps.note: Tapping a table is enough, and the Rhythm ladder shows how. If you play guitar, ukulele or keyboard, many songs work with just three chords; try the chords a beginner learns first on your instrument.

steps.test: Write the song out clearly, with the words, the chorus marked, and a recording, so somebody else could learn it.
steps.note: Write "Verse 1", "Chorus", "Verse 2", "Chorus" as headings. Add chords above the words if you use them. If you read music, write the tune of the chorus on a stave as well.

steps.test: Over one week, write a second song about somebody you know, using the same shape as your first.
steps.note: A grandparent, a friend, a brother or sister, a teacher. Choose a real thing they did or a day you shared, and keep every line kind. Go through the same steps: the sentence, the eight lines, the chorus, two verses.

steps.test: Sing or play that song to the person it is about, or send them the recording.
steps.note: In person, on a video call, or as a recording in a message. Tell them it is for them, then sing it through.

steps.test: Teach the chorus of one of your songs to two or more people until they can sing it back without you.
steps.note: Sing it one line at a time and have them copy each line, then two lines, then the whole chorus. Family at a meal table is a good place to start.

steps.test: Sing one of your songs for a group of three or more, and have them join in on the last chorus.
steps.note: Teach them the chorus first, as on the last rung, and tell them you will nod when the last chorus comes. A birthday, a family gathering, or friends round for a meal all work.

tracks.name: Reading music
tracks.line: From finding every C on a keyboard to playing a tune you have never seen, from the page, first time, for somebody.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts on a free piano app, finding the notes by letter, then the treble clef, middle C, and a note-naming quiz. Then comes rhythm: note lengths counted and clapped, time signatures, and dots, before playing tunes from the page, sharps and flats, repeats, and the bass clef. It ends with you writing out a tune of your own and playing a tune you have never seen, slowly, straight from the page, for somebody. A pencil, paper and a free piano app on a phone are all you need; where note names differ between countries, both are given.

steps.test: On a free piano app or website, find and play every C: the white key just to the left of each group of two black keys.
steps.note: Search "online piano". The black keys come in groups of two and three all along the keyboard. Music names notes with the letters A to G and then starts again, so there are many Cs, each one higher than the last. If you already read music, count this and go through the next rungs quickly.

steps.test: Play the white keys from one C up to the next, saying their names: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C.
steps.note: After G the letters go back to A. The two Cs sound like the same note, one higher. Do it three times, then play them down again, saying the names backwards.

steps.test: Draw a stave of five lines, draw a treble clef at the start, and write a note in each of the four spaces: F, A, C, E from the bottom up.
steps.note: A stave is five evenly spaced lines; lines and spaces are counted from the bottom. Copy the treble clef from any sheet of music; its curl wraps round the second line, which is G. The four spaces spell FACE, which makes them easy to remember. Write the letter under each note.

steps.test: Write a note on each of the five lines of your treble stave and name them from the bottom up: E, G, B, D, F.
steps.note: Some people remember them as "Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit". A note on a line has the line running through its middle. Now say all nine, lines and spaces, from the bottom: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F.

steps.test: Write middle C and the four notes above it on your stave, then play them from what you wrote.
steps.note: Middle C sits on a short extra line just below the treble stave. On a keyboard it is the C nearest the middle; on a phone app, the C labelled C4 if the keys have labels. Above it come D (just under the bottom line), E, F and G.

steps.test: Name twenty treble clef notes on a free note-reading quiz, getting at least eighteen right.
steps.note: Search "note reading quiz treble clef". Without a screen, ask somebody to draw notes on your stave for you, or write ten yourself, cover the letters, and come back to them the next day. Aim for accuracy first, then speed.

steps.test: Clap and count four bars of crotchets and minims that you have written out, counting "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud.
steps.note: A crotchet (called a quarter note in some countries) is a filled-in note with a stem and lasts one count. A minim (a half note) is an open note with a stem and lasts two counts: clap once and hold for the second count. A bar is the space between two upright lines, and here each holds four counts.

steps.test: Clap and count a line with semibreves and crotchet rests, keeping silent on every rest.
steps.note: A semibreve (a whole note) is an open note with no stem and lasts four counts. A rest is a silence of a set length; a crotchet rest is a zigzag shape and lasts one count. Keep counting out loud through every silence.

steps.test: Clap and count a line that mixes quavers with crotchets, saying "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and".
steps.note: A quaver (an eighth note) has a flag on its stem, or is joined to its neighbour by a beam, and lasts half a count. Two quavers fit in one count: clap one on the number and one on the "and". Start slowly with a metronome app at 60.

steps.test: Find three pieces of free beginner sheet music, read the time signature of each, and count one bar of each out loud.
steps.note: Search "free beginner sheet music", or use a songbook or hymn book. The time signature is the two numbers at the start. The top number says how many counts are in a bar; a 4 underneath means each count is a crotchet. So 4/4 is counted "1, 2, 3, 4" and 3/4 is "1, 2, 3".

steps.test: Clap and count a line in 3/4 that has dotted minims in it.
steps.note: A dot after a note makes it half as long again. A minim is two counts, so a dotted minim is three and fills a whole bar of 3/4. A dotted crotchet is one and a half counts. Write four bars yourself if you have no music to hand.

steps.test: Play the first eight bars of "Ode to Joy" from the page on your piano app, slowly and in time.
steps.note: Search for free easy sheet music for it in the key of C. Clap the rhythm first, then name the notes, then play. Bar four ends with a dotted crotchet, a quaver and a minim: hold the dotted note for one and a half counts.
how: Clap the rhythm, counting out loud.
Say the note names in order.
Play it with a metronome app at 60.

steps.test: Play an eight-bar tune you have never heard before, from the page, slowly.
steps.note: A beginner book or free beginner sheet music. Use the same three steps as the last rung: clap it, name it, play it. Do not look up a recording until you have played it through; then listen and check.

steps.test: Play C, C sharp and D, then E, E flat and D, saying each name as you play it.
steps.note: A sharp sign (like #) raises a note to the very next key up, and a flat sign (like a small b) lowers it to the very next key down; here both land on a black key. A natural sign cancels a sharp or flat. A sharp or flat written in front of a note lasts until the end of that bar.

steps.test: Play a simple tune with one sharp at the start of each line, playing every F as F sharp.
steps.note: The sharp sits on the top line of the treble stave, which is F. When a sharp or flat is written at the start of every line like this, it is called the key signature, and it applies to every F, high or low, all the way through. One sharp is the key of G major or E minor. Circle each F in pencil before you start.

steps.test: Play a tune that has a repeat sign and first and second endings, in the right order.
steps.note: A repeat sign is a thick and thin double line with two dots. Play to it, go back to the start or to the facing repeat sign, and play again. The first time through, play the bar marked 1; the second time, skip that bar and play the one marked 2. Trace the route with a finger before playing.

steps.test: Write the bass clef on a stave, name its lines G, B, D, F, A and its spaces A, C, E, G from the bottom, and find middle C just above it.
steps.note: The bass clef is for lower notes; its two dots sit either side of the fourth line, which is F. Some people remember "Good Boys Do Fine Always" for the lines and "All Cows Eat Grass" for the spaces. Middle C sits on a short extra line just above the bass stave, the same note as just below the treble stave.

steps.test: Play a four-bar bass clef line with your left hand, slowly, from the page.
steps.note: Piano music for beginners gives the left hand a bass clef line. Name the notes first, then play. On a phone app, use your left thumb or finger, and play the notes below middle C.

steps.test: Write out a four-bar tune of your own with a clef, a time signature and bar lines, and have it played back to check it.
steps.note: Make up a tune using the notes from middle C to G, and write it down neatly. Then have somebody who reads music play it, or type it into a free music-writing program or website that plays notes back. Fix anything that does not sound the way you meant.

steps.test: Play a simple tune you have never seen before, from the page, all the way through without stopping, in front of one person.
steps.note: Ask them to choose it from beginner sheet music. Take one minute to look: the time signature, the key signature, any repeats. Then play slowly and steadily, keeping the count going through any wrong note. That is reading music at sight.

tracks.name: Dance
tracks.line: From stepping in time to one song to teaching a group of five or more a dance and leading them through it.
tracks.who: For everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It starts with stepping in time to one song at home, then single steps and a short group dance learned from free videos, done without the video and without stopping after a mistake. After that come a dance from another part of the world, a dance of your own, a partner step, and joining in where other people are dancing. It ends with you teaching a dance to five or more people and leading them through it. Any style counts, from a circle dance to salsa to a line dance, and all you need is a clear space and music.

steps.test: Put on a song and step from one foot to the other on every beat, all the way to the end.
steps.note: Clear a space and wear bare feet or shoes that grip; socks slip on a smooth floor. The beat is the steady pulse you would tap your foot to. Let your arms move however they want. If you already dance, do it to a song you would not normally choose and count it.

steps.test: Learn one basic step from a free video and do it eight times in a row in time with music.
steps.note: Search the name of a step with the word "beginner": a side-together step, the grapevine, a box step, or the salsa basic step. Watch it through once, then copy it slowly with the video. Count the eight out loud.

steps.test: Do that step all the way through one song without counting out loud.
steps.note: Count in your head for the first few times through, then let the music tell your feet. If you lose the step, stand still, find the beat, and start again on a "1".

steps.test: Learn a second step and switch between the two every eight counts for a whole song.
steps.note: Choose a step that ends on the foot the first one starts with, so the change is smooth; a beginner video usually says. Count "1 to 8" for each, switching on every new "1".

steps.test: Learn a short group dance of three or four moves from a free video and dance it through once with the video.
steps.note: For example a line dance, a circle dance from Greece or the Balkans, or a beginner routine from a Bollywood film. Each is danced in a group, but you can learn it alone. Learn one move at a time with the video slowed down, then join them together.

steps.test: Dance that group dance to the music alone, with the video turned off.
steps.note: Play the song on its own. If you forget a move, keep stepping on the beat until the part you remember comes back. Then check the video once for the part you forgot.

steps.test: Dance it through three times in a row, and each time you go wrong, carry on from the next count instead of stopping.
steps.note: Stopping is the habit to lose. Keep your feet moving on the beat through the mistake and join the next move when its count comes round. Nobody watching notices a wrong step as much as a stop.

steps.test: Record yourself dancing it once on your phone, watch it back, and choose one move to tidy up.
steps.note: Prop the phone where it sees all of you. Many people dislike watching themselves at first, and that passes. Look for one thing only, such as a step too small or arms held stiff, practise that move ten times, and delete the video afterwards if you like.

steps.test: Dance the group dance all the way through for one person at home.
steps.note: A family member, a friend, or somebody on a video call. Tell them what it is first. Afterwards, offer to show them the first move.

steps.test: Dance for a whole song you have never heard before, using only the steps you already know.
steps.note: Ask somebody to choose the song, or play a radio station or a playlist you do not know. Listen for the beat in the first few seconds, start with your basic step, and change steps when the music changes.

steps.test: Learn a dance from a different part of the world from your first one, using free videos, over a week.
steps.note: If your first was a line dance, try a West African dance class, a Scottish or Irish folk dance, merengue from the Dominican Republic, or a Korean pop routine; if it was a Latin dance, try a circle dance. Read a few lines about where it comes from and when people dance it. A little each day for a week.

steps.test: Make up a dance of your own to one song: four sets of eight counts, using steps you know.
steps.note: Choose a part of the song, such as the chorus. Give each set of eight counts one step or move, and write the four down in order on paper so you remember them. Simple is fine; the rung is a dance you can repeat.

steps.test: Do your own dance the same way on two different days, from your written list.
steps.note: On the second day, read the list once, then put it away and dance. If it came out differently, decide which way you like and fix the list.

steps.test: Learn a short dance together with one other person from a free video, and dance it side by side in time.
steps.note: A child and a grown-up, two friends, or two family members. Learn it at the same time so neither of you is the teacher. Count "5, 6, 7, 8" out loud to start together.

steps.test: Learn the basic step of a partner dance, such as a waltz, salsa or swing, and dance it through one song holding hands with a partner.
steps.note: A family member or friend of any age. Stand facing each other holding both hands, arms relaxed, and step the basic from a beginner video. The aim is to stay together on the beat and not tread on each other's feet; going slowly is how you get there.

steps.test: Dance the partner step through one song leading, and through another following.
steps.note: The leader chooses when to start, turn or change, and shows it with a gentle push or pull of the hands; the follower feels it and goes with it. Both roles are skills and both people can learn each. Talk after each song about what was clear.

steps.test: Join in a dance where other people are already dancing, for at least one whole song.
steps.note: A family party, a wedding, a festival, a community dance evening, or a free dance event in a park. Many places run beginner dance classes, and the first one is often free to try. At a party, you can start with the steps from rung two.

steps.test: Teach your own dance from rung twelve to one person until they can dance it with the music.
steps.note: Teach one set of eight counts at a time, slowly and without music, then add the music at half effort. Praise what they get right before correcting anything.

steps.test: Teach a dance to two or three people together and get them dancing it through to the music.
steps.note: Your own dance or the group dance from rung five. Stand in front of them facing the same way, so your right is their right. Count them in with "5, 6, 7, 8", and run it three times before you stop.

steps.test: Teach a dance to a group of five or more at a gathering, and lead them through it to the music.
steps.note: A birthday, a family meal, a class, or a club evening. Ask the host first. Choose a simple dance, teach it in two or three short parts, then start the music and dance at the front. It does not need to be perfect; a room of people dancing together is the aim.

tracks.name: A song all the way through
tracks.line: From four, beside you. One song, sung whole, then sung to somebody.

steps.test: Sing one song all the way through with somebody singing beside you.
Sing it all the way through on your own, with nobody helping.
Sing it without forgetting any of the words.
Clap the beat while somebody else sings it.
Sing it and clap the beat at the same time.
Sing it as loud as you can.
Sing it so quietly that only the person next to you can hear.
Sing it fast, then sing it slow.
Sing it to somebody who has never heard you sing it.
Learn a second song all the way through.
Make up a new verse and sing that too.
Sing your song to a whole roomful of people.

categories.name: Magic and performance
categories.line: Card tricks, coins, sleight of hand, mind reading, mime, puppets.

tracks.name: Card tricks
tracks.line: From one trick that works by itself, to a five-minute card act for five or more people.
tracks.who: From about eight; children and grown-ups alike
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight, children and grown-ups alike. A pack of playing cards is the only kit. It starts with tricks that work by themselves, so the very first person you show is surprised, then adds a few simple secret moves: a way to find a card after the pack is cut, a way to make somebody take the card you want, shuffles that keep a card on top, and showing two cards as one. It ends with a five-minute card act for five or more people. Along the way you learn careful hands, clear speaking, and what to do when a trick goes wrong.

steps.test: Learn the 21-card trick and do it three times on your own, finding a card you picked yourself.
how: Deal 21 cards face up into three columns of seven, one row at a time, left to right.
Remember one card, then pick up the three columns with that card's column in the middle.
Deal and pick up the same way twice more, always putting its column in the middle.
Count down from the top of the face-down pile: the 11th card is the one.
steps.note: It works by counting alone, so no skill is needed, which makes it the right first trick. Each deal moves the card nearer the middle of the pile until it has to be the 11th of 21. Keep each column together when you pick it up.

steps.test: Do the 21-card trick for one person, then spell A-B-R-A-C-A-D-A-B-R-A, dealing one card for each letter, and turn over the last one.
steps.note: Abracadabra has exactly eleven letters, so the card on the last A is theirs. Each time you deal, ask them only which column their card is in. If you already know this trick, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Do twenty overhand shuffles in a row without dropping a card.
steps.note: Hold the pack upright by its short ends in your right hand. Use your left thumb to pull a few cards at a time off into your left hand, again and again, until the right hand is empty. Practise over a bed or a sofa so a dropped card does not matter. Small hands can start with half a pack.

steps.test: Do the key card trick for one person, and let them cut the pack as many times as they like.
how: Shuffle, and secretly look at the bottom card. This is your key card.
Spread the cards, let them take one and look at it, and have them put it on top of the pack.
Ask them to cut the pack and put the bottom part on top, as many times as they like.
Deal the cards face up one at a time: the card straight after your key card is theirs.
steps.note: A complete cut moves cards from the top to the bottom but never changes which card sits next to which, so your key card stays just before theirs. If your key card is the very last card dealt, theirs was the first one. You can glance at the bottom card while you tap the pack square on the table.

steps.test: Do a card trick saying only what you are doing, never what is about to happen.
steps.note: Say "Take a card" and "Put it on top", never "Now I will find your card". When people know the ending, they know where to look for the secret. Try it with the key card trick.

steps.test: Practise the cross-cut force on your own ten times, until it feels like an ordinary cut.
how: Look at the top card of the pack before you start.
Cut off some cards and set them down, the way the other person will.
Put the rest of the pack across the top of that pile, in a cross.
Count five seconds, lift off the top pile, and turn over the top card of the bottom pile: it is the card you looked at.
steps.note: A force means a person seems to choose freely but gets the card you want. It works because the card they are shown was on top of the pack all along; the cross shape and the pause make everybody forget which pile was which. Practise the pause as much as the hands.

steps.test: Write the name of a card on paper, fold it, and use the cross-cut force so one person takes that card.
steps.note: Put the card you wrote down on top of the pack before they arrive, and leave the folded paper where they can see it. During the pause, talk about the paper: "I wrote that before you came in." Let them open the paper themselves at the end.

steps.test: Using two overhand shuffles, move a card from the top to the bottom and back to the top, ten times without losing it.
how: First shuffle: pull the top card off on its own into your left hand, then shuffle the rest on top of it. It is now on the bottom.
Second shuffle: shuffle normally until only one card is left in your right hand, and drop it on top. It is back on top.
steps.note: Turn over the top card after each try to check. To anybody watching, both look like ordinary shuffles, so shuffle at your normal speed.

steps.test: Have one person take a card and put it on top, shuffle it back to the top, then ask them to name it and turn the top card over.
steps.note: This uses the two shuffles from the rung before, with a card they really chose. After the shuffles, put the pack down and ask "What was your card?" before anybody touches it. Let them turn it over themselves.

steps.test: Practise a double lift at the mirror thirty times, turning over two cards so they look like one.
how: Hold the pack face down in your left hand, and with your right thumb lift the back short edge of the top two cards together.
Turn the two over as one onto the top of the pack, so the face shows.
Turn them back face down as one, square with the pack.
steps.note: Keep the edges of the two cards exactly together, and move at the same speed as when you turn over one card. Check in the mirror: turn over one, then two, and see if you can tell which is which. Older cards are easier than new slippery ones.

steps.test: Make a card on the table change into the chosen card for one person, using the two shuffles and a double lift.
how: Have them choose a card, put it on top, and shuffle it back to the top.
Double lift to show a card and ask, "Is this your card?" They say no.
Turn both back face down as one, take the top card alone, and lay it face down on the table.
Wave over it and ask them to turn it over: it is their card.
steps.note: The card on the table was theirs all along; the double lift showed them the card underneath it. Keep the moment slow: "Not yours? Watch." This one surprises grown-ups who already know the easy tricks.

steps.test: Do the 21-card trick with the other person doing all the dealing and spelling, while you never touch the cards.
steps.note: You only tell them what to do: deal into three columns, point to your column, pick up with that column in the middle. Because it works by counting, it works in anybody's hands. Stand back a little so everybody can see you are not touching anything.

steps.test: Borrow a pack of cards that is not yours and do two tricks with it.
steps.note: The 21-card trick and the key card trick work with any pack, so start with those. A borrowed pack shows there is nothing special about the cards. Give it back neatly in its box.

steps.test: Choose what you will do if a trick goes wrong, and practise it three times with the cards in your hands.
steps.note: Pick one line, such as "Let us try that another way", and one trick that cannot go wrong, like the 21-card trick. Practise saying the line and going straight into that trick. Then the day a trick really fails, you do not have to think.

steps.test: Put three or four tricks in order for a five-minute act, and write the order on a small card.
steps.note: One good order: the written prediction first, because its card must be on top before anybody arrives; then the key card trick; then the card that changes on the table; and the 21-card trick with its spelling to end. Plan one or two sentences to say between tricks. Your own words work better than anybody else's.

steps.test: Run your whole act on your own five times, speaking out loud, with a timer.
steps.note: Say every word as if people were there. Aim for about five minutes; if it runs long, cut words, not tricks. A run only counts if you do not stop and start again.

steps.test: Do your whole act for one or two people at home, from start to end.
steps.note: Afterwards, ask which trick they liked best and which moment felt slow. Change one thing in your notes before the next time.

steps.test: Do the changing-card trick with one person on your left and one on your right, and ask each if they saw anything odd.
steps.note: The double lift is easy to see from the side if the cards are tilted up. Keep the pack flat and low, and check which way you need to turn. When you perform, stand so that nobody is right beside your hands.

steps.test: Teach somebody the 21-card trick until they can do it for a third person.
steps.note: Deal it through slowly with them twice, then let them do it while you watch. Remind them that the column always goes in the middle. It counts when their trick works on somebody who has not seen it.

steps.test: Perform your five-minute card act for five or more people.
steps.note: A family meal, a birthday or a club you belong to all work; ask the host first. Sit or stand with everybody in front of you. Set the prediction card on top before you begin, and keep your small card of notes in your pocket.

tracks.name: Coin tricks
