tracks.line: From one coin passed hand to hand at a mirror, to a three-minute coin routine for five or more people.
tracks.who: From about eight; children and grown-ups alike
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight, children and grown-ups alike. It starts with one coin passed from hand to hand at a mirror, then builds three simple secret moves: the French drop, a coin held hidden in curled fingers, and a pretend hand-over. With those, a coin vanishes, comes back, travels, changes and goes through a table, and the ladder ends with a three-minute routine for five or more people. All you need is a coin or two, and the practice gives you steady hands and the calm to perform. Keep coins away from children under three, who may put them in their mouths.

steps.test: Stand at a mirror and pass a coin from your left hand to your right hand for real, ten times, watching how it looks.
steps.note: Hold the coin flat between the thumb and first two fingers of your left hand, then let your right hand take it and close round it. Watch the speed of your hands and where your eyes go. Every secret move later has to look exactly like this real one. If you are left-handed, swap the hands all the way up the ladder.

steps.test: Do the French drop slowly at the mirror ten times, until you cannot see the coin fall.
how: Hold the coin flat by its edges between your left thumb and fingertips, palm up, fingers a little curled.
Bring your right hand over as if to take it: right thumb under the coin, right fingers covering the top.
Just as the right fingers hide it, let the coin drop quietly into your curled left fingers.
Close the right hand and move it away as if it holds the coin, and let the left hand relax.
steps.note: The French drop is hundreds of years old and still works. Go at the same speed as your real hand-over from rung 1; rushing makes it look odd. The coin only falls a short way, into fingers already curled to catch it.

steps.test: Do the French drop ten more times with your eyes on the closed right hand, then open that hand slowly to show it empty.
steps.note: People look where you look. If your eyes stay on the hand that seems to hold the coin, theirs will too. Keep the left hand still and relaxed, and open the right hand one finger at a time.

steps.test: Show one person a coin, make it vanish with the French drop, and show your right hand empty.
steps.note: Start with somebody at home, standing in front of you rather than beside you. Say only "Watch this coin." Afterwards, put your left hand in your pocket and leave the coin there before you show that hand.

steps.test: Make the coin vanish, then bring it back from beside the person's ear.
how: Do the French drop, keeping the coin in your curled left fingers.
Show the right hand empty, then reach your left hand towards their ear.
As your hand arrives, push the coin to your fingertips with your thumb, and bring it forward slowly so it shows.
steps.note: Ask first, and do not actually touch their ear; your hand only needs to come near it. If somebody would rather you did not come close, bring the coin back from behind your own elbow instead.

steps.test: Keep a coin hidden in your curled right fingers for ten minutes while you use that hand for ordinary things.
steps.note: This is the finger palm. The coin lies across the middle and ring fingers, near where they join the hand, and the fingers curl just a little, like a hand hanging at your side. Turn pages, point, pick up a cup. When you forget the coin is there, the hand looks natural.

steps.test: Practise the pretend hand-over at the mirror ten times, until it looks the same as a real one.
how: Lay the coin on your open right hand, across the middle and ring fingers.
Turn the right hand over towards the left as if tipping the coin into it, and curl the fingers just enough to keep it.
Close the left hand as if it caught the coin, and move it away.
Let the right hand relax, with the coin still held in its fingers.
steps.note: Do one real tip-over first, then one pretend one, and compare them in the mirror. The left hand does the acting: it must close as if something landed in it, and your eyes follow it.

steps.test: Make a coin travel from your left hand to your right hand for one person.
steps.note: Do the pretend hand-over, so they think the coin is in your closed left hand; the coin is really in your right fingers. Close the right hand into a loose fist. Hold both fists out, open the left one slowly to show it empty, then open the right. If you already do this trick, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Change a small coin into a bigger coin for one person.
how: Before you start, hide the bigger coin in the finger palm of your right hand.
Show the small coin at your left fingertips.
Do the French drop: the right hand seems to take the small coin and closes.
Open the right hand to show the big coin, and while they look at it, put the left hand in your pocket and leave the small coin there.
steps.note: Any two coins that look clearly different will do, and a large button or a metal washer can be the big one. Everybody looks at the right hand when it opens, and that is the moment the left hand moves. Keep both hands slow.

steps.test: Ask a helper to stand in front of you, then on your left, then on your right, and do each trick once from each place.
steps.note: Ask them to say "stop" the moment they see a coin that should be hidden. Where they say stop is a bad angle for that trick. Write it down, and from then on keep people in front of you for that trick. A mirror cannot show you this; only a person can.

steps.test: Sitting at a table, make a coin pass down through the tabletop for one person.
how: Sit across the table from them, with the coin at your left fingertips.
Do the French drop, so the right hand seems to take the coin.
Let your left hand go under the table "to catch it", with the coin in its fingers.
Slap the right hand flat on the table, lift it to show nothing there, and bring the coin out from underneath.
steps.note: At the moment of the slap, tap the coin against the underside of the table for a small click. Keep your eyes on the right hand the whole time. Any table works, even the kitchen one.

steps.test: Borrow a coin from somebody and do two of your tricks with it.
steps.note: A borrowed coin shows there is nothing special about it. Ask plainly: "May I borrow a coin? You will get it back." Use tricks that need one coin, such as the vanish and the table, and hand it back straight after.

steps.test: Write down what you will say during three standing tricks, a few short sentences each, and read it aloud once.
steps.note: Choose three that can be done standing, for example the vanish and the ear, the coin that travels, and the coin that changes. Say what you are doing, never what is about to happen, so nobody knows where to look. A simple story helps, such as a coin that keeps escaping. Your own words work better than anybody else's.

steps.test: Run your three tricks as one routine at the mirror five times, with no stops in between.
steps.note: Plan where the coins are between tricks, so one trick ends where the next begins; for example, the ear production leaves the coin at your fingertips, ready for the pretend hand-over. If you stop and start again, that run does not count. Time it: about three minutes is right.

steps.test: Do your whole routine for one person, from start to end, without stopping.
steps.note: Somebody at home is ideal. If a move goes wrong, keep going to the end; not stopping is the thing you are practising. Afterwards, ask which moment surprised them most.

steps.test: When somebody asks to see a trick again, smile and show them a different trick instead.
steps.note: The second time, people know where to look, so the secret is easier to see. Have a line ready, such as "Here is another one." Practise saying it aloud now; the rung counts the first time somebody asks and you do it.

steps.test: When somebody asks how a trick works, keep the secret kindly and move on to talk about something else.
steps.note: A smile and "That part stays with me" is enough. Keeping the secret keeps the surprise alive for them. Never make the person feel silly for asking; it means they enjoyed it.

steps.test: During practice, drop a coin on purpose, pick it up with a smile, and go straight on to the next trick.
steps.note: Real coins fall, and an audience only minds if you do. Choose your line now, for example "That one wanted to see the floor", and practise it three times. Then the day a coin really falls, you already know what to do.

steps.test: Teach somebody the French drop until they can make a coin vanish for a third person.
steps.note: Show it slowly, then let them try while you watch from the front. Tell them the two things that matter most: go at the speed of a real hand-over, and look at the hand that seems to hold the coin. It counts when their vanish works on somebody who has not seen it.

steps.test: Perform your three-minute coin routine for five or more people.
steps.note: A family meal, a birthday or a club you belong to all work; ask the host first. Have everybody stand or sit in front of you, as you learned from your helper. Start with the trick you do best, and end with the one that got the biggest reaction at home.

tracks.name: Mind-reading tricks
tracks.line: From a number puzzle on paper, to a ten-minute set of mind-reading tricks for five or more people.
tracks.who: From about nine; children and grown-ups alike
tracks.about: For everybody from about nine, children and grown-ups alike. These are tricks that look like mind reading, and you always say so: every one works by maths, a helper with a secret signal, or a small hidden detail, never by any real power. It starts with a number puzzle on paper and ends with a ten-minute set of four tricks for five or more people. It builds careful counting, clear speaking and good manners in front of an audience. People only ever choose numbers, words, objects and animals; nothing here guesses at anybody's private life, feelings or worries.

steps.test: On paper, do the always-five puzzle with three different starting numbers, and check each answer is 5.
how: Think of a number and double it.
Add 10, then halve the result.
Take away the number you started with. The answer is 5.
steps.note: Doubling and then halving gives back your number plus 5, so taking your number away leaves 5. Try 37: double is 74, add 10 is 84, half is 42, take away 37 is 5. Knowing why it works lets you perform it calmly.

steps.test: Do the always-five puzzle with one person, saying first that it is a trick, and name their answer before they tell you.
steps.note: Start with: "Here is a trick that looks like mind reading." Let them use paper or a calculator, and give each step slowly. Then look at them for a moment and say, "You have 5." If you already know this one, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: On paper, do the 1089 puzzle with three different three-digit numbers, and check each answer is 1089.
how: Write a three-digit number whose first and last digits differ by 2 or more, such as 742.
Write it backwards (247) and take the smaller number from the bigger one (495).
Write that answer backwards (594) and add the two together: 1089.
steps.note: The rule about the first and last digits matters: with a number like 312 the subtraction gives 99 and the trick fails. Check each subtraction carefully, because one slip in front of people gives the wrong answer.

steps.test: Write 1089 on a paper and fold it, then lead one person through the 1089 puzzle and have them open the paper.
steps.note: Give them the folded paper to hold before they start, so everybody knows it was written first. Let them use a calculator if they like, and if the answer is not 1089, check the subtraction together. Say it is a prediction trick, and enjoy the moment with them.

steps.test: Before a reveal, ask the person to say their choice out loud, then wait for a slow count of three.
steps.note: The pause gives everybody time to remember that you could not have known. Try it with the 1089 paper: "Tell everybody your number." Count three to yourself. "Now open the paper."

steps.test: Find a book at home with at least 108 pages, and learn the ninth word on page 108 by heart.
steps.note: Count from the first word at the top of the page. Write the word nowhere; learn it, and check yourself again tomorrow. Choose a book you can leave on a shelf among others, because it sets up the next rung.

steps.test: Lead one person through the 1089 puzzle, then have them open the book at page 108, look at the ninth word, and name it for them.
steps.note: Say: "Use the first three numbers as a page, and the last one to count words." Let them take the book from the shelf themselves. Take your time before naming the word, and say at the end that it was a trick.

steps.test: Stack three dice, and work out the total of the five hidden faces from the top face alone, ten times.
steps.note: On an ordinary die, opposite faces add up to 7. Three dice have six top and bottom faces adding up to 21, and in a stack you can see only the very top one. So the hidden total is 21 take away the top number. Check each time by adding the hidden faces; dice from a board game are fine.

steps.test: With your back turned, have one person stack three dice, then turn round, look once, and name the total of the hidden faces.
steps.note: Ask them to stack the dice any way they like, then add up the hidden faces themselves and write the total down. Turn round, look at the stack for a second, then look away while you seem to think. Say the number and let them check.

steps.test: When somebody asks how you did it, say it is a trick, keep the secret, and never claim a real power.
steps.note: "It is a trick, and a good one, but the secret stays with me" is honest and friendly. If a child asks whether you can really read minds, say no, plainly. Practise the line now; the rung counts the first time somebody asks.

steps.test: Practise the one-ahead trick on your own three times, with three slips of paper and three questions.
how: Plan the last question to be the 1089 puzzle, so you already know its answer.
Ask for a colour, and while they think, write 1089 on the first slip.
When they say a colour, ask for an animal and write their colour on the second slip.
When they say an animal, lead them through the 1089 puzzle and write their animal on the third slip.
steps.note: You stay one answer ahead: each slip holds the answer to the question before. For practice, play both parts yourself, making up answers. At the end the slips are mixed and opened together, so nobody can tell which was written when.

steps.test: Do the one-ahead trick for one person: three folded slips, three questions, and three right answers.
steps.note: Hide each slip from view while you write, fold it straight away, and drop it in a cup so the order is lost. At the end, tip the slips out and let them open all three. Say it is a trick before you start.

steps.test: Agree a secret signal with a helper, and practise the black-object trick together five times.
how: You leave the room, and the others choose any object in it.
You come back, and your helper points at objects one at a time, asking "Is it this?"
Your helper points at something black just before pointing at the chosen object.
You say no to each one until the one straight after the black thing, and say yes to that.
steps.note: The helper must never point at anything black except as the signal. If the room has a lot of black things, agree on another colour. A grown-up and a child make a good team.

steps.test: Perform the black-object trick with your helper for two or more people, three times in a row.
steps.note: Doing it three times shows it is not luck. If somebody works out the secret, say "Well done" and let them be the next helper; that is part of the fun.

steps.test: Tear a sheet of paper into nine pieces, three by three, and with your eyes closed find the middle piece by touch, five times.
steps.note: The middle piece is the only one with torn edges on all four sides. The corner pieces have two smooth edges and the others have one. Tear along straight lines so the difference is easy to feel.

steps.test: Give four or more people a torn piece each, have the one with the middle piece write an animal, and find that piece without looking.
steps.note: Hand the middle piece to one person and ask them to write any animal; everybody else writes a food. Everybody folds their piece and drops it in a bowl. Reach in without looking, feel for four torn edges, and read out the animal slowly.

steps.test: Choose four tricks for a ten-minute set, put them in order, and write one opening sentence that says they are tricks.
steps.note: One good order: the always-five puzzle to start, the dice, the one-ahead slips, and the torn-paper animal to end. The book trick can take the place of any of them. An opening sentence might be: "None of this is real mind reading, but see if you can work out how it is done."

steps.test: Run your whole set on your own twice, speaking every line out loud, with a timer.
steps.note: Set out the paper, pens, dice and cup before you begin, and say the questions as if people were there. Aim for about ten minutes. Practise one line for when something fails, such as "Let us try another one."

steps.test: Teach a younger person the always-five puzzle until they can do it for somebody else.
steps.note: Do it on them first, then show them the steps on paper and why the answer is 5. Let them practise on you twice. It counts when their trick works on somebody new, and they say it is a trick.

steps.test: Perform your ten-minute set for five or more people, saying at the start that these are tricks.
steps.note: A family gathering, a birthday or a club you belong to all work; ask the host first. Choose people for each trick who look happy to join in, and never pick on anybody. Thank each helper by name at the end.

tracks.name: Mime and clowning
tracks.line: From one action mimed at a mirror, to a two-minute silent piece for five or more people.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. Mime is showing things with your body and face and no words; clowning is making people laugh at a clown's own small troubles. It starts with miming a cup at a mirror, builds the classic skills of the invisible wall, the rope pull and the walk on the spot, and ends with a two-minute silent piece for five or more people. It needs no kit at all, only a clear space, and it teaches you to notice how people really move. One rule runs through every rung: the joke is always on you, never on anybody watching or any real person.

steps.test: At a mirror, mime drinking from a cup, keeping your hand the shape of a real cup the whole time.
steps.note: Hold a real cup first and look at the shape of your hand, then put it down and make the same shape with nothing in it. Lift it, tip it, swallow, and put it down. The cup must not change size while you hold it.

steps.test: Mime five everyday actions for one person, and have all five named.
steps.note: For example: brushing your teeth, opening a door, putting on a coat, reading a book, eating an apple. Do each slowly, with real sizes and weights. If one is not guessed, do it again more slowly instead of adding sounds.

steps.test: Mime putting a cup down on a table, walk away, come back, and pick it up from exactly the same spot.
steps.note: Invisible things only seem real if they stay where you left them. Look at the spot as you put the cup down and again as you come back. A helper can watch and tell you if it moved.

steps.test: Hold the invisible wall at the mirror for thirty seconds, moving one hand at a time to new places on it.
how: Hold both hands up, fingers together, as if touching a window.
Let each hand arrive with a tiny stop, as if it has just touched glass.
Move one hand to a new spot on the wall while the other stays still, then move the other.
steps.note: Keep your palms flat and fingers straight while touching, and relax the hand as it comes off. Keep the wall the same distance from your body all the time. Look at the wall as if you can almost see it.

steps.test: Keep the invisible wall in exactly the same place for a whole minute while your head and shoulders move behind it.
steps.note: The whole effect depends on the invisible thing not moving; if it moves once, it is gone. Lean left and right, and look through the wall, while your hands stay fixed in the air. Watch your hands in the mirror, not your face.

steps.test: Mime lifting a heavy suitcase, then a feather, and have a watcher say which looked heavier and why.
steps.note: A heavy thing changes the whole body: the knees bend, the breath is held, and the hand is pulled down by the weight. A feather needs only fingertips and a light face. Bend your knees for the pretend lift too, the same as for a real one.

steps.test: Do the rope pull for thirty seconds, pulling an invisible rope towards you.
how: Grip the rope with both fists, one in front of the other, at chest height.
Pull both fists in towards your chest, leaning back a little.
Let go with the back hand, reach it forward past the front hand, grip, and pull again.
steps.note: The rope seems real when both fists grip the same straight line each time. Lean back as if the rope is heavy, and let your face show the effort. Do it in a clear space with nothing behind you.

steps.test: Walk on the spot for thirty seconds so that you look as if you are walking forward.
how: Lift your right foot and put it down flat a short step ahead.
As it lands, slide your left foot back along the floor, keeping it flat.
Lift the left foot and put it down a short step ahead, and slide the right foot back.
Swing your arms as in a normal walk, and keep your head at one height.
steps.note: Practise slowly at the mirror, standing side-on, because that is how it looks best. It takes many tries before it looks smooth. Socks on a smooth floor make sliding easier, so go carefully and keep your weight over your feet.

steps.test: Mime a short story with a beginning, a middle and an end, with no words, twice at the mirror.
steps.note: For example: you open a present, find a smaller present inside, then a smaller one, and at last a tiny one that makes you smile. Or you plant a seed, water it, wait, and pick the flower. Plan the three parts before you start.

steps.test: Practise a clown double-take ten times: look at something, look away calmly, then turn back quickly with a surprised face.
steps.note: Clowns show what they are thinking before they do anything. The first look must be calm, so the second one is a surprise. Try it with an odd thing on a table, such as a shoe on a plate. Turn your head gently; the surprise is in your eyes and mouth, not in your neck.

steps.test: Make one person laugh with no words by having a small pretend trouble with an invisible object.
steps.note: For example, an umbrella that will not open and then pulls you along, or a door that keeps swinging back at you. The laugh comes from you trying hard and staying cheerful. The trouble is always with a thing or with yourself, never with the person watching.

steps.test: Put three of your skills into a two-minute silent piece, and run it at the mirror three times with a timer.
steps.note: For example: walk on the spot to a door, find an invisible wall, pull it open with the rope, then have trouble with an umbrella outside. Plan where each part starts and ends. Music with no words can play in the background if you like.

steps.test: Run a mime-guessing game for three or more younger children, giving each a turn to mime and a turn to guess.
steps.note: Whisper each child an easy action: brushing teeth, eating a banana, being a cat. Clap for every try, guessed or not. Keep turns short so nobody waits long.

steps.test: Perform your two-minute silent piece for five or more people.
steps.note: A family gathering, a birthday or a school or club event all work; ask the host first. Clear a space with nothing to trip on. Stay silent all the way to your bow at the end.

tracks.name: Puppets
tracks.line: From an old sock on your hand, to a five-minute puppet show for younger children.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. You make your own puppets free from an old sock and a paper bag, learn the small things that make a puppet seem alive, and end by putting on a five-minute show for younger children and letting each of them talk to a puppet. Puppets are a gentle way to practise voices, stories and speaking to an audience, because everybody looks at the puppet, not at you. A grown-up does the cutting with young children, and buttons or other small parts are only for puppets kept away from children under three.

steps.test: Make a sock puppet by putting an old sock on your hand and giving it two eyes.
how: Put your hand in the sock with your fingers in the toe and your thumb in the heel. The gap between is the mouth.
Mark where the eyes go, just above your knuckles.
Take the sock off and add the eyes: paper circles stuck on with glue or tape, or two sewn-on buttons.
steps.note: An odd sock that has lost its partner is perfect. Eyes drawn with a marker pen work too, but take the sock off your hand first. A grown-up helps with the needle if you sew buttons on.

steps.test: Make the puppet count from one to ten out loud, opening its mouth for each word.
steps.note: Move your thumb down to open the mouth, rather than lifting your fingers; that looks like a real jaw. Open at the start of each word and close at the end, twice for "seven". Watch it in a mirror.

steps.test: Make the puppet look at five things in the room, one at a time, stopping on each.
steps.note: Where the puppet looks is what makes it seem alive; nothing else comes close. Point its nose, not only your wrist, and hold still for a second on each thing, such as the window, a lamp or your own face.

steps.test: Keep the puppet quiet for thirty seconds while it breathes, with a small, slow rise and fall of your hand.
steps.note: A puppet that freezes looks like a sock again. A small, slow movement every few seconds keeps it alive while it listens. Try it while somebody else is talking, or while music plays.

steps.test: Give the puppet a name and a voice that is not your own, and have it talk about itself for two minutes.
steps.note: Try a voice higher, lower, slower or faster than yours. Let it say what it likes, what it does all day, and where it lives, for example at the bottom of the washing basket. Keep the voice the same the whole time; a timer helps.

steps.test: Have the puppet ask one person three questions, and reply to each of their answers.
steps.note: Look at the person, and keep the puppet's mouth moving with the words. Easy questions work best: "What is your favourite food?" Children often answer a puppet more easily than a grown-up.

steps.test: Make a paper-bag puppet with a talking mouth and paper arms.
how: Lay a flat-bottomed paper bag down with the folded bottom on top, facing you.
Draw the eyes and nose on the folded flap, and the chin just below the flap.
Cut two strips of paper and tape one to each side as arms.
Put your hand inside with your fingers in the flap, and bend your fingers to make the mouth open and close.
steps.note: If you have no paper bag, make a second sock puppet and give it paper arms. A grown-up does the cutting with young children. Draw the face large and bold so it can be seen across a room.

steps.test: Give the second puppet a voice clearly different from the first, and switch between the two voices ten times.
steps.note: If the first voice is high and quick, make this one low and slow. Give it a different mood too: one cheerful, one grumpy but kind. Switching back and forth checks that you never mix the two up.

steps.test: With one puppet on each hand, have them talk to each other for two minutes.
steps.note: Only the puppet that is talking moves its mouth; the other turns to look at it and breathes. A simple subject works: the sock has lost its partner, and the bag thinks it knows where to look.

steps.test: Plan a five-minute puppet story with a beginning, a problem and an ending, written as six short lines.
steps.note: For example: the sock wakes up alone; it cannot find its partner; it asks the bag for help; they look in funny places; they find the partner in the washing; they celebrate. Add one moment where a puppet asks the audience a question, such as "Have you seen a sock?" Six lines are enough; you make up the exact words as you go.

steps.test: Make a stage you can kneel behind, from a table and a sheet or from a big cardboard box.
steps.note: The easiest stage is a table with a sheet hanging over the front to the floor, and you kneel behind it. A big box with a window cut in the front works too; a grown-up does the cutting. Check from the audience's side that the puppets show above the edge and your head does not.

steps.test: Rehearse the whole show behind your stage twice, from start to end, without stopping.
steps.note: Lay the puppets where you can reach them without looking. Arms get tired, so rest your elbows on the edge between lines. If you have a helper, each of you can work one puppet.

steps.test: Put on your show for two or more people.
steps.note: People in your family make a fine first audience. When a puppet asks its question, wait for the answers. Afterwards, ask what they liked best.

steps.test: Put on your five-minute show for three or more younger children, then let each child talk to a puppet.
steps.note: Ask their grown-ups first, and keep it cheerful, with nothing frightening for small children. After the show, bring a puppet out and let it say hello to each child by name. If a child is shy, the puppet can simply wave.

tracks.name: Circus skills
tracks.line: From a sock swung in circles, to a two-minute circus routine to music for five or more people.
tracks.who: From about seven; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about seven: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. It uses soft, safe kit in this order: socks swung in circles like poi, a hoop, a plastic spinning plate on a stick, and a diabolo, with nothing that uses fire or anything hard thrown high. Ball juggling has its own ladder. It ends with a two-minute routine to music for five or more people. It builds timing, balance and patience, and every rung is practised in a clear space, away from windows, lights, other people and anything that can break.

steps.test: Make a sock poi and swing it in circles beside your body twenty times with one hand.
how: Push a rolled-up pair of socks into the toe of a long sock, and tie a knot above them.
Hold the open end, with your arm hanging by your side.
Swing it in big circles beside you, like a wheel turning next to your leg.
steps.note: Poi come from the Māori people of New Zealand, who swing them in dance; this soft version is for safe practice. Give yourself a clear circle of space bigger than your arm and the sock together. The socks are soft, so a knock on the leg does not hurt.

steps.test: Swing the sock poi twenty times with your other hand, then twenty circles the opposite way round with each hand.
steps.note: The other hand feels clumsy at first, and it improves within a few days. Keep your wrist loose and your arm fairly straight. If you already swing both ways easily, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Make a second sock poi and swing both at once, one on each side, the same way round, twenty times.
steps.note: Keep the two socks level with each other, like two wheels on a cart. If they bump, hold your hands a little further apart. Counting out loud keeps them in time.

steps.test: Swing both poi twenty times so that one is at the top whenever the other is at the bottom.
steps.note: Start one sock swinging, then start the second half a circle later. If they keep matching up again, slow down and let one hand lead.

steps.test: With one poi, swing ten figures of eight in front of you, one circle on your left side and then one on your right.
steps.note: Turn your wrist across your body to move from one side to the other, and keep each circle the same size. Go slowly at first; it looks good even at a gentle speed.

steps.test: Spin a hoop around one wrist and forearm twenty times without it dropping.
steps.note: Hold your arm straight out, start the hoop turning with the other hand, and move your wrist in a small circle to keep it going. Any hula hoop works; if you do not have one, a school, youth club or friend may lend one.

steps.test: Roll a hoop away across the floor so that it stops and rolls back to you, five times.
how: Hold the hoop upright in front of you, with one hand on top.
Push it forward, and pull your hand down the back of it as you let go, so it spins backwards.
It moves away, stops, and rolls back towards you.
steps.note: Use grass or a long floor with nothing breakable at the far end. A sharper pull down gives more spin and a quicker return. Stop it with your hand when it comes back.

steps.test: Keep a hoop turning round your waist for thirty seconds.
steps.note: Stand with one foot a little in front of the other. Push the hoop round against your back, and rock your weight forward and back in time with it, rather than moving your hips in circles. A bigger, heavier hoop turns more slowly and is easier to learn on.

steps.test: Spin a hoop on one raised arm and pass it over to the other arm without it stopping.
steps.note: With the hoop turning on your right wrist and your arm up, bring your left hand up to touch your right hand, and let the hoop move across onto the left wrist. Keep both wrists circling while it passes. A lighter hoop makes it easier.

steps.test: Start a plastic spinning plate on its stick and keep it spinning for ten seconds.
how: Hold the stick upright, with its tip inside the ring on the underside of the plate.
Move the stick in small, quick circles so the plate starts to turn with it.
When it spins well, hold the stick still and straight. Circle again to speed it up.
steps.note: Use only a plastic plate made for spinning, never a kitchen plate. They cost little, and schools, youth clubs and circus groups often lend them.

steps.test: Keep the plate spinning for one minute, passing the stick from one hand to the other twice.
steps.note: Speed the plate up before each pass. Hold the stick near the bottom and pass it upright, with no tilt. If the plate slows, give it a few small circles again.

steps.test: Toss the spinning plate a short way up off the stick and catch it back on the stick, five times.
steps.note: Spin it fast first. Flick the stick up so the plate rises about a hand's height, then bring the tip back under the middle as it falls. Practise over grass or a bed, and keep it well away from faces.

steps.test: Get a diabolo spinning on its string and keep it going for ten seconds.
how: Lay the diabolo on the ground in front of you, with the string under its middle.
Lift the right stick so the diabolo rolls along the ground to your right, then lift it into the air.
Keep it spinning by pulling the right stick up quickly and letting it down slowly, while the left stick stays nearly still.
steps.note: Borrow one if you can; many schools, youth clubs and circus groups have them. If you are left-handed, swap the work over to the left stick. If it starts to tip, turn your body slowly one way, then the other, until you find which way straightens it.

steps.test: Keep the diabolo spinning and level for a whole minute.
steps.note: Keep the sticks at about waist height and the string fairly tight. A few quick pulls with the right stick every second or two keep the speed up. If it tips, move one stick a little towards you or away from you until it is level again.

steps.test: Toss the diabolo a short way into the air and catch it back on the string, five times.
steps.note: Spin it fast, then pull the sticks apart quickly so the tight string throws it up, only a little way at first and never above your head. Watch it, and bring the tight string under it, letting the sticks move down a little as it lands. Use a soft rubber diabolo, and keep other people well back.

steps.test: Choose your three best tricks from any of the props and join them into a one-minute routine without stopping.
steps.note: For example: poi circles into the figure of eight, then put the poi down and pick up the hoop for the waist spin. Lay the props out in order before you start. Plan your ending: a still pose with your arms up shows people it is over.

steps.test: During practice, drop a prop on purpose, pick it up calmly, and go straight on with the routine.
steps.note: Choose what you will do: a small shrug and a smile, or a bow to the prop. Practise it three times. Audiences like a performer who carries on; they only mind if the performer does.

steps.test: Make your routine two minutes long and do it to a piece of music three times, starting and ending with the music.
steps.note: Choose music with a clear, steady beat, suitable for children to hear. Plan one trick for each part of the music, and play it from a phone or any music player.

steps.test: Teach somebody to swing a sock poi until they can do twenty circles on their own.
steps.note: Make them a sock poi first, and show them in a clear space. Stand beside them rather than facing them, so they can copy your arm. It counts when they do twenty circles without your help.

steps.test: Perform your two-minute routine to music for five or more people.
steps.note: A garden, a park or a big room works; check the space is clear and people stand well back. Ask the host first if it is not your own home. Finish with your still pose and a bow.

categories.name: Food and the kitchen
categories.line: Knife skills, cooking, baking, growing, preserving, hosting.

tracks.name: Real food, part one
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From one honest look at a label to an eight-hour eating window.

steps.test: Read the ingredients of everything you eat today. Change nothing.
steps.note: Just read. If you cannot picture an ingredient growing, or being made in a kitchen, it is one to notice. Today is looking, not fixing.

steps.test: Drink only water, tea, coffee or herbal tea for a whole day.
steps.note: No fizzy drinks, no juice, nothing sweetened. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it. Already done is still done, and it is the ground the rest stands on.

steps.test: Eat one meal slowly: fork down between mouthfuls, taste every one.
steps.note: Twenty minutes for a plate. Notice when you are full; it arrives earlier than the empty plate does.

steps.test: Swap one thing in one meal for something more real.
steps.note: Cereal for eggs, crisps for nuts or cheese, a sauce from a jar for butter and salt, white bread for a plate of vegetables. One swap, one meal.

steps.test: Nothing to eat for the first three hours after waking.
steps.note: Water, tea or coffee are fine. If you already skip breakfast, count it. Notice that hunger comes in waves and passes.

steps.test: Nothing to eat in the three hours before you sleep.
steps.note: Finish dinner, close the kitchen. Herbal tea if you want something. Most people sleep better for it the very first night.

steps.test: A whole day without snacks: meals only, as many as you like.
steps.note: Three meals, or two, or four; the rule is nothing between them. Snacking is the habit most worth breaking, so this is a big rung.

steps.test: A day sweetened only by honey, fruit, or nothing.
steps.note: No sugar, no sweeteners, no syrups. If you already live like this, do it on purpose and count it. Read the labels; sugar hides under twenty names.

steps.test: A day where nothing you eat has more than five ingredients on its label.
steps.note: Food with no label (meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit, butter) counts as zero. This is the rung that empties the biscuit tin.

steps.test: Cook one meal from real food only.
steps.note: Meat, fish or eggs; vegetables; butter, cream or olive oil; salt. Nothing from a packet with a list on it. It can be simple: eggs, spinach and butter is a meal.

steps.test: Both edges in one day: nothing for three hours after waking, nothing for three hours before bed.
steps.note: Rungs five and six together. You have done each already; today they meet.

steps.test: A twelve-hour window: first bite and last bite twelve hours apart.
steps.note: Eight to eight, nine to nine. Most people are nearly there already; this makes it deliberate. Water and tea outside the window are fine.

steps.test: A day where every carbohydrate is a vegetable or a piece of fruit.
steps.note: No bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, cereal or sweets. Plenty of everything else: meat, fish, eggs, cheese, butter, vegetables. Eat enough of the real things and you will not be hungry.

steps.test: Skip one meal on purpose and notice what actually happens.
steps.note: Not a snack instead; nothing until the next meal. Hunger rises, peaks, and goes. Write down what you noticed.

steps.test: Two big meals and nothing else, for one day.
steps.note: Make them proper meals, plates full of real food. This is how most people ate for most of history.

steps.test: Do one food shop buying only real food.
steps.note: Nothing that needs its label read. Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, vegetables, fruit, nuts, butter, olive oil. Look at the trolley at the end.

steps.test: Three days in a row with no snacks.
steps.note: Rung seven, held. By the third day the pull between meals has mostly gone.

steps.test: A ten-hour window: first bite to last bite in ten hours.
steps.note: Nine to seven, or ten to eight. Move the edges to suit your day; the width is the rung.

steps.test: Sixteen hours without eating, once.
steps.note: Dinner at seven, nothing until eleven the next morning. Water, tea and coffee throughout. Sleep does most of it for you.

steps.test: An eight-hour window for a full day: sixteen hours off, eight on.
steps.note: Two or three real meals inside the eight hours, nothing outside them. That is the far end of this ladder. Past here is part two; and if you have a health condition or take medicine, a doctor before you go further.

tracks.about: For grown-ups. Twenty rungs from one honest look at a label to an eight-hour eating window, in an order that never jumps. If a rung is already how you live, you do it on purpose that day and it counts. Real food, fewer snacks, a bit of space between meals; nothing extreme until the very end, and a doctor before going further if you take medicine.

tracks.name: Real food, part two
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From an eight-hour window to a way of eating that is yours.
tracks.about: Part one changed single days; part two makes it a week at a time and then a month. Real breakfasts, meals you cooked, no snacks for five days, a week of twelve-hour windows, then ten, then eight; a real-food kitchen, a whole chicken or a pot of beans used up, and one quiet day of twenty-four hours without food. Anybody on medicine, pregnant, diabetic, or under eighteen asks a doctor before the long ones. It ends with you writing down how you eat now.

steps.test: A week where every breakfast is real food, or no breakfast at all.
steps.note: Eggs, meat, fish, yoghurt, fruit, nuts, butter; or nothing until lunch. No cereal, no toast, no bars. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Cook three real meals in one week.
steps.note: Meat or fish or eggs, vegetables, a fat you can name, salt. Nothing from a packet with a list. Three, on three different days.

steps.test: Five days running with no snacks.
steps.note: Meals only, as many as you need. By day five the pull between meals has mostly gone.

steps.test: A week without sugar, honey included; fruit is fine.
steps.note: Read every label. Sugar hides under twenty names. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: A twelve-hour eating window every day for a week.
steps.note: Eight to eight, nine to nine. Seven days in a row. Water, tea and coffee outside the window are fine.

steps.test: Make one thing you usually buy.
steps.note: Bread, yoghurt, stock, a sauce, pickles, granola without the sugar. Once, properly, and taste the difference.

steps.test: Eat a big plate of vegetables with butter or olive oil as a whole meal.
steps.note: Roasted, steamed, fried, whatever you like; a lot of them; fat on top. Notice that it is a meal.

steps.test: Three days running where every carbohydrate is a vegetable or a piece of fruit.
steps.note: No bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, cereal, sweets. Plenty of everything else. Eat enough and you will not be hungry.

steps.test: Cook a whole chicken, a whole fish, or a pot of beans from dry, and use all of it.
steps.note: The carcass becomes stock, the leftovers become tomorrow. This is how food was cooked for most of history.

steps.test: A ten-hour window every day for a week.
steps.note: Nine to seven, ten to eight. Move the edges to fit your days; keep the width.

steps.test: A day of two meals, no snacks, both cooked by you.
steps.note: Proper plates. Real food. Nothing between.

steps.test: Read one book, or listen to one long talk, on fasting or real food by a doctor or scientist who has studied it, and write down three things.
steps.note: One who has treated patients or run studies, not a seller of plans. Three things you did not know, in your own words.

steps.test: Sixteen hours off, eight on, three days running.
steps.note: Dinner at seven, first bite at eleven. Sleep does most of it. Water, tea and coffee in the gap.

steps.test: Keep a real-food kitchen for a week: nothing in it with more than five ingredients.
steps.note: Clear the cupboards first. What has no label counts as zero. Everybody in the house eats better without deciding to.

steps.test: Eat only what you cooked yourself for three days.
steps.note: Nothing bought ready, nothing from a café or a van. A flask and a box when you are out.

steps.test: Twenty-four hours without eating, once, on a quiet day.
steps.note: Dinner to dinner. Water, tea and coffee throughout; rest; nothing heavy planned. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, on medicine, or under eighteen: a doctor first, always.

steps.test: A month without sugar.
steps.note: Thirty days, fruit allowed, honey not. After a month the sweet things you used to want taste like what they are. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Cook a real-food meal for other people and say nothing about it being healthy.
steps.note: Roast chicken, vegetables in butter, a good salad, cheese and fruit after. Let them enjoy it. The word healthy ruins a dinner.

steps.test: Sixteen hours off, eight on, for a full week.
steps.note: Seven days. This is the far end of the ladder and most people find, by now, that it is simply how they eat.

steps.test: Write down how you eat now, what changed, and what you will keep.
steps.note: One page. That page is your way of eating, and it is yours to defend. From here a facilitator, if you want to go further, and a doctor beside you if you do.

tracks.name: Knife and board
tracks.line: From buttering bread properly to preparing a whole meal, and teaching a younger one.

steps.test: Butter a slice of bread properly, right to the edges.
how: Soft butter, not fridge-hard. Leave it out for half an hour first.
Spread from the middle outwards, right to every edge and corner.
No tearing the bread.
steps.note: The smallest possible knife job, and the one that teaches a light hand. Spread a hard butter and you tear the bread; that is the whole lesson in one slice.

steps.test: Learn the claw grip, with your fingertips tucked under.
how: Curl the fingers of your holding hand so the knuckles stick out and the fingertips hide behind them.
The flat side of the blade rests against your knuckles and slides along them.
Practise it on a carrot with somebody watching before you speed up at all.
steps.note: This one grip is why professional cooks can chop fast and still have ten fingers. Learn it before anything else and you never have to unlearn a bad habit.

steps.test: Cut a flat side onto a round vegetable first so it cannot roll.
how: Take a slice off one side of the onion, carrot or potato.
Turn it onto that flat side. Now it sits still.
Every round thing gets this treatment, every time.
steps.note: Rolling vegetables cause most kitchen cuts. This takes two seconds and removes the problem entirely.

steps.test: Cut something soft — a banana, a mushroom, a tomato — with the claw grip.
how: Slow. Speed comes from not stopping, never from moving fast.
Let the knife do the work — a sharp knife needs almost no pressure.
Fingertips tucked the whole time.
steps.note: Soft things show you whether the knife is sharp: if a tomato squashes rather than slices, the knife is blunt and that is more dangerous than a sharp one.

steps.test: Peel a vegetable without taking half of it away.
how: Peeler away from you, long strokes, light pressure.
Turn the vegetable rather than moving your hand about.
Look at the peelings — thin ribbons, not chunks.
steps.note: The peelings are the evidence. Thick peelings are money in the bin, and on a potato most of the good is just under the skin anyway.

steps.test: Chop an onion without help.
how: Top off, leave the root end on — it holds the whole thing together.
Halve it through the root, peel, flat side down.
Cuts towards the root but not through it, then across. It falls into dice.
steps.note: The onion is the test everybody is measured by, and the root-end trick is the whole secret. Once you can do an onion you can do anything on a board.

steps.test: Cut everything for one dish to roughly the same size.
how: Look at the biggest piece and the smallest piece before it goes in the pan.
Same size means everything is cooked at the same moment.
Take an extra minute rather than fixing it later.
steps.note: This is the actual difference between a decent home cook and a poor one, and it has nothing to do with recipes. Even pieces cook evenly. That is most of cooking.

steps.test: Prepare all the vegetables for a whole meal before anything goes in the pan.
how: Everything chopped, in bowls or piles, before the heat goes on.
Board wiped and clear before you start cooking.
It will take longer than you think the first time.
steps.note: Getting everything ready first is what stops a meal turning into a panic. It also means you can cook things that need your attention rather than only things that wait for you.

steps.test: Sharpen a knife, and cut the same vegetable before and after.
how: A cheap steel or a pull-through sharpener, or the back of a ceramic mug in a pinch.
Same angle each stroke, both sides evenly.
Cut a tomato before and cut one after.
steps.note: A blunt knife needs force, slips, and is how people get cut. A sharp knife is the safe one. Almost every kitchen in the country has only blunt ones.

steps.test: Wash, dry and put away your knife and board properly, every time, for a week.
how: By hand, dried immediately, never left in the sink for somebody to reach into.
Never in the dishwasher — it ruins the edge and the handle.
Board scrubbed and stood on its edge to dry.
steps.note: A knife left in a sink of water is the classic way somebody else gets hurt. This rung is about the person who washes up after you.

steps.test: Chop for somebody else who is cooking, at their pace.
how: Ask what size they want things and do it that way rather than your way.
Keep ahead of them so the pan never waits.
Clear your board as you go.
steps.note: Being the useful pair of hands in somebody else's kitchen is a social skill as much as a knife one, and it gets you fed in a lot of houses.

steps.test: Teach a younger child to chop safely.
how: Sitting down, at a table, with something soft and a small knife.
The claw grip first, the flat side second, and never anything else until both are automatic.
Your hand over theirs for the first few cuts, then your hands behind your back.
steps.note: Children are far better at this than adults expect and far safer once shown properly. The ones who are never taught are the ones who get hurt at fifteen.

tracks.about: Almost everything that gets called cooking is actually chopping, and almost nobody is ever taught how. A fortnight of this and a meal takes half as long and costs half as much, because real ingredients are cheaper than prepared ones and it is the chopping you were paying to avoid. It also happens to be the safest thing in the kitchen to learn properly and the most dangerous to pick up by accident.

tracks.name: Cooking a meal
tracks.line: From a cold breakfast to putting a hot meal in front of eight people.

steps.test: Make yourself a cold breakfast and clear it away afterwards.
how: Anything that needs no heat: eggs boiled the night before, yoghurt, fruit, cheese, oatcakes.
Eat it sitting down rather than standing up.
Everything washed, dried and put away before you leave the kitchen.
steps.note: Clearing away is half of this ladder and the half people skip. A cook who leaves a wreck behind stops getting to cook.

steps.test: Make a hot drink safely for yourself and somebody else.
how: Kettle filled above the element, lid down, handle turned in.
Pour slowly, away from you, with the cup on the worktop rather than in your hand.
Ask them how they take it rather than guessing.
steps.note: The first hot thing you handle. Handle turned in, pour on the worktop — two habits that prevent almost every kitchen scald.

steps.test: Boil an egg exactly the way you like it, twice running.
how: Water at a gentle boil, egg in, timer on. Six minutes runny, eight soft, ten hard.
Write down the time that worked.
Do it again two days later using your own number.
steps.note: Cooking is timing more than anything else. This is the smallest possible lesson in it: same time, same result, every time.

steps.test: Read a recipe all the way through before you start.
how: Every line, including the last one, before you touch anything.
Note the bits that need waiting — resting, rising, soaking, marinading.
Check you actually have everything.
steps.note: Almost every kitchen disaster is a recipe read one line at a time. Two minutes of reading saves the meal where the last step turns out to be 'leave overnight'.

steps.test: Get everything out, chopped and weighed before the pan goes on.
how: Every ingredient in its own bowl or pile, in the order it goes in.
Pans out, utensils out, bin within reach.
Only then turn the heat on.
steps.note: This is how every professional kitchen in the world works and it is why they are calm. Cooking is easy once the chopping is behind you.

steps.test: Make beans on toast with both parts ready at the same moment.
how: Work backwards: the toast takes two minutes, the beans take four. Beans first.
Butter on the plate and the table set before either is ready.
Hot food on a warm plate.
steps.note: The humblest possible lesson in timing two things, and it is exactly the same skill as getting a roast and its vegetables to land together.

steps.test: Cook pasta and a sauce and get them together hot.
how: Sauce on first, pasta into properly salted boiling water second.
Taste the pasta a minute before the packet says.
Drain, then straight into the sauce pan and toss — never sauce sitting on top.
steps.note: Salting the water and finishing the pasta in the sauce are the two things that separate a decent plate of pasta from a sad one, and both are free.

steps.test: Fry something without burning it or leaving it raw.
how: Pan properly hot before anything goes in — a drop of water should dance.
Do not crowd the pan. Two batches beats one steamed mess.
Leave it alone. Turn it once, when it lets go of the pan by itself.
steps.note: Turning things over and over is the commonest mistake there is. A thing that is stuck is not ready to turn; when it is ready, it releases.

steps.test: Taste as you go, and change it — more salt, or something sharp.
how: Taste before it goes on the plate, every single time.
Flat and dull usually means salt. Heavy and rich usually means something sharp: lemon, vinegar, mustard.
Add a little, stir, taste again.
steps.note: This is the rung that makes you a cook rather than a recipe follower. Nobody can taste your food from a page in a book.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for yourself, start to finish.
how: Something real: meat or fish or eggs, a vegetable, something to cook it in.
Everything ready first, taste before serving, sit down to eat it.
Clear the kitchen afterwards.
steps.note: A whole meal on your own is the middle of this ladder. If this is already routine for you, cook something you have never cooked before and count that.

steps.test: Clean as you go, so the kitchen is nearly clear when you sit down.
how: Wash each thing while the next thing cooks.
Bin, cloth and hot soapy water within reach from the start.
The rung is what the kitchen looks like when the food goes on the table.
steps.note: This is the habit that decides whether cooking feels like a pleasure or a chore, and it costs no extra time at all — only different timing.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for your family.
how: Something you have cooked before rather than a first attempt.
Ask beforehand what nobody will eat, so you are not surprised.
Plates warm, everything landing together, table laid.
steps.note: Feeding people is the oldest way there is of saying something you might not say out loud. This rung is worth more than the four above it.

steps.test: Cook the same meal again, better.
how: Write down one thing you would change before you forget it.
Cook it again within a fortnight with that one change.
Ask whether they noticed.
steps.note: Cooking the same thing three times beats cooking three different things. The second and third times are where the skill actually appears.

steps.test: Time three things so they are all ready together.
how: Write the times backwards from when you want to eat.
The longest thing goes on first. Everything else fits around it.
One timer per thing if you need it.
steps.note: This is the whole difficulty of cooking a meal, in one rung. Once you can do this with three things, a Christmas dinner is only the same problem with eight.

steps.test: Cook a meal out of whatever happened to be in the house.
how: Look at what you have first, then decide, rather than deciding then shopping.
Eggs, onions, a tin of something and whatever vegetable is going over is a meal.
No shopping trip allowed.
steps.note: This is where cooking starts saving you real money and real waste. It is also the skill that means you are never stuck.

steps.test: Cook for somebody who cannot eat something, and get it right.
how: Ask exactly what they cannot have, and whether it is a preference or a medical matter.
Read the labels on anything from a packet — it hides in sauces, stock and bread.
Clean board, clean pan, clean knife if it is serious.
steps.note: Being cooked for safely is rare enough that people remember who did it. Take it seriously and ask rather than assuming.

steps.test: Cook a roast, with the vegetables, all ready together.
how: Work backwards from the time you want to eat, on paper.
Meat rests for fifteen or twenty minutes — that is when the vegetables finish and the gravy happens.
A cheap cut cooked slowly beats an expensive one cooked badly.
steps.note: The roast is the traditional test and it deserves its reputation: six things, one oven, one moment. The resting time is the trick that makes it possible.

steps.test: Cook three courses and get them all to the table hot.
how: Pudding made first and left. Starter prepared cold or nearly cooked.
Main the only thing actually happening while people are in the house.
Written plan on the worktop.
steps.note: Doing the work in advance is the whole answer. Three courses is not three times the cooking, it is one course cooked while people are there and two done that morning.

steps.test: Cook a meal for eight people.
how: Choose something that scales and waits: a stew, a curry, a big tray bake, a pot of soup and good bread.
Cook it the day before if you can — most of these are better for it.
Count the plates, forks and chairs before the day.
steps.note: Numbers are not the hard part. Choosing a dish that forgives being held for half an hour is the whole skill of cooking for a crowd.

steps.test: Cook for the whole group at a day out.
how: A big pot of something, or a fire and something to grill, or a proper picnic you actually made.
Plan for it being cold, wet, and later than intended.
Bring more than you think, and something hot to drink.
steps.note: Feeding people outdoors is the oldest version of this and the one nobody forgets. It is also the end of the ladder: you can now feed anybody, anywhere.

tracks.about: Being able to feed yourself and other people well, from real ingredients, without a recipe in your hand. This is the most immediately useful ladder in the school: it saves real money every week, it is the practical half of Real food, and a person who can cook is welcome everywhere. It goes from boiling an egg to a roast and three courses, in about three months of cooking a few times a week — which you were going to do anyway.

tracks.name: Baking
tracks.line: From weighing accurately to a loaf of your own, and selling what you made.

steps.test: Weigh five things accurately on a scale, to the gram.
how: Bowl on the scale, zero it, then add. Zero it again for the next thing.
Get it exact rather than close. Baking is the one place where close is not good enough.
No scale? Kitchen scales are cheap second hand and most charity shops have one.
steps.note: Cooking forgives, baking does not. Everything above this rung depends on the weighing being honest.

steps.test: Bake something from a packet mix, exactly as it says.
how: Read it all the way through first. Then follow it to the letter.
Oven on early — it takes fifteen minutes to get properly hot.
Set a timer and check five minutes before it goes off.
steps.note: A packet mix takes all the decisions away so that you learn the oven, the tin and the timing without anything else to go wrong.

steps.test: Line and grease a tin so nothing sticks.
how: Butter the tin, then a circle of baking paper in the bottom, then butter that too.
For a loaf tin, a long strip up and over both ends acts as handles.
No paper? Butter and a dusting of flour, tapped out.
steps.note: More home baking is ruined at the turning-out stage than at any other. Two minutes of lining saves the whole thing.

steps.test: Bake something by following a written recipe on your own.
how: Everything weighed and lined up before you start.
Follow it exactly, even the bits you would change.
Write on the recipe afterwards what you noticed.
steps.note: Follow it exactly once before you ever improvise. You cannot tell what a change did unless you know what the original does.

steps.test: Rub butter into flour until it looks like breadcrumbs.
how: Cold butter, cut into small cubes, straight from the fridge.
Fingertips only, lifting the mixture up and letting it fall as you rub.
Stop when it looks like coarse breadcrumbs — a few bigger lumps are fine.
steps.note: Cold hands and cold butter. This one technique is the base of scones, shortbread, crumble and pastry, so it is worth ten minutes of practice.

steps.test: Make scones or shortbread that come out right.
how: Handle the dough as little as possible — the less you work it the lighter it is.
Hot oven, high shelf, and do not open the door for the first ten minutes.
Cut straight down with the cutter, no twisting, or they rise crooked.
steps.note: The first thing you will make that people ask for again. It is also the quickest: twenty minutes from a cold kitchen to something on a plate.

steps.test: Know when something is done without cutting it open.
how: A skewer into the middle comes out clean. A sponge springs back when pressed.
Bread sounds hollow when you knock the bottom of it.
Colour first, then the test. Pale means underdone whatever the timer says.
steps.note: Ovens all lie by ten or twenty degrees. Learning the tests rather than trusting the timer is what makes your baking work in anybody's kitchen.

steps.test: Bake a sponge that rises.
how: Butter and sugar beaten until genuinely pale and fluffy — a good five minutes.
Eggs added a little at a time so it does not split.
Flour folded in gently at the end. Beating here knocks the air out.
steps.note: A risen sponge is air, and the air went in during the beating. This is the rung that teaches why a method is in the order it is in.

steps.test: Bake something twice, and make the second one better.
how: Write down one change before you forget: five minutes less, a little more salt, a hotter oven.
Same recipe, one change only, within a fortnight.
Note which was better.
steps.note: One change at a time is the only way to learn anything from your own baking. Two changes and you will never know which did it.

steps.test: Make a dough and knead it for ten full minutes.
how: Timer on. Ten minutes is much longer than it feels — most people stop at three.
Push it away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it a quarter, repeat.
It goes from a shaggy lump to smooth and springy. That change is what you are looking for.
steps.note: Kneading is the whole of bread and there is no shortcut worth having. Ten minutes of it is also a remarkably good way to be in a bad mood less.

steps.test: Make a loaf of bread from flour, water, salt and yeast.
how: Four ingredients only. Nothing else belongs in a loaf.
Knead ten minutes, rise until doubled, knock back, shape, rise again, bake hot.
It costs very little and takes fifteen minutes of actual work spread over an afternoon.
steps.note: A shop loaf has a label with twenty things on it. Yours has four. This one rung is the whole argument of Real food, made edible.

steps.test: Make a loaf where the crumb is even all the way through.
how: Knock the air out properly before the second rise, and shape it tightly.
Do not let the second rise go too far — it should spring back slowly when pressed.
Cut it only when it is cool, however hard that is.
steps.note: Big holes at the top and dense at the bottom is the classic second loaf. Proper shaping and not over-proving is the fix.

steps.test: Bake something with a filling that does not leak.
how: Cold pastry, cold filling, and seal the edges with a wet finger and a fork.
Cut a hole or two in the top so the steam has a way out.
Do not overfill. Everybody overfills.
steps.note: Leaks come from steam with nowhere to go. A couple of slits in the lid is the difference between a pie and a tray to scrub.

steps.test: Ice or decorate something so it looks like it was meant to.
how: Completely cold before any icing goes near it, or it slides off.
A thin first coat to catch the crumbs, then the real coat on top.
Simple and neat beats elaborate and messy every time.
steps.note: Looking deliberate is mostly patience: cold cake, thin first coat, one colour done neatly. It doubles the pleasure for the person receiving it.

steps.test: Bake something without looking at the recipe.
how: Pick the thing you have made most often.
Write the recipe out from memory first, then bake it and check.
Whatever you got wrong is the bit you never actually learned.
steps.note: Having one thing in your head that you can make in anybody's kitchen with no book is worth more than twenty recipes you can follow.

steps.test: Bake for somebody's birthday.
how: Ask what they actually like rather than baking what you like making.
Make it the day before so you are not rushing.
Bake a small test version first if it is a new one.
steps.note: A baked thing made by a person is one of the few gifts nobody has ever had too many of, and it costs very little.

steps.test: Work out what a batch costs you to make.
how: Weigh the flour, butter, sugar and eggs you used and price each from the receipt.
Add something for the electricity and the paper.
Divide by the number of pieces.
steps.note: This is where baking meets Money and value, and the numbers usually surprise people in both directions. You cannot price anything until you know this.

steps.test: Bake to order for somebody else, to exactly what they asked for.
how: Write down what they asked for and read it back to them.
Agree the day and the time before you agree anything else.
Deliver it when you said, not when it is convenient.
steps.note: Somebody else's specification is a different job from your own baking. Getting the brief right, and on time, is most of what being paid for anything is.

steps.test: Price what you baked and sell it to people who are not related to you.
how: Cost plus your time, then a real price, written on a card.
A stall, a second-hand sale, a school fair, a sign at the gate, a message to the street group.
Say the price out loud without apologising for it.
steps.note: The nerve is not in the baking, it is in saying the number. That is the rung. Money earned from something you made changes how you see your own hands.

steps.test: Teach somebody to bake one thing, start to finish, hands off.
how: Your hands behind your back. Say it, do not do it.
Let them make the mistakes — the crooked scones teach more than your perfect ones.
They take the whole batch home.
steps.note: Hands off is the hard part and the whole rung. Something somebody made themselves, badly, with you beside them, is what makes them a baker.

tracks.about: Baking is chemistry that you get to eat, and unlike cooking it rewards exactness rather than judgement, which makes it the better one to learn with children. The ladder goes from a packet mix to a proper loaf of bread from flour, water and salt — which costs very little and beats anything in a shop — and ends by selling what you made to somebody who is not related to you, which is a different kind of nerve entirely.

tracks.name: Cooking on fire
tracks.line: From toast on a stick to running the fire and the food for a whole day out.
tracks.who: Grown-ups, and teenagers with a grown-up
tracks.about: For grown-ups, and for teenagers with a grown-up beside them at every lit fire; a child never lights or runs a fire alone. It follows on from the Fire ladder: every rung is on a fire lit only where fires are allowed, with water ready, and put out cold at the end. A charcoal barbecue counts for every rung. The climb goes from toast on a stick to cooking on embers, keeping food clean, bread and foil parcels, meat cooked all the way through, a pot over the heat and a hot meal for two, then a meal for six. It ends with you running the fire and all the food for a whole day out, and it is one of the best ways there is to make a day outside feel like an occasion.

steps.test: Toast a piece of bread or a marshmallow on a long stick over a small fire and eat it.
steps.note: Only where a fire is allowed, with water ready, as in the Fire ladder; a charcoal barbecue works just as well. Use a long metal toasting fork, or a clean stick from a tree you know. Some trees and shrubs are poisonous, so if you are not sure what a stick is from, use metal. Hold it above the flames, not in them, and turn it.

steps.test: Let a fire burn down to glowing embers, and test the heat with your hand before cooking.
steps.note: Flames burn the outside and leave the middle raw; embers cook evenly. Hold your palm at cooking height above the embers and count slowly. If you have to pull away in two or three seconds, the heat is high; in five or six, it is medium. This usually takes twenty to thirty minutes after lighting.

steps.test: Before cooking outdoors, wash your hands and set out a clean board or plate for raw food and a separate one for cooked food.
steps.note: Bring a bottle of water and a little soap for hands, or use hand wipes if that is all there is. Raw meat never touches cooked food, the same plate or the same tongs. Keep raw meat cold in a cool bag until it goes on the heat.

steps.test: Bake a twist of bread dough on a stick over embers until it pulls off cleanly and sounds hollow when tapped.
steps.note: Mix flour, a pinch of salt, a spoon of baking powder and enough water to make a soft dough at home. Roll a sausage of it and wind it round a thick clean stick or a metal skewer. Turn it slowly above the embers for ten to fifteen minutes. Pale and doughy inside means it needs longer.

steps.test: Wrap a potato or a mix of chopped vegetables in foil and cook it in the edge of the embers until soft.
steps.note: Two layers of foil, sealed well. Push it into the edge of the embers with a stick or tongs, turn it every ten minutes, and test with a knife: a whole potato can take forty minutes or more. Use gloves or tongs to lift it out; the foil stays very hot.

steps.test: Keep a fire at steady cooking heat for twenty minutes by adding small pieces of wood little and often.
steps.note: Check with the hand test every five minutes. Add one or two small pieces to the side of the fire, not on top of your cooking spot, so there are always new embers coming. A big log thrown on makes flames and smoke, not heat.

steps.test: Cook sausages over embers until they are cooked all the way through, and cut the thickest one open to check.
steps.note: Turn them often. Cooked through means no pink in the middle, and the juices run clear. Food-safety guides generally say meat like sausages, burgers and chicken should reach about 75 degrees in the middle; a food thermometer shows this if you have one. Blackened outside is not the same as cooked.

steps.test: Set up a pot so it stands or hangs steady over the embers without tipping.
steps.note: Use a metal grill resting on stones, or a metal camping pot stand; a wooden stick can burn through. If you use stones, choose dry ones from a dry place, never from a river or the shore, as wet stones can crack in the heat. Push the pot gently: if it rocks, fix it before any water goes in.

steps.test: Boil water in a pot over the fire and make a hot drink.
steps.note: A lid makes it much quicker. Lift the pot with a thick cloth or gloves, and pour away from yourself and other people. Keep children back from the fire while the water is hot.

steps.test: Cook a one-pot meal over the fire for two people.
steps.note: For example: a chopped onion softened in a little oil, sliced cooked sausages, and a tin of beans or tomatoes, stirred until everything is hot through. Or pasta boiled, drained and mixed with cheese. Stir often and move the pot to a cooler edge if it starts to stick.

steps.test: Cook two things at once over the same fire, one on the hottest part and one on a cooler edge, and have both ready together.
steps.note: For example: sausages on the grill over the hot middle, and beans in a pot at the edge. Work backwards from what takes longest. This is the rung that makes a real meal possible.

steps.test: Wash up outdoors and leave no sign of the cooking behind.
steps.note: Heat water on the fire, use a little soap, and scrape food scraps into a bag to take home. Pour the used water onto open ground well away from any stream, pond or lake, never into the water. Pack every scrap of rubbish and foil away with you.

steps.test: Cook a full meal outdoors for six people, with everybody fed at about the same time.
steps.note: Plan the menu at home, and prepare what you can there: vegetables chopped, dough mixed, meat kept cold. A simple plan works best: a one-pot main, bread twists or foil potatoes, and fruit or something sweet toasted at the end. Ask the others to help with jobs, but you run the fire.

steps.test: Run the fire and all the food for a whole day out: at least two hot meals or drinks, the fire put out cold, and the spot left clean.
steps.note: You check the rules and the fire danger that morning, pack the food and the water, light and keep the fire, cook, wash up, and put the fire out cold at the end. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Growing
tracks.line: From cress on a windowsill to giving away food and plants you grew yourself.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up can grow side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, each with their own pot. Every rung up to the last few works on a sunny windowsill, with no garden at all. It starts with cress on damp paper, then a pot of salad or radishes, kitchen scraps that grow again, a herb from a cutting, and one bigger plant like a tomato or beans, with a notebook of what happened. Then it looks outwards to your own seasons, compost and a bigger space, and ends with enough grown to share and seed saved for next time. Watching food come out of a pot of soil is a quiet daily pleasure, and it changes how you look at every vegetable you buy.

steps.test: Sow cress seeds on damp kitchen paper in a saucer, and put it on a windowsill.
steps.note: Fold two sheets of kitchen paper into the saucer, wet them, pour off the extra water, and sprinkle the seeds thinly over the top. Cress or mustard seed is cheap and quick. No seeds at all: a spoonful of dried lentils or chickpeas from the cupboard will sprout on damp paper too, but those are for watching, not for eating raw.

steps.test: Check the saucer every morning for a week, keep the paper damp but not swimming, and write down the day the first shoots appear.
steps.note: Touch the paper each morning: damp like a wrung-out cloth is right; a puddle is too much. A few drops from your fingers is usually enough. A child can keep the chart on the fridge.

steps.test: Cut the cress with scissors when it is about a finger tall, and eat it.
steps.note: Usually about a week after sowing. Rinse it, then put it in an egg sandwich, on a cheese cracker, or on top of soup. Wash your hands before you cut it.

steps.test: Fill a pot with compost and sow radish or salad leaf seeds at the depth the packet says.
steps.note: The pot needs holes in the bottom and a saucer under it; a yoghurt pot or a cut-down milk carton with holes poked in by a grown-up works fine. Fill it to a finger below the rim, press it down lightly, water it, then sow. Garden soil will do if you have no compost. Salad leaves and radishes are some of the easiest seeds to grow indoors.

steps.test: For a week, push a finger into the soil every day and water the pot only when the top is dry to your first knuckle.
steps.note: More pot plants die from too much water than too little. Water slowly until a little comes out into the saucer, then stop, and tip away what is left in the saucer after half an hour. If you already water plants this way, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Stand the root ends of some spring onions in a glass with a little water, change the water every two days, and cut the green tops once they have grown back.
steps.note: Keep the white root end, about a thumb long, after you cook with the rest. Water only up to the roots, not over the top. The green grows back in about a week, and you can cut it more than once. The root ends of celery and leeks do the same.

steps.test: When the seedlings in your pot have two or three leaves, pull out the weakest so each one left has room to grow.
steps.note: Radishes need about a thumb width between them; salad leaves a little less. Hold down the soil next to the one you keep with one finger while you pull. The small salad leaves you pull out can be rinsed and eaten.
