steps.test: For one week, each time you meet a long word you do not know, break it into parts in your notebook and write your guess before you look it up.
steps.note: Words from books, school, work, the news or packets all count. Aim for at least one a day. Tick the ones you guessed right; the ticks grow as the week goes on.

steps.test: Teach somebody five roots and how to break a long word into its parts, until they can work out one new word on their own.
steps.note: Choose roots from your notebook and a test word that uses them, such as bipedal or telegraph. Let them guess before you help. A child can teach a grown-up as well as the other way round.

tracks.name: One beautiful thing a day
tracks.line: From one beautiful thing in the room you are in, to sixty days of them in a notebook and the three best chosen.
tracks.who: From about eight; a family can do it together
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight; a family can do it together, each with their own page. You start with one beautiful thing in the room you are in and one sentence on why. The rungs go from ordinary things, sounds and things nobody made, to a notebook kept every day, drawing, a line copied from a poem, a famous painting or piece of music looked at slowly, and showing somebody what they had walked past. It ends with sixty days in the notebook and the three best chosen. This is not about what went well; it is about training your eyes and ears to find beauty wherever you are.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing in the room you are in, and say in one sentence why it is beautiful.
steps.note: The light on a glass of water, the grain in a wooden table, the curve of a cup handle, a plant against the window. "Why" can be the colour, the shape, a pattern, how the light falls on it, or how well it is made.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing outside today and say in one sentence why.
steps.note: On a walk, on the way to school or work, or from a window: the shape of a cloud, moss on a wall, a well-made gate, a bird. Stop for a moment when you find it.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing in an object people use every day.
steps.note: A spoon, a door handle, a stair rail, a jug, an old tool, a pair of scissors. Look at how the shape fits the hand or the job. Things made to be useful are often the most beautiful.

steps.test: Find one beautiful sound today, and stop to listen to it until it ends.
steps.note: Rain on a roof, a bird singing, a bell, wind in trees, somebody laughing in the next room. Close your eyes if it is safe to.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing made by a person and one that nobody made, and say which you would rather keep looking at.
steps.note: A bridge and a tree, a painted door and a shell, a bowl and a leaf. There is no right answer; say why.

steps.test: Start a notebook for beautiful things, and write today's in it with the date and one line on why.
steps.note: Any notebook, a few sheets of paper folded and stapled, or a note on your phone. One line is enough: "Tuesday. Frost on the car roof, like feathers."

steps.test: Write one beautiful thing in the notebook every day for seven days.
steps.note: Pick a time: before bed, or on the way home. If you miss a day, write the next one and keep going. A family can each write their own and read them out at dinner.

steps.test: Draw one of your beautiful things in the notebook instead of writing it.
steps.note: Roughly, in pencil, in a few minutes. Drawing makes you look at it for longer than writing does, and you will see more.

steps.test: Copy into the notebook one line from a poem, a book or a song that you think is beautiful, and write why.
steps.note: From a book at home, a library book, a hymn, a song you love. Write the name of the person who wrote it underneath.

steps.test: Look at one famous painting or listen to one famous piece of music for ten minutes without doing anything else, and write down what you noticed.
steps.note: For example, Vermeer's "The Milkmaid", Hokusai's "The Great Wave", Bach's "Air on the G String" or Beethoven's "Moonlight Sonata". Many great museums show their paintings free on their websites, and music is free to listen to online or on the radio.

steps.test: Show somebody one beautiful thing near home that they walk past every day, and tell them why you think it is beautiful.
steps.note: The carving over a door, a tree in a certain light, a pattern in the paving. Take them to it; do not just describe it.

steps.test: Write one beautiful thing in the notebook every day for thirty days.
steps.note: Carry on from your first week. Try to find a new kind of thing now and then: a sound, a person being kind, something small. Mark the days on the page.

steps.test: Describe the painting or music from rung ten to somebody from memory, for one minute.
steps.note: What is in it, the colours or the sounds, what happens in it, what you like. Look again first if you need to, then put it away and describe it.

steps.test: Reach sixty days in the notebook, read every page back, and choose the three best to show somebody.
steps.note: Carry on from thirty days. Read it all in one sitting. Pick the three you would most want to see again, and tell somebody at home why you chose them.

tracks.name: Thinking on your own
tracks.line: From five minutes with one question to twelve weekly pages of your own thinking, read back and written about.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten who can write a page. It starts with five minutes on one question with no screen, then ten minutes and three written sentences, then a walk with the phone left behind. Next you learn to write down what you think before you look anything up, to read somebody else on the same question, and to change your mind on paper. A thinking notebook starts in the middle, one page a week, and the ladder ends when it holds twelve pages that you read back and write about. Working out what you think before you hear what everybody else thinks is harder than it sounds, and it gets easier with practice.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten

steps.test: Pick one question, set a timer for five minutes, think about it with no screen, then say out loud what you think.
steps.note: Any question with more than one answer: "Should children get pocket money?", "Is it better to have a few close friends or lots of friends?", "What would make our street a nicer place?", "What would I do with a whole free Saturday?". Sit or stand anywhere, phone out of reach. Say your answer to yourself or to whoever is there.

steps.test: Think about one question for ten minutes, then write three sentences: what you think, why, and what might change your mind.
steps.note: Pen and paper, no screen. The third sentence is the useful one: "I would think differently if I found out that most people who tried it were unhappy." A child can say the three sentences for a grown-up to write.

steps.test: Go for a twenty-minute walk with no phone, thinking about one question, and say or write what you worked out when you get back.
steps.note: Choose the question before you leave. Take a route you know. If you need a phone for safety, take it switched to silent in a bag and do not look at it; a child walks with a grown-up or on a route the family has agreed. If you cannot go out, walk slowly up and down a room or garden.

steps.test: Before you look anything up about a question, write down what you already think; then look it up and mark what you got right and wrong.
steps.note: For example: "Why do leaves change colour in autumn?", "How does a fridge keep things cold?", "Why do some countries drive on the left?". Find out what you think before you find out what everybody else thinks; it is much harder afterwards. Getting things wrong on this rung is fine, and usually interesting.

steps.test: Write a whole page by hand on what you think about one question, without looking anything up.
steps.note: One side of paper is enough. Example questions: "Should everybody learn to cook?", "What makes a good neighbour?", "Is it ever right to break a rule?". Do not tidy it up; the point is to see what you actually think.

steps.test: Read one thing somebody else has written on the same question, then add three lines to your page: where you agree, where you do not, and one thing you had not thought of.
steps.note: An article, a chapter of a book, a letter to a newspaper, or ask somebody older to write you a paragraph. Read it slowly. Add your three lines under your own page, so you can see both.

steps.test: Write down one idea about the world you have repeated many times, then write the best reasons for it and against it.
steps.note: Ideas like "things were better in the past", "people are more selfish than they used to be", "the expensive one is always better" or "you need a degree to do well". Two columns on a page, three reasons in each if you can. You do not have to decide at the end.

steps.test: Start a thinking notebook and write one page in it each week, on a different question, for four weeks.
steps.note: Any notebook or a stack of paper in a folder, with the date at the top of each page. Keep a list of questions at the back to choose from: things you wondered about, overheard or argued about. The pages from this rung onward count towards the twelve at the end of the ladder.

steps.test: Find one place in your notebook where you now think you were wrong, cross it out neatly, and write what changed your mind.
steps.note: Something you read, somebody you talked to, or just thinking about it longer. "I wrote that dogs are easier than cats. My aunt has both and says the opposite, because cats do not need walking." Changing your mind for a good reason is part of thinking well.

steps.test: Sit for twenty minutes with one question, a pen and paper, and nothing else.
steps.note: Write only when something new comes; long gaps with nothing written are normal. If your mind drifts, read the question again. A question you care about works best, for example a choice coming up in your own life.

steps.test: Spend one hour of free time with no screen and nothing planned, then write down what you ended up thinking about.
steps.note: Sit in a chair, lie on the grass, look out of a window. The first twenty minutes often feel restless and slow; notice that and stay. Afterwards, list the things that went through your head, even the small ones.

steps.test: Choose one practical thing you have been avoiding thinking about, write it down, and write one small next step.
steps.note: Something practical: a form, a decision about a course, a conversation that needs having, a plan for the holidays, a cupboard of paperwork. Keep painful things like a loss for a time when you have somebody to talk them through with; this rung does not need them. The next step should be small enough to do this week.

steps.test: Make one decision you have been putting off by writing the choices, what each would likely lead to, and what you chose and why.
steps.note: A small or middle-sized decision: which club to join, whether to change a routine, which of two things to save for. Two or three choices, a few lines each. Then write the decision and act on it or tell somebody.

steps.test: Tell one person, calmly, something you think that most people around you do not, and give your reason.
steps.note: Something ordinary, not something to start a row: "I think we should eat together more", "I think the park is better in the rain". Say it once, give the reason, and then listen to their answer properly. You do not need them to agree.

steps.test: Spend one whole day using screens only for calls and what work or school needs, and write a page that evening.
steps.note: Tell the people you live or work with the day before. Put the television remote and the tablet in a drawer. In the evening, write a notebook page on anything the quiet day gave you time to think about.

steps.test: Reach twelve weekly pages in your thinking notebook, read all twelve back in one sitting, and write one more page on how your thinking changed.
steps.note: This is the end of the ladder, about three months after you started the notebook. Notice which questions you kept coming back to and where you changed your mind. The last page can start: "Three months ago I thought ..., and now I think ...".

categories.name: Nerve
categories.line: Small brave things, done on purpose, until they stop being brave. The later levels are for older ones and adults.

tracks.name: Asking out loud
tracks.line: From asking somebody to say that again to asking for something you really want from somebody who can say yes.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child has a grown-up close by for any ask of a stranger. It starts with the smallest ask there is, "Sorry, could you say that again?", then free things in a café, a shop checking the back, a hand from a stranger, and a question in front of a group. In the middle you learn to ask and then wait in silence for the answer, and to ask for a better price and take no cheerfully. It ends with asking somebody for half an hour of their time, then asking for something you really want from somebody who can say yes, and then helping somebody else make their first ask. Many of the things people want, they would get simply by asking.

steps.test: The next time you do not catch what somebody said, ask them to say it again instead of nodding.
steps.note: "Sorry, could you say that again?" At a counter, on the phone, in class, at the table. Most people nod and guess. Today you ask, and you listen to the whole answer the second time.

steps.test: In a café or shop, ask for something small that is free.
steps.note: A glass of tap water, an extra napkin, a spoon, the wifi password, a pen to borrow. Ask clearly and say thank you. If you already do this without thinking, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Ask a shop assistant to check whether they have something in a different size or colour.
steps.note: Shoes in the next size up, a jumper in another colour, the last one of something in the back. You do not have to buy it when they bring it; "thanks, I will think about it" is fine.

steps.test: Ask a stranger for a hand with something.
steps.note: Reaching a high shelf in a supermarket, taking a photo of your family, holding a door while you get a buggy through, which platform the next train goes from. A child asks with a grown-up standing beside them.

steps.test: Ask one question out loud in front of a group.
steps.note: In a class, at a club, on a guided tour, at a parents' evening, at the end of a talk. Have the question ready before the moment comes. One sentence is enough.

steps.test: Ask for a small change to what you have been given: a different table, a different seat, or a swap on a plate.
steps.note: A table by the window instead of by the door, salad instead of chips, a seat that is not in the draught. Politely, without a reason if you do not have one. Most places say yes when they can.

steps.test: Ask for something today, then say nothing at all until the other person answers.
steps.note: The hard part is the pause. Most people fill it with "it is fine if not" and answer for the other person. Ask, close your mouth, and count slowly in your head. Any ask counts: a lift, a favour, a question at a counter.

steps.test: Ask politely for a better price, and take no cheerfully if that is the answer.
steps.note: A stall at a market or a second-hand sale ("would you take eight for it?"), a quote from a tradesperson, or a phone or broadband contract when it is due to renew ("is that the best you can do for me?"). Smile, ask once, and say thank you either way. A child can do the second-hand sale with a grown-up.

steps.test: Ask a neighbour, friend or relative for a favour you would normally talk yourself out of asking for.
steps.note: Borrowing a ladder or a drill, a lift to the station, somebody to water the plants while you are away, a hand moving a sofa. Say exactly what you need and when, and make it easy to say no.

steps.test: Ask somebody who knows how to do something for half an hour of their time, and say what it is for.
steps.note: A neighbour who grows vegetables, a relative who fixes cars, somebody who does a job you are curious about. "Could I have half an hour one evening to ask how you started? I would like to try it." Offer a cup of tea or help with a job in return.

steps.test: Ask for something you really want from the person who can say yes to it.
steps.note: Extra hours or a change of hours from a manager, a place on a course or a team, a stall at a local fair, a trial day somewhere you would like to work, more pocket money for a job done at home. Say what you want, why, and then wait for the answer. A no today is still the ask done.

steps.test: Stand beside somebody while they make their first ask of a stranger.
steps.note: A child asking for tap water, a friend asking for a size in the back, a teenager asking a question at a counter. Let them choose the ask, stay close, and say nothing unless they look at you for help. Afterwards, tell them what they did well.

tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten

tracks.name: Walking in
tracks.line: From ten minutes inside a building you have never entered, to bringing somebody new to a group you now belong to.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child goes into a new group with a grown-up who meets the person running it and waits nearby. It is about the moment of going through the door: first into buildings and shops you have walked past for years, then a public event on your own, then a group that meets every week. The middle rungs are staying for the chat afterwards, going back a second time and walking into something already under way. It ends four weeks into a group you joined alone, bringing somebody who would never have walked in on their own. Almost everything good that happens with other people starts with somebody walking into a room.

steps.test: Walk into a free public building you have never been inside, and stay for ten minutes.
steps.note: A library, a museum, a gallery, the entrance hall of a town hall, a place of worship that is open to visitors. Look at one thing properly while you are there. If you walk into new places all the time, pick one you have walked past for years and never entered, and count it.

steps.test: Go into a small shop or café you have walked past but never been into, and look round for five minutes.
steps.note: A bookshop, a hardware shop, a bakery, a shop that sells things you know nothing about. You do not have to buy anything; "just looking, thank you" is all you need to say. A child goes in first with the grown-up behind.

steps.test: Sit at a table on your own in a café, a library or a public square for twenty minutes, with your phone away.
steps.note: Bring a book or a notebook if you want something in your hands. A café needs a drink, but a library table or a bench in a square costs nothing. Notice that after the first few minutes nobody is looking at you. A child sits with their grown-up at a table nearby.

steps.test: Go on your own to a free event that is open to the public, and stay until the end.
steps.note: A talk at the library, a concert in a park, a gallery opening, a local history society evening, a service open to all. Arrive five minutes early: walking into a room that is filling up is easier than walking into a full one. A child goes with a grown-up, who sits a few seats away.

steps.test: At an event with seats, sit next to somebody instead of choosing an empty row.
steps.note: "Is anybody sitting here?" is the whole sentence. You do not need to talk any more than that. If you already do this, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Find one group that meets every week and welcomes new people, and write down when and where it next meets.
steps.note: A walking group, a choir, a beginners' night at a running club, a chess club, a craft morning at the library, a volunteering session, a youth club for a child. Look on the library or community noticeboard, your local council's website, or ask at the library desk.

steps.test: Go to that group for the first time, and tell the person running it that it is your first time.
steps.note: Arrive a few minutes early. "Hello, I am new; is this the right place?" People who run groups are glad of new faces, and they will usually show you what to do. A child's grown-up meets the leader at the door, then waits nearby or comes back at the end.

steps.test: After the group, stay for the tea or the chat for ten minutes instead of leaving as soon as it ends.
steps.note: Stand near the kettle or wherever people gather. One sentence about the session is enough: "That was harder than I thought" or "How long have you been coming?" If there is no tea, help put the chairs away.

steps.test: Go back to the same group a second time, within two weeks.
steps.note: The second visit is the one most people skip, especially if the first felt awkward. This time you will recognise a face or two, and somebody may recognise you. If you did not like that group at all, go to a different one for its first time, then go back to that one.

steps.test: Walk into a drop-in session that is already under way, find the person in charge, and ask what you can do.
steps.note: A community garden work morning, a repair café, a litter pick, a craft drop-in, a charity sorting morning. People will already be busy when you arrive. "Hello, I have come to help; what would be useful?" A child goes with a grown-up, and they are given a job together.

steps.test: Go to a gathering where you know only one person, and stay at least an hour without standing next to them the whole time.
steps.note: A friend's birthday, a neighbour's barbecue, a school fair, a work evening, a friend's club night out. Say hello to your friend, then spend part of the hour somewhere else in the room: at the food, helping, looking at the view.

steps.test: Go to a group where you are clearly the youngest or the oldest there, and take part fully.
steps.note: A teenager at a local history society, a grandparent at a beginners' climbing night, a grown-up at a family craft session. Nobody minds; most groups are pleased to have somebody different. Take part as you would anywhere, without apologising for being there.

steps.test: Go to your weekly group four weeks in a row.
steps.note: The group from rung nine, or any group you have found since. If it meets every two weeks or once a month, four meetings in a row counts. By the fourth time, somebody will usually know your name, and you will know theirs.

steps.test: Bring somebody who would not have walked in on their own to your group, and introduce them to the person running it.
steps.note: A neighbour who lives alone, a friend who has just moved, a relative who has been meaning to try it, a child's friend. Meet them outside and walk in together. That is the far end of this ladder: you are now the person who makes it easy for somebody else to walk in.

tracks.name: On the phone
tracks.line: From ringing a friend instead of sending a message, to making every call you have been putting off in one sitting.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child makes calls to businesses with a grown-up in the room. It starts with ringing somebody you know instead of sending a message, then a written first sentence, notes during the call, a clear voicemail and a booking. In the middle come the harder calls: getting through a menu and a wait on hold, ringing somebody you have never spoken to, and reporting something that has gone wrong. It ends with calling for somebody who finds the phone hard, and then clearing every call you have been putting off in one sitting. A five-minute call often settles what would take days of messages.

steps.test: Phone somebody you know instead of sending the message you were about to send.
steps.note: A friend to fix a time to meet, a grandparent to say how your week went, a relative to say happy birthday. If they do not pick up, ring again later or leave a short message; making the call is the rung. If you already ring people all the time, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Before your next call, write down your first sentence and the one thing you need to find out, then make the call.
steps.note: "Hello, my name is Sam, I am ringing to ask whether the pool has a lane swim on Saturday." Keep the paper in front of you while you talk. Good calls to try this on: the dentist to check an appointment time, the library about a book you reserved, a club about when it next meets. Most nerves are about the first ten seconds, and the written sentence gets you past them.

steps.test: During a call to a shop, office or service, write down the answer and the name of the person you spoke to before you hang up.
steps.note: Have a pen and paper beside you before you dial. Near the end, ask "Sorry, who am I speaking to?"; people are used to being asked. A name and a note mean you never have to ring twice to find out what was said.

steps.test: Leave a voicemail under thirty seconds that says your name, why you are calling, and your number twice, slowly.
steps.note: Write it out first in three lines. Ringing a business outside its opening hours is an easy way to get a voicemail to practise on, as long as you have a real reason to call. A child gives a grown-up's number, with their say-so, not their own.
how: Say your name and the reason in one sentence.
Say the number slowly, in small groups of digits.
Say it a second time, then say goodbye.

steps.test: Phone to book something, then repeat the day, time and name back to them before you hang up.
steps.note: A haircut, a doctor's or dentist's appointment, a swimming lesson, a table for a family meal. Free ones count just as well: a computer slot at the library, a place on a free museum tour or a council-run walk. "So that is Tuesday the fourth at ten, under Morgan." If your name gets misheard, spell it out.

steps.test: Phone somewhere you already have a booking, an account or a loan, and ask them to check or change one detail.
steps.note: Renew your library books by phone, confirm when your next dental check-up is due, move an appointment by a day, ask a school or club to update your address. Say who you are, what you want changed, and check they have done it before you say goodbye.

steps.test: Get through a menu of numbers to press, wait on hold, and ask your question to a real person.
steps.note: A bank, an energy or water company, your local council, a phone company. Listen to the whole list of options once before you press anything, and write the numbers down as you go. Do something with your hands while you wait, like washing up or folding laundry. If they offer to call you back instead, saying yes counts too.

steps.test: Phone somebody you have never spoken to, by name, to ask about joining something they run.
steps.note: The secretary of a walking club, the leader of a choir, the coach of a children's team, the person who runs a community garden. Their number is usually on the group's website or a noticeboard at the library. Start with where you found it: "I saw your number on the library board; I would like to ask about joining."

steps.test: Phone to report something that has gone wrong, and before you hang up, find out what happens next, by when, and get a reference number.
steps.note: A parcel that never arrived, a bill that looks wrong, a repair that did not last, a broken streetlight reported to your local council. Say what happened in two or three calm sentences, facts first. Write down the date, the name of the person and the reference. A teenager can make this call for a household problem, with a grown-up's say-so.

steps.test: On the day they said it would be sorted, ring back, give your reference number, and ask where things have got to.
steps.note: Use the notes from rung nine. "I rang on the third, reference 4417; you said it would be done by today. Could you tell me where it has got to?" If it was already put right, ring anyway to say thank you and check it is closed. Most people never ring back, and ringing back is often what gets a problem put right.

steps.test: Make a call for somebody who finds phoning hard, with them sitting beside you.
steps.note: A grandparent booking a doctor's appointment, a friend whose first language is not yours, a neighbour sorting out a delivery. Say at the start "I am calling on behalf of" and their name; never pretend to be them. Some places need to hear the person say yes themselves, so have them close enough to take the phone.

steps.test: Write a list of every call you have been putting off, then make all of them in one sitting.
steps.note: Start with the easiest to get going. Put a line through each one as you finish, and write what it settled beside it. If a place is closed, leave a voicemail the way you learned on rung four and cross it off. That is the far end of this ladder: no call left waiting because you would rather not make it.

tracks.name: Getting told no
tracks.line: From writing down what you have never asked for, to putting yourself forward for something most people are turned down for.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child asks strangers only with a grown-up beside them. It starts at home with a list of things you have never asked for and a no you answer with "fair enough". Then it goes outside: an ask that will probably be refused, three noes in a week, asking for the reason, asking what would change the answer, and asking again later. It ends with twenty noes in four weeks and then putting yourself forward for something where most people are turned down. The rule on every rung is that a no is always allowed: one friendly question, then thank them and leave it.

steps.test: Write down three things you have not asked for because you expected the answer to be no.
steps.note: A later bedtime, a different job at work, a place in a team, a neighbour's spare apples, a lift, help with something. Small or big, just write them. Keep the list; later rungs use it.

steps.test: Ask somebody at home for something small you expect a no to, and when the no comes, say "Fair enough, thanks" and nothing more.
steps.note: A child asks to choose the film, or to stay up half an hour; a grown-up asks somebody else to cook tonight. The rung is the answer you give: no arguing, no sulking, no asking twice. If you get a yes, enjoy it, and try again with something bigger.

steps.test: After your next no, write two lines: what you were afraid would happen, and what actually did.
steps.note: Use the no from rung two, or any no this week. Most of the time the second line is short: "They said no. We carried on." Seeing it written down is the point of the rung.

steps.test: At a quiet time, ask a place for a look behind the scenes that they probably do not give, and thank them whatever they say.
steps.note: A bakery's kitchen, a fire station, a print shop, a farm, the back of a theatre, a bike repair workshop. "Would it be possible to have a quick look at where you make the bread?" A yes happens more often than you think. A child asks with a grown-up beside them.

steps.test: Collect three noes in one week, from three different people, and tick each one off.
steps.note: Use the list from rung one. Ask the library whether they would buy a book you want, a friend whether they would swap a job with you, a neighbour whether you could pick some fruit from their tree. Only ask for things where a yes would be fine for them too. A yes does not count towards the three, so ask again elsewhere.

steps.test: When you are told no, ask in a friendly voice whether there is a reason, and listen to the whole answer.
steps.note: "That is fine; can I ask why?" Then stop talking and listen. People are allowed not to give a reason; if they would rather not say, thank them and leave it.

steps.test: After a no, ask "What would need to be different for it to be a yes?" and write down the answer.
steps.note: "Not this week" might mean next week works. "Not until you are twelve" is a date. "Not without a written plan" tells you exactly what to bring. Ask once, write it down, and do not argue with it.

steps.test: Go back to somebody who told you no, now that something has changed, and ask again.
steps.note: The answer from rung seven is your guide: the week has passed, you have written the plan, you are a year older. Say what changed: "Last time you said not until it was lighter in the evenings; could I ask again now?" A second no is fine; this rung is the asking again.

steps.test: Put yourself forward for something where you might not be picked.
steps.note: Try out for a team, audition for a choir or a school or community play, apply for a volunteer role, enter a local art or baking competition, apply for a job. Most of these are free to enter. Whatever the result, the rung is putting your name down.

steps.test: When a no comes to something you care about, write three things you could do next, and do the first one within a day.
steps.note: Ask what would have made the difference, practise and try again next season, try a different team or role, ask somebody who got in how they prepared. If rung nine got you a yes, use the next no you are given that matters to you.

steps.test: Over four weeks, collect twenty noes, and keep a tally on paper.
steps.note: About five a week. Mix the kinds you have practised: asks at home, asks in shops and places, putting yourself forward. Every ask must be one where a yes would be fine for the other person. By the end, notice how small a no now feels.

steps.test: Put yourself forward for something where most people are turned down, and send it off.
steps.note: A place on a course that takes few people, a job you are only just ready for, a scholarship or grant, a story or photo sent to a magazine or a competition with judges. Do your best work on it, send it, and write down the date. That is the far end of this ladder: going for the thing that will probably say no, because you no longer mind if it does.

tracks.name: Speaking up on the spot
tracks.line: From saying one thing at the table without being asked, to two minutes standing up in front of ten people on a subject handed to you there and then.
tracks.who: From about eight; the early rungs happen at home
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, and for grown-ups; the early rungs happen at home, the later ones in a class, a club, a meeting or a family gathering. This ladder is speaking in a group with no time to prepare. It starts at the family table, then a topic game at home with a simple shape for any answer: one point, one example, stop. In the middle you take that shape into groups outside home: adding to what somebody said, going first, offering an idea, summing up. It ends with two minutes standing in front of ten people on a subject you were given a moment before.

steps.test: At a family meal, say one thing about your day before anybody asks you.
steps.note: "Something funny happened on the bus." "I found out how bread rises." One or two sentences, then let somebody else talk. If you are always the one who talks first, let everybody else speak first and say yours at the end.

steps.test: In a conversation with three or more people, when there is a pause, be the one who speaks.
steps.note: Friends at lunch, family in the car, a break at work. Say anything that fits: a question, something you noticed, a thought on what was just said. A pause of two or three seconds is your moment; you do not need a clever line.

steps.test: Play the topic game at home: somebody gives you a subject you have not seen, and you talk about it for thirty seconds straight away.
steps.note: Write twenty subjects on slips of paper: your favourite meal, the best day out you have had, rain, a thing you would invent, your first memory. Somebody draws one and starts a timer. Take turns if there are two or more of you.

steps.test: In the topic game, answer three subjects using one point, one example, then stop.
steps.note: "Rain is better than people think. Last Saturday we stayed in and built a den all afternoon. That is why I like rain." The stop is the hard part; most people ramble because they have not decided how to finish.
how: Say your point in one sentence.
Give one real example of it.
Say your point again in a few words, and stop.

steps.test: In the topic game, talk for one full minute on a subject drawn from the pile.
steps.note: Use the shape from rung four, with two or three examples instead of one. When you want to say "um", pause instead; a pause sounds like thinking. If you cannot think what to say next, give another example.

steps.test: Have somebody ask you three questions on subjects you know little about, and answer each one with what you do know, in two sentences.
steps.note: How does a plane stay up? Why is the sea salty? Who built the first bridge? "I am not sure of the whole answer, but I know the wings are shaped to push air down." Being honest about the edge of what you know, and still saying something, is the skill.

steps.test: In a class, club or meeting, add to what somebody else just said: agree with them by name and give one more reason.
steps.note: "I agree with Priya; it would also be quicker." You do not need a new idea, only one more reason for theirs. It is the easiest way to speak in a group you do not know well.

steps.test: When a group goes round the room introducing themselves or answering a question, go first.
steps.note: Classes, clubs, courses, meetings and training days often start like this. As soon as the leader asks, say "I will start" and use the shape from rung four. Going first means nobody has set a pattern to follow, and it is over before the nerves build.

steps.test: When a group is deciding something, say an idea of your own that nobody has mentioned.
steps.note: Where to go on a family day out, a name for a team, what to do at a club's next session, how to split a job at work. "What about the beach, if the weather holds?" Say it once, clearly, and let the group decide.

steps.test: When a group discussion keeps coming back to the same points, sum up out loud what has been said so far.
steps.note: "So we have two ideas: the park or the museum. The park is free, the museum is dry." Two or three sentences. It is often the most useful thing anybody says, and it needs no preparation, only listening.

steps.test: At a gathering, stand up and say a few words of thanks to somebody, with no notes, for about thirty seconds.
steps.note: At a birthday, the last session of a club, the end of a talk, a family meal somebody cooked. "Can I just say thank you to Dad for this meal..." What they did, why it mattered, thank you. A child can do this at a family gathering.

steps.test: Speak for two minutes, standing, to a group of at least ten people, on a subject somebody gives you there and then.
steps.note: A family gathering playing the topic game, a class, a youth group, a club night. Many towns have a public speaking club where guests can have a go at this, often for free. That is the far end of this ladder: handed a subject, you stand and speak without a word prepared.

tracks.name: Not minding what people think
tracks.line: From humming a tune as you walk past people, to a month of the harmless thing you had put off because of what people might think.
tracks.who: Everybody; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and it is especially good for teenagers. Every rung is harmless, kind and cheerful, and something people might look at. It starts small, with humming as you walk and stopping to look properly at something, then wearing what you like, singing outdoors, playing in a park, drawing in public, and being the first to clap, cheer and dance. It ends with a month of the one harmless thing you have put off only because of what people might think. Nothing on this ladder frightens anybody, gets in anybody's way or makes fun of anybody, and if it would embarrass the person you are with, do it another day on your own.

steps.test: Hum a tune while you walk somewhere with other people about.
steps.note: Down a street, through a shop, along a park path. Loud enough that somebody passing might hear, not so loud that it bothers anybody. If you hum all the time already, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: In a busy place, stop and look properly at one thing people walk past, for two full minutes.
steps.note: A carving over a door, the top of an old building, a flower growing out of a wall, a spider's web, clouds. Stand to one side so nobody has to walk round you. People may look to see what you are looking at, and some will stop too.

steps.test: Wear something you like but usually leave at home, for a whole day out.
steps.note: A bright colour, a hat, a scarf you love, odd socks, a badge. Use what you already have; nothing needs buying. Notice how few people notice.

steps.test: Sing a whole song out loud, at an ordinary volume, outdoors where a few people might hear.
steps.note: On a park path, in your garden, on a beach, walking along a quiet road. Not in a quiet place like a library, and not right beside somebody. A child and a grown-up can sing it together.

steps.test: In a park, do something playful that people your age do not usually do, for five minutes.
steps.note: A grown-up rolls down a grassy slope, skips along a path, or plays on a climbing frame in a park where grown-ups are allowed; a teenager plays hopscotch or a game of tag with younger children in the family. Only where it is allowed and safe, and never take a swing or a slide a child is waiting for.

steps.test: Sit in a public place and draw what is in front of you for twenty minutes, letting people look.
steps.note: A building, a tree, a boat, people's shoes at a bus stop. A pencil and any paper will do. If somebody looks over your shoulder, say hello and carry on; how good it looks does not matter.

steps.test: At the end of something, be the first to clap, clearly and warmly.
steps.note: A busker's song, a school concert, a talk, a street performer, a friend's football match. Start as soon as it ends. Others usually join in within a second, and the person who performed will notice.

steps.test: Cheer out loud for people you do not know at a race, a parade or a match.
steps.note: A local fun run, a charity walk, a children's sports day, a cycling race passing through. Shout the numbers or names on their shirts: "Keep going, number 42!" Runners say it helps.

steps.test: Dance where people can see you, when others are dancing too.
steps.note: At a wedding, a party, a festival, a street fair, next to a busker playing a good tune, in the kitchen with the family and the window open. Any dancing counts; nobody is judging the steps.

steps.test: Be the first to join in when a dance, a song or a game is started for everybody.
steps.note: The first onto an empty dance floor, the first to join a community sing, the first to try the game at a fair. Somebody has to go first, and the rest follow faster than you think. If you are with a friend, take their hand and go together.

steps.test: Write down three harmless things you would do if nobody ever looked, and do the smallest one this week.
steps.note: Learning to ride a bike as a grown-up, running in the streets, swimming, singing in a choir, practising an instrument with the window open, going to a class people think you are too old or too young for. Only things that are kind and safe. Do the smallest one once.

steps.test: Do the biggest thing on your list at least once a week for a month.
steps.note: Four times, on four different weeks. If it needs money, choose the free version: running outside instead of a gym, a library class instead of a paid one, a borrowed bike. That is the far end of this ladder: the thing you once put off because of other people is now part of your week.

categories.name: Negotiation
categories.line: Almost everything is flexible — the price, the terms, the timing. Most people simply never ask.

tracks.name: Asking for a better price
tracks.line: From knowing the usual price to getting money off something with a printed price tag.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for a child from about ten spending their own pocket money, with a grown-up beside them for every rung in a shop or at a stall. Every rung is done on something you were going to buy anyway, so it needs no extra money. It starts with finding out what a thing usually costs, then saying a lower number for something second-hand, then asking a shop to match a price, asking about discounts, marked goods and quotes, and ends with money off something that had a printed price tag on it. Asking politely is always allowed, and the worst answer is the price you were going to pay anyway.

steps.test: Pick one thing you are going to buy soon, and write down what you expect to pay for it.
steps.note: School shoes, a bike, a game, a tank of heating oil, a haircut, a second-hand pram. Just your guess, written down. The next rung checks it.

steps.test: Find three prices for that exact thing: from shops, websites, or second-hand.
steps.note: Same make, same size, same model. Write down where each price was and the date. Compare with your guess from rung one. This list is what you bring to the later rungs.

steps.test: Ask somebody you know what they paid for something like it, and where they got it.
steps.note: A parent, a neighbour, a friend at school, a colleague. "What did you pay for your bike?" People are often glad to tell you, especially when they got a good deal.

steps.test: Write down the one sentence you will use to ask for a lower price, and say it out loud three times.
steps.note: "Would you take 30 for it?" or "I have seen this for 45 elsewhere; can you do that?" Saying it at home first makes it much easier to say in front of somebody. Keep it short and friendly.

steps.test: Offer a lower price for something second-hand: at a second-hand sale, a market stall, or on an online listing.
steps.note: Say a number, about a quarter under the asking price: for something marked 20, offer 15. You do not need a yes; the rung is saying the number. Only offer on something you would actually buy at your price. A child does this with a grown-up beside them.

steps.test: Get a second-hand price lowered by agreeing a number between yours and theirs.
steps.note: They ask 20, you offer 15, they say 18, you say "17 and we have a deal". Then pay and say thank you. If they will not move at all, that is their right; try somewhere else another day.

steps.test: Write down the exact words that got you the lower price.
steps.note: The words you said, what they said back, and what you paid. Keep it with the sentence from rung four. Next time you use the words that worked.

steps.test: In a shop, show a lower price you found somewhere else, and ask whether they will match it.
steps.note: Use the list from rung two, on your phone. "I have seen this for 45 in another shop; will you match that?" Some large shops have a rule that they will. Never say you saw a price you did not see.

steps.test: Ask what the price would be if you bought two or more.
steps.note: Plants at a garden centre, eggs at a farm gate, tins of paint, a second ticket, two haircuts for brothers. Only ask about things you would use two of.

steps.test: Ask whether there is a discount you might be able to get.
steps.note: "Do you do a discount for students, or for pensioners, or for families, or for a first order?" Many places have one and do not put it on the sign. On the phone counts too.

steps.test: Ask for money off something marked, scuffed, the last one, or on display.
steps.note: A dented box, a scratched table, the floor model, the last pair in your size. "Would you take something off for the mark?" Check it still works before you ask.

steps.test: For a job you need done, get two written quotes, and ask the dearer one whether they can come down.
steps.note: Cutting a hedge, fixing a car, clearing gutters, repairing a bike. Written means an email or a text with the price. Tell them honestly what the other quote was. A teenager can make the calls for a grown-up's job, with the grown-up's say-so.

steps.test: When the person serving you says they cannot change a price, ask politely who can.
steps.note: "I understand. Is there somebody who can decide on the price?" A manager, the owner, a supervisor. Wait while they fetch them, then ask again.

steps.test: Get money off something that had a printed price tag on it, in an ordinary shop.
steps.note: Use anything you have learned: a lower price elsewhere, buying two, a mark, a discount, asking the manager. Only on something you came in to buy. That is the far end of this ladder: a printed price is one you can ask about.

tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from ten with a grown-up

tracks.name: Asking for more instead of less
tracks.line: From noticing what came with the last thing you bought to buying something that matters with two extras added in.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from ten with a grown-up
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for a child from about ten with a grown-up beside them in any shop or at any stall. This ladder is about getting more for the same money, not paying less: a spare part, a set-up, the old one taken away, a small extra added to a bag. It starts with noticing what already comes with things, moves to asking what comes with them, then asking for small extras, then offering more yourself when somebody asks you for money off. It ends with a purchase you were making anyway that comes with two extras you asked for. A seller can often add something that costs them little far more easily than they can lower a price.

steps.test: Pick something you bought in the last month and write down everything that came with it apart from the thing itself.
steps.note: A phone came with a charger and a case, a bike came with lights, a haircut came with a wash, a sofa came with delivery. Some things came with nothing extra at all, and that is worth noticing too. This list shows you the kind of extras that exist.

steps.test: Before you pay for something today, ask the person serving you what comes with it.
steps.note: "Does this come with anything else?" works for a pair of shoes (spare laces, a shoe bag), a coffee machine (a descaler), or a plant (a pot). You are only asking, not bargaining. A child asks with a grown-up beside them.

steps.test: For something you plan to buy soon, write down three extras you would value more than money off.
steps.note: For a bike: a lock, a first service, lights. For a washing machine: carrying it in, plumbing it in, taking the old one away. For a lesson or a course: a practice session, the notes to keep. Keep this list; rung eight uses it.

steps.test: When you buy several things at a market stall, bakery or farm shop, ask politely whether they could add one small thing in.
steps.note: "I am taking six rolls; could you add a seventh?" or "Could you add a bunch of parsley with the vegetables?" Small shops and stalls often say yes, and a no is fine. Say thank you either way. A child asks with a grown-up standing beside them.

steps.test: When you book a service you were going to pay for anyway, ask whether a small extra could be included.
steps.note: A trim of the fringe with a haircut, the tyres pumped up with a bike repair, the inside wiped with a car wash, one more window with a window clean. Ask when you book or before they start, not after. Ask for something small that takes them a few minutes, not a second job.

steps.test: For something that will be delivered, ask whether they will carry it in, set it up, or take the old one away at no extra charge.
steps.note: Beds, fridges, washing machines, a garden shed, a large piece of furniture. Some sellers do this as standard and do not advertise it. Ask before you pay, by phone, email, online chat or in the shop.

steps.test: When a seller tells you the price cannot come down, ask what else they could include instead.
steps.note: "I understand the price is fixed. Is there anything you could include with it?" Then wait for their answer and let them suggest something. Use it only on something you were going to buy anyway at that price.

steps.test: Ask for one of the three extras you wrote down in rung three.
steps.note: Name the exact extra: "Could the lock be included with the bike?" Ask once, plainly, and say thank you whatever the answer. If that purchase has already happened, choose three extras for the next one and ask for one of those.

steps.test: The next time you have already paid for a seat, a room or a table, ask whether a better one is free at no extra cost.
steps.note: A better seat at a show or a match when the hall is half empty, a quieter room when you check in somewhere to stay, a bigger table when the room is empty. Ask only when you can see or reasonably expect that one is free. A no is the usual answer and is still the rung done.

steps.test: When somebody asks you for money off something you are selling or doing, offer them something extra instead.
steps.note: Selling a bike second-hand: offer the lock and the pump with it. Charging for babysitting, dog walking or a lift: offer an extra half hour or a stop on the way. Pick an extra that costs you little and is worth something to them. If nobody has asked you for money off yet, offer an extra to the next person who buys from you and count it.

steps.test: On a real purchase, say exactly which extra would make you buy today, and let the seller decide whether to add it.
steps.note: "If it came with fitting, I would buy it today." Only say it if it is true, and then buy it if they agree. If they say no, you can still buy it without the extra or leave; both are fine.

steps.test: Buy something that matters, which you were going to buy anyway, and come away with two extras you asked for.
steps.note: A bike, a washing machine, a course, a car service, a set of school uniform. Use anything from the ladder: asking what comes with it, your list of three, the extra that would make it a yes. Make sure both extras are written on the receipt or in an email. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Bills by phone and email
tracks.line: From working out what one bill costs a year to going through every regular bill in one afternoon and getting at least one lowered.
tracks.who: Grown-ups who pay household bills
tracks.about: For grown-ups who pay household bills; a teenager from about sixteen can sit beside them and do the looking-up. Every rung is done from home, by phone, email or a company's online chat. It starts with one bill: what it costs in a year, when the contract ends, and what new customers pay. Then you write down what you will say, ask, ask for the right team, and say honestly whether you would leave. It ends with a list of every regular payment, the end dates in a calendar, and one afternoon spent going through them. Companies often keep a better price for customers who ask, and it takes a phone call or an email to find out.

steps.test: Pick one bill your household pays every month and work out what it costs in a whole year.
steps.note: The phone, the internet, insurance, a television service, a gym, energy. Multiply the monthly amount by twelve and write the answer down. Seeing the yearly number is often enough to make the next rungs feel worth doing.

steps.test: Find out the date that bill's contract ends and whether there is a fee for leaving before then.
steps.note: Look in your online account, on a recent bill, or in the email you got when you signed up. Write down the date and the fee. Some things have no contract at all and can be changed any month; write that down if so.

steps.test: Look up what a new customer would pay today, with the same company, for exactly the same thing.
steps.note: Use the company's own website: same speed, same cover, same number of minutes. Write the price and the date you saw it. If it is lower than what you pay, that is the number you ask about.

steps.test: Look up what two other companies would charge you for the same thing.
steps.note: Their own websites or a price comparison website both count. Write each company's name, the price and the date. You will only ever quote a price you have actually seen.

steps.test: Write down the price you would be glad to pay and the three sentences you will say.
steps.note: Keep it short and every word true. Read it out loud once so it sounds like you.
how: "I have been with you for [how many] years."
"New customers pay [price], and [other company] offers [price]."
"What is the best price you can offer me to stay?"

steps.test: Contact the company about that bill by phone, email or their online chat, say your three sentences, and ask for their best price.
steps.note: Use the phone number or website printed on your bill, never one from a message somebody sent you, and never give out a full password. Be friendly; the person answering did not set your price. Write down their name, the date and what they offered.

steps.test: If the first person cannot lower the bill, ask politely to speak to the team that deals with customers who are thinking of leaving.
steps.note: Many companies have one, with names like "customer loyalty" or "cancellations". Those staff are often the ones allowed to offer a different price. "Could you put me through to the team that can change the price?" is enough.

steps.test: If you really would move to another company for a better price, say so plainly and ask what they can do.
steps.note: "I am ready to move to [company] at [price] unless you can come close." Only say it if it is true, and if they cannot help, then move. Whatever you agree, ask for it by email or letter, and check the next bill shows the new price.

steps.test: Ask about a second bill in writing, by email or online chat, using the same three sentences.
steps.note: Choose a different bill, and first look up its new-customer price and two other prices, as in rungs three and four. Writing gives you a record of every word, and some people find it easier than a call. Save the reply.

steps.test: Using your last two bank statements, write a list of every regular payment, with what each costs in a year.
steps.note: Include the small ones: online storage, a streaming service, a charity, a magazine, a phone insurance. Some bills have a price nobody can change or only one supplier where you live; mark those and leave them out of the asking.

steps.test: Put the contract end date of every bill on your list into a calendar, with a reminder one month before each.
steps.note: A paper calendar or the calendar on your phone. A month is usually enough time to look up prices and ask. If you do not know an end date, finding it is part of this rung.

steps.test: Spend one afternoon going through every bill on your list that is out of contract or ends within two months, and get at least one lowered or changed.
steps.note: Use the same steps each time: the new-customer price, two other prices, your three sentences, the right team, and the agreement in writing. Moving to a cheaper company counts as lowering it. That is the far end of this ladder: every regular bill looked at, not left alone.

tracks.name: Terms, not just the price
tracks.line: From noticing what a deal was apart from its price to agreeing a job or a bigger purchase with your three most important terms written down before you pay.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers; a teenager does any rung about a job at home with the grown-up whose home it is. A deal is more than its price: when you get it, how you pay, what happens if it goes wrong, how long you have to change your mind, and who does the work. The ladder starts with noticing those things, then reading returns rules and small print, then asking about dates, guarantees and who does the work. It ends with a job or a bigger purchase where your three most important terms are agreed and written down before you pay anything. Getting the terms right often matters more than a few coins off the price.

steps.test: Pick the last thing you paid a fair amount for, and write down two things about that deal that were not the price.
steps.note: When you paid, how it reached you, whether you could return it, how long it was guaranteed, who fitted it. A pair of trainers, a phone, a repair, a holiday booking all count. These are the terms of the deal.

steps.test: Find the returns rules of a shop or website you often use, and write down how many days you have to return something.
steps.note: They are usually on the website under "Returns" or on the back of a receipt. Note whether you need the receipt and whether you get money back or only a credit note. Now you know before you buy, not after.

steps.test: Before you buy something that has to be ordered or delivered, ask when it will arrive and whether it could come sooner.
steps.note: A pair of glasses, a sofa, a part for a bike, a school blazer. In a shop, on the phone or in an online chat. Write down the date they give you.

steps.test: Before you buy something that costs a fair amount, ask what happens if it breaks or goes wrong.
steps.note: "If this stops working in the first year, what happens?" Listen for who fixes it, who pays, and whether you go back to the shop or to the maker. If the answer is unclear, ask them to show you where it is written.

steps.test: Before you agree to something with a sign-up, read its terms all the way through and write down one thing you did not expect.
steps.note: A gym, an app, a hire car, a club, a booking. Look for the notice needed to cancel, whether it renews by itself, and any fees. Take as long as it takes; this is the part most people skip.

steps.test: Ask somebody to confirm by text or email something they told you out loud.
steps.note: A price for a job, a date they will come, a promise that a part is included. "So we both have it, could you send me that in a text?" Most people are glad to, because it protects them too.

steps.test: For a job at your home, ask who will do the work, what day they will arrive, and how long it will take.
steps.note: A plumber, a painter, a gardener, somebody fitting a carpet. The person who gives the quote is not always the person who does the work. Write the three answers down.

steps.test: Before a bigger purchase or a job, write down the three terms that matter most to you, in order.
steps.note: For example: finished before a certain date, paid when the work is done, and the mess cleared away. Or for a purchase: delivered on a Saturday, a long guarantee, thirty days to return it. Putting them in order tells you what you could let go of.

steps.test: Ask to pay for a job in stages as it is done, or when it is finished, rather than all of it before the work starts.
steps.note: "Could I pay half when you start and half when it is finished?" A deposit for materials is normal and fair. Never borrow money or sign up to a credit plan for this rung; it is only about when you pay.

steps.test: Ask for longer to return something or to change your mind.
steps.note: "It is a present; could I have thirty days to return it instead of fourteen?" Some shops will write it on the receipt. If they say yes, check it is written down before you leave. A polite no still counts as the rung done.

steps.test: Offer to let go of a term that matters less to you in return for one that matters more.
steps.note: "I can wait two extra weeks if you can do it on a Saturday." "I will collect it myself if you can keep it for me until the end of the month." Use your ordered list from rung eight. Only offer what you really can give.

steps.test: Agree a job or a bigger purchase with your three most important terms settled and written down before you pay anything.
steps.note: A text, an email, a written quote or the receipt all count, as long as all three terms are there. Check it before you hand over money. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Being ready to say no to a deal
tracks.line: From spotting the words that try to hurry you to saying no to something you really wanted because the price or terms were past your limit.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from about ten
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about ten; a child does the shop rungs with their own pocket money and a grown-up nearby. It starts with noticing the signs and words that try to make you decide fast, then writing your limit and your other option before you buy. Then you practise leaving: an online basket left overnight, a shop left with "I will think about it", a decision left until the next day, an extra at the till turned down. It ends with saying no to something you really wanted, because it was past your limit, and looking back on it a week later. Being ready to say no is what keeps every other deal honest and calm.

steps.test: Find three signs, adverts or emails that try to make you buy quickly, and write down their exact words.
steps.note: "Only two left." "Offer ends tonight." A clock counting down on a website. A child can hunt for these with a grown-up in a shop or on a screen. Once you have seen them written down, they are easier to spot.

steps.test: Before you next buy something, write down the most you will pay for it.
steps.note: A second-hand game, a coat, a bike, a used car. Write the number on paper or in your phone before you look at any price tag. The number is yours to keep to.

steps.test: For that same thing, write down what you will do instead if you cannot get it at your price.
steps.note: Buy it somewhere else, wait for a second-hand one, borrow one, save for another month, or do without. Having another option written down is what makes saying no possible.

steps.test: Put something in an online basket and leave it there overnight before you decide.
steps.note: Close the page. In the morning, decide with a clear head whether you still want it at that price. Both answers count; the rung is waiting.

steps.test: In a shop, say "I will think about it", and leave without buying.
steps.note: Choose something you are not yet sure about, and really think about it once you are home. Say it kindly and say thank you. A child does this with a grown-up nearby.

steps.test: When somebody wants an answer today, tell them you will decide tomorrow, and then decide tomorrow.
steps.note: A salesperson on the phone, a club asking you to sign up, a friend selling something. "I do not decide on the same day; I will tell you tomorrow." A fair offer is usually still there the next day, and if it is not, that tells you something too.

steps.test: When a price is over the limit you wrote down, say "That is more than I want to spend, thank you", and leave.
steps.note: At a market stall, a second-hand sale, a shop. Say it only when it is true. If they come down to your limit, you may buy it; if they do not, you go, and stay friendly.

steps.test: Turn down an extra you are offered at the till or at an online checkout.
steps.note: Extended warranty, insurance for a small item, a bigger size of drink, a membership card with a fee. "No, thank you" is a whole sentence. If you had already decided you wanted it, it does not count; pick the next one.

steps.test: The next time you notice yourself hurrying to buy something, put it down and walk around for ten minutes before you decide.
steps.note: Hurry often feels like a racing heart, a quick "just get it", or not reading the price. Ten minutes away is enough to know whether you still want it. A child can take the ten minutes with a grown-up.

steps.test: Say no to something you could afford but do not need.
steps.note: A third pair of shoes, a gadget, a treat at the till. Hold it, think about it, and put it back. Nobody else has to know.

steps.test: Stop offering or bidding when the price goes past your limit, even if somebody else then gets it.
steps.note: An online auction, a second-hand listing with several people interested, a sale where people make offers. Write your limit before it starts. A child does this with a grown-up and the grown-up's account.

steps.test: Say no to something you really wanted because the price or the terms were past your limit, and a week later write down how you feel about it.
steps.note: A car, a holiday, a phone, a flat, a bike you wanted very much. Say no kindly and leave. After a week, write a few lines: what you did instead and whether you are glad. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Both sides pleased
tracks.line: From one swap you are both glad of to a regular arrangement with somebody that has run for four weeks and that both of you still want.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight. A child does the early rungs at home with a grown-up (swaps, turns, family plans), and the later rungs suit grown-ups and teenagers. It starts with a small swap, then asking what the other person wants, saying their side back, and finding what costs you little and is worth a lot to them. In the middle you settle family plans so everybody gets what they care about, tell the truth when it costs you, and put right a deal that went badly for the other person. It ends with a regular arrangement, such as a lift share or a swap of help, that has run for four weeks and that both of you still want. Deals like this are the ones people come back for.

steps.test: Swap something with somebody so that you are both glad of the swap.
steps.note: Stickers, cards, books, a jumper you never wear for a game they have finished, a job at home for another job. Ask "Are you happy with that?" before you both agree. A child does this with a friend, brother or sister, with a grown-up nearby.

steps.test: Before you ask somebody at home for something, first ask what they would like out of it.
steps.note: Before you ask for the television, ask what they were hoping to watch. Before you ask for help with the washing up, ask what they need done tonight. Then say what you want.

steps.test: In a disagreement, say the other person's side back to them in one sentence, and ask whether you have it right, before you give yours.
steps.note: "So you want to go to the park because you have been inside all day; is that right?" If they say no, try again until they say yes. Only then give your side.

steps.test: Settle a small disagreement at home by finding what each person actually wants from the thing.
steps.note: Two children want the last orange: one wants to eat it, the other wants the peel for baking, so both get all of what they wanted. Ask "What do you want it for?" This works for the front seat, the bathroom, the last slice, the laptop.

steps.test: For a real deal coming up, write two short lists: what matters to you, and what you guess matters to the other person.
steps.note: A trade with a neighbour, a price for a job, a plan with a friend, pocket money for jobs at home. Three items on each list is plenty. The next rung checks your guesses.

steps.test: Ask that person what matters most to them in the deal, and compare it with your guess.
steps.note: "What is the most important thing for you here?" Listen to the whole answer. Mark on your list where you guessed right and where you guessed wrong.

steps.test: Find one thing that would cost you little and is worth a lot to them, and offer it before they ask.
steps.note: Being flexible about the day, collecting instead of having it delivered, leaving a tool with them for a week, doing the part of the job they dislike. Offer it plainly: "I can easily do Saturday if that is better for you."

steps.test: Offer two different deals that are both fine for you, and let the other person choose.
steps.note: "I can do it for 40 on Saturday, or 35 if you can wait until next week." "You can have the front seat there or on the way back." Make sure you would be glad of either answer.

steps.test: Tell the other side something true that makes your own position weaker.
steps.note: The bike you are selling has a slow puncture. The job will take longer than they hoped. The thing they want is cheaper somewhere else. Say it before they agree, not after.

steps.test: Plan something as a family or a group so that every person gets the part they care about most.
steps.note: A day out, a weekend, a meal, the jobs in the house. Ask each person for the one thing that matters most to them, then build the plan around those. A child can run this with a grown-up helping to keep the list.

steps.test: Write down, before you talk to them, the one thing you will not do in a deal, and tell the other person at the start.
steps.note: "I cannot do weekends, but everything else is open." Saying it first saves both of you from building a deal that could never happen. Keep it to one thing and keep it true.

steps.test: Agree a deal with somebody you see every week.
steps.note: A neighbour, a colleague, another parent from school, a housemate: sharing a lawnmower, a rota for putting the bins out, taking turns driving the children to school. Use what you have practised: ask what they want, offer what costs you little.

steps.test: A week after a deal, ask the other person whether it is still working for them.
steps.note: "Is the Tuesday lift still suiting you?" If something is not working, change it together now, while it is still small. If it is all fine, you have both heard that it is.

steps.test: Keep a promise you made in a deal even though something better for you came up afterwards.
steps.note: You agreed to sell a chair for 30, then somebody offered 50. You said you would help on Saturday, then another invitation came. If nothing better comes up, keeping the promise to the end still counts. Your word is worth more than the difference.

steps.test: Go back and put right a deal that turned out unfair on the other person.
steps.note: You sold something that broke a week later, a job took them far longer than either of you expected, you got much the better side of a swap. Offer something back: money, a repair, another turn. If no deal of yours has gone that way, count this rung the first time one does.

steps.test: Say no to a deal you do not want, in a way that leaves the other person glad to deal with you another time.
steps.note: Thank them, give the honest reason in one sentence, and say what might work in future: "Thank you for thinking of me. It is more than I need right now; I would be glad to hear from you if you have a smaller one."

steps.test: Help two other people reach an agreement without making the decision for them.
steps.note: Two children who both want the same toy, two housemates arguing about cleaning, two friends planning a trip. Ask each what they want and why, say each side back, and let them find the answer. A teenager can do this for younger children with a grown-up around.

steps.test: Do a second deal with somebody you have dealt with before, and make it better for both of you than the first.
steps.note: The same neighbour, the same seller, the same person you swap help with. Use what you learned last time about what matters to them. Ask afterwards whether it was better for them.

steps.test: Ask somebody you have dealt with what would make them glad to deal with you again.
steps.note: "Was there anything I could have done to make that easier for you?" Listen, say thank you, and write down what they said. Do not argue with the answer.

steps.test: Set up a regular arrangement with somebody that has run for four weeks and that both of you still want.
steps.note: A lift share, a swap of childcare, lessons in return for help in the garden, a rota for a shared vegetable plot. Use the rungs: ask what matters, offer what costs you little, check in after a week. At four weeks, ask "Shall we keep going?" and hear a yes from both sides. That is the far end of this ladder.

categories.name: You belong here
categories.line: Fine shops, grand rooms and expensive things — so you never again decide somewhere is above you.

tracks.name: Your town, part one
tracks.line: From a street you have never walked to being greeted by name.

steps.test: Walk one street in your own town that you have never walked.
steps.note: Ten minutes. Look up: the upper floors are where the old town still is. If you have walked every street, walk one at a different time of day.

steps.test: Learn the names of five streets or places you pass every week.
steps.note: Say them out loud as you pass. Most people can name three streets in the town they have lived in for years.

steps.test: Say hello to the person who runs one shop, stall or café you pass often, by name if you can.
steps.note: No need to buy anything. "Morning, I walk past every day and never say hello." That is the whole rung.

steps.test: Find out one thing about your town's history and tell somebody.
steps.note: Why the name, what the oldest building was for, who the statue is. One fact, told once.

steps.test: Walk into a building you have never been in and look around for two minutes.
steps.note: A library, a town hall, a church, a hotel lobby, an auction house. You are allowed. Nod to somebody, look, leave.

steps.test: Sit somewhere public for fifteen minutes and just watch who comes and goes.
steps.note: A bench, a square, a station, the steps of somewhere. A bench costs nothing and a café is not required.

steps.test: Find three groups that meet in your town and write them down.
steps.note: A choir, a club, a parkrun, a class, a market, a men's shed, a mums' group. The library notice board, a search, or asking somebody.

steps.test: Ask somebody local for their best recommendation.
steps.note: A walk, a view, a shop, a person worth knowing. "You've lived here a while, what should I not miss?"

steps.test: Pick up litter for ten minutes on one street and leave it better.
steps.note: A bag and, if you have them, gloves. Nobody will thank you and that is rather the point.

steps.test: Go to one thing that is on, and stay half an hour.
steps.note: A market, a match, a talk, a service, a fair, a carol concert. Pick one that is free.

steps.test: Find out who actually runs things in your town.
steps.note: The council, your councillor, the group behind the events, who owns the big empty building. Names, written down.

steps.test: Send one message of thanks to a local person or group for something they run.
steps.note: The market, the run, the choir, the litter pick. Three sentences. Local people answer.

steps.test: Walk into somewhere you feel you do not belong and ask one question.
steps.note: A fine shop, a golf club reception, a grand hotel. "Is the restaurant open to non-residents?" Smile, thank them, go.

steps.test: Introduce yourself to a neighbour two doors further than you have ever gone.
steps.note: Your name, how long you have been here. In a flat, the floor above or below counts.

steps.test: Go to one group's meeting once. Say your name. Stay to the end.
steps.note: One from rung seven. Free ones exist everywhere: a run, a choir, a walking group, a class at the library.

steps.test: Offer to help at one thing.
steps.note: Set out chairs, hand out water, tidy up, hold a banner. "Do you need a hand with anything?" is the whole rung.

steps.test: Go back to the same group a second time.
steps.note: The second visit is when people start to remember you. Say your name again anyway.
