steps.test: Bring somebody with you to something local.
steps.note: A friend, a child, a neighbour. Being the one who knows what is on is a kind of belonging.

steps.test: Learn ten local names.
steps.note: The butcher, the postal worker, the librarian, the coach, the people at the bus stop. Write them down; use them.

steps.test: Be greeted by name by three people on one walk through town.
steps.note: Nothing to put on, nothing to organise. When it happens, you belong here. Part two builds something for the town.

tracks.about: Your own town, walked, learned, and joined. From a street you have never walked to a meeting you went back to twice, to being greeted by name on one walk through. Free things only; no group needs paying for and no shop needs buying from.

tracks.name: Grand places, from home
tracks.line: From looking up opening times at home to booking the visit you would have talked yourself out of.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers. Every rung but one is done from a chair at home with a phone or a computer. It starts with finding out which grand buildings near you are open and when, what a free way in looks like, and what good things really cost, which is often less than people assume. Then a list of places you had assumed were not for you, an email and a phone call to one of them, a free tour booked, a date in the diary, and one person told. It ends with booking the visit you most doubted was for you. Many of the places people feel shut out of are open to anybody who asks.

steps.test: Look up one grand building near you that is open to the public, and write down its opening times and whether it is free.
steps.note: A city hall, a cathedral, an old library, a big country house, a grand hotel lobby. Many city halls and parliament buildings run free public tours. Check the building's own website for the times. Write them down with the date you looked.

steps.test: Find one grand place within an hour of you that has a free way in, such as a free tour, a free day or an open day.
steps.note: Many countries hold heritage open days once a year, when buildings that are usually closed open for free. Some country houses have free gardens or grounds even when the house costs money, and many parliaments and city halls run free tours. Check the dates before you plan anything.

steps.test: Look up the real price of something you would never normally look up.
steps.note: A made-to-measure suit, a good watch, a grand piano, a week on a sailing boat, a meal in the best restaurant in your area. Write the price down. Some will be what you expected and some will not be; either way you now know instead of guessing.

steps.test: Look up what afternoon tea or a coffee costs in the grandest hotel near you.
steps.note: Many good hotels let anybody sit in the lounge for a coffee, not only people staying there. Write down the price of a coffee and of afternoon tea. It is often much less than people assume.

steps.test: Look up what one night in the best hotel within an hour of you costs, and what is included.
steps.note: Pick a date a few months ahead. Write down the cheapest room price and what comes with it: breakfast, the spa, parking. You are not booking; you are replacing a guess with a number.

steps.test: Write down three places near you that you had assumed were not for you, and one fact you found about each.
steps.note: For example: "The hotel lounge: anybody can have a coffee, and here is the price." "City Hall: free tours, times on its website." "The golf club restaurant: open to non-members." Keep the list; the next rungs use it.

steps.test: Email one place on your list with a real question.
steps.note: A real question is one you want the answer to: "Can I look round the ballroom when there is no event on?", "Is there a dress code in the lounge?", "Do you run tours for families?" Keep it to three or four lines, sign with your name, and send it.

steps.test: Phone another place on your list and ask two questions.
steps.note: Write the two questions down first. For example, to a hotel: "Can non-residents have afternoon tea, and do I need to book?" To a car showroom: "Can I come in and sit in one without booking a test drive?" Say thank you, and write the answers down.

steps.test: Book a place on something free at one of the places you found: a tour, an open day or a talk.
steps.note: From your list or from what you found on rung two. Many are booked online in a couple of minutes. If nothing free is coming up, put your name on the mailing list so you hear about the next one.

steps.test: Put the date in your diary, and work out how you will get there and back.
steps.note: Bus or train times, parking, how long it takes, what time to leave. Write it on the calendar where the house can see it, not only in your head.

steps.test: Tell one person you are going, and ask whether they would like to come.
steps.note: A friend, a parent, a partner, a grandparent. Saying it out loud makes it real. If they say no, you are still going.

steps.test: Book, in advance, a visit to the place on your list you most doubted was for you.
steps.note: The lounge for afternoon tea, the guided tour of the big house, a concert in the grand hall, a meal in the good restaurant. If money is tight, pick the free or cheapest way in: a coffee instead of afternoon tea, the free lunchtime recital instead of the evening concert. The end of the ladder is the booking made and the date in the diary.

tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers

tracks.name: Fine shops
tracks.line: From looking up one fine shop at home to taking somebody round one who would never have gone in on their own.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for a child from about ten with a grown-up beside them. Fine shops are open to anybody who walks in, and looking is what they are there for, so no rung needs any money and nobody pretends to be buying. It starts with one shop looked up at home, then walking in and looking properly, a question, holding one thing, a second kind of shop, and learning how the best things are made. It ends with taking somebody round a shop they would never have gone into on their own. Knowing what fine work looks like, and that you are welcome to look at it, is worth having whatever you earn.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from ten with a grown-up

steps.test: Find one fine shop near you on its website, and write down three things it sells and one you would like to see up close.
steps.note: A jeweller, a watchmaker, a tailor, a shop selling good furniture, pianos, pens or kitchen knives, a fine food hall, a gallery that sells paintings. Write the shop name, its opening hours and the three things. No shop like this near you: do the next rungs in the best shop of any kind you can reach.

steps.test: Walk into that shop, look closely at three things for about a minute each, and walk out at an unhurried pace.
steps.note: Look at how each is made: the stitching, the finish, the weight of it on the stand. You do not need to speak to anybody on this rung. If somebody says hello, say hello back. A child does this with a grown-up.

steps.test: When somebody offers to help, say "I am just looking today, thank you", and stay at least five more minutes.
steps.note: It is true, it is polite, and it is what shop staff hear all day. Then keep looking at your own pace. If you already go into shops like this without a second thought, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Ask a member of staff one question about something in the shop.
steps.note: For example: "What is this made of?", "Where is this made?", "How long does this take to make?" Listen to the whole answer and say thank you.

steps.test: Ask what the difference is between two similar things at very different prices, and listen to the whole answer.
steps.note: Two watches, two coats, two pans, two pens. People who work in good shops usually like explaining this. Afterwards, say in one sentence what you learned.

steps.test: Ask whether you may hold or try one thing, saying honestly that you are not buying today.
steps.note: A watch on your wrist, a coat on, a pen in your hand, a leather bag on your shoulder. Most shops say yes. Have clean hands, hold it over the counter, and hand it back carefully. If they say no, say thank you; the rung is the asking.

steps.test: Go into a second, different kind of fine shop, look properly, and ask one question.
steps.note: If the first was a jeweller, try a tailor, a piano shop or a shop selling good tools. Same as before: look closely, one question, thank you, and leave at an easy pace, with no apology and no excuse.

steps.test: Ask somebody who works there which thing in the shop they would choose for themselves, and why.
steps.note: Their answer usually tells you what really matters about the thing, which is often not the most expensive one. Write down what they chose and their reason.

steps.test: Go back to one of the shops a second time and say hello to somebody you spoke to before.
steps.note: Tell them something you remembered from last time: "You told me about the stitching on the coats; I have been noticing it since." Being remembered works both ways.

steps.test: Find out how the best version of one thing you saw is made, and explain it to somebody at home in two minutes.
steps.note: From a person in the shop, the maker's own website, or a video of the workshop. How a watch movement is put together, how a suit is cut by hand, how a good knife is forged. Two minutes, out loud.

steps.test: Spend half an hour in a fine shop or the fine department of a large store, looking and asking, with nothing bought and nothing to apologise for.
steps.note: Take your time with each thing. Ask two or three questions across the half hour. When you leave, say thank you to whoever helped you.

steps.test: Take somebody who would never have gone in on their own round one of your shops, and let them ask the first question.
steps.note: A friend, a grandparent, a teenager, a neighbour. Tell them beforehand what to say if staff come over. That is the far end of this ladder: you are the one showing somebody else that they are welcome there too.

tracks.name: Cars
tracks.line: From looking up one car you admire to taking somebody else for their first look round a showroom.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for a child from about ten with a grown-up; the drive near the end needs a driving licence, and its note gives a way for non-drivers. Showrooms and car shows are there to be looked round, and every rung here is done honestly, saying you are not buying today. It starts with one car you admire looked up at home and what it really costs to run, then looking at one up close, walking into a showroom, sitting in it, asking owners and staff what they know, and learning how one part works. It ends with an honest test drive or ride, and then taking somebody else for their first look. By the end you know what the car you admire is like to sit in, how one part of it works, and what it costs to keep.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from ten with a grown-up

steps.test: Choose one car you admire and write down three facts about it: the price new, what drives it, and where it is made.
steps.note: Any car at all: a family estate, an electric car, a classic, a sports car. The maker's website has the price and the engine or battery. Write the three facts on paper with the date.

steps.test: Find out roughly what that car costs to run for one year: fuel or charging, insurance, tax, servicing, and the value it loses.
steps.note: Owners' clubs, running-cost calculators and motoring magazines online give rough figures. Write one number for each, then a total. Rough is fine; the point is a real number instead of a guess.

steps.test: Find the car you chose, or one like it, on show somewhere free and look at it closely for five minutes.
steps.note: A showroom window, a car museum, a classic car meet in a car park, a motor show on its free day. Look, but never touch or lean on a car that belongs to somebody unless they invite you to.

steps.test: Walk into a car showroom and look round one car for ten minutes, saying "just looking today, thank you" if somebody comes over.
steps.note: Walk round it slowly: the wheels, the lights, the boot, the inside through the window. Showrooms expect people who are years away from buying. A child does this with a grown-up.

steps.test: Ask the salesperson one question you actually want answered about that car.
steps.note: For example: "How far does it go on a full charge in winter?", "Why is this one dearer than that one?", "What is the warranty?" Listen to the whole answer and thank them.

steps.test: Ask whether you may sit in the car, saying plainly you are not buying today, then adjust the seat and mirrors and stay for three minutes.
steps.note: Most showroom cars are left open for exactly this. Notice what you can see from the seat, where your hands fall, how the door sounds when it shuts. If they say no, thank them; the asking is the rung.

steps.test: Ask somebody who knows the car what owners like most about it and what they wish were different.
steps.note: A salesperson, a mechanic, or an owner at a car meet. Owners are usually glad to talk about their cars. Write down one thing from each side.

steps.test: Go to a different kind of place where cars are on show, and talk to one owner or member of staff.
steps.note: A classic car show, a car museum, a club meet, or a different brand's showroom. Many club meets are free to walk round. Ask one question and listen.

steps.test: Learn how one part of that car works well enough to explain it to somebody at home in one minute.
steps.note: How the brakes put charge back into the battery, what a turbocharger does, how four-wheel drive decides which wheel to push. A diagram on paper helps. One minute, out loud.

steps.test: Write down, on paper, what it would honestly take to own that car: the price, a year of running costs, and how long you would need to save.
steps.note: Use your numbers from rungs one and two. Divide by what you could put aside each month to get a date. The answer may be next year or twenty years away; either way it is now a number, not a feeling.

steps.test: Ask a showroom for a short test drive, saying honestly how far away you are from buying, and take it if they say yes.
steps.note: "I am saving towards one in a few years; could I take a short drive so I know what I am saving for?" Some will say yes and some no, and both are fair answers. Needs a full licence. A non-driver or a teenager asks instead to sit in the passenger seat while a member of staff drives, or to sit in it with the engine running.

steps.test: Take somebody for their first look round a showroom, and let them ask a question and sit in a car.
steps.note: A friend, a son or daughter, a parent who never goes in. Tell them beforehand to say "just looking today". That is the far end of this ladder: you are the one who knows the way in and shows somebody else.

tracks.name: Grand rooms
tracks.line: From looking up at one grand ceiling to an evening event in the grandest room near you, stayed to the end.
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight; a child goes with a grown-up to every place on this ladder. It is the going-in that follows Grand places, from home: cathedrals, city halls, old libraries, grand hotels, university halls and galleries, most of which let anybody in for nothing. It starts with one grand ceiling looked at properly, then details, a question, a free tour, a public meeting, a talk or recital and an exhibition opening, an hour on your own, and the story of the room. It ends with an evening event in the grandest room near you, stayed to the end. These rooms were built to be walked into, and they are at their best with people in them.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child with a grown-up

steps.test: Go into one grand building that is free and open to the public, and look up at the ceiling for one full minute.
steps.note: A cathedral, a city hall, an old public library, a museum's main hall, a railway station built long ago. Stand still and look up. If you did Grand places, from home, use a building from your list.

steps.test: In a grand building, find three details somebody put there on purpose, and draw or write down each one.
steps.note: A carved face above a door, a painted name, a coloured window, a clock, a pattern in the floor. A quick sketch is enough. A child can look for the smallest detail they can find.

steps.test: Ask a member of staff or a volunteer one question about the building.
steps.note: For example: "When was this room built?", "What was this room used for?", "Which part is the oldest?" People who work in grand buildings are often glad to be asked.

steps.test: Go on a free guided tour of a grand building and ask the guide one question during it.
steps.note: Many city halls, parliament buildings, libraries and cathedrals run free tours; check the building's website for times. If you booked a tour on Grand places, from home, this is that tour: count it.

steps.test: Walk into the lounge of a grand hotel and ask at reception whether people who are not staying there may sit in it.
steps.note: Ask honestly: "Is it all right for non-residents to sit in the lounge?" If they say yes, sit for ten minutes. If they say you need to order something, you choose: a glass of water or a coffee, or thank them and go. The rung is the asking.

steps.test: Go to a free talk, lecture or lunchtime concert held in a grand room.
steps.note: Universities, cathedrals, libraries, museums and city halls often hold them, many free and open to anybody. Check their websites for "public events". Arrive ten minutes early and sit near the front half.

steps.test: At the end of a talk or concert, speak to one person: the speaker, a player, or somebody sitting near you.
steps.note: One sentence is enough: "Thank you, I enjoyed the part about the organ." or "Have you been to one of these before?" A child can thank a player with a grown-up beside them.

steps.test: Sit in the public seats of a council meeting or a court for half an hour.
steps.note: Many local councils and courts let the public watch; check the rules and times on their website first. Arrive early, turn your phone off, and stand when others stand. Many courts do not let children in, so a child goes to the council meeting instead.

steps.test: Go to the opening of an exhibition that says it is open to the public.
steps.note: Galleries and museums list openings on their websites and noticeboards. Only go if it says open to all; if it says by invitation, choose another. Look at the work, and say hello to one person.

steps.test: Go into a grand building on your own and stay for one whole hour.
steps.note: The reading room of an old library is ideal: sit at a table and read. A cathedral, a museum hall or a gallery also works. A child does the hour with a grown-up in the same room, each on their own.

steps.test: Find out the story of one grand room you have been in: who built it, who it was for, and who may use it now, and tell somebody.
steps.note: The building's own website, a guidebook from the library, or the guide on your tour. Tell it at home in two minutes.

steps.test: Go to an evening event in the grandest room near you, and stay to the very end.
steps.note: A concert, a public lecture, a debate, a carol service, an organ recital. Many are free; for the rest, choose the cheapest seat or a free one. Wear what you are comfortable in. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: Carrying yourself
tracks.line: From one minute standing well at home to seven days of walking, sitting and speaking the same calm way everywhere you go.
tracks.about: For anybody from about ten: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side. How you stand, walk, sit and speak is a set of habits, and habits can be practised. It starts at home with standing and walking and sitting properly, then takes them out: into a shop, through a whole conversation, saying your name, being served without apologising, asking plainly, letting a pause be. Later rungs use them in rooms where you feel out of place, and it ends with seven days of carrying yourself this way everywhere. It is not about looking richer or grander than anybody; it is about standing, moving and speaking as calmly in a grand room as in your own kitchen.
tracks.who: From about ten; a child and a grown-up side by side

steps.test: Stand with your feet under your hips, your weight even on both feet, your shoulders relaxed and your head level, for one minute.
steps.note: Anywhere at home, in front of a mirror if you have one. Let your arms hang. Breathe normally. Notice where you usually lean or tip your head.

steps.test: Walk across a room at home five times at an easy, unhurried pace, with your head up.
steps.note: Look at the far wall, not the floor. Let your arms swing a little. If it feels slow, it is probably right.

steps.test: Sit properly for five minutes: back against the chair, both feet on the floor, hands still.
steps.note: During a meal, a programme or a phone call. Not perched on the front edge of the seat. A child can do it at the table while a grown-up does the same.

steps.test: Walk into a shop or café at that same unhurried pace, head up, and say hello to the first person you meet.
steps.note: Walk in as you practised at home. The person at the counter, at the door, or the person you step aside for. If you already walk in like this, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Stand with your weight even and your shoulders relaxed for one whole conversation.
steps.note: Any conversation where you are standing: at the door, in a queue, in a corridor. Notice if you start to fold your arms or lean away, and come back to standing evenly.

steps.test: For one conversation, look at the other person's face while you are speaking, for the whole of each sentence.
steps.note: Look at the face, not a stare into the eyes; between the eyebrows works if eye contact feels hard. In some families and places a steady look at an older person is rude, so do what is respectful where you are.

steps.test: Say your own name slowly and clearly to somebody you have not met before, with the greeting that is usual where you are.
steps.note: A handshake, a nod, a bow, or just "Hello, I am Sam." For example: a new neighbour, a shopkeeper, a parent at the school gate, a new player at a club. Practise saying your name at home first.

steps.test: Let somebody serve or help you, and say "thank you" instead of "sorry for the trouble".
steps.note: Somebody bringing a drink, holding a door, giving you a lift, passing the salt. It is their job or their kindness; a thank you is the right answer to both.

steps.test: When somebody gives you a compliment, say "thank you" and nothing after it.
steps.note: No "oh, this old thing", no pointing out what is wrong with it. Just thank you, and a smile. A grown-up can give the child a compliment to practise on, and the other way round.

steps.test: For one whole day, say sorry only for things that really were your fault, and say "excuse me" or "thank you" in place of the rest.
steps.note: Bumping into a door is not a sorry. Asking a question is not a sorry. Somebody waiting for you: "thank you for waiting". Keep a count of the sorries you swapped.

steps.test: Ask for something you want as a plain sentence, with no apology in front of it.
steps.note: "I would like the table by the window, please" instead of "Sorry, is there any chance we could maybe sit there?" At home: "Please could you pass the bread." Do it three times today.

steps.test: When a conversation goes quiet, count three seconds in your head before anybody fills it, including you.
steps.note: Most pauses feel longer than they are. Often the other person says the more interesting thing in that gap. Do it in one conversation today.

steps.test: Wear something you already own and feel good in to something ordinary, on purpose.
steps.note: A good shirt to the supermarket, a favourite jacket to school or work. Nothing bought. Walk and sit the way you practised.

steps.test: Walk into a place where you feel out of place, and walk, stand and sit there the way you practised.
steps.note: A grand hotel lobby, a fine shop, a meeting where everybody is older than you, a club you have never been to. Stay at least ten minutes. The ladders Fine shops and Grand rooms are full of places to try.

steps.test: In a place like that, ask a member of staff for something you want, as a plain sentence.
steps.note: "Could you tell me where the reading room is, please?", "I would like to see the blue one, please." Standing evenly, looking at their face, no apology first.

steps.test: At a gathering, introduce yourself by name to the person running it.
steps.note: The host at a party, the chair of a meeting, the coach at a club, the head teacher at a school event. "Hello, I am Sam, I came along for the first time today." A child does this with a grown-up nearby.

steps.test: Disagree once, calmly, with somebody older or in charge of you, in a normal voice and with your reason.
steps.note: "I see it differently, because…" and then listen to their answer. Not to win; just to say it plainly. A child picks something small and safe: which way to walk, what the answer to a quiz question is.

steps.test: In a room where you are fairly new, make somebody who looks even newer feel welcome.
steps.note: Say hello, tell them your name, show them where the water or the seats are. You remember exactly how it feels, which makes you the right person to do it.

steps.test: For one whole day, carry yourself this way everywhere you go: unhurried walk, head up, sitting properly, your name said clearly, no needless sorry.
steps.note: In the morning, read the list once. In the evening, write down where it was easy and where you forgot.

steps.test: For seven days running, carry yourself this way everywhere you go, and write one line each evening about where it was easy and where it was not.
steps.note: Same list as the single day. At the end of the week, read the seven lines and notice which places no longer feel out of place. That is the far end of this ladder.

tracks.name: The story you tell yourself
tracks.line: From writing down one "not for people like me" to doing three of them and telling somebody what really happened.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers. Most of us have places and activities we have quietly decided are "not for people like me": a gallery, a gym, a smart hotel lobby, a running club, a lecture. This ladder starts by writing one of them down, with exactly what you think would happen there and the words you say to yourself about it. Then you find out the facts, go, and write what really happened under what you predicted; then a second one, a weekly habit, and a person who does it. It ends when you have done three things from your list and told somebody the old story and what really happened. Pick ordinary, safe things; a fear that is strong or linked to something that hurt you is better talked through with somebody you trust than tested here.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers

steps.test: Write down one place or activity you have decided is "not for people like me".
steps.note: Ordinary, safe and legal: an art gallery, a golf club open day, a smart hotel for a coffee, a gym, a dance class, a public lecture at a university, a theatre, a running club, a big library. Pick something you would quite like to try if the thought were not there. One is enough.

steps.test: Under it, write exactly what you think would happen if you went there, and keep the paper.
steps.note: Be specific: "People would stare when I walked in", "I would not know where to go or what to do", "It would cost more than I have", "Everyone would already know each other". Put the date on it. You will need this page later.

steps.test: Write down, word for word, the sentence you say to yourself about it.
steps.note: The exact words, even if they sound blunt: "People like me don't go there", "I would look stupid", "That is for rich people", "I am too old for that". Seeing the sentence on paper is different from hearing it in your head.

steps.test: Write where you think that sentence first came from, if you know.
steps.note: Something a parent, teacher or friend said, somewhere you felt out of place once, a film, or nowhere you can remember. This is not about blaming anybody; they may have been trying to protect you. "I don't know" is a fine answer.

steps.test: For one day, write down every time a thought stops you doing something, with the exact words of the thought.
steps.note: Carry a scrap of paper or use a note on your phone. Small things count: not asking a question in a shop, not joining in a conversation, not trying on a colour. Look at the list in the evening and notice any sentences that repeat.

steps.test: Next to your prediction from rung two, write the evidence you have for it and the evidence against it.
steps.note: Evidence means something that actually happened or that you know for certain, not a feeling. "I went to a gallery once as a child and got told off for touching" is evidence of something; "I just know" is not. Often the against column is empty only because you have never checked.

steps.test: Find out three facts about the place before you go: when it is open, what it costs, and what people do or wear there.
steps.note: Its website, a phone call, or asking somebody who has been. Many galleries, museums, libraries and lectures are free; many clubs and classes offer a free first visit. If a visit would cost more than a normal household can spare, pick a free thing from your list instead.

steps.test: Go to the place, or do the activity, once, and stay for at least fifteen minutes.
steps.note: Go alone or with one friend. In a hotel or café, a glass of water or the cheapest drink is enough; in a gallery, look at three things properly. If you feel very uneasy, notice it and stay for the fifteen minutes; if you ever feel unsafe, leave.

steps.test: Under your prediction, write down what actually happened.
steps.note: The same day if you can, while you remember. Go line by line: did people stare, did you know what to do, did it cost what you thought? Write the surprises as well as anything that was as you expected.

steps.test: Write a new sentence about that place that is true now, and say it out loud.
steps.note: Not a slogan, just what is true: "I went to the gallery, nobody looked twice, and I liked the big room upstairs." Say it out loud once. Keep it on the same page as the old sentence.

steps.test: Pick a second "not for me" from your list, write down your prediction, go, and write what actually happened.
steps.note: Choose one a little bigger than the first: a class instead of a visit, or staying an hour instead of fifteen minutes. Same method: prediction and date first, facts found out, go, then what happened.

steps.test: Write down one thing you were right to be careful about, and one thing you were wrong about.
steps.note: Being careful is sometimes right: a place really was expensive, or a class really was for a higher level. This ladder is about checking, not about ignoring every warning. Both lines are useful.

steps.test: Find somebody who does the thing you thought was not for people like you, and read or listen to how they started.
steps.note: An interview, a short biography, a club's page about its members, a talk online. Look for somebody whose start looks like yours: late, nervous, with no money or no family who did it. Write down one thing they did at the beginning.

steps.test: Ask one person who does it how they got started.
steps.note: Somebody at the club, the person at the gallery desk, a friend of a friend, a colleague. "I am thinking of trying this; how did you start?" is enough. Listen to the whole answer and say thank you.

steps.test: Go to one place from your list every week for four weeks.
steps.note: The same place each week, or a different one; both work. Put it in your calendar like any other appointment. By the third week, notice whether the old sentence still turns up and how loud it is.

steps.test: Tell one person something you want to do that the old story said you could not.
steps.note: A friend, a partner, a parent, a colleague. Say it plainly: "I want to join the choir", "I want to go to the lecture series at the university". You are not asking permission, just saying it out loud to somebody.

steps.test: Do a third thing from your list, bigger than the first two.
steps.note: Join the class for a term, book the concert, enter a charity run, go to the members' evening. Same method: prediction first, then go, then what happened written underneath. If it costs money, choose the free version.

steps.test: Read your first page again, then tell somebody the old story and what actually happened.
steps.note: This is the end of the ladder. Somebody who might have a "not for me" of their own is a good choice. Tell them the prediction, the sentence, and what really happened at your three places, and if they want, help them write down their first one.

categories.name: Home and repair
categories.line: Keeping a place, mending, tools, bikes, first aid, engines.

tracks.name: A home that works, part one
tracks.line: From a made bed to a place that is ready for anybody in ten minutes.

steps.test: Make your bed and clear the floor of your room.
steps.note: Everything off the floor, into its place or a bag. Two minutes, and the whole room looks different.

steps.test: Empty one drawer and put it back in order.
steps.note: Everything out, wipe it, only what belongs goes back. One drawer, not the kitchen.

steps.test: Wash up everything and leave the sink empty and dry.
steps.note: Dry and empty is the rung. A dry sink is the sign of a kitchen somebody runs.

steps.test: Fix one small broken thing.
steps.note: A loose handle, a squeaking door, a wobbling chair, a blown bulb. Ten minutes and a screwdriver.

steps.test: Find out where the water stopcock and the fuse box are, and how they work.
steps.note: Turn the stopcock and back. Open the fuse box and read the labels. Renting counts just the same.

steps.test: Give away five things.
steps.note: A bag to a charity shop, a neighbour, a friend. Things you have not used in a year.

steps.test: Clean one window until you forget it is there.
steps.note: Inside and out if you can reach. Newspaper and vinegar work. Then look through it.

steps.test: Sort the phone: delete twenty things and turn off ten notifications.
steps.note: Apps, photos, old messages. Then the notifications that were never your idea.

steps.test: Cook, and leave the kitchen as you found it.
steps.note: Cooking is half the job. The other half is a kitchen that does not know you were there.

steps.test: Learn one house skill: change a fuse, reset a trip switch, or bleed a radiator.
steps.note: Ask somebody, watch a video, then do it yourself. One is enough today.

steps.test: Sew on a button or mend one hem.
steps.note: Needle, thread, five minutes. Nobody will see the stitches and you will know they are there.

steps.test: Clear one forgotten place.
steps.note: Under the bed, the top of the wardrobe, the cupboard under the stairs, the glove box. One.

steps.test: Keep a plant alive for a fortnight.
steps.note: A cutting in a jar of water counts. Water it, look at it, notice when it wants something.

steps.test: Sharpen the knives, oil a hinge, and tighten whatever wobbles.
steps.note: Three small things in one go. A home stays working through small things done early.

steps.test: Do one whole room properly: cleared, cleaned, everything with a place.
steps.note: Half a day. Choose the room you use most. Take a photo before and after.

steps.test: Make a first-aid kit that would actually help.
steps.note: Plasters, a bandage, antiseptic, painkillers, scissors, tweezers, a foil blanket. Check what is out of date.

steps.test: Deal with the pile: every letter and paper opened, filed, or binned.
steps.note: One sitting. Three piles: act, keep, bin. The bin pile is bigger than you think.

steps.test: Make one thing for the home.
steps.note: A shelf, a frame, a cushion, a hook, a bird box. Made by you, in use.

steps.test: A full week with the place tidy every night before bed.
steps.note: Ten minutes each night. By the seventh night it takes five.

steps.test: Have somebody round, and be ready in ten minutes.
steps.note: Tea, a clear table, a chair to sit in. When ten minutes is enough, the place works. Part two makes it beautiful.

tracks.about: A home that works: the bed, one drawer, the sink dry, one thing fixed, the stopcock found, five things given away, and on to a whole room done properly and a week of tidy nights. It ends with somebody round and ten minutes to be ready. Renting counts exactly the same.

tracks.name: Keeping a place
tracks.line: From sweeping a floor properly to looking after the whole house for a day.
tracks.who: From about eight; grown-ups who never learnt, too
tracks.about: For anybody from about eight, with a grown-up showing them each job the first time; grown-ups who were never taught these count exactly the same. This is the ladder for the housework jobs themselves, done properly: sweeping, wiping, washing up, a basin, a toilet, a floor, the laundry from basket to drawer, a duvet cover and the rubbish. Then the jobs become a weekly habit, and it ends with looking after the whole house for a day. A person who can do these is a help in any home they live in, now and later.

steps.test: Sweep one floor into a single pile and get all of it into the dustpan, with no line of dust left behind.
steps.note: Start at the edges and sweep towards the middle, then into one pile. Hold the dustpan flat, sweep in, pull the pan back a little and sweep again for the last line. A damp piece of kitchen roll picks up what the brush will not.

steps.test: Clear a kitchen table or counter, wipe it properly, and dry it.
steps.note: Move everything off first, not round it. Brush the crumbs into your hand or a dustpan, then wipe with a damp cloth and a little washing-up liquid in lines from the back to the front, then dry it with a tea towel. Put back only what lives there.

steps.test: Wash up a full sink of dishes in the right order: glasses, then cutlery, then plates and bowls, then pans.
steps.note: Hot water with a squeeze of washing-up liquid; the cleanest things go first so the water stays clean for longer. Change the water when it goes greasy or cold. Take care with knives: wash them one at a time and never leave them hidden under the bubbles. If your home has a dishwasher, load it, run it, and empty it into the right cupboards instead.

steps.test: Clean a bathroom basin until it shines, including the plughole, round the taps and behind them.
steps.note: A cloth with a little washing-up liquid does most basins; an old toothbrush gets round the taps and into the plughole. Rinse and dry the taps so they shine. If a grown-up gives you a bathroom cleaner, use only that one: never mix two cleaning products, because some give off harmful fumes together.

steps.test: Clean a toilet: the outside, the seat on both sides, then the bowl and under the rim with the brush.
steps.note: Rubber gloves if the house has them, and a cloth kept only for the toilet. Outside and seat first with the cloth, bowl last with the brush, then flush and rinse the brush in the clean water. Wash your hands well afterwards. A grown-up chooses the cleaner the first time.

steps.test: Hoover or mop the floor of a whole room, moving the chairs and small things out of the way first.
steps.note: Chairs on the table or in the hall, shoes and bags out, then start at the far corner and work back towards the door so you do not walk on what you have done. No hoover or mop: a broom and then a damp cloth on your hands and knees does the same job.

steps.test: Sort a basket of washing by colour and by the label, and put one load through the machine or wash it by hand.
steps.note: Whites and pale colours together, darks together, anything with a low temperature on the label kept apart. Check every pocket. A grown-up shows you the machine and the amount of powder the first time. No machine: warm water and a little soap in a basin or bath, then rinse and squeeze.

steps.test: Hang that load to dry so it creases as little as possible, then fold it and put every piece away where it lives.
steps.note: Shake each piece out hard before it goes on the line or the rack, and hang shirts from the bottom or on a hanger. Fold when fully dry. Every piece goes to its own drawer or its owner's room, not into a pile on a bed.

steps.test: Put a clean cover on a duvet and pillows on your own.
steps.note: The easy way: turn the cover inside out, put your hands inside to the two far corners, grab two corners of the duvet through the cover, then shake it so the cover falls down over the duvet. Pillows go in corner first. If your bed has sheets and a blanket instead, make it with the top sheet tucked in and count it.

steps.test: Take out the rubbish and the recycling, sorted the way your local council asks, on the right day.
steps.note: Look up what goes in which bin on your council's website or the leaflet that came with the bins, and which day they are collected. Squash the boxes, rinse the tins. A child can do the small bins round the house and a grown-up takes the big one to the street.

steps.test: Pick three jobs from this ladder that your home needs every week, and do them each week for four weeks without being asked.
steps.note: For example: the bathroom basin, the hoover in the living room, and the bins. Write the three on the fridge and tick each week. If you already do weekly jobs at home, take on one more and count the four weeks.

steps.test: Look after the house for a whole day: meals cleared away, floors swept, a load of washing done, bins out, and any pets and plants looked after.
steps.note: Agree the day with the grown-ups or the people you live with, so they can have a day off from it. Write your list the night before. At the end of the day, walk them round: the kitchen clear, the floors done, the washing folded. A child does this with a grown-up at home, who stays out of the jobs.

tracks.name: Mending
tracks.line: From fresh batteries in something that stopped to teaching somebody else a repair, hands off.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers; a child from about eight can do many of the rungs with a grown-up beside them, and each note says where a grown-up is needed. The climb starts with batteries and the right screwdriver, then learns where the line is (gas, mains electrics and roofs are always for a qualified person), then glue, cloth, zips, a sink trap, a sticking door, a hole in a wall, and a part replaced rather than the whole thing. It ends with fixing something for somebody else, and then teaching them to fix one thing themselves. Most of it needs only what is already in a drawer at home, and every repair is one less thing bought.

steps.test: Change the batteries in something that has stopped working, and put the cover back on properly.
steps.note: A remote control, a torch, a kitchen scales, a toy, a bathroom scale. Match the size printed on the old batteries (AA, AAA, a round button cell) and the plus and minus marks inside. Old batteries go to the battery box at a supermarket, not the bin. Button batteries are dangerous if swallowed, so keep them well away from small children.

steps.test: Find three screws in the house and the screwdriver that fits each one with no wobble.
steps.note: Try a cupboard hinge, a battery cover on a toy, or a door handle; screw heads are either a straight slot or a cross, and they come in sizes; the right one sits deep in the head and does not slip. With no screwdriver, a coin often fits a straight slot. Leave the screws on light switches and sockets alone.

steps.test: Write down the repairs in your home you should never do yourself, and who you would ring for each.
steps.note: Anything to do with gas, the fixed mains electrics (sockets, switches, the fuse box wiring), and anything on a roof or up a tall ladder. Gas work needs a registered gas engineer; wiring needs a qualified electrician. If you smell gas, open windows, do not touch switches, and ring the gas emergency number for your area: look it up now and write it on the list. Keep the list on the fridge or in your phone.

steps.test: Glue one broken thing with the right glue, leave it the full time on the tube, and check it still holds a week later.
steps.note: A plant pot, an ornament, a toy, the sole of an old shoe. Read the tube: some glues are for paper and wood, some for ceramics, some for shoes. Hold or clamp it (rubber bands, a pile of books) for the whole time the tube says. A grown-up handles superglue, which sticks skin in seconds; anything used for hot food or drink is better replaced than glued.

steps.test: Mend a book: glue a loose page back in, or tape a torn page from the back.
steps.note: A thin line of white PVA glue along the edge of a loose page, pushed back in, then the book closed under something heavy overnight. For a tear, clear tape on the side with less printing, or thin paper and glue. A child can do this one alone with a glue stick.

steps.test: Fix a screw that just spins in its hole, so it holds tight.
steps.note: Common on cupboard hinges and door handles. Take the screw out, push two or three wooden matchsticks or cocktail sticks dipped in wood glue into the hole, snap them off level, leave it an hour, then put the screw back in. If you have no wood glue, the sticks alone often work for something light.
how: Take the loose screw out.
Push glued matchsticks into the hole until it is full.
Snap or cut them off level with the surface and wait an hour.
Drive the screw back in gently until it is firm.

steps.test: Patch or darn one hole in a piece of clothing so it can be worn again.
steps.note: A sock heel, a jumper elbow, the knee of a child's trousers. For a small hole, sew back and forth across it, then across those stitches the other way, like weaving. For a bigger one, sew a piece of fabric from an old garment over it. A needle and thread are the only kit; a sewing kit from a hotel or a cracker is enough.

steps.test: Put a zip back on its track, or give a zip with a broken pull a new one.
steps.note: If one side has come out, open the zip fully, ease the slider back over both rows of teeth at the bottom, and pull up gently. If the pull tab has snapped off, a key ring, a paper clip or a loop of string through the hole works. Coats, bags and pencil cases are good places to find one.

steps.test: Clear a slow sink: take the hair out of the plughole, then undo and clean the U-bend underneath and put it back without drips.
steps.note: Put a basin under the curved pipe under the sink first, because it is full of water. Unscrew the two plastic rings by hand, rinse the bend out in a bucket (not in the same sink), and screw it back hand-tight. Run the tap for a minute and check for drips. Wear rubber gloves, never mix drain cleaners, and a child does this one with a grown-up.

steps.test: Fix a door that sticks or a drawer that does not run smoothly.
steps.note: For a door: tighten every hinge screw first, since a loose hinge is the usual cause, then rub chalk on the edge, close it, and look where the chalk has rubbed off. For a drawer: take it out, clean the runners, and rub a candle or a bar of dry soap along them. If a door needs planing, that is a job to watch somebody do first.

steps.test: Take one small thing apart to fix it, keep the screws in order, and put it back together so it works.
steps.note: A pepper grinder, a torch, a toy, a stapler, a pair of glasses with a loose arm. Photograph each stage with your phone and put the screws in an egg box, one cup per stage. Never open anything that plugs into the mains, a microwave, a television or a phone charger: they can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged. A child does this with a grown-up.

steps.test: Fill a small hole or crack in a wall and sand it flat.
steps.note: A screw hole from an old picture or a dent from a door handle. Scrape out loose bits, press ready-mixed filler in with a knife so it stands a little above the wall, leave it as long as the tub says, then sand it smooth with sandpaper wrapped round a block. Filler is cheap; ask a neighbour or a relative for the end of a tub. If you rent, ask the landlord first, and wear a dust mask when sanding.

steps.test: Paint over the patch you filled so the edges cannot be seen.
steps.note: Use leftover paint from that wall; many houses have the tin in a shed or under the stairs. Paint a little wider than the patch and spread the edges out thin with an almost dry brush. Let it dry, then look from across the room in daylight. A child can do this with a small brush and a grown-up nearby.

steps.test: Fix three broken things in one day.
steps.note: Walk round the house first and write down every small broken thing you have been meaning to fix, then pick three you now know how to do. A loose handle, a stuck drawer, a torn page all count. Tick them off as they are done.

steps.test: Replace one worn-out part instead of replacing the whole thing.
steps.note: A shower hose, a vacuum cleaner belt, a cupboard handle, a toilet seat, the rubber feet on a chair. Take the old part with you to the shop, or search the model number printed on the thing for the exact part. For free, take a part from a broken one of the same kind, or ask at a repair café.

steps.test: Watch somebody who knows how to mend something, and ask them to explain each step while they do it.
steps.note: A grandparent who darns, a neighbour who fixes bikes, a relative who does DIY. A repair café is ideal if there is one near you: search "repair café" and the name of your town. Bring one of your own broken things if you can, and write down one thing you learned.

steps.test: Put together one box of the things you kept needing on this ladder.
steps.note: Look back at what you used: two screwdrivers, glue, a needle and thread, tape, sandpaper, a few spare screws, matchsticks, a torch. One shoebox is enough. Keep it somewhere everybody in the house knows about.

steps.test: Fix one thing that somebody in the house had already given up on and put aside to throw out.
steps.note: Ask around: there is usually something in a cupboard or a bag by the door. Look it up, try, and if it cannot be fixed, find out why before it goes. Working again is the rung; learning exactly why it cannot be fixed also counts.

steps.test: Fix something for somebody else who could not fix it themselves.
steps.note: A neighbour's sticking door, a grandparent's torch, a friend's coat zip. Take your box from rung seventeen. Only take on repairs you have already done on this ladder, and say so if it is beyond you.

steps.test: Teach somebody to fix one thing themselves, with your hands off it the whole time.
steps.note: Pick a repair from this ladder that you are sure of: a patch, a spinning screw, a stuck drawer. Talk them through it and keep your hands in your pockets, even when it is slow. It is finished when the thing works and they did every part of it.

tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from eight with a grown-up

tracks.name: Tools
tracks.line: From finding five tools at home to teaching somebody to carry, pass and put away tools safely.
tracks.who: From eight with a grown-up; power tools for grown-ups only
tracks.about: For grown-ups, and for children from about eight with a grown-up beside them. The rungs with a blade are for grown-ups and older teenagers, and the power drill rung is for grown-ups only: a child never uses a power tool. You start by finding five tools at home and writing your own safety rules, then learn safety glasses, the tape measure, the level, pliers, a spanner and a hammer, then a craft knife, drill bits and a drill, then cleaning and storing, and one real job from start to finish. It ends with teaching somebody else to carry, pass and put away tools safely. Sawing and joining wood are in the Wood ladder, and repairs are in Mending; this one is the tools themselves.

steps.test: Find five tools in your home and say what each one is for.
steps.note: Look in a drawer, a cupboard, a shed or a garage: a hammer, a screwdriver, pliers, a tape measure, a spanner, a torch, scissors. Put them together in one place while you name them. A child does this with a grown-up and leaves anything with a blade or a plug for the grown-up to move. If your home has almost none, look through a relative's or a neighbour's toolbox with them.

steps.test: Write five safety rules for tools in your home and put them where the tools are kept.
steps.note: Good rules: carry anything sharp or pointed with the point down and away from you; pass a tool handle first; never leave a tool on the floor or on a stair; nothing with a plug or a battery is used by a child; every tool goes back when the job is done. Add one of your own. A child and a grown-up can write them together, and the child can read them out.

steps.test: Find a pair of safety glasses and a pair of work gloves, and put both on to check they fit.
steps.note: Eyes are the part most easily hurt by tools: a chip from a nail, dust from a drill, a spring that jumps out. From now on, glasses go on before any hammering, cutting or drilling. Borrow a pair if you have none; ordinary glasses give a little protection while you find some, and the measuring rungs need none. Gloves protect against splinters and rough edges, but never wear gloves with a drill or anything that spins, because a glove can catch and pull your hand in.

steps.test: Measure the length and width of a table with a tape measure, twice each, and get the same numbers both times.
steps.note: Hook the metal end over one edge, pull the tape straight and flat, and read where it meets the other edge, looking straight down at it. The hook at the end is loose on purpose: it moves by its own thickness so the reading is right whether you hook it on or push it against something. If your two tries differ, measure a third time. Use centimetres or inches, whichever your tape shows. Let the tape roll back slowly with your hand on it, because its edge can cut.

steps.test: Use a spirit level to check whether a shelf and a table are level, and use it to straighten one picture frame.
steps.note: When the bubble sits exactly between the two lines, the surface is level. To check the level itself, read it, turn it end for end on the same spot, and read it again: the bubble should sit in the same place. With no spirit level, many phones have one built into their measuring app, or you can find a free one. Straighten a frame that already hangs on a hook or nail; putting up new fixings comes later.

steps.test: Bend a paper clip into a hook with a pair of pliers, then straighten it again as well as you can.
steps.note: Grip near the tip of the pliers for small bends and near the joint for strength. Keep the fingers of your other hand away from the jaws, which pinch hard. Many pliers also have a wire cutter near the joint: leave that for a grown-up, who cuts with the loose end pointing down so it cannot fly up. Already easy? Bend the clip into the first letter of your name.

steps.test: Loosen and tighten a nut with a spanner that fits it exactly, without wearing down the corners of the nut.
steps.note: A bicycle seat, a garden chair or a scooter often has one. A spanner of the right size, or an adjustable one closed up tight on the nut, grips it firmly; a loose one slips and rounds off the corners. Turn anticlockwise to loosen and clockwise to tighten, as you look at the nut, which is true for almost every nut. Pull the spanner towards you rather than pushing, so your knuckles do not hit anything if it slips. Anything that carries weight or a person goes back fully tight, and a grown-up checks it.

steps.test: Hammer a nail straight into a scrap of wood, holding the nail with a clothes peg so your fingers are clear.
steps.note: Safety glasses on. Hold the hammer near the end of the handle, not near the head. Tap gently until the nail stands up by itself, then take the peg away and hit more firmly, watching the nail head, not the hammer. A child does this with a grown-up beside them, using a short nail in soft wood. Places that sell timber will often give away an offcut if you ask.

steps.test: Pull a nail out with the claw of a hammer, with a thin scrap of wood under the hammer head to protect the surface.
steps.note: Slide the claw under the nail head, put the scrap of wood under the curve of the hammer head, and pull the handle back slowly. The scrap stops a dent and gives more lift; for a long nail, use a thicker scrap halfway out. Keep your glasses on, because a nail can spring out. Do not use a bent nail again: keep bent nails in a tin for metal recycling.

steps.test: Cut a straight line in thick card with a craft knife against a metal ruler, then put the blade away.
steps.note: This rung is for grown-ups, or a teenager with a grown-up beside them. A younger child cuts the same line in thin card with scissors instead, and that counts. Put the card on a cutting board or an old magazine, hold the ruler down with your fingers spread flat on the side away from the blade, and make two or three light cuts rather than one hard one. Slide the blade back in, or cover it, the moment you stop cutting.

steps.test: Tell a wood drill bit, a masonry drill bit and a metal drill bit apart, and say what each one is for.
steps.note: A wood bit usually has a sharp spike in the middle of its tip, to start the hole in the right place. A masonry bit, for brick, stone and concrete, has a flat tip slightly wider than the rest, often a different colour. A metal bit has a plain cone-shaped point with no spike, and can also drill wood. A child can do this rung by looking and pointing with the bits left in their case. With no bits at home, look at them in a hardware shop or in pictures online.

steps.test: Drill one hole in a scrap of wood with a power drill, wearing safety glasses and no gloves, with long hair tied back.
steps.note: This rung is for grown-ups only. A child never uses a power tool: a child can choose the right bit, hold a torch, and watch from a step back with safety glasses on. Clamp the wood or hold it firmly on a bench, hold the drill with both hands, start slowly, and take the battery out or unplug it before changing the bit. Before you ever drill a wall, remember that wires often run straight above, below and beside switches and sockets, and pipes run to taps and radiators: do not drill there, and if in doubt, ask somebody qualified.

steps.test: Clean and dry every tool you have used on this ladder, wipe the metal parts with a little oil, and put each one back in its own place.
steps.note: Wipe off dust and dirt with a dry cloth; water left on metal causes rust. A thin wipe of light machine oil keeps rust off; a drop of cooking oil will do for a while if that is all you have. Blades and bits go back in their covers or case. Give each tool one place, so a gap shows what is missing: a box with sections, a shelf, or a board with the outline of each tool drawn on it.

steps.test: Do one real job at home from start to finish: choose the tools, lay them out, do the job, and put everything back.
steps.note: Pick a job this ladder has trained you for: tighten a wobbly chair, straighten a picture, measure a space for a piece of furniture, pull an old nail from a board. Lay the tools out before you start, glasses included. A child chooses the job with a grown-up and does the parts that are safe for them. If you already do jobs like this, do one on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Put every tool back clean and in its place after every use for four weeks.
steps.note: Keep a tick on a calendar or a note on the fridge each time. The day you need a tool in a hurry, it is where it should be. A child can be the one who checks the tool box once a week. If you forget once, put it back when you notice and keep going; the count does not start again.

steps.test: Teach somebody to carry a sharp tool, pass a tool and put tools away safely, and watch them do all three.
steps.note: Show each one first, then let them do it while you watch without taking over: point down and away when carrying; handle first when passing; clean and back in its place when done. A younger brother or sister, a friend, a grandparent or somebody you live with all count, and a child can teach a grown-up. Ask them to tell you one of your safety rules back.

tracks.name: Bike mechanics
tracks.line: From reading the pressure on a tyre to teaching somebody to mend their own puncture, with your hands off.
tracks.who: From about eight with a grown-up; teens and grown-ups
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers, and for children from about eight with a grown-up beside them. You need a bike, and a borrowed one is fine. The climb starts with the tyre pressure and a check before every ride, then the saddle, the chain, taking the wheels out, a puncture found and mended at home and then away from it, the brakes, and the gears. It ends with teaching somebody to mend their own puncture while you keep your hands off. Every time the brakes or a wheel have been touched, a grown-up who knows bikes checks the brakes before anybody rides it, and a bike that fails that check is not ridden.

steps.test: Find the tyre pressure printed on the side of a bike tyre, and write it down.
steps.note: Look round the side of the tyre for small raised writing such as "40-65 PSI" or "2.8-4.5 bar": that is the range the tyre is made for. While you are there, look at the valve: a fat one like a car's, a thin one with a tiny nut on the top, or an older type with a cap and a collar. Note which it is, because the pump has to fit it.

steps.test: Pump both tyres to within the pressure range written on them.
steps.note: A pump with a gauge is best; many bike shops let you use theirs for free. For the thin valve, unscrew the tiny nut first, and screw it back after. With no gauge, pump until the tyre is firm and your thumb only just dents it, and never go over the top number on the tyre.

steps.test: Do the check before a ride: tyres firm, both brakes stopping the wheels, the chain on and oiled, and the wheels tight.
steps.note: Squeeze each brake lever and push the bike forwards: the wheel should not roll, and the lever should stop well before it touches the handlebar. Lift each end and spin the wheel: it should turn freely and not wobble, and any quick-release lever should be closed firmly. A child does this with a grown-up, who checks the brakes again. Do it before every ride from now on.

steps.test: Set the saddle height so the rider's leg is almost straight with their heel on the pedal at its lowest point.
steps.note: Loosen the saddle clamp, a lever or a bolt under the saddle, set the height, and tighten it so the saddle cannot twist. Never raise it above the line marked on the seat post. When the rider pedals normally with the ball of the foot, the knee will then be slightly bent at the bottom, which is comfortable. A child still learning may want it lower, so both feet can touch the ground.

steps.test: Clean the chain with a rag and oil it, one drop on each link while you turn the pedals backwards, then wipe off what is left on the outside.
steps.note: Hold a rag round the chain and turn the pedals backwards to wipe it. Use oil made for bike chains, borrowed if you have none; cooking oil goes sticky and holds dirt. The oil is needed inside the links, not on the outside, so wiping the outside afterwards stops grit sticking to it. Lean the bike against a wall; keep fingers away from where the chain meets the teeth.

steps.test: Lift the chain off the front ring on purpose, put it back on, and wash your hands.
steps.note: With the bike still, lift the chain off the teeth of the big front ring and let it hang. To put it back, hook it over the top teeth of the front ring and slowly turn the pedal by hand so the chain climbs back on. If there is a gear mechanism at the back, pushing it forwards gives the chain some slack. Turn the pedal, never the chain, so fingers stay clear of the teeth.

steps.test: Take the front wheel out and put it back, centred, with the brake working again, and have a grown-up check the brake.
steps.note: If the brakes grip the rim, open the small release on the brake first (on V-brakes, unhook the curved metal pipe from its holder) so the tyre fits past the pads, and close it again at the end: this is the step people forget. Undo the quick-release lever or the nuts (a spanner that fits exactly), drop the wheel out, then put it back fully into the slots and tighten. With disc brakes, do not squeeze the brake lever while the wheel is out. Spin the wheel to check it is centred, and squeeze the brake.

steps.test: Take the back wheel out and put it back, with the chain on the smallest back gear and the wheel straight in the frame, and have a grown-up check the brake.
steps.note: Change to the smallest back gear before you start, which makes it easier. Open the rim brake release, undo the lever or nuts, push the gear mechanism back and let the wheel drop out. Going back, lay the chain over the smallest gear, pull the wheel into the slots, check it sits straight, tighten, and close the brake release.

steps.test: Take the tyre off the rim with tyre levers, take the tube out, put both back and pump the tyre up.
steps.note: Let all the air out, push the tyre edges into the middle of the rim all round, then hook a tyre lever under one edge and lever it over; a second lever a hand's width along does the rest. Never use a screwdriver, which cuts tubes. Many tyres go back on by thumbs alone: start at the valve and finish opposite it. Before pumping, check all round that no tube is caught between the tyre and the rim, or it will burst.

steps.test: Find the hole in an inner tube, then find what made it in the tyre.
steps.note: Pump the tube up a little and listen and feel for the hiss, or push it through a bowl of water a bit at a time and watch for bubbles. Mark the hole with a pen. Line the tube up with the tyre to see where the hole was, and look slowly inside the tyre there for a thorn or a bit of glass; wipe with a cloth rather than bare fingers. Bike shops often have old punctured tubes to practise on for free if you ask.

steps.test: Mend a puncture with a patch kit, and check the next day that the tube still holds its air.
steps.note: Rub the area round the hole with the sandpaper in the kit, spread a thin layer of the glue wider than the patch, and wait until it looks dry, usually a few minutes. Press the patch on hard, from the middle out, for a minute. Self-adhesive patches skip the glue but still need the sanding. Pump the tube up a little, leave it overnight, and check it is still firm.

steps.test: Away from home, replace an inner tube using only what you carried, and ride home.
steps.note: Carry tyre levers, a spare tube or patches, and a pump that fits your valve, in a small bag or tied under the saddle. To practise, choose a safe spot such as a park path, let the air out on purpose, and swap the tube. Before riding home, check the wheel is tight and the brake works, and a child has a grown-up do that check.

steps.test: Look at all the brake pads on a bike and say whether each one needs replacing.
steps.note: Rim brake pads have grooves: when the grooves have worn away, the pad needs replacing. Disc brake pads are small and sit inside the brake; look through the gap with a torch, and when the pad material is thinner than the metal plate behind it, it needs replacing, though the maker's instructions give the exact limit. Check too that rim pads hit the rim squarely, not the tyre.

steps.test: Adjust a rim brake with its small barrel adjuster so the lever stops well before it touches the handlebar, and have a grown-up check it.
steps.note: The barrel adjuster is the small round part where the cable goes into the brake or the lever. Turning it anticlockwise pulls the cable tighter and brings the pads closer to the rim; clockwise lets them move away. Turn half a turn at a time, then squeeze and spin the wheel: the pads should grip firmly and not rub when you let go. Brakes that work by oil in a pipe (hydraulic) are for a bike shop or somebody experienced.

steps.test: Take the brake pads out of one rim brake and put them back lined up so they hit the rim squarely, and have a grown-up check before riding.
steps.note: Loosen the nut holding the pad, set it so the whole pad meets the rim flat and does not touch the tyre, and tighten it while holding the pad in place. If the pads are worn out, this is when new ones go in, and new pads usually cost little; putting the old ones back lined up counts for this rung. Squeeze the lever hard afterwards and check nothing has moved.

steps.test: Adjust the back gears with the barrel adjuster so the chain moves cleanly onto every gear, up and down.
steps.note: Lift the back wheel off the ground and turn the pedals while you change gear. If the chain is slow to climb to the bigger gears, turn the barrel adjuster on the gear mechanism or the shifter a quarter turn anticlockwise; if it is slow to drop to the smaller ones, turn it clockwise. Leave the two small screws marked H and L alone: they stop the chain falling off the ends. You need a borrowed bike with gears on the outside for this rung.

steps.test: Find where a noise on a bike is coming from, and fix it.
steps.note: A squeak from a dry chain wants oil; a rub on every turn of the wheel is often a brake pad touching or a wheel sitting crooked; a click with every pedal turn can be a loose pedal or a loose bottle cage. Lift the bike and turn one part at a time to narrow it down, and ask the rider when it happens: going uphill, over bumps, when braking.

steps.test: Get a bike that nobody has ridden for a long time ready to ride again, and have a grown-up check the brakes before it goes out.
steps.note: Borrow one from a relative, a neighbour or a shed. Pump the tyres and look for cracks in the rubber, which mean new tyres; clean and oil the chain; check every brake and gear; tighten the saddle, handlebars and wheels. Write a list of anything it needs that you cannot fix, such as a rusted cable, and give that list to the owner.

steps.test: Teach somebody to mend their own puncture, with your hands off the bike the whole time.
steps.note: Choose a friend, a child with their grown-up, or anybody who has never done it. Tell them each step and let them get it wrong and try again; you may point but not touch. It is done when their tube holds air and the wheel is back in, with the brake checked.

tracks.name: First aid
tracks.line: From saying the emergency call out loud to being the trained first-aider on a family day out.
tracks.who: Grown-ups, and anybody from about eight with a grown-up
tracks.about: For grown-ups, and for anybody from about eight doing it with a grown-up beside them. An app is not a first-aid course: these rungs help you remember and practise, and one of them is booking a proper hands-on course with a trainer. The climb starts with the emergency call and the first-aid kit, then the everyday injuries (cuts, bleeding, burns, nosebleeds, stings, bumps on the head), then the signs that mean call for help now, then the recovery position, choking and CPR, always practised on a cushion or a training dummy and never on a person. It ends with you as the first-aider for a family day out. The steps here follow mainstream first-aid teaching such as the Red Cross and Red Crescent; if your course or your emergency operator tells you something different, follow them.

steps.test: Say out loud, as if to the emergency operator, what you would tell them: the number you ring, where you are, what has happened, and who is hurt.
steps.note: Find out your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999) where you live; in many countries 112 also works from a mobile phone. Where you are comes first, because they can send help before they know anything else. Never ring the real number to practise.

steps.test: Next time you are out, stop and say exactly how you would tell the operator where you are.
steps.note: Away from home you may not know the address. Use a street name, a shop, a bus stop or a landmark, or open the map on your phone and read out where the blue dot is. In a park or on a path, say the entrance you came in by and roughly how far you walked.

steps.test: Find the first-aid kit at home, say what each thing in it is for, and tape a card inside the lid with your emergency number and your address.
steps.note: Take everything out and name its use: plasters for small cuts, a dressing and a bandage for bleeding, gloves, scissors, tweezers. Throw out anything past its date and write down what needs replacing. If you have no kit yet, "A home that works" has a rung for putting one together; do that first.

steps.test: Draw a small "cut" on your arm in pen and go through cleaning and covering it: hands washed, rinsed under the tap, patted dry, a plaster on.
steps.note: For a real small cut or graze: wash your hands, rinse the cut under clean running water, pat it dry with something clean, and cover it with a plaster or a clean dressing. A deep or gaping cut, one with dirt or glass stuck in it, or an animal bite needs a doctor or nurse. A child can do the pen practice on their own arm.

steps.test: With a partner, press firmly on a pretend wound on their arm with a folded clean cloth for one full minute, as you would to stop bleeding.
steps.note: Firm enough to hold the cloth still, never hard enough to hurt your partner. For real bleeding: press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or cloth and keep pressing; if blood comes through, put another pad on top and do not lift the first. For heavy bleeding, ring your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999), or get somebody else to, and keep pressing until help takes over. Wear gloves if you have them.

steps.test: Say out loud the steps for a burn, then set a timer for twenty minutes and see how long the cooling really takes.
steps.note: Cool the burn under cool running water for at least twenty minutes, straight away. Take off rings or clothing near it unless they are stuck to the skin. Then cover it loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag. No ice, butter or creams. Get medical help for a burn bigger than the person's hand, one on the face, hands, feet or private parts, or any burn on a baby or young child.

steps.test: Sit in the position for a nosebleed and hold it for one minute: sitting, leaning forward, pinching the soft part of your nose.
steps.note: Lean forward, not back, so blood does not run down the throat. Pinch the soft part just below the hard bridge of the nose and breathe through your mouth; for a real nosebleed, keep pinching for ten minutes before you check. If it is still bleeding after about half an hour, or it started after a hard knock to the head, get medical help.

steps.test: Say out loud what to do for a bee sting, and the signs of a serious allergic reaction that mean ringing for help straight away.
steps.note: If a sting is left in the skin, scrape it out sideways with a fingernail or the edge of a card, then hold something cold wrapped in a cloth on it. Ring your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999) at once if the person has swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, or feels faint. If they carry an adrenaline pen for allergies, help them use it. A sting in the mouth or throat needs medical help too.

steps.test: Write on a card, and keep it with the kit, the signs after a bump on the head that mean getting medical help.
steps.note: For a small bump: rest, and hold something cold wrapped in a cloth on it. Get medical help straight away if the person was knocked out even for a moment, is sick, is sleepy and hard to wake, is confused, has a headache that gets worse, has trouble seeing, speaking or walking, has blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears, or has a fit. Keep an eye on them for the next day or two.

steps.test: Say out loud the signs that somebody is getting too hot, and what to do while they cool down.
steps.note: Signs: headache, dizziness, feeling sick, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, cramps, being very thirsty. Move them somewhere cool, lie them down with their feet raised a little, give them sips of water, and cool their skin with water and a fan. If they are not better within half an hour, or they become confused, stop sweating while very hot, or collapse, ring your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999). The signs of getting too cold are on the "Weather and tide" ladder.

steps.test: Learn the signs of a stroke, and say them to somebody else.
steps.note: Many countries teach them as FAST: Face, one side has dropped or they cannot smile evenly; Arms, they cannot lift both and keep them there; Speech, it is slurred or muddled. Time: ring your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999) straight away and note the time it started. Some places teach two more, sudden loss of balance and sudden trouble seeing.

steps.test: With a grown-up lying on the floor pretending, go through checking for a response and for breathing.
steps.note: Kneel beside them. Ask loudly "Can you hear me? Open your eyes" and tap their shoulders gently. Then tilt their head back gently with a hand on the forehead and two fingers under the chin, and look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to ten seconds. In a real emergency, somebody rings your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999) as soon as the person does not respond.

steps.test: Roll a willing partner into the recovery position on a soft floor, and back again.
steps.note: This is for somebody who is not responding but is breathing normally. Take it slowly and gently; a course trainer will check your hands.
how: Kneel beside them. Put the arm nearest you out at a right angle, and bring their far hand across to rest against the cheek nearest you.
Bend their far knee up, keep their hand on their cheek, and pull on the knee to roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt their head back a little so the airway stays open, and keep checking their breathing until help arrives.

steps.test: Say out loud what to do if somebody has a fit, and when to ring for help.
steps.note: Move hard or sharp things away, put something soft under their head, and note the time. Do not hold them down and do not put anything in their mouth. Ring your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999) if the fit lasts more than five minutes, it is their first one, they are hurt, or they do not wake up properly after. When the shaking stops, if they are breathing, put them in the recovery position and stay with them.

steps.test: Act out the steps for a choking person on a big cushion or the back of a chair, never on a person.
steps.note: For a choking adult or child over one year old: if they can cough, tell them to keep coughing. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, lean them forward and give up to five firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If that does not clear it, give up to five pulls inwards and upwards with your fist just above the belly button. Keep repeating, and ring your emergency number (such as 112, 911 or 999) if it has not cleared. Babies under one are done differently, and a course shows how.
