Then it gets longer: three days, a week of a private promise, and at the end one chosen hard thing done on twenty-eight days out of thirty. If life is already hard right now, getting through the day counts, and this ladder will still be here later.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side

steps.test: Pick one job you have been putting off that takes under ten minutes, and do it now, all the way to the end.
steps.note: A reply to a message, a drawer sorted, a form filled in, homework handed over, a plant repotted. All the way means finished and put away. If you have no put-off jobs, do the one you least want to do today, on purpose, and count it.

steps.test: The next time something you are doing stops being fun, keep going for ten more minutes, with a timer.
steps.note: Practising an instrument, a long jigsaw, weeding, reading a hard chapter, times tables. Set the timer at the moment you want to stop. Something you must not carry on with, like anything that hurts, is not what this rung is about.

steps.test: Write one big job you have been avoiding as five small steps on paper, and do the first step today.
steps.note: For example "clear the shed": empty one shelf, sort it into keep and go, take the rubbish out, and so on. For a child: "tidy my room" becomes floor, bed, desk, clothes, bin. Each step should take less than half an hour.

steps.test: Do the other four steps of that job within the next seven days.
steps.note: One a day, or two on a free day. Tick each one off on the same paper. If a step turns out to be bigger, split it again rather than stopping.

steps.test: Do something you are a beginner at while somebody else watches.
steps.note: Juggling, a song on an instrument, a cartwheel on grass, a few words of another language, a new recipe, a game with a child who is better at it than you. Laughing at how it goes is fine. If it goes well, try the next bit that is harder.

steps.test: Go to a class, club or session where you will be one of the least skilled people, and stay to the end.
steps.note: A chess club, a choir, a dance class, a climbing wall taster, a sports session, a language evening at a library. Many clubs let you try once for free. A child goes with a grown-up, and the grown-up can join in too.

steps.test: Ask somebody to explain something you feel you should already know.
steps.note: How to check the oil in a car, what a word at work means, how the heating timer works, the way a child is taught to do long division now. Say it plainly: "I have never understood this properly, could you show me?". Say thank you and try it while they are there.

steps.test: Get something wrong in front of somebody, say "I got that wrong", and do it again.
steps.note: A sum said out loud, a card trick, a word in another language, a tune, a catch. The words matter: say it simply, without a long excuse, then try again straight away. Grown-ups doing this in front of children shows them it is safe to do.

steps.test: Choose one hard thing and do it three days running.
steps.note: Ten minutes of instrument practice, a page of a difficult book, ten press-ups, ten new words, making the bed properly, tidying for ten minutes. Something safe, in your control, and small enough to do on a busy day. The same one each day.

steps.test: On a day you feel like doing nothing, do one small thing you had planned, then rest.
steps.note: A walk round the block, the washing-up, one piece of homework, a short practice. Then rest properly. This is for an ordinary low-energy day, not for illness, grief or exhaustion; on those days, looking after yourself is the right thing to do and counts.

steps.test: Choose the harder of two options on purpose once today, and write down why.
steps.note: The stairs, not the lift; cooking, not a takeaway; walking a short distance, not a lift in the car; finishing the chapter, not picking up the phone. One line: "I took the stairs because I want to be able to climb hills with my kids."

steps.test: Do one safe but uncomfortable thing outdoors on purpose: a walk in the rain, up early for a sunrise, or the steepest street near you.
steps.note: Dress for the weather and tell somebody where you are going. Not in storms, ice or dangerous heat; in a hot climate, go at dawn and carry water. A child does this with a grown-up.

steps.test: Say yes to one chance this week that makes you nervous, and go through with it.
steps.note: Reading out loud at a group, joining a game in the park, speaking up at a meeting, inviting somebody round, trying out for a team. Nervous, not unsafe: never something you have a good reason to refuse. Tell one person afterwards how it went.

steps.test: Make yourself a promise that nobody else knows about, and keep it for seven days.
steps.note: Out of bed when the alarm goes, no phone at the table, ten minutes of practice, the bed made. Write it on a card only you will see. If a day slips, carry on the next day and add a day at the end.

steps.test: Go back to something you once gave up on and do one session of it.
steps.note: An instrument in a cupboard, a half-read book, a language, drawing, a sport. Stopping before was not a failure; starting again is part of doing hard things. Keep this session short, about fifteen minutes, so there is a second one.

steps.test: Help somebody else keep going at the moment they want to stop.
steps.note: A child stuck on homework, a friend learning to drive, a colleague on a long task. Do not lecture: say what they have already done, suggest ten more minutes, or do ten minutes alongside them. Then let them decide.

steps.test: Write down one thing that used to be hard for you and is not hard now, and what made the difference.
steps.note: It might be from this ladder or from years ago: swimming a length, a phone call, getting up early, reading a whole book. Keep the paper with the card from your seven-day promise.

steps.test: Choose one hard thing and do it on at least twenty-eight of the next thirty days.
steps.note: This is the end of the ladder. The same kind of hard thing as rung nine, perhaps a bit bigger, marked on a calendar each day. Two missed days are allowed so that one bad day does not end it; if you are ill, stop the count and pick it up again when you are well.

tracks.name: Noticing the good
tracks.line: From one good thing said out loud to a daily habit you have started at somebody else's table.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can climb it side by side, and a family can climb it together. It starts with saying one good thing about today out loud, then making it specific, then doing it three days running. Then it turns outwards: thanking the person at home whose work nobody mentions, and the people outside who are rarely thanked at all. A jar of good things for a week, a letter by post, thirty days, and reading the month back. It ends with you starting the same habit at somebody else's table. What you notice every day tends to become what you expect, so this is worth the one minute it takes.

steps.test: Say out loud one good thing that happened today, to whoever is in the room.
steps.note: Small is best: the bus was on time, the soup was good, a dog was glad to see you. At the tea table works well for a family. On your own, say it out loud anyway, or send it to one person as a message. If this is already part of your day, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Say today's good thing with one detail: what it was, when, and who was there.
steps.note: Not "it was a good day" but "at lunch Sam gave me half his chips without being asked". The detail is what makes you notice it and remember it. A child can be asked "what exactly?" until there is a detail.

steps.test: Say one good thing, with its detail, three days running.
steps.note: Same time each day helps: tea, bedtime, the drive home from school. If you miss a day, the three start again, with no fuss.

steps.test: Make today's good thing about a person, not a thing.
steps.note: Somebody who did something, said something, or was simply there: a teacher, a neighbour, a stranger who held a door, somebody at home. Say their name and what they did.

steps.test: Thank somebody at home for one job they do that nobody mentions.
steps.note: The bins, the washing, the packed lunches, the lifts, walking the dog, fixing the wifi. Name the job and say what it saves you: "Thanks for always doing the bins. I never have to think about Tuesday." Children can thank grown-ups and grown-ups can thank children.

steps.test: Thank somebody outside who is rarely thanked for what they do.
steps.note: The bin crew, the school crossing guard, the bus driver as you get off, the cleaner at the leisure centre, the person stacking shelves. Short and clear: "Thanks, you keep this place lovely." If you already do this, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Think of the hardest day you had this month, and find one good thing in it.
steps.note: Somebody who helped, something you learned, something that went right in the middle of it, or simply that it ended and you got through it. Write the one thing down or say it to somebody. This is not pretending the day was good; it is finding the good that was there.

steps.test: Keep a jar of good things for a week: one slip of paper from each person, every evening.
steps.note: Any clean jar, box or bowl and scraps of paper. Each evening, everybody writes one good thing from the day with the date and drops it in. Children who cannot write yet can draw it or say it for a grown-up to write. On your own, one slip a day is plenty. Do not read them yet.

steps.test: Write a thank-you letter by hand to somebody who helped you this year, and post it.
steps.note: A coach, a neighbour, a nurse, a colleague, a grandparent. Say what they did and what difference it made, in five or six sentences. A letter by post is kept in a way a message is not. A stamp costs money; if that is a problem, hand-deliver it or leave it where they will find it.

steps.test: Keep the jar going every day for thirty days.
steps.note: Same jar, same time, one slip each. If a day is missed, add it the next morning and carry on; the thirty is days with a slip, not days in a row.

steps.test: Empty the jar, read every slip out loud, and pick the three best.
steps.note: A family can take turns reading. Notice what kinds of things came up most often: people, food, being outside, something funny. Keep the three best somewhere you will see them, like the fridge door.

steps.test: Start the good-thing habit at a table where nobody was doing it before.
steps.note: Grandparents' Sunday dinner, a meal with friends, a club or team night, a break at work. Go first, keep it to one sentence, and then ask the person beside you. The end of the ladder is somebody else carrying on doing it after you have gone.

tracks.who: For everybody; a family can do it together

tracks.name: Fasting
tracks.line: For grown-ups. From a comfortable sixteen hours to thirty-six, done properly.
tracks.warn: Adults only past step five. Not if you are pregnant, diabetic, underweight, still growing, on medication that needs food, or have ever had trouble with eating. Children stop at step four — going without snacks is theirs; going without meals is not.

steps.test: Go sixteen hours with nothing but water, tea or black coffee, and work a normal day inside it.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until eleven the next morning. Sleep does most of it.
No milk, no sugar, no sweeteners — they end the fast in your head even when they barely do in your body.
Do it on an ordinary working day, not a quiet one.
steps.note: You have done sixteen hours before; this rung is doing it while life carries on around you. If this is already how you live, do it on purpose today and count it.

steps.test: Drink a large glass of water with a pinch of salt in it during a fast.
how: A good pinch of ordinary salt in a pint of water, drunk over an hour.
Do it at the point in the fast where you usually start feeling flat.
Costs nothing and you already have both ingredients.
steps.note: Most of what people call hunger past about eighteen hours is thirst and salt, not food. This one trick removes most of the headaches people blame fasting for.

steps.test: Sit through one wave of hunger without eating, and time how long it lasted.
how: When it arrives, look at the clock and write the time down.
Do something with your hands until it passes, then write that time down too.
Most waves are fifteen to twenty minutes.
steps.note: Hunger comes in waves and goes again whether you eat or not. Watching one arrive and leave is the single most useful thing on this ladder, because after it you stop believing hunger is an emergency.

steps.test: Go eighteen hours, water only.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until one the next day.
Water, black tea, black coffee, herbal tea. Nothing else.
Plan what you will do at the hour it gets hard — a walk is the best answer.
steps.note: Eighteen is where sixteen stops being mostly sleep and starts being a decision. The salt water from rung two matters here.

steps.test: Take a walk in the middle of a fast rather than sitting through it.
how: Twenty minutes, outside, at the hour you would normally be eating.
Notice that the hunger is quieter while you are moving.
Any weather, any route.
steps.note: Moving while fasted feels wrong and is not. A walk is the cheapest and fastest way to send a wave of hunger away, and it fills the time the meal used to take.

steps.test: Do eighteen hours on three separate days in one week.
how: Three days, with ordinary eating in between. Not consecutive.
Same edges each time so your body knows what is coming.
Write the three days down and tick them off.
steps.note: Repetition is what makes this comfortable. The third one is always much easier than the first, and it is the rung where fasting stops being an event.

steps.test: Break a fast properly: a real meal, eaten slowly, not a feast.
how: Eggs, fish, meat, vegetables, butter. Something you cooked.
Eat it slowly, and stop at comfortably full rather than stuffed.
Nothing sweet as the first thing that goes in.
steps.note: Almost everybody undoes a good fast in the twenty minutes after it. How you break it matters more than how long it was.

steps.test: Go twenty hours, water only.
how: Dinner at seven, nothing until three the next afternoon.
Salt in your water once during the day.
Keep busy through the early afternoon — that is the hard hour.
steps.note: Twenty hours means one proper meal in a day. That is how a great many people have eaten for most of history and it is not an extreme thing.

steps.test: Do a full day on one meal, and make that meal a proper one.
how: One plate, real food, enough of it. Not a small plate.
Eat it at the time that suits your day, and nothing else all day.
Eat until you are properly full — this is not about eating less at the meal.
steps.note: The mistake here is a small meal, which leaves you hungry and cross and convinced fasting does not suit you. One big honest plate is the rung.

steps.test: Go twenty-four hours, from one evening meal to the next.
how: Seven in the evening to seven the next evening.
Water, salt, black tea and coffee. A walk in the afternoon.
Plan the meal at the end before you start, so you are not deciding while hungry.
steps.note: Evening to evening is much easier than it sounds because you sleep through a third of it and eat on both days. You did one of these in Real food part two — this is doing it deliberately.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours on an ordinary working day, not a quiet one.
how: A normal day of work, people and demands, with nothing to eat in it.
Do not tell everybody. This is not a performance.
Water and salt, and a walk at lunchtime instead of lunch.
steps.note: Finding out that you can work, think and be civil to people on an empty stomach removes a fear most people carry all their lives.

steps.test: Notice what you actually feel when you say you are hungry, and write down three words for it.
how: Do it in the last few hours of a fast.
Bored? Tired? Cold? Sad? Thirsty? Out of habit? Be specific.
Three words, written down.
steps.note: A good half of what gets called hunger turns out to be something else with a name. Naming it is what lets you answer it properly instead of with food.

steps.test: Do twenty-four hours twice in one fortnight.
how: Two full days, a week apart.
Same shape both times so you can compare them.
Write down which was easier and why.
steps.note: Twice tells you whether the first one was a fluke. For nearly everybody the second is markedly easier, which is the point of doing it.

steps.test: Go twenty-eight hours.
how: Evening meal, then through the next day, then sleep, then break it in the morning.
Salt water twice across the day.
Keep the day gentle — light work, walking, nothing heavy.
steps.note: Past twenty-four hours the hunger usually gets quieter rather than louder, which surprises everybody the first time.

steps.test: Sleep through part of a fast, and notice how you sleep.
how: Go to bed inside a fast rather than breaking it at dinner.
Write down in the morning how you slept and how you woke.
Warm room, extra blanket — you will feel the cold more.
steps.note: Some people sleep beautifully fasted and some sleep badly. Knowing which you are is worth more than any general advice about it.

steps.test: Go thirty-two hours.
how: Evening meal to the following morning, through a full day and a night.
Salt and water properly. Do not skip this — it is what keeps your head clear.
Stop if you feel genuinely unwell rather than merely uncomfortable. That is not failure, that is sense.
steps.note: Knowing the difference between uncomfortable and unwell is the real skill of this ladder. Uncomfortable you can sit through; unwell you eat.

steps.test: Do something you would normally need a meal for, while fasted.
how: A long walk, a day out with the children, a hard morning's work, a hill.
Water and salt with you.
Break the fast properly afterwards with a real meal.
steps.note: This is the rung where the point of the whole thing lands: your day stops being organised around the next meal, and that is a freedom you keep.

steps.test: Plan and cook the meal that will break your longest fast, before you start it.
how: Decide it, shop for it, and have it ready in the fridge.
Meat or fish, vegetables, butter or olive oil. Nothing sweet, nothing from a packet.
Write down the time you will eat it.
steps.note: Decisions made while hungry are bad decisions. Making this one in advance is what stops thirty-six hours ending in a takeaway.

steps.test: Go thirty-six hours, and break it with the meal you planned.
how: Evening meal, a full day, a night, and then breakfast the second morning.
Salt and water throughout, a walk each day, gentle work.
Eat slowly when you break it. Stop at comfortably full.
steps.note: Thirty-six hours done properly and broken properly is the far end of this ladder. Going further than this is a thing to do with a doctor, not with an app.

steps.test: Write down your own rules for fasting, and the ones you will not break.
how: How often, how long, and on which days of your week.
The stop rules: unwell rather than uncomfortable, ill, pregnant, on new medicine.
Who you would tell before a long one.
steps.note: The ladder ends where Real food ended: with your own written way of doing it rather than somebody else's. Rules you wrote while clear-headed are the ones that hold when you are not.

tracks.about: Real food part two took you to a sixteen-hour window and one twenty-four hour fast. This ladder is the craft of going further: what to drink, how to keep working through it, what to do when you feel rough, and — the part nearly everybody gets wrong — how to break a long fast without wrecking the good of it. It costs nothing; it is the only thing in the school that saves you money while you do it. If you are pregnant, underweight, diabetic, on medication, or have any history of disordered eating, this ladder is not for you. Talk to a doctor first.

categories.name: Creating order
categories.line: Clear it, mend it, give it away, clean the forgotten places. A life flows when the place is in order.

tracks.name: The bedroom
tracks.line: From one cleared surface to a bedroom that stays right for a fortnight.
tracks.about: For everybody: a child and a grown-up can each do their own bedroom, side by side. The climb starts with the surfaces and the piles, takes out what does not belong, cleans and washes what does, and then turns the room into a habit: a bed made properly each morning, clothes ready the night before, a place for every thing. It ends with the room kept right for two weeks. The bedroom is where the day starts and ends, and a clear one makes both easier; renting or sharing counts exactly the same.

steps.test: Clear every surface in the bedroom and put back only what you used this week.
steps.note: Bedside table, chest of drawers, windowsill, the top of the wardrobe you can reach. Everything off, then back only what you picked up in the last seven days. The rest goes where it lives, or into one bag to decide about at the weekend.

steps.test: Deal with the chair or corner where clothes pile up, until there is nothing on it.
steps.note: Every piece gets one answer: the wash basket, a hanger, or folded into a drawer. Clothes worn once and fine to wear again go on a hook, not back on the chair. A child can do their own with a grown-up saying where things go.

steps.test: Empty the box or bag where things wait to be dealt with: bin it, give it, or find each thing a real home.
steps.note: Every house has one: the box, bag or corner where things wait. Tip it out. Each thing gets one of three answers: bin, give, or a real home. No fourth pile.

steps.test: Take out anything that is not for sleeping or dressing.
steps.note: The bedroom is for sleeping and dressing. The ironing pile, the exercise bike used as a rail, the work bag, the laptop charger: take one of them out and find it a better place tonight. If your bedroom is also where you study or work, give that one corner and keep it there.

steps.test: Clean the bedroom to a close look: under the bed, the skirting, the corners, the light switch.
steps.note: Look where you never look: under the bed with a torch, along the skirting, into the corners, and the light switch that everybody touches. A damp cloth does all of it. The phone torch is enough light.

steps.test: Wash the bedding and pillow covers, and wash the curtains or wipe down the blind.
steps.note: Check the label on the curtains before they go in the machine; if they cannot be washed, shake them out of a window and hoover them. A blind wipes clean with a damp cloth, one slat at a time. If you did the bedding this week already, do the curtains and count it. A grown-up takes curtains down, not a child on a chair.

steps.test: Make the bed properly once: bottom sheet tight, pillows shaken, covers straight and turned down.
steps.note: Pull the bottom sheet tight at all four corners so there are no wrinkles, shake the pillows and put them straight at the top, and pull the duvet or covers flat and even on both sides. Then fold the top back a hand width. Once, as well as you can, is the rung.

steps.test: Make the bed properly every morning for a week.
steps.note: The same way as the last rung, as soon as you get up, before the phone. It takes about two minutes. If you already make your bed every day, do it to the proper standard on purpose this week and count it.

steps.test: Put out tomorrow's clothes the night before, three nights running.
steps.note: Everything, down to the socks, on the chair you cleared on rung two, or on a hook. Check the weather forecast when you do it. A child can choose theirs and lay them out with a grown-up.

steps.test: Walk round the bedroom and choose a place for every thing that does not have one.
steps.note: The things that end up anywhere: chargers, hair things, the book you are reading, glasses, jewellery, the bag you use every day. Give each one a spot, like a hook, a small dish, or one drawer. A shoebox or a mug is a perfectly good home.

steps.test: Sit in the finished room for ten minutes with nothing in your hands and notice how it feels.
steps.note: No phone, no book. Sit on the bed or a chair and look round slowly. Notice what your eye goes to first and whether anything still bothers you; if something does, that is the next job, not today's.

steps.test: Keep the finished bedroom right for two weeks: surfaces clear, bed made, clothes put away, every thing in its place.
steps.note: Five minutes before bed puts back whatever the day moved. Check it each morning when you make the bed. If one day slips, put it right the next morning and carry on; the fortnight does not start again.

tracks.who: For everybody; each person does their own room

tracks.name: The desk
tracks.line: From one bare, wiped surface to a desk left clear at the end of every day for two weeks.
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child with a homework table and a grown-up with a work desk can do theirs side by side. The desk is wherever you sit to write, study or work, and a kitchen table counts. The climb clears the surface, the floor round it, the papers, the drawers and the cables, then sets the chair, the screen and the light so sitting there is comfortable. It ends with the desk left clear at the end of every day for two weeks. A clear desk means you sit down and start, instead of tidying first.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child and a grown-up side by side

steps.test: Clear the desk to a bare surface, wipe it, and put back only the three things you use every day.
steps.note: Everything off: the pens, the mugs, the post, the charger. Wipe it with a damp cloth until it is bare. Then choose the three things you really use every day, and only those go back; the rest waits in a box on the floor for later. A kitchen table you work or do homework at counts.

steps.test: Clear the floor under and around the desk, and put each thing where it belongs.
steps.note: Bags, shoes, boxes, the bin that needs emptying, the things that slid off the desk. Each one goes to where it lives in the house, or into the bin. Your feet should have room to rest flat under the desk when you finish.

steps.test: Gather every loose paper on and around the desk into one pile and go through it once: bin it, file it, or do what it asks today.
steps.note: Put every loose piece of paper into one pile and go through it once, from top to bottom, touching each sheet only once. It goes in the bin, into a folder, or you do what it asks today. Tear anything with a name, address or account number into small pieces before it goes in the bin. A child does the same with school sheets and old drawings, with a grown-up saying what can go.

steps.test: Set up one tray, box or folder for papers that still need doing, and put everything waiting into it.
steps.note: One place only, so nothing waiting ever sits loose on the desk again. A shoebox lid or a cereal box cut down makes a free tray. Write on it what it is for, such as "To do", and keep it at the back corner of the desk. If you already have one, empty it out, check it, and count it.

steps.test: Sort the desk drawers: one drawer for what you use at the desk, and everything else out.
steps.note: Pick one drawer to hold what you use at the desk: the scissors, a notebook, the tape, the charger you need. Everything else comes out of the drawers and goes to its real place in the house, or goes. With no drawers, a mug or a small box on the desk does the same job.

steps.test: Gather the cables on and behind the desk so none lie across the surface or the floor.
steps.note: Unplug and put away anything you have not used this month. Coil the rest loosely, hold each one with a bread-bag tie or a strip of paper, and write on it what the cable is for. Keep cables out of the way of chair wheels and feet, never under a rug, and never bent tight or squashed. A child leaves the plugs to a grown-up.

steps.test: Sit at the desk and set the chair and the screen or page to the right height.
steps.note: Sit as you normally do. Your feet should be flat on the floor, your elbows about level with the desk, and the top of any screen at about eye level. A cushion raises you, a stack of books raises a screen, and a box under the feet helps a child whose feet do not reach. Nothing needs buying.

steps.test: Move the desk, the lamp or yourself so the light falls on your work from the side, not from behind you or into your eyes.
steps.note: Sit down with a page in front of you. If your head or your hand makes a shadow on it, the light is behind you or on the wrong side; if you are squinting at a bright window, it is in front of you. Most people find light from the side away from their writing hand works best. Moving the lamp or turning the desk is free.

steps.test: Put one thing on the desk that you are glad to look at.
steps.note: Not something useful, something you like: a stone from a walk, a photograph, a child's drawing, a plant cutting in a glass of water. One thing only, so the desk stays clear. If there is already something there you love, dust it and count it.

steps.test: At the end of one work or homework session, clear the desk and leave out only the one thing you will start with next time.
steps.note: The cup back to the kitchen, papers into the tray, pens into the drawer. Then put out the single thing you will pick up first next time, such as the book open at the right page. It takes about two minutes. If you already clear up at the end, leave the one thing out on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Clear the desk at the end of every day for a week, with one thing set out for the morning.
steps.note: The same two minutes as the last rung, every evening or when you finish for the day. On a day you did not use the desk, just check it is still clear. If you miss a day, clear it the next morning and carry on; the week does not start again.

steps.test: Keep the desk clear at the end of every day for two weeks, then write down one thing that was easier.
steps.note: By now it should take a minute. At the end of the fortnight, write one line about what changed: starting work faster, finding things, not moving piles before homework. Keep the line in the tray, so you see it next time the desk starts to fill up.

tracks.name: The wardrobe
tracks.line: From one sorted drawer of socks to a wardrobe where every piece has been worn in the last four weeks or kept on purpose.
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a child sorts their own clothes with a grown-up beside them, and a grown-up does theirs. The climb goes through the clothes one kind at a time, starting with the smallest drawer, then bags what is leaving, puts back what stays so every piece can be seen, and sorts out what needs mending and what belongs to another season. It ends four weeks later with a simple test of what really gets worn. Getting dressed becomes quicker, and clothes that sat unworn go to somebody who will wear them.
tracks.who: From about eight; a child with a grown-up

steps.test: Take every sock and piece of underwear out of the drawer, and put back only what is in good condition and gets worn.
steps.note: Tip the drawer out onto the bed. Match the pairs; single socks, holes, stretched or faded things go into a pile to leave. Put back what is left, folded or rolled so you can see each one. A child does their own drawer, with a grown-up checking what still fits.

steps.test: Take out every top, shirt and jumper, and put back only what fits now and you are glad to wear.
steps.note: All of them onto the bed, including the ones on the back of the door. Pick each one up and ask two questions: does it fit now, and have I worn it this year? Two yeses go back. Anything else goes in the pile to leave, or on a chair to try on at the next rung.

steps.test: Try on everything you are unsure about, including the trousers, skirts, dresses and coats, and keep only what fits now.
steps.note: Stand in front of a mirror and try each one properly, buttoned and zipped. Keep what fits your body today and that you would wear this month, not what might fit one day. A grown-up helps a child check sleeves and length, because children grow out of things quickly.

steps.test: Take out every pair of shoes, clean the ones that stay, and put aside any that hurt or have not been worn in a year.
steps.note: Line them up on some newspaper. A pair that gives you sore feet, or that has sat unworn for a year, goes in the pile to leave. Wipe the rest with a damp cloth and put them back in pairs. If your shoes are all already clean and worn, sort them anyway and count it.

steps.test: Bag the clothes that are leaving: one bag to give away, and the worn-out ones kept apart.
steps.note: Clean, wearable clothes go in one bag for a charity shop, a clothes bank, a younger cousin or a friend the same size. Clothes that are torn or worn thin go in a separate bag: many places have a clothes recycling bank, or cut them up into cleaning cloths. Tie the bags and put them by the front door to go out this week.

steps.test: Put back everything that stays so you can see every piece at once.
steps.note: Hang things of the same kind together: tops with tops, trousers with trousers. In drawers, fold each piece into a small rectangle and stand it on its edge, like files in a box, so you see every one when you open the drawer. Nothing hidden under anything else.

steps.test: Check every kept piece for a missing button, a loose hem or a broken zip, and put those in one bag to mend.
steps.note: Look at buttons, hems, seams under the arms and zips. Put anything that needs work into one bag and write on it the date you will mend them by, within two weeks. The Mending ladder shows how to do zips and patches; buttons need only a needle and thread.

steps.test: Pack the clothes for the other season away somewhere else entirely.
steps.note: Thick jumpers and coats in the warm months, light clothes in the cold months. Fold them into a bag, a box or a suitcase and put it under the bed or on a shelf you can reach from the floor. Where the weather is much the same all year, put away the clothes you only wear for rare occasions instead. What is left is only what you can wear this month.

steps.test: Work out what you are really missing, and write the list.
steps.note: Look at what you wear every week and ask what would make mornings easier. A plain jumper that goes with everything, a pair of shoes that do not hurt. Write the list; buying is not today, knowing is. Many things on it can come from a friend, a family member or a clothes swap for free.

steps.test: Wash, dry and put away one whole load of washing on the same day, from the basket back into the wardrobe.
steps.note: The wardrobe stays sorted only if clean clothes reach it, instead of sitting in a pile. Fold or hang each piece as soon as it is dry, and put it back in its place from rung six. A child can match socks and put their own clothes away. If this is already how you do washing, do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: Turn every hanger in the wardrobe back to front, and turn each one round the right way when you wear what is on it.
steps.note: Turn the hook so it faces the other way. After you wear something and put it back, hang it the normal way round. For folded clothes, keep what you have worn at the front of the drawer. Out-of-season clothes are not part of this test.

steps.test: Four weeks after turning the hangers, take out everything still back to front and decide about each piece.
steps.note: Whatever is still on a back-to-front hanger has not been worn for a month. For each one, either choose to keep it for a reason you can say out loud, such as a wedding outfit, or put it in a bag to give away. The wardrobe that is left holds clothes you wear.

tracks.name: Broken things
tracks.line: From a written list of every broken thing to a broken-things page cleared every week for two months.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers; a child from about ten can walk the house and help with the list, with a grown-up for anything electrical or sharp. This ladder is about deciding, not repair skills (the Mending ladder teaches those). It starts with a list of every broken and half-working thing in the house, makes the dangerous ones safe, gives each thing an answer (fix, repair shop, replace or let go) and works through them until the list is empty. It ends with looking after things before they break and a page for broken things cleared every week for two months. A house where things work is calmer, and so is the person who lives in it.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from ten with a grown-up

steps.test: Walk the whole house with a notebook and list every broken or half-working thing.
steps.note: Room by room with a pen: the dripping tap, the door that sticks, the lamp with a dead bulb, the drawer that jams, the phone with a cracked screen. Add the things that only half work, like the remote you have to press twice. Just the list tonight. Seeing it all written down is the job.

steps.test: Circle anything on the list that could hurt somebody, stop using it, and put it out of reach today.
steps.note: A frayed or melted cable, a cracked plug, a heater or charger that smells hot, a chipped glass, a loose stair rod, a wobbly chair. Unplug electrical things at the wall and stick a note on them saying "Do not use". Anything to do with gas or the wiring in the walls is for a qualified person, never a home fix. A child tells a grown-up instead of touching it.

steps.test: Beside every thing on the list, write one word: fix, shop, replace, or go.
steps.note: "Fix" means you can do it at home. "Shop" means somebody else could repair it for less than a new one. "Replace" means it is worn out but you still need one, and "go" means you can live without it. Decide quickly; you can change a word later.

steps.test: Fix the quickest thing marked "fix", today.
steps.note: Pick the one that takes under ten minutes: a new bulb (switched off and cool first), fresh batteries, a loose screw on a cupboard handle. Do it now, and cross it off the list. If you have already fixed the easy ones, pick the next quickest and count it.

steps.test: Let one thing marked "go" leave the house the right way.
steps.note: Most broken things can go in the ordinary bin, but electrical things, batteries and light bulbs should not. Your local council lists where to take them, and many shops that sell electrical things take old ones back. Cross it off when it has left the house, not when it is bagged.

steps.test: For one thing marked "shop", find out where it could be repaired and roughly what it would cost.
steps.note: First look for a receipt or email: it may still be under guarantee and be repaired for free. Then search for a shoe repairer, a phone or bike repair shop, the maker's own repair service, or a repair café, where volunteers fix things for free. Ask on the phone or by message what they think it would cost. Write the place and the cost beside it on the list.

steps.test: Take that thing to be repaired, or send it off.
steps.note: Take the receipt if you found one, and the charger or any parts that go with it. Ask when it will be ready and write it on the list. If the repair would cost more than it is worth, change its word to "replace" or "go" and count the rung.

steps.test: For one thing marked "replace", look for a second-hand or free one before buying new.
steps.note: Ask family and friends first; somebody often has a spare kettle, lamp or bike light in a cupboard. Then look at free-giving groups and second-hand shops online or nearby. Buying new is fine when there is no other way, but look first. When the new one arrives, the broken one leaves the house the right way.

steps.test: Find the instructions for one thing on your list by searching its model number, and read what they say about its fault.
steps.note: The model number is on a small printed label, often on the back or underneath. Search it with the word "manual", and most makers' instructions come up for free. Look for the part called "troubleshooting" or "problems". Sometimes the fix is a reset button or a blocked filter.

steps.test: Fix something you have walked past for a year.
steps.note: Every home has one thing everybody has stepped round for a year: the loose handle, the wobbly chair, the cupboard door on one hinge. Today, fix that one. A free video search for the exact problem, with the make or model if it has one, usually shows how. If it turns out to need a person with a trade, book them today and count it.

steps.test: Let go of one thing you have been keeping "to fix one day" for more than a year.
steps.note: The radio in the cupboard, the chair in the shed, the watch in the drawer. If a year has passed and nobody has fixed it, give it a real answer now. It goes, the right way, or it goes to a repair shop this week. Keeping it for another year is not one of the answers.

steps.test: Get the list down to nothing: every thing fixed, at a repair shop, replaced, or gone.
steps.note: Do one thing a day, or a few at the weekend, until every line is crossed off. Anything waiting for a repair shop or a delivery counts as done once it is arranged. Tick the date at the bottom when the last line goes.

steps.test: Pick one thing that broke because it was never looked after, and do the looking-after job on another thing like it.
steps.note: A vacuum cleaner that stopped because the filter was never cleaned: clean the filter on the one you have now. A bike chain that rusted: oil the chain on the other bike. A knife that went blunt: sharpen the others. Unplug anything electrical first.

steps.test: Write a short list of the jobs that stop things in your home breaking, and how often each one needs doing.
steps.note: Five to ten lines is plenty. For example: clean the vacuum cleaner filter every month, tighten loose handles every few months, oil the bike chain every month, check the tyres on the bike or car. The instructions you found earlier often say how often. Keep the list with the broken-things page.

steps.test: Keep one page for broken things, and clear it every week for two months, doing one job from your list each week too.
steps.note: Anybody in the house can write on the page when something breaks. Once a week, at the same time, give each new line its word and do what it says, plus one job from the looking-after list. If a week slips, do it the next day and carry on; the two months do not start again.

tracks.name: Giving away
tracks.line: From one bag by the front door to a giving bag kept by the door, and emptied when full, for eight weeks.
tracks.about: For everybody from about eight: a family can do it together, each person deciding about their own things. It starts with one bag of things nobody has used in a year and getting it out of the house the same day. Then it goes room by room: the kitchen, the books and games, the bathroom, the towels and sheets, the cupboard everybody avoids. The later rungs are the harder ones: a good thing given to somebody who will use it more, things kept only because they cost a lot or "just in case", and one thing sold. It ends with a giving bag that lives by the front door for eight weeks. Less to look after at home, and useful things in the hands of people who will use them.
tracks.who: From about eight; a family can do it together

steps.test: Fill one bag with things nobody has used in a year, and put it by the front door.
steps.note: Any bag. Walk the house and fill it with things you have not used in a year: the spare mugs, the gadget still in its box, the clothes that have not fitted for a year. Only your own things, or things everybody in the house agrees about. Tie it and put it by the front door.

steps.test: Take the bag to a charity shop, a friend, or somebody from a free-giving group the same day.
steps.note: A charity shop or second-hand shop that raises money for a good cause, a school, a place of worship's collection, or a friend who wants something in it. Online free-giving groups let people collect from your doorstep; a grown-up arranges that and hands it over at the door. Check what a place accepts before you go. Out of the house today is the rung.

steps.test: Go through the kitchen cupboards and fill one bag to give away.
steps.note: Open every kitchen cupboard. The third spatula, the mugs nobody picks, the machine used twice, the extra lunch boxes without lids. Unopened food that is still in date can go to a food bank. Anything past its date goes in the bin, not the giving bag.

steps.test: Go through the books, games, toys and hobby things, and pass on the ones you have finished with.
steps.note: Books you will not read again, board games nobody asks for, toys a child has grown out of, the kit from a hobby you have stopped. A child chooses which of their own toys go; nobody gives a child's things away for them. Check games have all their pieces. A friend, a school, a library or a charity shop are all good homes.

steps.test: Clear the bathroom cupboard and the medicine box.
steps.note: Take everything out. Half-used bottles you do not like go in the bin, and unopened soaps and toiletries can go to a food bank or a shelter. A grown-up checks the dates on every medicine: out-of-date or unwanted medicines go back to a pharmacy, never in the bin or down the sink. Put what stays back out of reach of children.

steps.test: Go through the towels, sheets and blankets, and keep only what gets used.
steps.note: Two towels and two sets of sheets per bed is plenty for most homes. Clean spares in good condition can go to a charity shop. Old, worn towels and blankets are often welcome at animal shelters: ask yours first. If your cupboard is already down to what gets used, check it and count it.

steps.test: Clear the cupboard, shed or garage corner everybody avoids, keeping to what you can reach from the floor.
steps.note: Pick one corner or one shelf and take everything out into the light. Heavy things are a job for two people, and nobody climbs up for the top shelf. Old paint and garden or car chemicals do not go in the bin or down a drain; your local council says where to take them. Whatever is left goes back in with space around it.

steps.test: Give away one thing that is good and that you like, to somebody who will use it more.
steps.note: Not the thing you do not want. Something good that you like and hardly use: a book you loved, a good coat, a tool, a game. Pick the person who will use it more and send them a message to say it is theirs. Then hand it over.

steps.test: Ask each person in the house to fill one bag of their own things too.
steps.note: Ask, do not tell, and say what you have given already. Each person decides about their own things, and nobody sorts somebody else's bag. Offer to take the bags out for them. If you live alone, ask a friend or family member if they want to do a bag the same week.

steps.test: Let go of one thing you have kept only because it cost a lot.
steps.note: The expensive coat that never felt right, the exercise machine used as a shelf, the camera kept in its box. The money was spent the day you bought it; keeping the thing does not bring it back. Give it to somebody who will use it, or sell it at the next rung.

steps.test: Let go of one thing you keep "just in case" that you could easily borrow or get again.
steps.note: The second set of kitchen scales, the pile of spare cables, the suitcase you use once every few years. Ask: if I needed this, could I borrow one from a friend, or get one again easily? If yes, it can go. Write down who you would borrow it from.

steps.test: Sell one thing worth selling, instead of keeping it.
steps.note: A second-hand selling site or app, a notice board, or a friend who wants it. Take a clear photograph in daylight and write two honest lines about it, including any faults. When somebody comes to collect, a grown-up hands it over at the door or in a busy public place, and never shares bank passwords or codes. A young person sells only with a grown-up doing the arranging.

steps.test: A month after the first bag, write down anything you have missed from all the bags.
steps.note: Think back through every bag and every room. Write down each thing you have wanted since it left, and what you did instead: borrowed it, did without, or got one again. For most people the list is short or empty, and that is useful to know for the next rung.

steps.test: Keep a giving bag by the front door for eight weeks, and take it out each time it is full.
steps.note: Whenever anybody in the house finds something that is not used, it goes in the bag straight away. When the bag is full, it goes out that week, and a new empty bag takes its place. Count the bags at the end of the eight weeks.

tracks.name: The phone and the inbox
tracks.line: From deleting the apps you never open to a ten-minute phone and inbox tidy every week for two months.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and anybody from about twelve with their own phone or email. It starts with the quick jobs on the phone itself: apps you never open, notifications that are not people, the home screen, and the apps that take the most time. Then the inbox and photographs, then the safety jobs: a backup of the photographs that matter, a forgotten subscription, old sign-ins and two-step sign-in. It ends with a short weekly tidy for two months. A phone with less on it asks for less of your attention, and the things that matter are safe.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and anybody from twelve with a phone

steps.test: Delete every app you have not opened in a month.
steps.note: Go through your apps page by page. If you cannot remember opening it in the last month, delete it. An app you paid for can usually be downloaded again for no cost from the same account. Many phones can show apps by last use in the settings.

steps.test: Turn off every notification that is not a person talking to you.
steps.note: Open settings, then notifications, and go down the list. Messages and calls from people stay on. Shops, games, news and anything else that buzzes you: off. You can still open the app whenever you choose.

steps.test: Clear the home screen to one page of the apps you use every day.
steps.note: Keep only the apps you use every day on the first page, eight or so. Everything else goes onto the second page or into one folder. The first page is what you see every time you pick the phone up, so make it only what you need.

steps.test: Move the two apps that take up most of your time off the first page and into a folder on the last page.
steps.note: Most phones show which apps you spend the most time in, under screen time or digital wellbeing in the settings. Take the top two off the first page. You can still open them; it just takes a moment longer, and that moment is the point.

steps.test: Delete the screenshots and extra copies of photographs from the last month.
steps.note: Open your photographs and scroll back one month. Delete the screenshots you no longer need, the blurry ones, and all but the best of the near-identical shots. Many phones have a screenshots album that makes this quick. Check the recently deleted album too, and empty it.

steps.test: Unsubscribe from twenty emails you never read.
steps.note: Open your email and search for the word unsubscribe. For every newsletter or shop email you never read, open one and press the unsubscribe link at the bottom. Only use the link in emails from companies you know you signed up with. Count to twenty.

steps.test: Get the inbox to empty once: every email archived, deleted, or dealt with.
how: Search or sort your email by date, oldest first.
Select everything older than a month that needs nothing from you, and archive it.
Go through the rest one at a time: reply, delete, or archive.
steps.note: Start with the oldest. Anything older than a month that needs nothing from you: select it and archive it all at once, which keeps it searchable. Then go through what is left, one email at a time: reply, delete, or archive. The goal is an empty inbox once, tonight.

steps.test: Back up the photographs you would be most sorry to lose.
steps.note: Children growing up, family occasions, the people who are gone. Turn on your phone's photo backup (most come with some free space), or copy them onto a computer or a memory stick you already own. Two copies in two different places is safer than one.

steps.test: Sort one year of photographs, one month at a time, keeping the best of each set of near-copies.
steps.note: One month a sitting takes about ten minutes, so a year is a couple of weeks of short sittings. Keep the best of each set of near-identical shots and delete the rest. Leave any photograph of a person who has died until you feel ready; nothing has to go today.

steps.test: Find one subscription you had forgotten about, and cancel it.
steps.note: Look through a month of your bank statement, or the subscriptions list in your phone settings. Find the one you forgot about: an app, a channel, a free trial about to start charging. Cancel it today. If somebody else pays for your subscriptions, look through the list with them.

steps.test: Check where your main email account is still signed in, and sign out of what you do not use.
steps.note: Open your main email account's security settings. It lists the devices and apps still signed in. Sign out of old phones, old computers, and apps you no longer use. If you see a device you do not recognise, sign it out and change your password.

steps.test: Turn on two-step sign-in for your main email account.
steps.note: It is in the same security settings. After your password, the account also asks for a code from your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough. Never give that code to anybody who asks for it, by phone, message or email, whoever they say they are. If it is already on, check the phone number on it is still yours and count it.

steps.test: Get the inbox back to empty by the end of each day for a week.
steps.note: Five minutes in the evening: reply, delete, or archive each email that came in. If something needs longer, archive it and write it on your list for tomorrow instead of leaving it in the inbox. If one evening slips, catch up the next day and carry on.

steps.test: Do a ten-minute phone and inbox tidy once a week for two months.
how: Delete apps you have not opened, and turn off any new notifications that are not people.
Delete the week's screenshots and extra copies.
Unsubscribe from anything new you did not read, then empty the inbox.
steps.note: Same day each week, with a timer. New apps you have not opened, new notifications that are not people, the week's screenshots, any new emails to unsubscribe from, and the inbox back to empty. Stop when the ten minutes are up.

tracks.name: The forgotten places
tracks.line: From every light switch in the house wiped to one forgotten place cleaned every week for two months.
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers; a child from about ten can do most rungs with a grown-up nearby, and the oven and anything electrical are for grown-ups. These are the places ordinary cleaning misses: behind, under, on top of and inside. It starts with the things everybody touches and nobody wipes, then the windows and blinds, under the sink, the fridge, the tops and edges of a room, under the furniture, the front door, the kettle and filters, and the oven. It ends with a list of your own forgotten places and one done every week for two months. Every rung uses warm water, washing-up liquid and ordinary cloths; nobody stands on anything, and cleaning products are never mixed.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; from ten with a grown-up

steps.test: Wipe every light switch, door handle and stair rail in the house.
steps.note: A cloth in warm water with a drop of washing-up liquid, wrung out well so it is only damp. Go room by room: the switches, both sides of every door handle, the cupboard handles, the stair rail. Keep water away from the inside of light switches and sockets.

steps.test: Wipe the blinds slat by slat, and the curtain rail if you can reach it from the floor.
steps.note: Close the blinds and wipe each slat with a damp cloth, or a sock over your hand. Then run a cloth along the top of the curtain rail, where the dust has been sitting for months. For a rail you cannot reach standing on the floor, tie a cloth over the head of a broom; never stand on a chair.

steps.test: Clean the windows in one room, inside and out.
steps.note: Warm water with a drop of washing-up liquid, a cloth, and a dry tea towel or newspaper to finish. Inside first, then outside only where you can reach from the ground. Never lean out of an upstairs window or climb up to reach. Pick a dry day that is not freezing.

steps.test: Empty and clean the cupboard under the kitchen sink, then wash the kitchen bin inside and out.
steps.note: Take everything out. Wipe the floor of the cupboard, bin what is empty or dried up, and put back only what you use. Never mix two cleaning products, because some, such as bleach, give off dangerous fumes when mixed; keep them all where children cannot get to them. Then wash the bin itself with warm soapy water and dry it.

steps.test: Empty and wipe the fridge shelf by shelf, and bin what is past its date.
steps.note: Take everything out of one shelf at a time. Check dates, bin what is past, wipe the shelf, and put back what is good. Do the door shelves last. Warm water and a spoonful of bicarbonate of soda cleans it well, if you have some; plain soapy water works too.

steps.test: In one room, dust the top of the cupboards, the light shade and the skirting all the way round, from the floor.
steps.note: One room. Stand on the floor, not on a chair or a step: for high places, use a long-handled duster or a damp cloth over the head of a broom. Dust the light shade with the light switched off and cool. Then go all the way round the skirting boards with a damp cloth.

steps.test: Move the furniture in one room and clean what was under and behind it.
steps.note: The sofa, the armchair, the small table, the television stand. Lift the sofa cushions too. Anything heavy is a job for two people: slide it on a folded towel rather than lifting it alone. Switch off and unplug electrical things before moving them.

steps.test: Clean the front door, the handle and the doorstep.
steps.note: The front door is the first thing you touch coming home. Wipe the door, polish the handle, the letterbox or the doorbell, and sweep the step. In a flat, do your own door and the bit of floor outside it. A bucket of warm soapy water and a cloth is everything.

steps.test: Descale, empty or clean the filter on one thing that needs it.
steps.note: The kettle with white scale inside, the cooker hood filter, the shower head, the vacuum cleaner filter. Pick one, and unplug or switch it off first. For a kettle: half water, half white vinegar, boil, leave an hour, rinse well and boil fresh water twice before using it. Never add any other cleaner to vinegar.

steps.test: Clean the oven, or the microwave if you have no oven.
how: Oven off and cold; take out the shelves and soak them in hot soapy water.
Spread bicarbonate paste inside, avoiding the heating parts, and leave it overnight.
Wipe it all off with a damp cloth, rinsing the cloth often, then put the shelves back.
steps.note: Oven off and completely cold. Mix bicarbonate of soda with a little water into a paste, spread it inside away from the heating parts, leave it overnight, then wipe it off with a damp cloth. For a microwave, heat a bowl of water with a slice of lemon for a few minutes and wipe the inside. A grown-up does the oven; no shop oven cleaner is needed.

steps.test: Wash the things that clean other things: the washing-up bowl, the dish rack, the cutlery tray and the toothbrush holder.
steps.note: These get wet every day and almost never get washed themselves. Hot soapy water and an old toothbrush for the corners. Leave each one to dry fully before it goes back. Add the soap dish and the nail brush if you have them.

steps.test: Clean the one place in the house nobody has looked at in years, if you can reach it from the floor.
steps.note: Behind the sofa, the back of the cupboard under the stairs, the drawer under the oven, the gap beside the fridge. Pick the one place nobody in the house has looked at in years. Take everything out, clean it, and put back only what belongs there. Twenty minutes, and it is done.

steps.test: Write a list of the forgotten places in your home, with how often each one needs doing.
steps.note: Go through the rungs you have done and add anything else you noticed: the bath panel, the rubber seal inside the washing machine door, the car mats if you have a car. Beside each one write weekly, monthly or twice a year. Aim for about ten places, so there is one for each week and a few to spare.

steps.test: Clean one forgotten place from your list every week for two months.
steps.note: Pick the same day each week and do the next place on the list, about twenty minutes. Tick it and write the date. If a week slips, do it the next day and carry on; the two months do not start again.

tracks.name: Keeping it
tracks.line: From a home for the five things that never get put away to a place that stays right for three months.
tracks.who: Grown-ups and teenagers; children join the evening round
tracks.about: For grown-ups and teenagers who run a home, whether you own it, rent it or share it; children can join in with the evening round. This ladder is not about cleaning or clearing out: it is about the small systems that stop the mess coming back once a place is right. It starts with a home for the five things that never get put away, then builds an evening round, a weekly round, one in and one out, and a way of dealing with post the day it comes. It ends with the whole household keeping the place right for three months, with both rounds running and no big clear-out needed.

steps.test: Choose a home for the five things in your house that never get put away.
steps.note: Keys, glasses, chargers, the post, shoes: the things that always end up on the table. Walk the house and choose one spot for each, close to where you use it. A bowl by the door for keys counts, and so does a shoebox for chargers.

steps.test: Put each of those five things back in its home every time you finish with it, for three days.
steps.note: Every time, not just at bedtime. Keep a tally on a scrap of paper by the door if it helps. If you already do this with all five, do it on purpose for three days and count it.

steps.test: Move the home of any of the five that kept ending up somewhere else, to where it actually lands.
steps.note: If the keys went on the kitchen counter all three days, their home belongs on the kitchen counter, not by the door. A home only works if it is where your hand already goes. If all five stayed put, check them once more and count it.

steps.test: Choose three spots to put right every evening, and do it once, timing how long it takes.
steps.note: Pick the three that spoil the room most when they are covered: the kitchen table, the counter by the kettle, the sofa. Tie it to something you already do every evening, like after the washing up or before you brush your teeth. Most people find it takes under ten minutes.

steps.test: Put those three spots right every evening for seven evenings in a row.
steps.note: Same three spots, same moment in the evening. If you missed a night, start the count again. If you already did a week of tidy nights on "A home that works", this is the shorter version tied to a fixed moment; do it on purpose and count it.

steps.test: For one whole day, put everything away as soon as you finish with it, and count the times you nearly put something down to do later.
steps.note: The cup goes to the sink, not the side table; the coat goes on the hook, not the chair. Make a mark on a piece of paper each time you catch yourself about to leave something. The count is the point: it shows where the evening round comes from.

steps.test: For one week, bring nothing new into the home without one thing of the same kind going out.
steps.note: A new mug in, an old mug out to give away; a new jumper in, an old one out. Food and everyday things that get used up do not count. Buying nothing new for the week counts too.

steps.test: Write a list for a half-hour weekly round that puts the whole place right, and do it once.
steps.note: Choose a day that suits your week. A good list: every surface cleared, bags and coat pockets emptied, the fridge checked, the washing started, the evening spots done. Set a timer for thirty minutes and stop when it rings, even if the list is not finished.
how: Choose the day and the time.
Write the list, no more than eight things.
Set a timer for thirty minutes and work down the list.

steps.test: For two weeks, deal with every letter and piece of paper on the day it arrives.
steps.note: Open it where it comes in. It goes one of three ways: do it, keep it in one folder, or recycle it. School letters and receipts count. This is the daily habit; a big pile that has built up is a one-off job on "A home that works".

steps.test: Walk the whole home slowly, find the spot where things have started to pile up again, and put the worst one right today.
steps.note: Walk every room the way a visitor would see it. Where are the piles back? The chair in the bedroom, the bottom of the stairs, the end of the kitchen counter. Pick the worst one and put it right today.

steps.test: Find the one spot that always goes wrong, and give it a new job.
steps.note: Every home has a spot that always goes wrong: the hall table, the end of the kitchen counter. Watch what lands there. Then give it a new job: a hook for bags, a basket for post, or nothing on it at all.

steps.test: Catch a pile three times in one week, when it is only two things, and put both away.
steps.note: Two things on a chair is the start of a pile. When you see two, put both away there and then, and make a mark for it. Three marks by the end of the week is the rung.

steps.test: Keep one in, one out going for a whole month.
steps.note: The same rule as the week, held for four. Keep a short list on your phone of what came in and what went out. By the end, you will notice you think twice before bringing things home.

steps.test: Do the weekly round four weeks running.
steps.note: Same day each week if you can. Change the list after the first two weeks if something on it never needs doing. If one week is missed, do it the next day and carry on.

steps.test: Agree with everybody you live with on one shared surface that stays clear, and keep it clear for a week.
steps.note: The kitchen table and the hall shelf are good choices. Ask, do not tell: "Can we keep the table clear so we can all eat at it?" Children can be in charge of checking it each evening. If you live alone, choose the surface a visitor sees first and tell a friend you are keeping it clear.

steps.test: Give everybody in the home one small evening job that is theirs, and keep it going for two weeks.
steps.note: Shoes into the rack, cushions on the sofa, the table wiped, the dishwasher emptied. Choose jobs that suit each person; a child of four can put the shoes away. Thank people for doing theirs. If you live alone, give yourself one job at a second moment in the day, like a morning one, and count it.

steps.test: Leave every room as you found it, or better, every time you leave it, for a week.
steps.note: Before you leave a room, look back from the door and take one thing with you if it does not belong. It adds a few seconds each time. This is what makes the evening round shorter.

steps.test: After a week when things slipped, do a weekly round and start the evening round again on the same day.
steps.note: Visitors, being ill, a trip away or a busy week all break the habit, and that is normal. The rung is starting again on one day, not waiting for next week. If nothing has slipped yet, do it after your next busy weekend and count it then.

steps.test: Keep the evening round and the weekly round going for a month, and write down the one change that made the most difference.
steps.note: Tick each evening and each week on a calendar. At the end, write one sentence: "The bowl by the door made the most difference", or "the jobs for the children did". That sentence is what you tell the next person who asks how you keep the place right.

steps.test: Keep the whole home in a state you are glad to walk into for three months, with both rounds running.
steps.note: Evening round, weekly round, one in and one out, the post dealt with each day. A slipped day is put right the next morning and the three months carry on. At the end there should be nothing for a big clear-out, because nothing has built up.

tracks.name: Your own things
tracks.line: From four, beside you. Shoes, cover, clothes, books, and one box put right.

steps.test: Put your shoes side by side by the door, the same way round.
Hang your coat up on a hook.
Pull the cover up straight on your bed when you get out of it.
Put your clothes in the wash basket at bedtime, without being asked.
Put the books back on the shelf the right way up.
Put the lids back on the pens and the tops back on the tubs.
Empty one box of toys onto the floor and put every single one back in.
Find a home for one thing that never had one.
Put away what you were playing with before the next thing comes out.
Do that for a whole afternoon.
Tidy your room with somebody, and stay until it is finished.
Do all of it one whole day without anybody reminding you.

journey.name: Easy wins
journey.line: Every one of these is a decision rather than a skill. Minutes each, nothing to buy, nothing to learn first. Most people are surprised they had never done them.

journey.name: Courage, worth and asking
journey.line: Deliberately early. Once you can ask for things, walk into anywhere and hear no without flinching, a great many things that looked like they cost money turn out not to. This stage quietly changes what everything after it is worth.

quick.test: Slide your back down a wall until your knees are bent at a right angle, and hold it for thirty seconds.
quick.note: Feet a little in front of you and hip-width apart, knees over your ankles. If a right angle is too deep, hold it higher up the wall and go lower another day. Stop if anything hurts. Seated version: sit tall on the front edge of a chair and press both feet hard into the floor for thirty seconds.

quick.test: Rise up onto your toes and lower yourself slowly, fifteen times, with one hand resting on the back of a chair.
quick.note: Take two counts to go up and three counts to come down. Keep your knees straight but not locked. Stop if anything hurts. Seated version: sit with feet flat and lift both heels as high as they go, fifteen times.

quick.test: Stand on one foot for thirty seconds with your eyes shut, then do the same on the other foot.
quick.note: Stand beside a table or a wall so you can put a hand out if you wobble. If thirty seconds is too long, start with ten and count how far you get. Stop if anything hurts. If standing is not possible, sit and lift one foot just off the floor for thirty seconds instead.

quick.test: Turn your head slowly to look over your left shoulder, then over your right, five times each side.
quick.note: Move slowly and only as far as is comfortable, with your shoulders staying still. Breathe out as you turn. Stop if anything hurts. This works just as well sitting at a table.

quick.test: Roll both shoulders slowly backwards ten times, then forwards ten times.
quick.note: Make each circle as big as you can: up to your ears, back, down, and round. Keep your arms loose by your sides. Stop if anything hurts. You can do this sitting down, and if you already do it at your desk, doing it now on purpose counts.

quick.test: Stand for one minute with your heels, your back and the back of your head all touching a wall.
quick.note: Tuck your chin in slightly so your head can reach the wall without tipping up. Let your arms hang and breathe normally. Stop if anything hurts. When you step away, try to keep that same tall shape for the next few steps.

quick.test: Stand up from a chair and sit back down ten times without using your hands.
quick.note: Cross your arms over your chest, feet flat and a little apart. Sit down slowly rather than dropping. Stop if anything hurts. If it is hard without hands, use one hand on your knee and count how many you manage.

quick.test: Walk ten steps in a straight line, placing each heel right up against the toes of the other foot.
quick.note: Use the edge of a rug or a line between floorboards as your guide. Look ahead, not down at your feet, and hold your arms out to the side. Stop if anything hurts. Walk beside a wall so you can touch it if you need to.

quick.test: Raise your arms slowly above your head as you breathe in, and lower them as you breathe out, eight times.
quick.note: Breathe in through your nose for a count of four while the arms go up, and out for a count of six while they come down. Let the arms follow the breath, not the other way round. Stop if anything hurts. Sitting on a chair works exactly the same.

quick.test: Stretch the back of each lower leg against a wall for thirty seconds a side.
quick.note: Hands on the wall, one foot forward with the knee bent, the other leg straight behind with the heel pressed flat to the floor. Lean in until you feel a gentle stretch, not pain. Stop if anything hurts. Seated version: sit with one leg straight out, heel on the floor, and pull your toes back towards you.

quick.test: Stand in a doorway with your forearms on the frame at shoulder height and lean gently forward for thirty seconds.
quick.note: Step one foot through the door and let your weight move slowly onto it until you feel the front of your chest open. Keep your head up and breathe slowly. Stop if anything hurts. Without a doorway: clasp your hands behind your back and lift them a little away from you.

quick.test: March on the spot for two minutes, lifting your knees as high as your hips.
quick.note: Swing your arms as you go, right arm with left knee. Put on one song and march until it is two minutes in. Stop if anything hurts. Seated version: sit near the front of a chair and lift your knees in turn, arms swinging.

quick.test: Lie on your back with your knees bent, and lift your hips until you make a straight line from knees to shoulders, ten times.
quick.note: Feet flat and hip-width apart, arms by your sides with palms down. Hold each lift for two seconds at the top, then lower slowly. Stop if anything hurts. A rug or a folded towel under your back is plenty.

quick.test: On your hands and knees, stretch your right arm forward and your left leg back, hold for five seconds, then swap sides, six times each.
quick.note: Keep your back flat enough that a cup could sit on it without sliding. Look at the floor, not ahead. Stop if anything hurts. Seated version: sit tall and lift your right arm and left knee together, then swap.

quick.test: Sit on a chair, lift one foot, and draw ten slow circles with your toes each way. Then change feet.
quick.note: Make the circles as wide as the ankle will go, moving only the foot, not the whole leg. Then write the letters of your name in the air with your toes for a change. Stop if anything hurts. This one is made for sitting, so it suits a desk or a sofa.

quick.test: Sit down on the floor and stand back up again, three times, using your hands as little as you can.
quick.note: Cross your legs or kneel on the way down, then find the easiest way up. Count how many hands or knees you needed and see if it gets fewer by the third go. Stop if anything hurts. Skip this one if your knees are sore, and do the chair stand instead: up and down from a chair ten times.

quick.test: Draw a cup in one line, without lifting the pen off the paper.
quick.note: Put a real cup in front of you and let the line wander round the rim, down the side, round the handle and back. It will look a bit wobbly, and that is how these drawings are meant to look. Any pen and the back of an envelope will do.

quick.test: Fold a square of paper into a small open box with no glue or tape.
quick.note: Fold the corners to the centre, then fold two sides in to meet the middle, open out, and lift the ends to form walls. Look up a masu box if you get stuck, and follow one set of steps at a time. A page from an old magazine or a sheet of printer paper cut square is plenty.

quick.test: Turn a rectangle of paper into a perfect square with one fold and one tear.
quick.note: Fold one corner down so the short edge lies exactly along the long edge. Crease the fold hard, then tear off the strip left below it. Open it out and you have a square, ready for the next folding item.

quick.test: Fold a sheet of paper into a boat that stands up on the table.
quick.note: Fold the sheet in half, fold the top corners down to make a triangle, fold the bottom strips up on each side, then open the middle and flatten it into a square before pulling the two points apart. Look up a paper boat if you lose your place. Printer paper or a page of an old newspaper both work.

quick.test: Tie a figure-of-eight knot in a shoelace or a piece of string.
quick.note: Make a loop, pass the end round behind the standing part, then feed it back down through the loop. Pull both ends and it should look like the number eight. Untie it and tie it again with your eyes shut.

quick.test: Tie a shoelace bow with your eyes shut, and check it is tight.
quick.note: Take your shoe off and put it on your lap, or tie it while it is on your foot. Go slowly and feel each loop with your fingers. If you already tie laces without looking, try the double bow that does not come undone.

quick.test: Draw your own hand as it rests on the table, in three minutes.
quick.note: Start with the shape of the gaps between the fingers rather than the fingers themselves. Look at the hand more than you look at the paper. Pencil or pen both work, and nobody needs to see it.

quick.test: Draw a circle and shade it so it looks like a round ball.
quick.note: Pick one side for the light to come from. Leave a small white spot near that side, shade darker the further you get from it, and add a dark shadow on the table under the ball. An ordinary pencil pressed harder or softer is all you need.

quick.test: Write your first name in big hollow block letters and shade them in.
quick.note: Draw each letter as a thin outline first, then go round it to make it thick. Shade in stripes, dots or solid colour. A biro is fine; felt tips are a bonus if they are already in the house.

quick.test: Fold a sheet of paper back and forth into a fan, with every fold the same width.
quick.note: Make the first fold about two fingers wide, then turn the paper over and fold again along the edge. Pinch one end together when you finish and open the other end out. Try to make every fold line up exactly with the last.

quick.test: Draw a map of the room you are in as if looking down from the ceiling, with every piece of furniture in its place.
quick.note: Start with the walls, then mark the door and the window, then the big things like a bed, a table or a sofa. Use squares and rectangles only. Check it by standing where the map says the door is.

quick.test: Fold a sheet of paper into an envelope with no glue.
